ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address
as follows:
/ll'1"//1rcn of the Grand Lodge:
Today we assemble for the Sixty-ninth Annual Communication of
th<' Grand Lodge o\ California to pass in review the work of a busy and
nnxious year, to deliberate upon subjects of importance to the welfare
nncl happiness of the Craft, to enact necessary legislation, and to enjoy a
clt•li!{htful season of friendly and fraternal intercourse. It is with great
pl<•asure that I greet and welcome you all. Amid the clash of arms and
t hl' sore affliction of a distressed and war-torn world, our Institution
rontinues a very Republic of the Humanities upon which the Giver of
all Cood has showered His manifold blessings. Our powers have been
·'' rl'llgthened and vitalized, within our peaceful walls harmony and
hrothcrly love reign undisturbed, and before us lies the open way to a
prart ical exemplification of our principles and professions. A Mason's
lirst clnty is to his God, next to his country and then to suffering humanit.Y. Our country is in danger and calls all its sons to sacrifice and service·. Humanity everywhere is suffering calamities and woes, unrests
1111<1 upheavals, physical and mental agonies and the oppression of gross
111al<'rialism. Let us pray our Father to protect and bless our country,
to solace the suffering and to hasten the day when right and freedom
~hall triumph.and peace and happiness be restored to all lands and peop'.t•s; and let us. at this session devote our hearts and minds to the
111T11111plishment of the great mission of Masonry.·
T am before you at this hour to present for your approval an
111·1·01111t of my official acts during the year, to exhibit the general condit i1111 of Masonry within the Jurisdiction, and to re~ommend such legislat i1111 as I deem expedient for the welfare of the Craft. One year ago
wlll'11 you installed me in this honorable station, I expressed to you the
111is1.:ivi11gs and fears which beset my heart and voiced my sense of
l1111dl'q11acy and frailty as I faced the responsibilities and duties you
li111h· me assume. It is appropriate for me now to say to you that no
11111• rl'grets more than myself the shortcomings and failures and mis-

takes with which I can be justly charged, yet I have redeemed in full
my promise to you by enlisting in your service every faculty I poss:ss.
and bv diligent and painstaking effort striving to meet every require·
ment ;ml demand with loyalty, zeal and a singleness of purpose to pe~­
form my duty. The nature and extent of the functions and opportumties of the Grand Master are so vast that no person without abundant
leisure and superior spiritual and intellectual endowments can hope to
measure up to the full standard set by the honor, digni~y and ir;iporta'.1ce
of the office. I have done my utmost, and my confess10n of d1sappo.mtment is joined to a fervent hope that you, in your generosity and. kindness, will applaud my sincere endeavors and forget that I have failed to
accomplish all you expected.

Necrology
We enter upon our deliberations today saddened and chastened by
the appalling sacrifice and wastage of human life on the battle fields of
Europe, but we find some consolation in the knowledge that t~ose w~o
fight and fall for Right do not die in vain. The noble sacrifices laid
upon the altar of country insure a safe and peaceful worl.d a;id the ha?piness of unborn millions of men. Brethren of our mystic tie have laid
down their working tools in the full strength of young manhood and
gone to rest in the earth of sunny France. vVe can not call them back,
but we who mourn them with so much pride can devote the remammg
span of our lives to build upon their deeds a nation of imperishable
worth and renown.
"God grant we may rest as sweetly
vVhen our work, like theirs, is done."
Vve thank the Supreme Grand Master that the official family of
this Grand Lodge has been unharmed and untouched by the shaft~ of
Death, and that for a full year all have been spared for further patient
and useful labor in the cause to which they have consecrated themselves.
The King of Terrors has invaded many of our sis.ter jurisdictio~s and
has slain some of our noblest and best. It was with a deep feeling of
personal loss and bereavement that I learned of the death of two of my
dearly loved friends-General Thomas J. Shryock, who had been Gran.d
Master of Maryland for thirty-three years, and Judge Charles Francis
Buck, who was for six years Grand Master of Louisiana. Mighty towers of strength have fallen and all Masonry mourns. As I contemplate
the saddening toll of the inexorable years and the departure of our
brothers for a higher Lodge, I am reminded of the words of George D.
Prentice:
"It cannot be that earth is man's only abiding place. It cannot be
that our life is a mere bubble cast up by eternity .to. float a mo men! on
the waves and sink into nothingness. Else why 1s 1t that the glorious
aspirations which leap like angels from the temple of our hearts are fo:ever wandering unsatisfied? Why is it that the stars that hold t~e1r
festival around the midnight throne are set above the grasp of our ltm-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

ited faculties, forever mocking us with their unapproachable glory?
And finally, why is ~ that bright forms of human beauty presented to
our view are taken from us, leaving the thousand streams of our affections to flow back in Alpine torrents upon our hearts? There is a realm
where the rainbow never fades; where the stars will spread out before
us like the islands that slumber in the ocean; and where the beautiful
beings which pass before us like shadows will stay in our presence
forever."

Special Communications
During the year I have convened the Grand Lodge in special session
on several occasions to perform ceremonies in accordance with our
established forms. \Vithin the constitutional time after the close of the
last annual communication of the Grand Lodge I constituted Lodges as
follows: Rockridge No. 468, at Oakland, on October 13th; Libertas
No. 466, at Bakersfield, on October 30th; and Culver City, at Los
Angeles, on November 6th, and I installed the officers of these several
Lodges.
On June 12th I convened the Grand 'Lodge at Healdsburg a'nd laid
the corner-stone of the magnificent new High School building in that
city. The occasion was notable. Many organizations were in the line
of march and the attendance was large and representative of the best of
the city and community.
On September 7th I convened the Grand Lodge at Sacramento and
laid the corner-stone of th~ splendid new Masonic Temple now being
erected by the Masons of the capital city. Many of the officers of the ·
Grand Lodge participated in the ceremonies, an eloquent oration was
delivered by Past Grand Master Burnett, a patriotic address was delivlivered by Wm. D. Stephens, Governor of California, and the ceremonies were ornamented by brilliant music and enjoyed by a large concourse of people. Sacramento was the birthplace of the Grand Lodge
of California and has ever been foremost in all matters Masonic, and
the brethren of this generation are emulating the spirit of those who
have gone before by erecting an edifice worthy of our Institution and
that great city, as our brethren fifty-three years ago laid the cornerstone of a Masonic Temple in Sacramento which is still in use and
which was then a great ornament as well as a credit to the city and to
the Craft.
On Septemher 28th I convened the Grand Lodge and laid the
corner-stone of the new High School building at Barstow. There h
no Lodge at Barstow, but the Masonic spirit of our many members in
this community is superb and there was a gratifying attendance of
Masons from San Bernardino and vicinity.
During the year I have also convened the Grand Lodge and have
taken great pleasure in participating in the ceremonies of dedicating the
Masonic Temple at Merced, the Masonic Hall at Holtyille and the
Masonic Temple at Vallejo. I desire at this time and in this place to

10

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

pay a tribute of admiration to our brethren in these three cities for
their accomplishments in a material way for the Craft, and for their
zeal, enthusiasm and fine Masonic spirit. These dedications in every
instance were festivals of brotherly love.
On June 22d I convened the Grand Lodge an,d dedicated the
Lodge room of Golden State Lodge No. 358, at Los Angeles. This
Lodge has recently· acquired the valuable property in which is situated
the hall where .the Lodge has met for many years. The Lodge is to be
congratulated on securing this fine property and on enjoying the privilege of meeting in its own home.
On June 8th I convened the Grand Lodge and dedicated the Hall
of Fullerton Lodge No. 339. This Lodge has also acquired the property in which is situated its place of meeting, and they have remodeled,
re-fitted and furnished a beautiful temple for their enjoyment. Good
fortune has been the portion of Fullerton Lodge, and we rejoice in the
prosperity which has attended their vigilant efforts and their zealous
devotion to the true interests of Freemasonry.

Recess Appointments
Because of the lamented death of Bro. Ralph Lowe, I appointed
Bro. John H. McGehee a member of the Finance Committee to succeed
our departed brother; because of the resignation of Bro. Geo. L. Jones
as Grand Orator, which I most reluctantly accepted, I found great
pleasure in appointing Bro. Charles H. Victor to be your Grand Orator;
and when Bro. Neuberg joined the service and left the State, I appointed Bro. W. T. Osterholt Grand Sword Bearer.
Dispensations
During the year I have issued dispensations for the formation of
Yorba Linda Lodge, at Yorba Linda, Orange County; Lincoln Lodge
at San Francisco, and Delta Lodge at Stockton. A petition for a new
Lodge at Hermosa Beach was, after long deliberation and much hesitation, d.enied. Several other new Lodges are in process of formation,
but the desires of the brethren interested have been held in check because of the unpropitious nature of the times. No new Lodge should
now be organized unless a clear and undoubted necessity exists therefor.
This is no time for unnecessary expense or Masonic experiments.
I have been called upon to issue many special dispensations to per·mit balloting upon petitions without reference to investigating committees, and also to permit Lodges to receive petitions from members
of the army and navy who did not possess the required qualification of
residence. I have exercised my discretion in these matters in the most
generous manner. These requests all grow out of our present state of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

11

war and I have felt disposed to gratify as far as possible the laudable
ambitions of our fighting men as well as the natural desire of the
Lodges to receive them into the bonds of our fellowship. I have
learned that the :Masonic tie is the strongest bond of union between the
men and officers in the army, and I have aided in bringing something of
the spirit and purpose of our Institution into the hearts and lives of
men who are going far from home in a noble cause.
Vacancies in the official corps of Lodges ·have been numerous because so many of our officers have joined the colors, and I have in all
cases upon proper request issued dispensations for elections to. fill
vacancies. No dispensations have been issued to re-ballot upon candidates except upon a clear showing of mistake. I entirely agree with the
observations which have been made by my predecessors on the subject
of granting permission to re-ballot, and I feel that the interests of the
Craft are best served by a policy of non-interference with the judgment of the members of the Lodge expressed through the ballot box,
unless it can be shown that an unjust result was occasioned by inadvertence or innocent mistake. The Grand Secretary will make a detailed report of all dispensations issued during the year.

Condition of the Craft
The year now closing has been one of great activity and considerable prosperity to the Craft in this Jurisdiction. Everywhere we have
been blessed with peace and harmony, our gains in membership have
been the largest in our history, and our influence has been felt and
appreciated in a fuller measure than ever before. The gains of the year
amount to 3,591, and we now number 63,984 Masons on our rolls. In
not a single instance have disciplinary measures been required of the
Grand Master, but the Lodges and officers have been as responsive as
could be expected to the criticisms and suggestions made for the improvement and benefit of ·l\fasonry.
At the request of different departments of the Government and in
furtherance of what I conceived to be my duty, communications have
been addressed from time to time to the Masters and Lodges dealing
with various governmental and Masonic subjects of present interest
and importance, a detailed report of which at this time would accomplish no useful purpose. Letters addressed by the Grand Master to
Masters and Secretaries are entitled to acknowledgment, and too often
there has been a breach of courtesy in this respect, and I am sorry to
report that through inadvertence or carelessness many of my communications have remained unanswered and unacknowledged. The simple
proprieties of human and fraternal intercourse should never be neglected, for when observed they add to the sum of happiness and foster
and encourage pleasant relations.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our Institution has not escaped the blighting effects of war. More
than 5350 of our members have put aside their professions and vocations, have renounced the peace and joy of their homes and domestic
cireles, and have gone forth from their Lodges to respond as patriotic
and loyal citizens to the call 'of duty and the defense of civilization.
The severance of business relations, home ties and fraternal bonds has
brought tragedy into thousands of lives. The absence of our brethren is
felt in all the spheres of their activity and influence, and in none more
than in their Lodges. The official corps of many of our Lodges in this
way have been sadly depleted. Few, if any, of our Lodges fail to exhibit
·service flags upon which are many stars. The ranks of the Inspectors
have a!so been broken, and some of our most efficient and noble work··
men have laid down their inspectorial duties to follow a higher and
nobler duty. The strong Lodges have withstood these inroads upon
the working forces without disaster, but many of the smaller Lodges
have been sadly weakened in their powers. The call of duty to our older
members has now become clear and insistent. They must return to
their former activities in Lodge work and again assume functions and
responsibilities which they had passed on to their younger brothers.
While our young men are out battling for the right, those who are
left at home owe to them the obligation of maintaining and supporting
in full power and efficiency the organization and work of Masonry, that
when the boys come home victorious, they will not be disheartened by
the wreckage of the Lodges they love.
For several years a problem has been presented by some of the
weake~ Lodges of the Jurisdiction· and consolidations have been more
or less urgently recommended. These particular Lodges have long led
a precarious existence and are now in worse condition than ever before,
and unless a number of consolidations are effected within a short time
the drastic remedy of arresting charters must be applied by the Grand
Master. The Grand Lecturer and the Inspectors should be charged with
the duty of prosecuting a diligent examination and advising the Grand
Master relative to needful consolidations.
The condition of the Craft that most impressed me during the year
was the need for a greater educational and social function on the part
of the Lodges. Everywhere Masons are eager to receive Masonic instruction. They desire to pr<'gress beyond the essentials of ritualism, to
know more of the history an<l philosophy of our Institution, to learn the
hidden meaning of its symbols and ceremonies, to be informed respecting its achievements and purposes, to study its landmarks and its laws
and to be led through the treasure chambers of its wisdom and divinity.
The complaint is heard in many quarters that no opportunities are
afforded at Lodge meetings for educational privileges or even for
soc;al intercourse. The complaint is well justified. The Lodges
throughout the Jurisdictior are devoting an immense amount of time

to .the work of initiating, passing and raising Masons, but find little time
We should not be too
n·a<ly to censure a member for his indifference or non-attendance when
the only opportunity offered him by his Lodge is the privilege of hearing the repetition of the rituals of three degrees, and the only service
ht.' is permitted to render is that of listening to the officers recite ritualistic work. A Mason receiving the third degree should be entering upon
a lifetime of study, self-improvement and service to his fellows, and his
l,odge is intended to be and should be the source of light and instruct ion and a field for serious and devoted work for the principles which
our Institution inculcates and upon which it is founded. The conception that the prosperity and greatness .of a Lodge is measured by its
large membership and its wealth is erroneous. That Lodge is prosperous and great which commands the affections of its members and displays spiritual rather than material wealth. The conferring of degrees
is essential and desirable, but a Lodge abrogates some of its responsihilities and neglects its fairest opportunities when it devotes its entire
time to the conferring of degrees and fails to unite its membership into
an homogeneous spiritual and working whole. This homogeneity can be
accomplished only by as assiduous attention to the needs and desires of
those who are already Masons as it does to the prayers of those seek·
ing to become Masons. By failing to respond to the intellectual and
spiritual demands of their members some of our Lodges are losing the
interest and active support of many of the best Masons of California,
and are in danger of becoming the patrons of the mediocre. The Committee on Masonic Education was organized for the purpose of assist
ing the Lodges in their intellectual and educational work, but this Com
mittee has failed to accomplish any conspicuous success because very
little interest is taken in the reading of lectures or themes, no matter
how excellent the subject matter or how attractive the method of its
presentation. To be of value there must be a personal touch, and many
will throng to hear a speaker or teacher who is a master of his subject
and imbued with the Masonic .spirit, but they .will not attend Lodge to
listen to the. reading of £fie printed page. The desire of the members for
instruction ·~o keen, the subjects for study are so many and varied,
and the sources of information are so easily obtainable, that I marvel at
the difficulty which is being experienced in instituting and carrying on a
wonderful revival of Masonic learning,
to instruct or help or minister to their members.

is

Visitations
Because of the example set by my predecessors, the manifest desire
of the Lodges, the promptings of my duty to the Craft, and my own
inclination, I endeavored to visit as many of the Lodges of the jurisdiction as possible. It will ever be a matter of regret to me that the
demands of my private business and my duties in the service of my

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

country conspired to prevent my acceptance of many urgent and cordial
invitations to visit Lodges and Masonic districts. Such visitations are
of great value and benefit to the Grand Master, for in no other manner
can he learn the actual conditions of the Lodges under his charge and
establish an· intimate and desirable personal touch with those active in
Masonic work. They should be helpful to the Lodges, and from personal experience I am persuaded that they quicken the fraternal spirit
and stimulate the Masonic impulses of the brethren. The very thorough
manner in which Grand Master Keesling covered the State last year,
his powerful influence for good, his sympathetic and intelligent attention to the needs of the Lodges and the Craft, not only endeared him
to the brethren and laid them all under a debt of gratitude, but at the
same time he relieved his successor of the necessity of making so many
visitations and lightened all the burdens of my high office. The more
widely I extend my knowledge of the true conditions of the Craft in
California and observe the effects of his devotion to his duty, the more
I am amazed at the wonderful achievements accomplished in one short
year by Brother Keesling and the greater my admiration for his zeal,
intelligence, firmness, good sense, breadth of vision and love of
Masonry.

Our great State is an empire in the length and breadth of its vast

otherwise could not have been visited. During the year I have had the

Tax on Fees and Dues
On January 19, 1918, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue made a
ruling with reference to Section 701 of the War Tax Law, that the dues
and d'ees of fraternal orders were taxable thereunder, and that the
Masonic Lodges did not come within the exemption provided in said
section. The Collectors of Internal Revenue notified the Lodges of said
ruling and demanded the payment of a tax on fees and· dues. Believing
that our Lodges were exempted by the terms of the statute from the
payment of taxes, and that the ruling made by the Department was
erroneous, I immediately protested the ruling on behalf of the Grand
Lodge of California and its subordinate Lodges, and in support of such
protest sent several letters and telegrams to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue and to other persons, and wrote and filed an exhaustive
brief covering the points of law involved. On March 24th the Commissioner of Internal Revenue reversed his ruling and decided that our
Lodges were not subject to the tax.
I took the position that the Congress did not intend to tax our
Lodges, and that the construction made by the Department broadened
the scope of the law far beyond the intent of the statute, and there.by
worked an injustice against our Institution. The effect of the .ruling
was to lay a tax on Masonic Lodges and to exempt therefrom most
other secret societies. I represented to the Department that this Grand
Lodge and its subordinates would not protest or in any manner seek
to evade the payment of any tax provided for in the law, but, on the
other hand, that we would gladly and promptly pay any levy that might
be fixed by the Congress. However, we did earnestly object to paying
a tax not intended by the law to be levied upon our fees and dues,
and particularly a tax of such a highly discriminatory and unjust nature.

Decisions
Many questions of Masonic law have been propounded during the
year, most of which could be answered by reference to the Constitution
and Decisions, and by the application to the facts submitted of the clear
provisions of our law. The comprehensive character of our Constitution and regulations, the clarity of their expression and the familiarity
of the Inspectors and Masters with their provisions, combined to render
my duties in this field light and pleasant. The following decisions are
the only ones rendered during the year that are of sufficient importance
to justify reporting:

1. Army and Navy men-distinction between members of Regular
Army and National Army: The exception in favor of persons in the
Army and Navy of the United States provided in Section 96 of the Constitution does not apply to officers and men of the Army and Navy, who
are residents of other States, and have volunteered for service during
the period of the present o/ar, or who are members of what was known
as the Federalized National Guard, or who have enlisted under the
Selective Draft. The exception was made for the benefit of professional
soldiers and sailors whose place of abode is always temporary and is
selected by the order of the Government and not by the desire of the
individual, who by reason of his service could not acquire a permanent
residence. The exception was not made for the benefit of nor intended
to apply to patriotic citizens who join the armed forces of the nation
in time of war, with the expectation of serving during the period of
hostilities and returning as soon as the enemy is conquered to their
homes and to the vocations which were temporarily suspended. It was
decided in 1917 that the exception in Section 96 applied only to members
of the Regular Army and Navy, and by Regular Army and Navy was
meant the permanent military establishments of the Government, composed of officers and men who serve both in war and in peace and follow no other vocation. The men and officers who enlist for service
during the present war have not abandoned their places of residenc~ and
are only temporarily absent therefrom, and the Lodges of their domiciles, wherever they may be, still retain jurisdiction over them, and petitions for the degrees should be made to the Lodge of the home of such
soldier or sailor.

2. Dedication of halls-improper unless property of Lodge: It is
not a proper function of the Grand Lodge to dedicate a Lodgeroom

h' · n a orma they can not with1,odge without a waiv:r n~; ~an. ~·ey, app(ly for advancement in another
Juris 1ct1on Sec. 162). Membership in a

Lodge can be terminated by a voluntary withdrawal therefrom (Sec.
158), and a <limit is a certificate of the fact of such withdrawal (Sec.
159). An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft of a California Lodge
can not be granted a <limit, and in the event he desires to receive the
remaining degrees and is unable to do so in his Lodge, he may receive
the same in another Lodge upon the request of his Lodge, or his Lodge
may waive jurisdiction over him and permit him to petition another
Lodge for the remaining degrees (Sec. 155). It has been held (Proc.
1913, p. 77) that a <limit issued to an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft by a legitimate Lodge may be accepted as a waiver by the Lodge
issuing it of jurisdiction over him. Such a <limit wou'.d be issued only
by a Lodge under a Grand Jurisdiction whose law is different from
that of California, and the effect of such <limit would be to terminate
the membership of the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft in the Lodge
in which he had received degrees, and would be a general waiver of all
except penal jurisdiction over him, and his petition for the remaining
degree or degrees, accompanied by such <limit, could be accepted by a
California Lodge without any further waiver on the part of the Lodge
issuing the <limit. Section 95 of the Constitution applies not only to those
persons who have not received any of the degrees of Masonry, but applies also to any Entered Apprentice or ,Fellow Craft who applies for
the remaining degrees. The only exception to the rule is stated in
Section 96, providing that in the case of one who has the qualification
of residence, the Lodge within whose jurisdiction 'he resides may, upon
his request in writing and for good cause shown, authorize another
Lodge to receive and act upon his application. This exception applies
only to Lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California.
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts of Lodges under jurisdictions
other than that of the Grand Lodge of California can not apply for the
remaining degrees in a California Lodge unless (1) they have the residential qualification provided in Section 95, and (2) unless they present
a <limit or a waiver of jurisdiction from the Lodge in which they received the degree or degrees already conferred upon them. Entered
Apprentices or Fellow Crafts of California Lodges· before applying for
the remaining degree or degrees in another Lodge, must secure a
waiver of jurisdiction as provided in Section 155, and in addition thereto
must possess the residential qualification provided in Section 95, either
in the territorial jurisdiction of the Lodge to which application for degrees 1s made, or in that of the Lodge granting the waiver of jurisdiction.

blue and one of gold. Tears dimmed many eyes as we looked upon the
proud banner which commemorated one of our boys whose life was
claimed by a criminal pirate of the underseas, and the fifteen others
whom we reared and fostered and who volunteered to serve our country in the ranks of the brave.
The members of the Grand Lodge should be profoundly grateful
to the Trustees of the Masonic Homes for their unselfish and valuable
services, and should accord them a generous and whole-hearted support.
Their duties are onerous and exacting and their responsibility is tremendous. They administer our most important trust. Upon their zeal
and wisdom depend in no small measure the happiness and wellbeing
of more than two hundred human lives; into their keeping is entrusted
the fair fame and age-old reputation of our Institution for benevolence;
and upon their business judgment and administrative skill rests the
management of half a million dollars in property and the expenditure
of $90,000 of annual revenue. It is a matter of congratulation that the
Board is so well fitted for the holy and arduous work we have set them
to do, but we should never fail to spur them on to a realization of their
obligations and greater endeavor to measure up to our expectations.

The Trustees will make to you a detailed report, which will disclose matters requiring your serious consideration. During recent
years the .expense of maintaining the Homes has constantly increased.
Tbe cost of labor, food, clothing and other commodities mounts higher
and higher. The per capita tax of one dollar per member has remained
unchanged for many years. The revenues for maintaining the Homes
have not increased materially, while the buying power of the dollar has
decreased alarmingly.
Moreover, 5300 of our members have joined
the Colors, and on most of these no per capita tax is payable. Owing
to these conditions we have accumu!ated in three years a deficit of
$13,000. A deficit is the vacuum abhorred by good business. Because
of the crowded condifion at Decoto, a distressing water famine and the
removal of the children to Covina, as reported to you by my predecessors, the Masonic Home building program was accelerated far beyond the financial provisions made therefor by Grand Lodge. This
necessary construction work has been completed and the revenues from
the special building tax have been anticipated to the extent of about
$102,000. It is, therefore, necessary that the said tax be levied annually
for at least three years more in order to cover the deficiency, and I
believe that an affirmative commitment on this subject by this Grand
Lodge would be proper at tbis time.
It may be that we will soon be called upon to forther enlarge our
housing facilities at both the Homes. The time is drawing nearer when
large numbers of our brave brethren will return from European battle

I direct each Master to appoint a committee or committees to proceed forthwith to solicit cash donations from the members of his Lodge
and from Masons sojourning in his jurisdiction. I urge that so far as
possible solicitation be made in person instead of by letter or circular,
and that every Mason be urged as a Masonic duty to make a donation.
I do not wish an unreasonable demand made on any person nor do I
want any Mason to avoid his plain duty. All moneys shall be paid to
the Secretary of the Lodge, who shall keep a just and faithful list of the
names of the donors and the amount paid by each. On the first day of
February, 1918, and on the first day of each month thereafter, the Secretary shall forward all the moneys then collected and in his hands to the
Grand Secretary for the account of the Masonic War Fund, and shall
report the amount of each remittance at the next stated meeting of the
I,odge thereafter, and shall cause a note thereof to be entered in the
minutes of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary will pay over all moneys
received by him for said fund to the Grand Treasurer, who will open
and carry an account of the same under the name of Masonic \Var Fund,
and all moneys in such account shall be subject to the draft of the Grand
Master, countersigned by the Grand Secretary. In the event of the termination of war leaving an unexpended balance in said fund, the same
shall be donated pro rata to the Lodges collecting the same or shall be
paid into the Masonic Home Fund, in the discretion of the Grand
Master.
I urge the Masters to interest themselves diligently and wholeheartedly in this important matter and to try to complete their collections during January and February. The Inspectors of the several Districts and the officers of the Grand Lodge will cooperate in this work.
It is my order that this letter be read by the Master in open Lodge
at the first stated meeting after its receipt, and at such other meetings
as the Master may elect, and that an entry be made in the minutes of
such reading.

demand for service overseas. The work already inaugurated must be

Recommendations
That the fund raised at the request of the Grand Master by voluntary subscriptions and now in the hands of the Grand Treasurer, be
known as the "Masonic War Fund", and that the rules and regulations
governing its administration be as follows :

Uses of the Fund: (a) For the support and maintenance at or
near military and naval establishments of Masonic headquarters, social
rooms and other instrumentalities of Masonic hospitality and brotherly
attention to members of the Craft in the Army and Navy of the United
States and its Allies. A portion of the fund may b~ used overseas, if
deemed desirable.
(b) For the assistance of Lodges located at or near military or
naval establishments in their work of entertaining visiting soldiers and
sailors and in conferring degrees by request of and as a courtesy to other
Lodges.
(c) For the relief of California Masons who, by reason of their
service in the allied armies during the great War, are in need as a consequence of such service, and whose Lodges are unable to provide the
necessary assistance.
(d) For the relief of widows !ind orphans of California Masons
who have died in the service of the United States or its Allies during
the great \Var, in those cases where the Lodges of which the deceased
Masons were members are unable to provide the necessary assistance.
War Fund Committee: The Grand Master shall appoint a Committee of three members to be known as the "\Var Fund Committee."
This Committee shall administer the War Fund under the direction of
the Grand Master, shall approve of payments of money therefrom, and
shall render to the Grand Lodge at its annual communication a complete statement of its transactions during the preceding year.
Rules of Administration: (a) Moneys belonging to the l\fasonic
War Fund shall be paid to the Gran_d Secretary and by him deposited
with the Grand Treasurer. The Grand Treasurer, with the consent ·and
approval of the Grand Master, may invest the surplus moneys of said
fund in bonds of the United States, of any State or County or municipality or school district. or in interest-bearing certificates of deposit of
any national bank or savings bank, but not less than five thousand dollars

rn11f1•rence was to enlist the aid and co-operation of fraternal societies in

New York Conference
A conference of Grand Masters was held at New York City on
May 9, 1918, on invitation of M.'.W.'.Thomas Penney, of New York.
The purpose of this conference was to consider the means which could
properly be taken by our Institution for the aid, care and comfort of
our members in the Army and Navy. The invitation came after I had
sailed for Hawaii and the conference was held prior to my return therefrom, otherwise I should have attended the same. Although I was not
present and this Grand Lodge was not represented thereat, yet you can
not fail to be interested in knowing that such a conference was held and
that fourteen Grand Lodges were represented, because it illustrated the
spirit of service to our enlisted men which has swept over the Masonry
of the entire country and the earnest efforts being made to definitely
ascertain the duty of Masonry in this great emergency and then to generously and fully perform our every obligation. It had been ascertained
by the Grand Master of New York that the Government would permit
and welcome the activity of our Institution in serving our brethren who
had been sent overseas. The meeting soon divided into two groups, one
holding to the op.inion that there was a work of great importance to be
done b:y us in France and that the same should be undertaken at once
by theiiQ.,and Ledges of the United States in co-operation. The other
group held to the opinion that the present was not the time to engage in
such work and that our efforts should be expended in this country until
future events or a more complete understanding of the subject would
lead to a contrary opinion. As in the case of the Washington meeting,
the conference adjourned without taking definite action except to pass
a resolution, which was not unanimously supported, to the effect that
there is a present need for Masonic service overseas, that such service
lies in the cities and recreation centers, where there should be established general Masonic headquarters for the welcome, comfort and encouragement of Masons, that there should be no duplication of such
headquarters, but they be manned from time to time by workers from
any and all of the American jurisdictions, that the expenses be paid out
of a general fund dedicated to Masonic Fraternal Service, that the management of the fund be in a Committee representing the several contributing jurisdictions, that the contributions to the fund be on some annual
basis, that the service be rendered without regard to territorial divisions,

as demand may appear, and that the plan be presented to the several
jurisdictions.
At this meeting many gratifying statements were made respecting
work already done or in contemplation on behalf of our brethren in the
service. The Grand Master of Oklahoma reported that the Grand
Lodge of Oklahoma had converted a large school-house in the town
near Fort Sill into a place for the reception and entertainment of soldiers, that they paid the Secretary $200.00 per month and his expenses,
·and that Grand Lodge had made an appropriation of $20,000 for the
entertainment of the men. Past Grand Master Bell of Illinois stated
that his Grand Lodge had already raised a fund of $150,000 and was
then engaged in raising another fond of $250,000, which would soon be .
completed, so that they had actually or potentially about $400,000 in
Illinois that is at the service of. the Fraternity whenever they know just
how to use it, and that Illinois had sent men abroad to represent and
work for the Grand Lodge. Grand Master Rice of Rhode Island said
that he had created a War Board, and the Grand Lodge had ratified his
action and had created a War Fund which was collected by assessment
upon the Lodges in the form of a per capita tax, and that they had collected $20,000 from a membership of 10,000 Masons. Rhode Island has
gone deeply into this work and has become the adviser and next friend
of all its Masons in the service, and seems to have established a personal contact with most of them. The smallness of the territorial jurisdiction and of the membership in Rhode Island makes this practicable.
Deputy Grand Master Moyle reported that Connecticut was attempting
to raise $5,()0 per member, to tear down the Masonic Home <1~d rebuild
it so as properly to care for the men coming back from the war. Grand
Secretary Robinson of Oregon reported that his Jurisdiction is maintaining the Acacia ·Club near Vancouver Barracks, and that they were
raising $50,000 for a Home to care for Oregon Masons who return
incapacitated from the war. Deputy Grand Master McPherson of
Michigan stated that his Grand Lodge was maintaining a Service Station at Camp Custer, Battle Creek, and has asked the Lodges of the
State to pay in $5.00 per member to raise a fund to provide needed entertainment for the Masons in camp, and that a War Council would be
established to administer all funds collected for war relief purposes.
Past Grand Master Scudder of New York, Chairman of the meeting,
reported that his Grand Jurisdiction was going to send a Commission
to France to open headquarters, not in the name of nor for New York,
but just in the name of and for Masonry, and he invited all other Grand
Jurisdictions to join with New York and to participate in the work of
the "Masonic Mission to Freemasons Overseas in the Forces of the
United States." He also reported that his Grand Lodge had voted to

Tenders of Masonic Service
The Grand Lodge Alpina of Switzerland has organized an<l maintains the "Swiss Masonic Office for the Search of the Missing." The
chief aim of this office is the search of missing soldiers and civilians
during the period of the war. It makes an effort to have sick war prisoners brought to Switzerland. It sends visitors and help to prisoners
of war, and does whatever lies in its power to help the victims of war
who are reported to the office. The office expresses a desire to be of
help to American Masonry and places itself at our disposal. The services are gratuitous and are covered by contributions of Lodges and
Freemasons who are interested in this particular work. The address
of the office is Alf. Moraz (Past Grand Secretary of Lodge Alpina),
Ave. Ruchonnet 26, Lausanne.
While we are not in fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge
Alpina, we deeply appreciate this offer to render a truly Masonic service, and commend the fraternal spirit and the benevolent activity uf the
Swiss Masons. In view of our action taken in 1917 relative to Masonic
intercourse in France, Belgium and Italy, it does not seem unwise that
we should extend the same privileges to Switzerland, and it certainly is
not inappropriate to express our deep sense of gratitude to the Masons
of Switzerland for their proffer of service to California Masons and
their families. This is not the first time that the Swiss Masons have
exhibited their fraternal spirit, and we are all familiar with the labor
on behalf of a universal Masonry and of the brotherhood of man which
has long been carried on by the International Bureau of Masonic Affairs
organized and maintained in Switzerland. The matter of the recognition by us of the Gran<'! Lodge Alpina is worthy of investigation.
The Grand Orient of France, at its headquarters in the City of
Paris, is maintaining a service of hospitality and fraternal aid to all
California Masons who can avail themselves of its courtesy. The report
on French Masonry which will be presented to you sets out in full a
courteous and kindly letter on this :subject.
Many of the Grand Lodges of the United States, in whose jurisdictions are situated cantonments and other military posts, have established Masonic service stations and have invited the Masons of California to partake of their hospitality. Communications from time to
time have been received by me from Grand Masters breathing in every
lin.e a superb spirit of fraternal regard and tendering through me to
our members in the service a warm Masonic welcome to their Lodges
and participation in their social activities. I hwe responded in every
case by offering the hospitality of our Lodges and service stations to all
our brethren whithersoever hailing.

I had the pleasure of visiting Lodge Maui in April of this year and
was received with the honors due to a Grand Master, and by invitation
accepted and wielded the gavel over said Lodge. I met the officers,
most of the Past Masters and many of the members of said Lodge, and
was gratified to find that the best men on the Island belonged to the
Lodge, and that it exercises a far-reaching and beneficial influence. This
Lodge is doing a truly Masonic work, it enjoys the respect of the entire
community, a splendid spirit of harmony and good feeling exists among
its officers and members, and it is prosperous. Three of the five Lodges
in Hawaii have by resolution requested this Grand Lodge to grant the
prayer of Lodge Maui.
At the time this Lodge was formed an attempt was made to organize under the California jurisdiction, but the assistance which should
have been freely given was denied, and as a result a Scottish charter
was obtained. It is the only regular Lodge not of its obedience working
in the territory of the Grand Lodge of California. I believe that the
interests of Masonry within our jurisdiction, and particularly in the
Hawaiian Islands, would be served by granting the petition of Lodge
Maui, and I, therefore, recommend that the petition of Lodge Maui for
a charter be granted, that the Past Masters of said Lodge Maui shall
have the same standing and rights as though Past Masters of a regularly
chartered Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California,
and that such charter be issued by the Grand Master when the Grand
Lodge of Scotland signifies its consent to the transfer of allegiance by
Lodge Maui.

Brother Henry M. Owens has been successful in stamping out clandestine and irregular Masonry in this Jurisdiction. He has devoted
much time to prosecuting cases in the courts and curbing the activities
of the vendors of fake Masonry. His professional skill and arduous
industry in this cause entitle him to the thanks and gratitude of all
members of the Craft. Brother Owens has also put his heart into the
work of the Masonic Library, and, together with Brother Sidney B.
Force, is largely responsible for the development of the Library during
the year. He will report to you in detail the character and extent of the
work of the Library Committee, and you will repay their efforts by your
appreciation and approval.
The loyalty, industry and zeal of the Inspectors of the several
Masonic Districts are entit'.ed to our recognition and a generous meed
of praise. The work of the present year has been unusually hard, and
in some Districts difficult and trying, yet with few exceptions the
Inspectors have done all that could be done for the promotion of the
harmony, integrity and wellbeing of the Lodges over which they have
visitorial and inspectorial powers. The annual reports recently returned
to me exhibit a creditable and devoted year of service and usefulness.
There is found among the Masters a feeling of confidence in and a genuine respect for the opinion and advice of the Inspectors, and I believe
their efforts in the field of their duty are appreciated and cordially welcomed'. I am grateful to the Inspectors for numerous courtesies and
acts of helpfulness, and shall ever cherish the privilege of having been a
co-worker with them in the Masonic vineyard.

Recommendations
1. Mistakes are bound to be made in the selection by the Lodges
of material for the Masonic structure, notwithstanding all the precautions which are provided to be taken in such matters. The high prerogative accorded each Lodge to choose from out of the men in its
jurisdiction those who by reason of their character, reputation, intelligence and love of humanity are fitted to engage in the service of Freemasonry, reposes in it a confidence and trust which should never be disregarded. The Lodge is thus empowered to select and introduce to the
great brotherhood of Masonry a new member, and it vouches to the
entire Masonic world that suc·h brother is a true and worthy and dependab'.e man and Mason. The duties of the investigating committee should
be so carefully and cautiously performed that the Lodge can rely with
implicit faith upon its conclusions. Personal observation and the reports

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

42

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of my brethren compel the conviction in my mind that in_ far too ~any
instances investigating committees either do not appreciate or fail to
perform their plain duty. The Master and the Lodge can not ~now the
character and extent of the investigation made by a committeeman.
The facts respecting a petitioner, as well as the conclusions of the Committee, should be presented to the Lodge, and the members present at
the time of voting upon the petition should determine whether such
facts constitute a favorable or unfavorable report. I, therefore, recommend that Section 100 of the Constitution be amended to read as
fol1ows:
"See. 100. Which report shall set forth in detail the facts ascertained respecting the applicant and the fayorable or unfavorable conclusion of the committee, and shall be read m the Lodge; ~JUt the name~
of the brothers making the reports shall not be announced m the Lodge.
2. It is in consonance with the better business practice that persons
handling the fnnds of others should be reqnired to give security for the
faithful performance of their trust. This rule is applied to individ~als
of the highest standing and reputation for probity and honesty, and is a
precaution that few employers are willing to forego, even though books
and accounts are audited at frequent intervals. No reflection is thereby
intended to be or is cast upon one who handles the money of another.
The Treasurers and Secretaries of our Lodges in the performance of
their duty are constantly handling the moneys of the Lodge, and their
accounts are audited at infrequent intervals, and in many cases the
audit is more a form than a businesslike checking of accounts and
reports. I believe that every Treasurer and Secretary, no matter how
faithful and irreproachable he may be, should give bond to his Lodge.
The Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge are
required to execute and file an official bond, and the reason for. such
requirement applies equally well to the Treasurers and Secretaries of
subordinate Lodges. ·while derelictions of duty are extremely rare, yet
never a year passes that some Lodge would not have been benefited by
the application of this salutary rule. I, therefore, recommend that Section 149 of the Constitution be amended by adding thereto the following clause :
.
"6th. To execute and file with the !\faster within fift~en days after
his installation an official bond in such penal .s!.lm and with su~h s~re­
ties as shall be approved by the Master, cond1u_oned that he will. fa1~h­
fu!ly discharge the duties of his office as prescribed by the ~onst1tutio:i
of the Grand Lodge and the By-Laws of his Lodge; provided, that if
the Lodge selects a bank as depositary of its funds ~n~ deposits are
made with such bank by the Secretary and the funds m its charge are
subject to the check of the Master,, or a Warden, and the Secretary,
then such bond shall not be required. '
I also recommend that Section 150 of the Constitution be amended
by adding thereto the following clause:

43

"9th. To execute and file with the Master within fifteen days after
his installation an official bond in such penal sum and with such sureties as shall be approved by the Master, conditioned that he will faithfully perform the duties of his office as prescribed by the Constitution
of the Grand Lodge and the By-Laws of his Lodge."
3. One of the disturbing elements in the present condition of the
Craft in California is the serious financial predicament of many of the
Lodges growing out of their investments in temples and the stock of
kmple associations. Unfortunately the investment of the funds of
I ,odges in halls, temples or stock of temple associations is not always
wise or prudent. Our brethren, actuated by local pride or over-enthu~lasm or optimism, too often involve their Lodges in ambitious projects
which in the end prove to be a great burden and a handicap to the usefulness and progress of the Lodge. The Masonic generation which
incurs such a debt is seldom the one which pays it. The investment of
Lodge fonds should be conservatively undertaken, and no land or stock
should be bought or buildings erected without application of all prudent
business tests in the examination, planning and execution of the project.
The judgment of those who, uninfluenced by local conditions or the
enthusiasm of the lodge members, are competent to advise, should be
sought and followed. Such a course would tend to prevent the repetition of unfortunate ventures against the error of which some of our
Lodges are now struggling. I, therefore, recommend that the following
provision be added to Section 87 of the Constitution :
"No Lodge shall invest any part of its funds in the stock of any
corporation, nor purchase lands, nor erect any building without the
approval in writing of a majority of the members of the Finance Committee of this Grand Lodge.".
4. The revenues of a Lodge should be amply sufficient to pay its
operating expenses, its per capita tax to Grand Lodge, and to discharge
honorably and generously all the just claims of charity. Too much
dependence should not be placed upon funds derived from fees. Some
portion of every fee should be saved and treasnred against the days of
need or misfortune, and no Lodge should rest under the necessity of procuring petitions and electing many candidates in order to pay its ex·
pcnses. The annual dues should not only be commensurate with the
financial ob'.igations of the Lodge, but should allow a co-efficiency of
safety to meet unexpected or unusual demands. Dues of many Lodges
amount to six dollars per year, and an analysis o.f Lodge statements
discloses that few of the Lodges can be maintained in solvency and use·
fulness on such slender revenues. Moreover, the dues of soldiers and
sailors are being generally remitted, resulting in a loss of income. It is
apparent that if the war continues for any considerable time, the relief
work of our Lodges will be materially increased and further exactions
must be made of the subordinate Lodges by this Grand Lodge. Prep-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

aration should be made to meet the eventualities, whatever they may be.
All reports of Inspectors and Lodges are not yet in hand, but a study of
those already received shows that the annual dues of 131 Lodges are six
dollars, four Lodges eight dollars, fifty-nine Lodges nine dollars, four
Lodges ten dollars, fifty-four Lodges twelve dollars, two Lodges eighteen
dollars and one Lodge twenty-four dollars. Of the Lodges whose dues
amount to six dollars per year, sixty have an available cash balance,
including Liberty Bonds and War Savings Stamps, of less than $500.00,
thirty Lodges have less than $200.00 on hand, and three Lodges show a
large deficit. Generalizations are not always fair, but I believe that I
am well within the truth in stating that the Lodges charging dues of
nine dollars or more per year are, as a rule, in far better condition than
those charging six dol!ars, and that it would be highly beneficial to most
of the Lodges now charging six dollars to increase their dues to nine
dollars. A few Lodges are in splendid condition, notwithstanding dues
of only six dollars per annum, but most of them lack desirable financial
strength. The Lodges which charge twelve dollars or more for dues are
nearly all prosperous and financially independent.

became a member of the Army or Navy subsequent to the filing of his
petition and applies for such refund.

I received recommendations from many Masters of Lodges now
charging six dollars dues that the Grand Lodge increase the minimum
dues permitted to be charged by its subordinates. One Master stated
his recommendation as follows:
"Our dues are too low and our members will not raise them, and
our active members all favor the Grand Lodge raising the minimum dues
to $9.00. It seems that a Lodge which has exi~ted for more than 25
years, as this one has, and has not had more charity work to do than we
have had, shou!d have a stronger financia) reserve. 9ur finances are the
best in the history of the Lodge. Our bank balance is $95.00, the Secretary' is paid to July !st, 1918, and all bills are p~id. We have ma~e the
first investment in the history of the Lodge, havmg bought and paid for
20 War Savings Certificates."
For the foregoing reasons I earnestly recommend that Section 128
of the Constitution he amended by striking out the first sentence thereof
and inserting in lieu thereof the following:
"From and after the stated meeting of December, 1918, no Lo~ge
shall charge or collect as its annual dues from members less than nmc
dollars."
5. I recommend that such change as may be necessary be made in
ou.r law (Uniform Code of By-Laws) to permit an applicant elected to
receive the degrees to come forward for initiation at any time within
three months after his discharge from the Army or Navy, provided he
entered the military or naval service of the United States, or its Allies,
prior to or within three months after his e'.ection to receive the degrees.
Also, that the Lodges he authorized, if they so desire, to refund to an

45

6: At the annual communication of this Grand Lodge in 1917, permission was given to our members to hold fraternal intercourse and
visit in France, Italy and Belgium, notwithstanding the fact that we do
not recognize the Masonic Powers of those countries. Notwithstanding
the fact that we do not recognize the Masonic Powers of Holland and
Switzerland, I think the same privilege should be extended to our brethren serving or visiting in those countries, and I, therefore, recommend
that the members of Lodges of the obedience of this Grand Lodge be
allowed and permitted to hold Masonic intercourse with the Masons in
Holland and Switzerland, and to visit in all their Lodges.

Conclusion
One year ago, my brethren, you exalted me to the high and honorable stition of chief Craftsman of the Grand Lodge and my stewardship is now ending. I have spread before you, for your approval or
rejection, the record of my acts and now we stand on the threshold of
the hour when my powers will be translated and my duties shifted to
other and worthy hands. It is my prayer that my gratitude and appreciation of the honor done me and the great kindness displayed to me
may find some substantial reflection in my official acts and may shine out
clearly and unmistakably in the sincerity of my devotion to your interests and to the progress and wellbeing of the Masonic Craft of this
great State.
In conclusion, may I revert a moment to the subject which has
recurred again and again in this address and which has been uppermost
in your minds and hearts during all the anxious weeks and months of
the momentous Masonic year now closing? When we entered upon this
year our country was making herculean efforts to engage worthily and
forcefully in the combat for civilization, and all over our land thoughtful citizens were oppressed with a feeling of deep responsibility and
disquieted by fears of a long and sanguinary conflict. Twelve months
have sped away and now every breast is surcharged with emotions of
inexpressible joy and hope. The honorable purpose of our nation will
soon be accomplished, the goal of our desires lies not far before, the
gallant boys in khaki and blue have brought imperishable honor and
renown to our arms, our chosen leaders have given utterance to the
noble sentiments and declared the humanitarian purposes of the American people in words of candor and truth, our Commander in Chief has
pronounced the glorious Declaration of Independence of the world, the
treasured riches and brightest hopes 6f every hamlet and family have

struggle and fight unaided and alone for religious and political freedom
and the recognition in laws and institutions and governments of the
Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, but today the most
powerful peoples have seized her lighted torch, and with the rallying
cry of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, have marched on a new crusade
to redeem the world as a holy land and to establish the kingdom of the
brotherhood of man and of nations. Their swords avenge the wrongs
of the helpless; their cannons speak for those who are voiceless, and
their flags float above the land and sea as an assurance alike to tyrants
and their victims that the creed of human liberty is not an unmeaning
formula, nor the brotherhood of man an empty dream. Freemasonry
was first to deny the claim that a king's crown gave to any man a divine
right to rule ruthlessly over all other men and to mold their destinies
without their consent; the first human organization to recognize and to
proclaim that all worthy men should everywhere meet on a common
level and stand equal before the law. The battle of democracy against
autocracy is essentially Freemasonry's battle; and our institution through
the years has seen throne after throne either crumbling or surrendering
its powers to the people, and now the last great combat overspreads the
earth to free mankind from despotism born of ambition and lust for
power and to make possible a universal brotherhood of man.
I am proud beyond expression of the loyalty, devotion and sacrifice
of California Masons. They have put love of country above all save their
love of God, and in their hearts and lives sing the song of service. Civilization has not failed, religion has not been inept, Freemasonry has not
been discredited-for out of the welter of war emerges their vindication. Freemasonry has outlived many wars and revolutions and states
and will continue to bless mankind long after the ravages of this great
strife have been forgotten and its many wounds all bound up. Its ministry will not end so long as men need to be made more diligent, prudeqt, temperate and discreet and their lives blessed with harmony, duty
and equilibrium.
The world will never be again as it was before. This is a time of
hope and of perils-in the world there is a deep, unsatisfied longing and
hunger. The most stupendous problems that ever confronted a people
will meet us when we lay down our victorious arms. Social, civic and
economic issues wiJJ assume new faces and require the attention of the
profoundest wisdom and patience and courage of patriotic Americans.
Masonry must be again a guide to statesman and citizen and its principles must be the solvent for the difficulties and dangers of the pregnant
hours of stress and readjustment. The tasks of the immediate future are
a challenge to every lover of his country and his kind, and a call to
every Mason for reconsecration and rededication to his duty. For class
bitterness, social unrest, governmental vagaries, national divisions, religi-

ous bickerings-other hope there is none save in the spirit of friendship
and fairness, of democracy and the fe~lowship of man with man, of the
altar across which men can talk but not fight, discuss but not dispute.
If Masonry does not light the uncharted and obscure way of the world,
there be those ready and eager to seize her lamp and lead mankind along
other and devious paths. God grant that our hearts be attuned to His
will, that our minds realize the obligations and responsibilities of our
day, and that when we meet again the peace of the world may bi'
restored and the healing of the nations begun.
"We build our future, thought by thought,
Or good or bad, and know it noty et so the universe is wrought.
Thought is another name for fate,
Choose, then, thy destiny, and waitFor love brings love, and hate brings hate."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
The Grand Secretary then read his Annual Report as
follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I report herewith the transactions of the Grand Secretary's
office for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1918, together with a detailed account of all moneys received within the year, and a detailed and itemized statement of the disbursements of the Grand
Lodge. In addition thereto I have appended an account of receipts since the close of business July 31, to and including October 2, 1918; and all unfinished business of Grand Lodge.
The year has been a particularly busy one for the Grand
Secretary, the many war activities in which members of our fraternity have taken a leading and splendid part being largely responsible for the added work. But it has been a labor of love.
All that those of us whose age or bodily infirmities preclude active military service can do for the men-and women-who are
engaged overseas, should be done, and I am happy in knowing
that our members, old and young, are in no degree slackers;
on the contrary, Masons everywhere by personal service. by pen,
by tongue, by money unstinted, are standing loyally and wholeheartedly squarely behind the Government in all and every activity
to win the war and establish forever the doctrine of decent democracy.
Some notion of the extra correspondence may be noted from
the letters and answers written with reference to having degrees
conferred by courtesy by our Lodges for other jurisdictions, and
by other jurisdictions for California Lodges. \Ve have requested
930 degrees to be conferred outside of California as courtesy to
our Lodges, and likewise we have conferred 806 degrees as favor
to Lodges in other jurisdictions. In every instance these requests
have been cheerfully granted and without fee. Needless to say,
all this work was conferred upon men in the military and naval
service. In many instances several letters were necessarily written because of the uncertain location of candidates, and I am
happy to report that in most cases we were able to locate the
soldier candidates and have the degrees conferred before they
sailed for "over there."

GRAND I.ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

66

As required by an amendment to section 50 of the Constitution, I prepared standardized forms of all blanks required to be
used by Lodges, and placed them on sale at cost. Price lists have
heen sent to each Secretary, and many of them have taken advantage of this wise provision of the law.
Grand Lodge last year required the Grand Secretary to furnish at cost to the Lodges such numbers of the Constitution and
Ceremonies as might be required, for the purpose of carrying out
the provisions of the resolution "that hereafter it shall be obligatory on the part of each and every Lodge, on completing the confcrring of the degrees upon a candidate, formally to present to
him a volume of the Constitution and Ceremonies, properly inscribed by the Master and Secretary." For this purpose six
thousand copies of the book were printed, and on the 15th of
August, 1918, the entire lot was sold. Another edition will be
printed as soon as may be after this Communication.
Pursuant to a resolution of Grand Lodge, I caused to be
typed and sent to the Board of Relief of Los Angeles, a card index of the entire membership. Five hundred dollars was appropriated for this purpose, and the work cost for labor and postage $346.65 and for cards $82.70. The names added to the memhcrship this year will be carded and sent to that body.
As ordered by Grand Lodge, I prepared and caused to be
printed a form of diploma in English, French and Latin for the
use and benefit of members in the military or naval service of the
tr nited States and its allies. Three thousand eight hundred and
fifty of these diplomas had been issued to July 31st, but inasmuch
ns there are considerably more than five thousand members in the
M<-rvice, it is apparent that many have not availed themselves of
this privilege.
At the close of the last annual communication we had 379
Lodges under our obedience with a membership of 60,393. Chari 1·rs were ordered issued at that communication to three Lodges:
Lihertas No. 466, located at Bakersfield, constituted October 30,
f<IJ7; Culver City No. 467, located at Culver City, constituted Novt·mber 6th, 1917, and Rockridge No. 468, located in the Claremont district of Oakland, constituted October 13, 1917, all by
(;rand Master Hervey.
Three Lodges have been formed during the year: Yorba
1.inda, located at Yorba Linda, Orange County; Lincoln, located

A petition for restoration by a former member of Golden Gate
Lodge No. 30. (Proceedings 1917, page 522.)
A resolution "That a special committee of five members of this
Grand Lodge be appointed by the Grand Master to report at the
next Annual Communication some plan whereby, if possible, the
breach between French and Anglo-Saxon Masonry may be healed
without the sacrifice on either side of any essential principle or matter of conscience." (Proceedings 1917, page 566.)
A resolution "That a special committee be appointed by the
Grand Master to formulate ~nd present amendments to the existing law that will provide some method by which each member of
the fraternity shall be required to contribute one dollar a year to
the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund." (Proceedings 1917, page
523.)
The recommendation of Grand Master Keesling with reference
to permitting portions of the initiatory ceremonies to be conferred
on more than one candidate at a time. (Proceedings 1917, pages
274, 507.)
The suggestion of Grand Master Keesling that the functions of
the Finance Committee be enlarged to include consideration of
many problems that properly come under the classification of Ways
and Means, and to change the designation of the Finance Committee to Ways and Means Committee. (Proceedings 1917 . pages
275, 572.)

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

h111 has made the duties of my office a pleasure, and the attendant

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report as
follows:
To the M.'.W.". Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith present a detailed report of 111y official activities as
Grand Lecturer, concerning the condition of the Lodges a~d .the
District comprising the same, since our last Annual Commu111cat10n.
Never before in the history of the Grand Lodge have the Lodges
of this jurisdiction heen called upon to confer so many degrees,. or
had so many petitions, due in most instances to the draft and enlistments of the young men in this great War, many Lodges holding seve.ral
meetings a week in order to try if possihle to keep the work gomg
and confer the degrees upon the applicants before being called to the
colors. This is true of most of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction,
except in the mining districts, which are pract!cally at a. stan~still,
many of the mines having closed and the depletion .of the mhab1tants
of the community, have made it difficult to hold meetmgs. Some Lodges
in the old mining towns have Jost almost their entire corps of officers.
Most of them, however, are getting along as best they can under the
circumstances.
There have been three dispensations issued for new Lodges,
making a total now of 382, with a net gain of 3593, the largest ~n. the
historv of the Grand Lodge. I sincerely trust that all the novitiates
fully ;ealize the importance of the lessons an:t oblig~tions they receiv~d,,
not to consider these obligations as mere hp service, but to establish
the foundation for a better life, so that all may be· worthy of the
privilege of being a Mason and endeavor to . demonstrate . to those
around them, both in their home lives and busmess connections, that
it is not in vain that they have seen the light, but that the effect of
the revelation has been to purify their lives, to ennoble their characters,
and to make all better husbands, fathers and citizens.

I have visited all the Districts in the State, wi~h the exception of
the 45th, comprising Mono and Inyo counties, and have held schools
of instruction in most of the Lodges therein, both day and night
sessions which were always well attended by officers and members
eager t~ perfect themselves in the ritual. I have also given instruction
to Inspectors, officers and brethren in my office.
To each and every Inspector I wish to express my sincere appreciation for the uniform support I hiLVc received from them at all times,
and for the splendid work they are doing in their several districts,
which has not only been of vast benefit to the Lodges under their care,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND MASTER'S
ADDRESS
Brother Will H. Fischer, for the Committee on Address
of Grand Master and Report of Grand Secretary, presented
the following report :
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee to which was referred the Annual Address of the
Most Worshipful Grand Master and the Annual Report of the Very
Worshipful Grand Secretary, has had the same under consideration,
and hereby submits its report as follows:
As clearly reflected by the Address, the craft throughout the
jurisdiction is enjoying the b:essings of fraternal harmony and pros- '
perity. While the demands upon the activities, interests and financial
resources, not only of the Lodges but of the individual brethren, have
been heavy and unceasing, the Spirit of Masonry has risen to meet
them gloriously, and under the wise guidance and moving inspiration
of our Most Worshipful Grand Master, Masonry in California has
moved steadily forward to higher attainments and greater goals. J\t
the call of our country and at the beck of civilization it has poured
forth its material treasure in support of the great Cause of Man; and,
at the so1111d of the trumpet it has given near to 5400 of its bravest
sons and truest exemplars to serve tmder arms in a strnggle which tht•
conscience of Christendom recognizes as a holy war. Arni Masonry in
California stands ready to continue its efforts, not only in this present,
but in the months and years to come.
Circumstanced as we arc, among clonhts and fears, sorrows and
hopes, this is yet an era in which, alike, the remembered and the forgotten dead well might wish to live again. For we move and have our
being in the highest times of human history-times when the tide of
great opportunity washes all the shores of the world and reaches to
the feet of the humblest as well as the most exalted men.
It rejoicc-s your committrc to observe and to testify that our Most
Worshipful Grand Master, acting through and for Masonry in the
grand jurisdiction of California, has takrn the tide at its flood. With
his strong hand at the helm, controlled by a great intellect and guided
hy a gentle, compassionate and brave heart, the bark of Masonry has
been borne on toward the shining shores of its ordained destit1y. Unceasingly has our Crand Master labored, unceasingly has he loved ancl
taught, am! in consequence we have just ha<l cxhihitet! to us fruits of
reward which must inclct·d bring· us pridt• of our tilling, together with a
sense of ckqi ancl lasting gratitmk to him who has directed us in our .

lias our Most Worshipful Grand Master acquitted himself of a master
l.1sk.

California Masonry in support of the war and in aid of our Masonic
hrcthren now in the armed service of God and humanity.
The solicitude which our Grand Master has manifested for onr

Likewise your committee calls attention to the prompt, vigorous

Your committee feels that it would be remiss in its duty were it
not to mention with special approval the recommendation of our Grand
Master that the Constitution be so amended as to provide for minimum
dues, in subordinate Lodges, of $9 per annum. Our fraternity cannot
measure fuJ:y up to its wonderful opportunities unless its revenues be
sufficient. The sentiment of active Masons throughout the jurisdiction
strongly favors the step suggested, with which, as indicated, your committee is in complete accord. Our Committee on Jurisprudence, of
course, will later render its formal report upon this recommendation.
Your committee has listened, cnrapt, to the impiring message with
which our Grand Master concludes his address. It is, indeed, a mes-·
sage too broad i11 its appeal, too deep in its meaning, too pure in its
expression, to be relegated to the mere tome of official ·record. It is
our privilege, and we believe our duty, to transmit it to the Craft
throughout the jurisdiction. It will strengthen the faint-hearted, it wilt
raise the brave to more exalted deeds. Your committee therefore offers
as a part of the body of this report the following resolution:

Your Board of Trustees are. fully conscious of the importance of
this Trust, not only in the care of our dependents, which is the first

11111ke as useful as possible, consistent with efficiency and economy, and
•111'11 sacrifices as in our judgment we could make to meet the patriotic
