RJlSIDENTS AND CHILDREN

The existence of the Homes is not an idle monument, nor should
any one consider them a burden. It should be the same pleasure and
delight of the Fraternity to provide comfort and cheer in our Masonic
Home, for those too old and too young to produce, as it is for members
as individuals to comfort the venerable father or sweet old mother or
the bright-eyed, light hearted, child of their own homes. We are proud
to note that the kindliest spirit seems to pervade our membershi·p, and
every year brings added interest in those of our Fraternity who are sep-.
arated from their loved ones, and are sheltered in the Homes.
At Decato we arc pleased to report the Residents are now enjoying the comforts of the new buildings and equipment with a better
spirit than when disturbed with many inconveniences. Not all are happy.
It is not human to meet misfortunes and be happy. We can always attempt, however, by selected diet, by providing diversions, and by keeping live interest among the members of our big family, to keep a physical and mental standard that will best serve the greatest number.
They are well clothed, their quarters are kept comfortable, and the hospital accommodations are in the best condition we have ever had them.
An effort has been made to make their diversions useful ones, to help
produce for the Home. In some cases this has met with a cheerful response, but in many they have resented being asked "to work." The
spirit of "doing their bit" is, we believe, spreading and we trust our
Residents will co-operate to a better degree in the future.
At Covina the children are advancing in their development with the
advantages afforded by the new bui:dings. No member of the Fraternity should ever regret the portion he has contributed to the building
up of these sterling young boys and girls. The Board desires to endorse in the strongest manner the beneficial results obtained by following up the recommendations of members of the faculty of Stanford University, who made the survey of our children last year. A new survey
is being made at the time this report is being written to determine any
advancement made, and we trust our Grand Master will receive the
report of the examiners in time to include it in his address. Those ·in
charge at the Covina Home have worked most faithfully with the children, and they feel they have been materially assisted by the suggestions
accompanying the report of the survey last year. The children have
been given credit for raising the standard of the school they attend, and
their industry at home in their duties is commendable. The discipline

ADMISSIONS

We are facing unusual conditions, and the Board has been as genl'l'llllS to our lodges as the condition of Jhe applicant would permit, as
tl11· lodges have had many other unusual calls. We have had continuous
ll''lll<"sts to admit Masons from other Grand Jurisdictions, many of them
lwi11g- personally deserving, but the problem of providing buildings to
h• •llS(' the number of applicants would alone be an impossible one. Many
11f tl1l'se applicants seek to demit into our lodges, and we strongly urge
11111" subordinate lodges to use every care in receiving affiliates, as this
J11ris(liction in common with others, requires five years' membership
fr11111 affiliates to be entitled to admission to the Homes.
All applications this year have received prompt attention. Our
:41•(·rl'tary has referred the application to the Trustee living nearest the
11pplicant at once, and reports have been made at the following meet'111.is. There has been but one disputed point in eligibility. A ruling
was made by a Grand Master that a female orphan of a Mason was
11lways an orphan, regardless of age, and regardless of how many
I i111('S they may have married outside the fraternity, and were entitled
In relief.
Our regulations provide for admission of orphans under
•ixl1"<'n years of age, and we have not recommended any change. We
'"('l'i ved two applications this year for orphans seventy years of age,
wl111 by the ruling of the Grand Lodge were entitled to Masonic relief.
hut by our regulations not entitled to admission to the Homes. Unless
111 l1l'rwise instructed, the Board will continue under our present rcgu1111 i11ns.
Requests to admit boarders at different rates at both Homes come
fn·q11('ntly from Masons who are able to pay for their care, and some are
q11i11· insistent. Experience at our own and other institutions in this
111altl'r has been most unsatisfactory. It creates a caste, or isolated
d:iss, among the old people and disrupts discipline among the children.
Tiu· number of applications for boarding children would go into the
li1111dreds, and the task of pleasing exacting parents wou~d be a burden
wr should not assume.
PROPJlRT!ES AND IMPROVEMENTS

As to improvements, this year has been a quiet one. The new
huit.lings, water plant, heating, refrigeration, etc., at Decato, have been
111 almost perfect operation, and few repairs have been necessary.

At Covina, as reported last year, the buildings were complete<l,
dedicated and occupied. It remained only to complete the grounds and
walks, and to build our barns, dairy, sheds, chicken houses, fences, etc.
All these were built from the material taken from the old temporary
buildings, and the expense consisted only of labor, cement work, wire
for fencing, and necessary hardware.
At San Gabriel we naturally would make no improvement.s, but
we were called upon to pay for some street improvement. This property is now protected from damage by a concrete bri~ge over the wa.sh
going through it. We were again unfortunate in bemg unable to (\I~­
pose of this property. In one instanc~ the State refused. to grant a license to the Sanitarium purchasing it, because no patients are now
permitted to occupy a three-story frame building. !he di~ficulty of
new enterprises financing themselves during these times, discourages
the sale of a property this size, but it is well cared for and should
attract a person desiring this class of property.
The scattering properties coming into possession of the Home
through bequests, Rule 16, or other sources, have all been occupied if
rentable or cared for as economically as possible if not. We can not of
course ~ake desirable sales with present market conditions. These outside properties with one exception, are of small value an<l much care.
We will dispose of them at earliest opportunities.

ACCOUNTING AND I'INANCes

On another page of this report is printed a reproduction of an annual sheet showing the expenses of maintenance <listributed in items,
which readily determines the relative costs of the various <lepartments.
These segregations are desirahle and helpful in comparing the monthly
costs and assist in the economical handling of supplies. Our system
of st~res which enables us to purchase in larger quantities, then issuing
by requisition the needs of each month separately, makes these accounts
fairly accurate in food supplies and clothing, but is not dependable in
farm purchases that do not go through stores. This system was not
easily established, and represents much effort on the part of our accountant Bro. John R. Ruckstell, but it is now operating nicely. A
similar distribution is now being compiled to show all disbursements
made from the building fund, so that a separate account may be carried
for each building, farms, heating plants, laundries, water plants, grou~d
improvement, etc., which will show a monthly record of the cost o.f n:a11.1tenance, repair, renewal, or other expense of each. When this 1s 111
operation our full system of accounting will be ideal.
A record of our Finances is kept in Funds .. each representing a
distinct department of our work. We believe a brief explanation of
these funds for the benefit of new members of the Grand Lodge would

Our "General or Maintenance Fund" opened with a deficit of
$:i,175.18 carried from last year. The receipts cover the per capita

I l1an we feared it would be, but the co-operation of those at the Homes
a111l the aid of our friends among the dealers has aided much.
"Special Rule 16 Fund" is moneys coming to the Home through
applicants who are possessed of small holdings of Real Estate, X otes,
llonds, Insurance or other Securities which by our terms of admis,jon are turned over to the Homes. These properties are converted
into cash when practical or possible, and the amounts held in "Rule 16
Fund" until the death of the Resident. The Resident "receives the in·
nime from this fund while living, and at death of the Resident, the
principal passes to the Endowment Fund.
"Permanent Endowment Fund" has not shown the advance the
past year, largely because in the judgment of the Grand Master, and we
:1s Trustees were in accord, no call was made for an "Endowment
I lay." There being so many other calls on our hrethren, patriotic and
otherwise, this call was temporarily withdrawn. This met with object ion from many of the brethren who are enthusiastic for this fund,
and many remitted without the request. These funds are invested in dcpt>ndablc bonds except for the amot1nt loaned to the building fond for
the completion of the new buildings at Decoto and Covina. The
Building Fnnd pays the Endowment fund five per cent interest 011 the
amounts borrowed, that the income may in no way he disturbed. While
our regulations provide that the Income from the Endowment F1111d
may be used for the maintenance of the Homes, your Board of Trustees have never drawn on it, and have carried the income back into
the fund as a part of the new principal.
"Residents' Deposit F1111d." This is the aggregate of small sums
sent to residents hy lodges for the personal expenses or comforts of
individual rcsidt>nls, or from other sources such as pcnsions. donations,
etc. When a rcshknt receives the income from Ruic 16 Fund, it is

"Entertainment Fund" is the residue of the Christmas Donations
so generously given by Masonic Bodies and members, and is used all
through the year for the entertainment, instruction and amusei;nent ~f
the old people, and for taking the children on a month's camping trip
during their summer vacation. This balance is naturally much larger
immediately following Christmas time. Residents and children share a
great sense of gratitude for this fund, knowing it comes as a volur:tary
contribution to be used exclusively for their pleasure and diversions.
We can not express to the thoughtful donors of this fund, the great
amount of real enjoyment these moneys provide, and the Trustees join
b~th our big families in most sincere thanks for this fund.
"Building Fund." This fund is supplied by the collection of the
fifty cents per capita collected each year as a building fun.d, and. ~as
been augmented by donations from members of the Fraternity desmng
to add to the comforts of those left to our care, particularly one good
brother, who does not permit the use of his name, who contributed
$21,000.00 toward the Covina Building, and $19,000.00 for new cons~ruc­
tion at Decoto. This fund has provided not only the new Dormitory
Building at Decoto and made the cottages much more suitable to our
needs, but it provided the new water system which was so ur?ently
needed and which gave the fraternity the gravest concern before it was
establi~hed. It also provided the new heating system which meant
much comfort to our old people in winter time, and the new laundry
which saves us much in the care and treatment of clothing. The
changes in the Annex Building, the refrigeration plant, the proper housing of employees, grading of grounds, roads, etc., has made our ho:ne
complete as it should be, with many convenienc.es, the absence of ~vh1ch
subjected us to just criticism before these .things were .accomph~h.ed.
The erection of the new buildings for the Children at Covina, prov1dmg
them with proper care and training, is the pride of all who have seen
them, and makes it possible to do that real Masonic building, the bui~d­
ing of strong men and women, morally, physically and mentally, with
the children for whose future we have assumed responsibility. These
sums have been spent in goodly amounts, but the Fraternity has never
spent its dollars for a more deserving purpose, and we can i ustly feel
that in providing these things we reflect credit upon efforts to meet
the responsibilities we assumed at the altar, in the care of those who
could look no place else but a public charity for their sustenance.

"Special Home Fund." This is a fund of $19,000.00 previously

GENERAL CONDITIONS

Never in the history of the Homes have all departments been
working so efficiently, and so satisfactorily, but never before have we
possessed the working buildings and plants. All these thing make the
lwtter results possible. Our health records have been good, our produci11!-( facilities increased, and the conditions giving us most severe coni'<'rn have been removed. No person not familiar with the detail we
li:ivc met, can fully appreciate what the Fraternity has accomplished in
t liis branch of our work. We can not anticipate what the needs of the
war may bring to us, but our Grand Lodge has prepared us to meet the
1ww conditions in a splendid manner. Returning soldiers will need as~istance.
Old people whose support has been taken from them may
In• eompelled to seek the shelter of the Home. Soldiers killed in action
111ay leave dependent children. Thanks to a thoughtful Grand Lodge,
W<' have thoroughly caught ttp in our work, and are .ready to meet new
ll'•ponsibilities if they come to us. There are few vac~nt rooms at
I >.-coto, but the greatest call may be on our hospital, which is now filled
'" rapacity. The Home at Covina will care for more than twice the
1111111her of children by going to capacity in the new buildings. 'vV e are
111aking no recommendations on this matter, as the call has not come to
""· hut are stating the situation, that members of the Fraternity may
kuuw the actual conditions, should unexpected demands arise.

remain unchanged. The deficit'the past year is less than anticipated.

TH!\ COVINA HOM!\

The children were installed in their new buildings last year but
a few days before the meeting of the Grand Lodge. They were most
happy in - th~ culmination of a long anticipated event in which they
had each personally participated in some useful way to make complete.
The past year may be said to be the one of greatest development in the
history of the Home. ~ ot development alone in physical improvement
of the property, but a wonderful mental development of the child, that
can only be experienced or obtained in habilitating in a sensible and
suitable manner the buildings they had watched in construction in every
detail from cornerstone to dedication.
In the furnishing, decorating and draping, the children were taught
to ·study the harmony of color, the character of design, the symmetry
of hangings, and the placing of the several units of the furnishings. In
the care of the home, the value of saving, the economy of wear, and the
maximum of usefulness of all things provided for them, is emphasized
by their instructions.
With the increased facilities for industrial. musical, and social development, they have displayed a corresponding increased interest and improvement in these branches. Our boys have dug ditches for pipe lines,
the holes for trees in the new orchards, assisted in grading, weeding and
caring for the lawn, and in many small ways were helpful in our general
improvements. Our girls laundered and hung the curtains, made covers
and tops for tables, scarfs for dressers and chiffoniers, many choice hangings and room ornaments for their dormitories, and above all made and
sold enough aprons to furnish their own parlors at a cost of nearly
three hundred dollars. While doing all these things, and sharing a
delight in doing them, they have advanced in their school work, music,
and drills as well.
Our children enjoy and value the visits of our Grand Officers, .;ind
those of Lodges and Chapters. Some of these visits mark some very
happy events. 'vVe desire the Lodges and Chapters to know they are'
always welcome, and if our Matron may be informed in advance, the
children will be pleased to entertain them in some way. We desire to
mention some of the visits that delighted the children the past year.
September 14th, Most Illustrious Harvey Le Fevre Marvin, Grand
Master of Grand Council, R. & S. M., visited the Home and addressed
the children in a most appropriat1 and cordial manner.
September 19th, Jasmine Chapter No. 145 of Azusa called with a
generous supply of fruits and jells. A warm welcome and program was
given by the children.
October 28th, Brother James F. Fenwick of Honolu!J'Lodge No. 4al
gave the children a most pleasant and cordial visit.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

May 8th. A musicale given by the children under the direction of
Mrs. Lela Buckham. She brought some artists with her from Los Angeles, who took part, much to the. delight of the children.
May 18th. A reception to Dr. Samuel E. Burke, Grand Master oi
Grand Council. Our boys drill team did well. On this occasion gavels
made by the boys of the Home were presented to Brother Burke,
Brother Wm. Rhodes Hervey, Grand Master, and Brother E. B. Spencer, Grand High Priest.
May 22nd, County ~fatrons and Patrons Association, 0. E. S., of
Los Angeles were entertained by the children at Covina.
June 22nd. Children participated in reception to Grand Master
\Vm. Rhodes Hervey at Shrine Auditorium. Our girls gave some
c1a.ssic dancing, Our boys gave a drill and the Girls' Mandolin Club
played.
June 30th. Visit of Veteran Lodge No. 373 of Sawtelle. The
Lodge presented a splendid 68 foot steel flag pole and a beautiful 12x20
flag. Golden West Commandery Band accompanied them, also Columbia Chapter, 0. E. S.
July 7th. Claremont Lodge No. 436 and Claremont Chapter No. 324
visited the Home. Children gave a program. The visitors were pleased
with the home and the children.
July 19th. Euclid Chapter No. 179 of Ontario called in good numbers and had a picnic lunch on the grounds. This Chapter was generous with comforts, pillow cases, towels, etc., and a nice number of
fruits and jells. Every member who did not act like a kid was fined,
and $7.63 was collected arid left as treat money for the children.
July 24th to August 28th, marks the camp at Balboa. Here 9ur
Orange County brethren make their visits, and many of our friends
coming to this Beach from Los Angeles and other places called at Camp.
Our Grand Master was a frequent caller, and Past Grand Masters
Weller and Keesling visited the camp and were most heartily received
bv the children. On some Sundays we received as many as fifty visitors.
Mrs. Adams and Mrs. Wollenberg accompanied their husbands at a
Hoard meeting in camp. They enjoyed the children and the beach, but
they made no swimming records.

Other Donations were made, the value of which cannot be measured in dollars, and the increasing benefit of the services performed
will compound more than usury rates in exchange. The Mental and
Physical Survey made by the Department of Pediatrics of Stanford
University Medical School was given to us by that institution without
cost to us. Prof. Arthur J. Ritter and Dr. Harold K. Faber conducting the work, have rendered the Fraternity a splendid service, and our
gratitude to them is extended in fullest measure of expression. They
were generous, not only in their labors, but i11 their recommendations
and suggestions for our guidance in building up intellectual and physical standards.

of our big family. His capable and generous wife, Dr. Nannie C.

Petersen before her removal to the hospital. Dr. Henry Dietrick,
though unknown to us at the time, cared for Dorothy at the Hospital
up to the time of her death, without expense to the Home. All of these
physicians are Masons, and none of them would accept compensation for
their services.

THE DECOTO HOME
During the past year the work of service at the Dccoto Home has
lit•en carried on along the same lines as reported on heretofore.
Suitable entertainments, school instruction, out-of-doors recreations,
picnic parties, excursions to nearby places of interest, etc., have enriched
the social and family life of the Homes, affording diversion for those
rnfeebled by advancing years, and giving wholesome and beneficial exerdse to those who find their strength increasing as the years unfold.
Since our last report twenty-six persons have been admitted to the
I Tome. Eighteen men and eight women. Twenty-four have passed
away. There are now present ninety-four men an<l fifty-three women.

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The general health of the Home has been good, with the exception
of those who by reason of age have become infirm and helpless.
Though the past season has been an unusually dry one, and the
water levels in the wells in the vicinity of the Home have lowered, our
well continues to give its usual supply of water.
The greater portion of the hill ranch has been leased ejther \)n
shares or cash rental. The orchards, hay fields, the chicken and hog
ranch, vegetable and berry gardens have given good returns. The sur"
p!us being sold in the local and San Francisco markets.
Owing to the high price of feed and other expense in maintaining
our dairy, it was found advisable to sell the dairy herd and for· the present to purchase milk for table use.
·A large quantity of fruit has been dried and stored for future use.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the
Home by their labors in the carpenter, tailor, shoe and barher shops,·
picking fruit, watering lawns, garage, kitchen work and light chores,
also work in the drug, dental and optical departments. All mending
and the making of household linen has been done by the ladies of .tho;
Home.
The ladies of the Home have taken entire charge of the care of
not only their own rooms, but also the halls, stairways, wash ronms,
reading, linen, and reception rooms; also the Assembly hall in the
buildings occupied by them.
The library is well patronized, and the reading am! club rooms
are supplied with magazines and daily ~apers.
A complete dental outfit has been donated to the II ome by nrothcr
Jed C. Stanton, consisting of one dental chair, one instrument and
supply case, one bracket case, forceps and dental supplies, etc. A dental department has been opened up in one of the rooms in Cottage No.
1, where all who need dental work done can be attended to by him.
A large Packard Reed Organ has been donakd to the Home by
Brother Edwin D. Matthews. It has been placed in our Temple Lodge
room.
Gold Hill Lodge No. 32 donated seven cane and umbrella stands ..
These stands have been in and around the several buildings of the
Home.
The Lodges of the 28th District donated six settees, each six feet
long. They have been placed on the porches of the cottages and new
buildings.
Each Thursday afternoon a moving picture entertainment has been
given at the Temple. The Thursday evening socials and card parties,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The general health of the Home has been good, with the exceptiC>n
of those who by reason of age have become infirm and helpless.
Though the past season has been an unusually dry one, and the
water levels in the wells in the vicinity of the Home have lowered, our
well continues to give its usual supply of water.
The greater portion of the hill ranch has been leased either <;m
shares or cash rental. The orchards, hay fields, the chicken and hog
ranch, vegetable and berry gardens have given good returns. The sure
plus being sold in the local and San Francisco markets.
Owing to the high price of feed and other expense in maintaining
our dairy, it was found advisable to sell the dairy herd and for· the present to purchase milk for table use.
. A large quantity of fruit has been dried and stored for future use.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of the
Home by their labors in the carpenter, tailor, shoe and barber shops,
picking fruit, watering lawns, garage, kitchen work and light chores,
also work in the drug, dental and optical departments. All mending
and the making of household linen has been done by the ladies of .the
Home.
The ladies of the Home have taken entire charge of the care .of
not only their own rooms, but also the halls, stairways, wash rooms,
reading, linen, and reception rooms; also the Assembly hall in the
buildings occupied by them.
The library is well patronized, and the reading and duh rooms
are snpplied with magazines and daily papers.
A complete dental outfit has been donated to the Home by Brother
Jed C. Stanton, consisting of one dental chair, one instrument and
supply case, one bracket case, forceps and dental supplies, etc. A dental department has been opened up in one of the rooms in Cottage No.
1, where all who need dental work done can be attended to by him.
A large Packard Reed Organ has been donated to the Home by
Brother Edwin D. Matthews. It has been placed in our Temple Lodge
room.
Gold Hill Lodge No. 32 donated seven cane and umbrella stands.,
These stands have been in and around the several buildings of the
Home.
The Lodges of the 28th District donated six settees, each six feet
long. They have been placed on the porches of the cottages and new
buildings.
Each Thursday afternoon a moving picture entertainment has been
given at the Temple. The Thursday evening socials and card parties,

At the request of the Grand Master, Hon. William Rhodes
Hervey, a survey for the year 1918 was made of the Masonic Home
for Children at Covina, California. The purpose of the Survey was
to determine if the recommendations of the report of 1917 had been
carried. out by the management, what results had been obtained
therefrom, whether improvements had been made in the physical and
mental development of the children included in the former survey,
and recommendations and reports on those admitted subsequent to
the findings of last year.
Physical Status: This year's survey was conducted Oil the same
basis as that outlined last. year for both physical and mental examinations. The measurements of height and weight, girth of head,
chest and abdomen, tests of vision by Snellen types, and hearing

The survey of last year showed already an unusual rating of
intelligence in a group of children, and the improvement shown here
could not have been ordinarily expected. This exceptional improvement in the individual case is largely due to the co-operation of
management and continuous application and instruction of the
children. The increase in scores is particularly noticeable in reasoning power and judgment. The boys have industriously assisted
in building up the Home, and as compensation received thrift stamps.
They also had considerable experience in making monetary transactions,
thereby learning the value of coins, in which they were rather backward last year. The examiners were very happy to note the oppor-

lwl'n established. Irrigation system and pipe lines, grading of playi.:nntnds, paving of roads, cement sidewalks, and lawns arc noticealik improvements accomplished dnring the year.

Conclusion: Jn conclusion, we desire to state that the work
accomplished during the year 1917-1918 at the Masonic Home for
l 'hildren is beyond anything expected. It 11111st he admitted that the
;;!amling of the children in 1917 was considered high, hut increased
rnnsiderahly dne to the understanding, study, and attention given
In the individual child.

Ill' congratulakd hy having in charge of this llomc the Managing
Trustee, Mr. E. B. Spencer, and the Matron, Mrs. Maude E. Miller,

towards the children which made possible the standard shown in this
;;11rvey.

made by a Grand Master that the female orphan of a Mason
was always an orphan, regardless of age, and regardless of
how many times they may have married outside of the
fraternity, and were entitled to relief. Our regulations provide for admission of orphans under the age of sixteen, and
we have not recommended any change. Vv e received two
applications this year for orphans seventy years of age, who
by the ruling of the Grand Lodge were entitled to Masonic
relief, but by our regulations not entitled to admission to
the Homes. Unless otherwise instructed, the Board will
continue under our present regulations." The Grand Secretary moved that it is the sense of this Grand Lodge that
the daughters of J..faster Masons over the age of twentyone years, who by our regulations are entitled to relief, are
eligible to the Masonic Home. The motion was considered
at length and lost.

AN:'.'JUAL ORATION
The Grand Lodge was then favored by an interesting,
instructive, and eloquent oration delivered by Brother Chas.
H. Victor, Grand Orator, as follows:
Most Worshipful Grand 11-faster and Brethren:
Very earnestly and sincerely have I wished that the appointment
given me by the Grand -Ylaster and the duty and the responsibility
placed upon me might have carried with it the inspiration and wisdom,
the power and the vision to have gra~ped so great an opportunity, but
this is a vain wish and likewise a fntile one; hut yet, perhaps, after all,
it is well that it should he so, for in times like these men are learning
to attempt tasks that are unusual and are taking up duties that seem
almost impossible, even when they are aware of their own deficiencies.
This is an unusual communication of the Grand Lodge. There is a
different atmosphere ahout our meeting this year from that which has
been present heretofore. We cannot help but feel it and we cannot fail to
recognize it. We do not greet each other in that care-free, off-hand way
so common to good fellowship that has marked our greetings in the
past. We are not interested in the ordinary social diversions and conversations that have been so pleasant a feature of the recurring anniversary of our meetings heretofore. When we grasp each other by the
hand it seems as though we can look into each other's hearts and have
a response come back to us that we are standing together. There seems
to be a deeper sense of our relationship and our brotherhood than has
marked this relationship heretofore. On the lapel of the coats of many
of you is that little button with its bright star that marks the fact that
the boy is gone, the fact that he is willing to offer up on the altar of his
patriotism a devoted service. And that star represents more than words
can tell. That star is at once your pride and your despair. and so we
cannot help but recognize the one great, outstanding, ever-present, overpowering fact that our condition is different this year from previous
years.

It seems to me that every sentence that has heen uttered since we
first gathered together has heen directed toward the one thought, that
we were at war. The one hig thing that stands out in our minds is not
a discussion of the beautiful philosophy of Masonry, not a discussion

inspiring, not thinking even upon those things that intimately concern

fraternity, and although we have been inspired through our entire his-

world can be a great republic. \Ve say that it is on this basis of
brotherhood, that it is on this basis of mutual respect and understanding that we unite every race, sect and opinion, and cause true friendship to exist among those that might otherwise have remained at a
perpetual distance; and it is a broad interpretation of this ritual of
ours that enables us to stand firmly and squarely with our President in
the right of self-determination of peoples.
Now, we care not what the race may be; we care not what the
color of a man may be; we care not what his education and his culture
may have been, for we declare as Masons that that man has a right to
decide for himself and the nation for itself how they are to live, how
they are to act, what form of government they may want to have over
them in so far as their actions, their desires and their governments do
not interfere with the same liberty, and the same rights and the same
actions of other peoples and other governments. And that is the thing
we are fighting for today. That is the reason why we, as a country that
to a certain extent has a!ways been isolated from the great qnarrels of
the world, a country that has kept itself separated, that has not engaged
in the wars and the intrigues of other continents, have transported our
troops across seas to the continents of Europe and of Asia, and there
we are fighting battles, not for territory-because it has been clearly
stated that we do not want one foot of the territory of our enemies,
not for indemnity or money, because it has b(:en equally stated with as
great force that we do not want one penny of indemnity or pay for the
service we are rendering, hut rather that we might bear practical testimony to our consecration to the principles of liberty, fraternity, equality
and self-determination of all peoples of the earth.
And, Brethren, as we have waged this war, many from our own
ranks have gone; the report that was given by our Grand Secretary
showing that between live and six thousand Brethren arc now in the
active service speaks for itself. The same report has come from other
jurisdictions, and we have found our Brethren who arc capable of
arms springing to the defense of these princip'.es of ours.
Many of us have not been able to go, hut we have found consolation in
the effort and work behind the line. and that is perhaps the important
thing to you and to me this morning.
Oh, I know that it is inspiring and it just fills and it j{1st thrills
us when we hear the reports as they come to us of what the boys are
doing. It just makes us rise up and thank God that we are Americans.
It just makes us happy all over and proud to think that we have in this
country of ours raised a race of men of the power, of the heroism.
of the spirit and of the physical valor and courage that have made possible some of the brilliant exploits that our men have already experienced, and those of you who heard the story of our Marines at Chateau

Thierry were filled with that spirit, and I believe that It ts m keeping
with the spirit of the hour that the facts as they have come to us might
be repeated. Some of you know the story and some of you do not, but
over there on that eventful 15th day of July, ninety-five hundred of our
Marines were at Chateau Thierry faced by two divisions of the German
army-and crack divisions, we are told, the very flower and pick of the
Prussian army-and the order eame for the Germans to attack, and
that mighty horde came over, and nearly three to one, Brethren. With
strong arms and under the force of the compact the Marines yielded,
they reeled and went back about half a mile, and then the lines had
been re-formed and the order from the commander went out that they
go forward, and they started. Then the order came in from the French
general to retreat. The word went back from the commander of the
Marines that he regretted very much his inability to obey the order,
that his patrols had already gone forward and that his men were on
the march, and that he must save and protect those men whom he had
commanded to move, and so they went forward, and for three days
the battle raged. Then the fight was over, and what was the result?
The information that comes to us is just this: that but twenty-five
hundred of the ninety-five hundred Marines that went into that conflict were able to stand and answer roll call. Seven thousand of them
were either dead or wounded-a tremendous sacrifice laid upon the
altar of their country, but, Brethren, what of the horde that attacked
them? What of those two divisions that came over to drive them hack?
The story that comes to us is that not a squad could he gathered together
to answer roll call. The ninety-five hundred Marines had accounted
for two divisions, or twenty-four thousand Germans. That kind of a
story, Brethren, fills us with enthusiasm for our boys; it fills us with
enthusiasm for the American spirit, and I want to say to you that the
thing that put that kind of a spirit into the hearts of those men was
the free institutions that have hrought them up, the institutions that
have been nurtured, that have been fostered. that have hecn created
and hrought to fruition hy the principles laid down hy our Masonic
fraternity.

161

Immediately after entering upon its task the committee was
confronted with grave difficulties arising out of the disturbances
resulting from our present state of war, lack of authentic and detailed information relating to the subject matter, and the widely
variant attitudes assumed by Grand Lodges respecting French
Masonic powers. Because of these difficulties your committee
finds itself unable at this time, notwithstanding its serious and diligent efforts, to comply with the requirements of your resolution.
However, it may be profitable to present a discussion of the subject
and respectfully to recommend a present course of action for the
Grand Lodge of California without presuming in any degree to indicate the attitude which should be assumed by any other body, or
remotely to suggest the propriety of similar action by any other
Grand Lodge of the great family of Anglo-Saxon Masonry.
The work entrusted to your committee is one of vital importance at this time. More than 5,300 members of California Lodges
have enlisted in the military or naval service of our government,
and thousands more, in all probability, will soon join the colors.
Many of these Masons arc already serving in France, and our
brethren will be sent in increasing numbers to that distant land.
California 11asons arc companions in arms with French Masons
who owe allegiance to bodies with which this Grand Lodge has no
fraternal relationship. These men are engaged in the same high
enterprise in behalf of honor and civilization, their brave hearts beat
in unison, they confront the same foe and equal dangers, and the
ashes of lllftl'!Y of them will commingle in the sacred soil of France,
which is being hallowed hy their blood. They are entitled to exchange and enjoy all the royalties and generosities and amenities of
Masonic fellowship and social intercourse unless some insurmountable barrier of conscience lifts between them ..
We are face to face with new and unnsual conditions in the
Masonic world. Our soldier brethren in France are unfamiliar with
the points of difference which separate the Anglo-Saxon Masons
from their French brethren. and they arc entitled to have this vexed
and difiicult question settled or to he advised of the reasons for a
continued separation. The French hodics have made overtures for
recognition. It seems our plain dttty to leave nothing undone that
can consistently he clone to cement more firmly the bonds of universal brotherhood. We desire, in this report. to lay before you
the facts pertinent to this inquiry and to point ont the ohstacles
which must he overcl)llle if French Masonry is to be recognized by
this Grand Lodge. W c regret that this report will be fottnd lacking in definiteness, but authentic information is not always available
and many aspects of the question under consideration are veiled in

obscurity. We believe the statements herein· contained, gathered
from many sources, to be facts in the case, although we can not, in
every instance, prove their authenticity.

French Masonic Powers
There are three Grand bodies in France exerc1smg authority
over the degrees of Symbolic and Ancient Craft Masonry, to-wit,
the Grand Orient of France, the Grand Lodge of France, and the
Independent and Regular National Grand Lodge of France and the
French Colonies. These three bodies are independent of each other
and exhibit differences in method and principle. It appears that
very little is known about French Masonry by the members of the
Craft, and the fugitive items in the Masonic and secular press on
this subject have not always dealt fairly with our French brethren,
and oftentimes have echoed the complaints and misrepresentations
of the enemies of Latin Masonry. The history of these powers
may be briefly summarized as follows:
(a) The Grand Orient. It is claimed that a Lodge of Masons
was organized at Dunkirk in the early years of the eighteenth century, but we have been unable to verify such facts. It appears that
the first Lodge actually known in France was that established in
Paris in 1732 by Lord Derwentwater. In 1735 certain Lodges at
Paris applied to the Grand Lodge of England for the constitution
of a Provincial Grand Lodge, but the petition was refused for political reasons. The Grand Lodge of England reconsidered its action
and in 1743 granted authority for the organization of a Provincial
Grand Lodge under the name of the Grande Loge J\lnglaise de
France. We have been advised that the constitution of this Grande
Loge was modeled on that of the Anderson Constitutions of 1723.
Soon after the organization of this Grand body differences arose
between the Parisian and Provincial Lodges and there ensued years
of turbulence. In 1755 the Grande Loge declared its independence
of the Grand Lodge of England and changed its name to Grande
Loge de France, and excluded all the Provincial Lodges from its
membership. It seems that this body recognized only the first
three degrees of Masonry. The difficulties between the Parisian
Grand Lodge and the Provincial Lodges seem to have been finally
healed and all the factions of French Craft Masonry were united in
1771, in which year a new constitution was adopted and the Grande
Loge de France was merged into the Grand Orient of France. It
appears, however, that soon a faction arose which repudiated the
merger or change and perpetuated the existence of the Grande
Loge, which engaged in a struggle against the new Grand Orient
until 1779, when the Grande Loge was finally and completely united
with the Grand Orient. In 1804 a second Grand body was organ·

ized, but by treaty was soon after mer d .

the two great Masonic powers in France, and that. notwithstanding
the treaty they had made, each continued to confer and rule the
first, second and third degrees. Not being able to trace the history
of the relations between these powers, we assume that the independence gained by the Grand Lodge of the Grand Orient in 1895, and
of the Supreme Council in 1904, terminated what must have been a
long quarrel. W c believe that, by reason of violations of the treaty
of 1805, from 1841 both the Grand Orient and the Supreme Council
conferred and ruled Craft degrees, and that the Supreme Council
relinquished control over the degrees of Ancient 'Craft Masonry to
the Grand Lodge in 1904. The Grand Lodge is said to have 136
Lodges, with a membership in excess of 8,500. It is interesting to
note that one of these Lodges. "Anglo-Saxon No. 343," works in
the English language, and that its members are mostly British and
Americans, and we are happy to state that fraternal good will has
existed uninterruptedly between these Grand Bodies since 1904.
The Grand Lodge claims jurisdiction over only the first, second
and third degrees of Masonry.
(c) The Independent and Regular National Grand Lodge of
France and the French Colonies. This Body was founded in
December, 1913, and has been recognized by the Grand Lodges 'of
England, Scotland and other countries. It was organized by three
Lodges which withdrew from the Grand Orient, and it appears that
at the present time the jurisdiction of the new Grand Body extend~
over three or four Lodges, with a membership of less than 200
Masons. This Body claims to be the only regular Grand Lodge in.
France, and we are informed, has modeled itself upon the laws and
principles of the Grand I.ridge of England. l t has been more thaR
once intimated in high places that this is hardly a new ·Grand
Lodge, but rather a sort of colonization in France of new Lodges
under English patronage. It seems to us that this Body may be
considered a negligible quantity nntil a longer life and greater
growth may justify the attention of the Masonic world.

Reasons for Continuance of Breach with Grand Orient.
If the only differences between the Grand Orient of France and
the Grand Lodge of California were those growing out of the inva-·
sion of the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana,
then there would be no obstai;les in the way of immediate establishment of full fraternal relations with the Grand Orient of France.
It appears, however, that after the dissolution of relations in 1869,
certain changes were made in the Constitution of the Grand Orient
of France which are now the subject of controversy. For several
years the Grand Orient discussed the proposition of striking all
reference to the Deity from the rituals and the Constitution. In
1877 the Grand Orient, after a year of serious deliberation, by a vote
of 135 to 76 Lodges, resolved to make the change in the Constitution.
It seems that prior to 1849 the Constitution and rituals of the Grand
Orient were essentially the same as they stand today. In 1849,
probably because of growing closeness of political relations with
Great Britain, the Grand Orient amended its laws and practices so
as to more nearly conform to those of the Grand Lodge of England.
\Ve understand that, following the English model, the Grand Orient
adopted the following rule in 1849:
. "Freemasonry has for its principles the existence of God, the
immortality of the soul, and the solidarity of mankind."
In 1877 this provision of the Constitution was repealed, and in
lieu thereof the following was substituted:
"Whereas, Freemasonry is not a religion, and has, therefore, no
doctrine or dogma to affirm its constitution, the Assembly adopting
the Vaeu IX., has decided and decreed that the second paragraph
of Article I of the Constitution shall be erased and that for the
words of said article the following shall be substituted:
"'Freemasonry, an essentially philanthropical and progressive
institution, has for its object the pursuit of truth, the study of morality, and the practice of solidarity; its efforts are directed to the
material and moral improvement and the intellectual and social
advancement of humanity. It has for its principles, mutual tolerance, respect for others and for one's self. and absolute liberty of
conscience. Considering metaphysical conceptions as belonging
exclusively to the individual judgment of its members, it refuses to
accept any dogmatic affirmation. I ts motto is: Liberty, Equality,
Fraternity.' "
Upon making this change in the Constitution, the Grand Lodges
in English-speaking countries then in fraternal relations with the
Grand Orient, dissolved the same, and many of the Grand Lodges
in the United States, although having already severed relations
because of the Louisiana incident, protested the action of the Grancl
Orient. The attitude taken is not easily understood when we
remember that many protesting Grand Lodges held fraternal rela.
tions with the Grand Orient prior to 1849. and that the announced

Brother Frederic Desmons, a Protestant minister of reputation
and high character, who was nine times President of the Grand
Orient of France, strenuously urged the adoption of the amendment, and later said:
"In suppressing the formula respecting the G. A. of the U. we
did not mean to replace it by a materialistic formula. None among
us in proposing this suppression, thought of professing atheism or
materialism, and we declare formally and emphatically that we had
no other end in view than to proclaim absolute liberty of conscience."
Brother Maricault, the reporter of the committee on amendment of the law, in recommending a postponement in 1876 of the
question, made the following statement:
"Your Commission has recognized that bad faith alone could
interpret the suppression demanded as a denial of the existence of
God and the immortality of the soul; human solidarity and freedom
of conscience, which would be henceforth the exclusive basis of
Freemasonry, imply quite as strongly belief in God and in an immortal soul as they do materialism, positivism, or any other philosophic doctrine."
By "solidarity" Brother Maricault and his brethren mean
"brotherhood of man.''
The Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient wrote to an English
brother as follows:
"The Grand Orient of France has not abolished the Masonic
formula, 'To the glory of the Great Architect of the Universe,' as
you appear to believe, still less have they made profession of Atheism. ln their general assembly of September, 1877, they purely
and simply proclaimed absolute liberty of conscience as a right
belonging to every man, and out of respect for this liberty they
expunged from their Constitution a dogmatic formula, whicll seemed
to a great majority of the members to be in contradiction with liberty of conscience.
"In modifying an article of its statutes the Grand Orient of
France by no means intended to make profession of either Atheism
or materialism, as would seem to be understood. No alteration has
been made either in the principles or the practice of Masonry;
French Masonry remains what it has always been-a fraternal and
tolerant brotherhood."
We are informed that French Masons contend that prior to
1877 the Book of Constitutions had lain upon the altars, and that it
was interpreted as the "Book of the Law" or "Volume of Sacred
Law." In some quarters we find the claim made that the Bible was
taken from the altars of French Lodges because of the attacks of
the Catholic Church on Masonry in that Republic, and that because
the Bible was used on the altars of the Church Masonry could not
place it upon its altars and remain consistent in its defense of the
rights of conscience. It appears that no change of practice with
reference to the Bible has been made by the Grand Orient for

16, Rue Cadet, Paris, October 12, 1917.
Worshipful Sir and Brethren: The world-wide conflict for the
liberation of oppressed nations and for the triumph of the principles
of justice and liberty in which a good many allied countries now
take an effective part, has assembled on French soil most of the
glorious armies fighting for right, who are now to be joined by an
imposing contingent of your noble country.
In the first rank of these gallant troops. their arm strengthened
by their ideal, we are sure to find, more numerous every day, Freemasons of the United States of America. and we have thought of
offering them, as sqon as they arrive in the French capital, a warm.
fraternal welcome becoming amongst brother Masons.
Under the auspices of the Grand Orient of France our wo.rshipful "La Fraternite des Peuples" has formed a reception at the
Temple of the Grand Orient, 16, Rue Cadet, a real Masonic home.
Here your brethren will always find devoted Masons, speaking
their language, ready to answer all inquiries and furnish any u.seful
information they may require; to assure them a fraternal help m all
circumstances, to keep in touch hy corresponding with them: to
visit them in case they are ill or wounded, to serve as intermediary
between them and their relatives, etc.
The usefulness of this central bureau will at once he apparent
to you. not only for our brethren who are in the army, but also to
those near and dear to them and who in their thoughts will follow
them across the Atlantic. and who will know that they are not left
to themselves and abandoned amongst the dangers of every-day
life, but that a fraternal and helping hand is always extended to
them in case of need.

Territorial Jurisdiction.
/\II the Grand Lodges in English-speaking countries tenaciously
ntlhere to the principle that each Grand Lodge is sovereign and
1'11prcme throughout its territorial jurisdiction, and that an invasion
uf the territorial jurisdiction of any Grand Lodge by another
Masonic Power is an act of hostility and operates to place the
llH11rper outside the pale of fraternal recognition and brands it .as
1111 outlaw. This is a salutary doctrine, and in English-speaking
t·111111tries at least should be vindicated and perpetuated. In the
r .al in countries the doctrine of exclusive territorial jurisdiction
1loes not obtain, but in those countries each Grand Body is sover1•i).(n and supreme, not throughout the territory it occupies, but
ovl·r its subordinate Lodges and their members. This explains why
lhc Grand Orient of France and the Grand Lodge of France, occupying the same territory, are in fraternal and friendly relations
t'al'h with the other. It does not seem necessary to the integrity
1111<1 maintenance of our doctrine of exclusive territorial jurisdiction
that we shall force the same upon our brethren of the Latin countries of the world who prefer to give their adherence to a different
doctrine, which suits them better and under which they seem to
live together in Masonic peace and fraternal concord.
The California Policy Respecting Recognition.
In 1913 the Grand Lodge of California adopted a certain report
and recommendation made by the late M. W. Edward H. Hart,
( 'hairman of the Committee on Correspondence, and thereby fixed
the tests to he applied by the Grand Lodge of California in the
111atter of recognition of other Grand Lodges. These tests are as
follows:
.
First, the Gra_nd Body seeking recognition must he regularly
lnrmed by subordmate Lodges which trace their origin to regular
a11d legitimate l\ncient Craft Masonry.
Secondly, the Grand Body applying- for recognition must hold
1111disputed sway as the acknowledged Supr('me Power in Ancient
('raft Masonry in the territory in which it claims jurisdiction, and
must not render allegiance or obedience, in any sense whatsoever
lo any other Masonic Power, or Supreme Council, hut must be abso-

GRAND LODGJ'.l 01:<' Cl.ALIFORNIA

lutely sovereign and supreme within its territory. As a necessary
cor:<?llary of this condition, it must recognize the exclusive jurisdict10n of all other Grand Lodges in their respective territories, and
shall not presume to project its authority or sovereignty into the
territory of any other Grand Lodge.
Thirdly, the Grand Body applying for recognition as a sovereign Grand Lodge of Ancient Craft Masonry must confine its
authority, and the exercise thereof, to the three degrees of Craft 01
Symbolic Masonry.
Fourthly, the Grand Body applying for recognition must recognize and support the Ancient Landmarks, which include, particularly, the Three Great Lights, and belief in God, and the Immortality of the Soul.

The following Grand Lodges, in addition to California, have

An application of the foregoing rules promulgated hy the
Grand Lodge of California to the Grand Orient and the Supreme
Council of France shows that no recognition can be given to these
Bodies without a change of the policy of this Grand Lodge. The
Grand Orient is regular in its origin, but its sway as a Supreme
Power is acknowledged only by the Lodges of its obedience, and in
its territory it has concurrent jurisdiction with the Grand Lodge of
France. It does not appear to be invading the jurisdiction of any
regular Grand Lodge, and does not expressly and in terms profess
a belief in God and the immortality of the soul. The Grand Lodge
of France more nearly meets these requirements than does the
Grand Orient, for, as heretofore stated, the Grand Lodge confines
its jurisdiction to the three degrees of Symbolic Masonry and it
exhibits the Three Great Lights and obligates its candidates and
opens and closes its Lodges with appeals to the Great Architect of
the Universe, and requires the "Book oi the Law" upon its altars,
but it may trace its origin to a Supreme Council having jurisdiction
over many degrees instead of to Ancient Craft Masonry.

of the Grand Lodges during this year is significant of the widespread desire for harmonious relations with France. and is indica·
tive of ultimate concord between the Grand Lodges of France and
those of the United States.

with the Grand Orient of France: Louisiana, Rhode Tsland, Iowa,

Argument.
Notwithstanding the attitude assumed at different times in the
i'il'I hy the Grand Lodge of California with respect to the recogqillun of Grand Bodies of Masonry in Latin countries, the time has
1111w arrived when there must be a new examination of the question
111111 a revision of former judgments. Our past judgments correctly
n•flccted our best thought, but now a new spirit broods over the
world and the conditions growing out of the great war compel us to
rhange some of our rules and earlier determinations. The time has
Ol'rived when our brethren demand that the reality of universal
hrotherhood be substituted for empty words, phrases and expres"ions; that we be neither confused nor misled by catch words for
which we have developed an almost superstitious reverence. Now
IM a time for our Institution to show a broad catholicity of spirit
nnd not to reject any Masonic Power which holds sway over the
nffections of men and engages the attention of the world, if that
l'ower displays the principles of brotherly love, relief and truth, and
111 working for the benefit and happiness of humanity, and bases
Itself upon the .eternal and immutable principles of Freemasonry.
Masonic scholars and jurists are divided in their opinion
r<>specting the recognition of French Masonry. The members of
11ne group contend that there can be no recognition of these Powers
lwcause: (a) they are not sovereign and supreme within their territory; (b) that the Lodges of the obedience of the Grand Lodge
of France do not trace their origin to regnlar Ancient Craft
Masonry; (c) that the Grand Orient exercises power over degrees
other than the first three degrees of Symbolic Masonry; (d) that
I he Book of Constitutions, instead of the lloly nib le, is found upon
the altars of the Lodges: (e) that a belief in God and the immortality of the soul is a landmark and is fundamental in Masonry.
This group contends that when a Mason ceases to express a belief
in Deity, he ceases to be a Mason. It also asserts that an open
Bihle is an indispensable part of the furniture of a Lodge, and that
I hese rec1uireme11ts are immovahl<' landmarks. \Ve know that until
rccently most of the Grand Lodges in English-speaking countries
were to he found espousing these principles, am! they were sup-

175

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ported by innumerable determinations, precedents, statutory enactments and utterances of the sages of the Craft.
However, there is a second group, which is constantly growing
in size and importance, which has made new evaluations and formed
new conclusions since the war has thrust this subject into prominence and caused a demand for a better and wiser solution. Your
Committee feels that it is in harmony with the thought and spirit of
this second group. The requirement that Lodges must derive me'diately or immediately from regular organizations of Ancient Craft
Masonry does not find universal adherence among Grand Bodies.
The application of the doctrine would serve to arrest the growth
and development of Masonry in many parts of the world, and
might forever destroy the possibility of universal Masonry. No
harm could be done by adopting the principle of recognizing, in
countries where no Symbolic Grand Lodge exists, the Lodges and
members of a legitimate and regular Supreme Council. If we deny
the legitimacy of Lodges originally founded under the Supreme
Council or Grand Orient system, then a large part of the territory
of the world must, perforce, remain unrecognized, and we could
have no relations with the Masons of South America, France, Italy,
Greece, Spain, Belgium and other countries, in all of which lands
are Supreme Councils recognized by the two Supreme Councils of
the United States. It seems to your Committee that a just rule to
apply to the Masonry of Latin countries would be to recognize
Lodges and Masons of any country where no Grand Lodge of Symbolic Masonry exists, provided such Lodges and members are of the
obedience of a jurisdiction recognized by the Supreme Council of
that country, and such Supreme Council is affiliated with the
Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of
Freemasonry for the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States.
With respect to the acceptance on the part of Grand Bodies in
Latin countries of the principle of concurrent jurisdiction, we do
not see why the Grand Lodge of California can not tolerate the selfdetermination of this subject by such Bodies. It is true that the
Grand Orient and Grand Lodge of France have not at all times, nor
do they now in all respects, comport themselves in accordance with
the standards which we have set for the regulation of our principles
and practices, but we have no more right to demand that they
accept the principle of exclusive territorial jurisdiction than they
have to demand that we accept the principle of concurrent Grand
Lodge jurisdiction. Our Latin brethren seem to live in fraternal
concord under the rule they have seen fit to adopt, and we are per·
suaded that the Grand Orient of France and the Grand Lodge of
France, notwithstanding their adoption of this jurisdictional peculiarity. are not weakened in their Masonic powers, and they are

doing a great Masonic work in behalf of the distressed, of the
brotherhood of man, of the welfare of humanity and of the advance
of civilization.
On the subject of the exercise of authority over degrees of
Masonry other than the first three, we merely direct your attention
to the fa<;t that the Grand Orient of France, prior to 1877, ruled
more than three degrees of Masonry, that it placed the Book of
Constitutions, instead of the Bible, upon its altars, and operated
under the same form of government as that in force at the present
time, and yet, for generations prior to that date, it enjoyed the recognition of and held fraternal relations with the mother Grand
Lodge of the world-the United Grand Lodge of England.
Religious dogmatism was not introduced into Masonry until
1760, when the Holy Bible was, on motion of Preston, made a landmark, and as dear as this alleged landmark is to the hearts of
American Masons, we can not thrust outside the pale of brotherhood good men and true who have not followed this innovation in
the body of Masonry. The form and nature of our rituals as the
same have developed through the years have· operated to fix in the
minds of English-speaking Masons the belief that Masonry is a
religious institution, and that the Bible is a necessary part of the
furniture of a Masonic Lodge, yet the ritual itself is not fundamental, and "its biblical nature is largely due to the chance that
made its chief compilers a French Huguenot and a Scotch Presbyterian. . . . This holy and apparently indispensable book is quite
unnecessary for the validity of a Lodge which is neither Christian
nor Jew." If there has been a departure from the Ancient Constitutions, we, and not our French brethren, have drawn away "from
them and asserted a dogmatic landmark.
When we arrive at the ultimate and basic cause of the estrangement of the Anglo-Saxon Masonry and the French Masonry, we
find it to consist in the religious test applied by the English-speaking Lodges and renounced by the French Lodges. The Grand
Master of Louisiana, in addressing the Grand Lodge in 1918, said:
"I submit, my brethren, that in the misconception of the position of our French brethren regarding their interpretation of
Masonic philosophy, English-speaking Masonry is clearly in the
wrong, and we, as Masons, should be ready to admit it. While
French Masonry is religiously tolerant, it is not in itself a religion
in the restrictive sense of the word. It proclaims no dogma; it
demands no profession; it respects all opinions, and in that tolerance is an exemplar of that true religion which is the basis of
Freemasonry-the brotherhood of mankind, which leads us through
love of our fellow men-a spark of His own divinity-to the love,
honor and glory of the Great Architect of the Universe."
It is held by many of our best thinkers that no man's creed or
religious observances should be made an issue in any matter indirectly connected with religion; that Freemasonry is not a religion

174

176

177

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and, therefore, a religious test should not be applied to it, and that
while it is perfectly competent for any Masonic Body to require
such confession of faith from its own members as it deems expedient, yet it should not refuse the name of brother to those who act
on truly Masonic principles, but do not demand any confession of
religious faith as a condition of membership.
It is not possible for us, as deeply attached as we are to our
rituals, forms and professions, to affirm with any surety the attitude that we would take on the subject of religion, if we were
unhappily situated in a Catholic country, in the midst of an antagonistic population and subject to the vicious and continuous attacks
of powerful ecclesiastical and illiberal influences. Our brethren in
France suffer from slanderous reports and accusations and are the
objects of hatred and persecution. They should have our sympathy
and we should strive to view with brotherly concern the measure~
they have in good faith adopted. Because references to the Deity
have been stricken from the French Constitutions and the Bible
does not lie upon French altars. your Committee has no more right
to pronounce French Masonry godless and atheistic than it has to
assert that the people of the United States arc godless and atheistic
because there is no reference to the Deity in their Constitution, or
that the schools of our country are atheistic because the Bible is
not taught therein. We are not disposed to reverence the religious
sentiments nor admire the Christian kindness of the German militarists, no matter how loudly and frequently they call upon God;
but, on the other hand, we believe in the charity and tolerance and
brotherly love and love of liberty of our valorous French brethren,
who have omitted the name but not the service of God from their
rituals and Constitutions, and who are fighting for the very essence
of Freemasonry. Nob le Frarice is in the very forefront of the great
fight for humanity and is aiding in no uncertain or impotent way
the great cause of Masonic brotherhood and the universality of
Freemasonry. We are very hopeful that our French brethren, having been brought into new and intimate relations with their American brethren, will in the near future, out of a new-born love for
us, and inspired by a fraternal desire for a closer spiritual union,
alter their Constitutions and rituals to more nearly conform to those
which bind in fraternal bonds the hearts of more than a million
American Masons.
Conclusions.
It is the belief of your Committee that the Grand Lodge of California should retain the policy it adopted in 1913, hereinbefore set
out, as the test to be applied to any Grand Lodge of an Englishspeaking country seeking our recognition, but that such test should
not hereafter be the measure applied to Grand Lodges situated in
the Latin countries of the world. That each application for recog-

nition made by a Grand Lodge or Grand Orient located overseas or
in South America should be considered by this Grand Lodge on its
merits, and that if it appears that such Grand Body exercises authority over the three degrees of Symbolic Masonry, and is recognized
as a sovereign power over its Lodges and members, and exhibits
its adherence to the principles of protherly love, relief and truth,
and is engaged in the promotion of the happiness of mankind and
the brotherhood of man, then, unless objections of a character other
than dogmatic appear, such Grand Body should be entitled to recognition. We believe that the Grand Lodge of California should labor
unceasingly in behalf of the universality of Masonry and should
strive to promote fraternal relations between all the legitimate
powers of Masonry in the world, and to this end should examine
into the regularity and Masonic character of the Grand Bodies with
which it is not now in fraternal correspondence.

Recommendations.
Your Committee respectfully recommends the adoption of the
following:
I. That the action taken by this Grand Lodge in 1869, by
which fraternal relations with the Grand Orient of France were
severed and forbidden, be, and is hereby repealed.
2. That the Grand Lodge of California is hereby declared to
be in fraternal accord and relation with the Grand Orient of France,
and that an exchange of representatives be requested of said Grand
Orient. (Not adopted-See next paragraph.)
2. That the Grand Lodge of California establish fraternal accord
and relation with the Grand Orient of France and exchange representatives therewith when assured by the Grand Orient of France that it is
not invading the jurisdiction of any regular American Grand Lodge.
(Adopted.)
3. That the Grand Lodge of California is hereby declared to
he in fraternal accord and relation with the Grand Lodge of France,
and that an exchange of representatives he requested of that Grand
Lodge.
4. That the principles enunciated by this Grand Lodge in 191.3
as tests for the recognition of other Grand Lodges, be, and the same
are applicable only to Grand Lodges of English-speaking countries.
and that as to the Grand Lodges and Grand Orients of other countries, each application be considered upon its merits with relation
to the situation of the applicant and with a view to doing full and
complete Masonic justice.
5. That the permission granted by resolution in 1917 to our
brethren to hold Masonic intercourse with the Masons in Belgium
and Italy and to visit any of their Lodges, be continued until the
further order of this Grand Lodge.

Since compiling the foregoing report, a letter has been received from the President of the Grand Orient of France in response to inquiries recently made of him, and although this latest
communication does not add to our stock of information, yet it
conveys a message that will be heartening to all of us. A translation of the letter is as follows:

The b~lief in God is not with us a mandatory obligation. For
that reason we have been charged with harboring sentiments which
are not true: for example, we have been accused of being absolutely
atheistic, which is the gravest of errors. To disprove this unwarranted accusation, we can only quote to you the second paragraph of Article First of the Constitution, which says:
"Free Masonry has for its fundamental principle mutual tolerance, the respect of others and of one's self, and the absolute
freedom of conscience."
The Grand Orient of France is neither deist, nor atheist, nor
positivist; it respects all philosophical conceptions, proclaims the
absolute freedom of conscience, but that cannot be construed as
its exclusion of a belief in God from its Lodges; on the contrary,
it leaves to each and every one the free exercise of believing in
God or not, so as to respect in the broadest possible manner the
convictions, doctrines and beliefs of everyone.
We consider that this standpoint is not contrary to the traditions of the Order.
Besides, the Grand Orient of France, whose Constitution hears
the date of 1736, has such an ancient birthright that, in our belief,
it should assure it a place within the Masonic world.
We send you herewith a booklet, "The Masonic Tenets of the
Grand Orient of France," which will explain to you who we are and
what we stand for.
We are most willing to aecept your Grand Lodges as now operating; we deem that we have no jurisdiction, nor criticism to
make concerning the inner workings of your Lodges, which is your
own and sole concern, nor the laws that have been freely accepted
by you to govern them.
We, in return, deem it a matter of logical reciprocity that the
Grand Orient of France be accepted under the same conditions,
feeling, as it does-as well as you possibly can-that it has a
legitimate claim to be solely composed of Free Masons, faithful to
the fundamental tenets of Free Masonry.
We fondly hope that the frequent visitation of American Masons to our Lodges will greatly assist in removing the existing objections, which, we are certain, rest on false premises.
We receive a great many Americans in the Grand Orient, where
a room has been set aside for the sole use of all the Rrethren
among the Allies, and we extend them the warmest welcome of
fraternal love and interest.
Do you not believe. therefore. that it would be indeed a great
pity that French and American Masons sho11ld continue to ignore
one another, at this very moment when France and America are so
closely and so intimately united in the struggle for the defense of
Right, Justice and Civilization? No! That seems to us impossible.
Since friendship of the deepest character entwines the hearts
of our two peoples, amity between brother Masons of our two countries should be closer than ever.
Awaiting the official re-establishment of relations between
our two Grand Bodies, we ask you, very dear and Most Illustrious
Brother, to accept the assurances of our best and most fraternal
sentiments.
The President of the Council of the Order.
(Signed) CORNEAU.

It is with the greatest pleasure that at its last meeting .the
Council of the Order took cognizance of your fraternal commumcation informing it that your Grand Lodge had authorize.d and permitted to the Brethren of its jurisdiction to have Masomc relat10ns
with the Masons of France, Belgium and Italy.
Ily this measure you have re-established the right of visitat\on
in our respective lodges; a right, by the way, we never ha~ demed
your Brethren of California, who have always been permitted, as
visitors, to witness the work in our lodges.
We rejoice to note this handsome Masonic and fraternal act. of
yours. We eagerly hope that it is only the prel_ude of forthcommg
relations far more close between our two Obediences (Grand Bodies); this re-establishment which we desire from the bottom of
our hearts.
We have already taken a new official contact and assum~~ exchange of amicable relations with the Grand Lodges of LoU1s1ana,
New Jersey and Iowa.
We ardently hope that such relations will soon be extended
to all the Grand Lodges of the United States.
It only remains for ~s to a?swer fully, .and with .the frankness
which pertains to Masomc relat10ns, the various questions you have
propounded to us.
In the matter of territorial jurisdiction, we beg to refer you to
paragraph one of Article 45 of our Copstitution: .
"The Grand Orient of France will not constitute any lodges
in foreign countries where there is a regularly constituted Masonic
Grand Body which is in fraternal int~rcourse w~th it.''. .
It is in the absence of such relat10ns of amity ex1stmg between
us and the Grand Lodges of the United States that a lodge was
created in New York in 1900, and another in San Francisco in
1911, otherwise these two lodges would not have had Charters
granted them.

Past Grand Master Murphey presented the report of

RESOLUTIONS
Brother Leo Bruck presented the following resolution:
Whereas, This Most Worshipful Grand Lodge has by its vote
decided that the daughter of a Mason after becoming of age, is not
entitled to admission to the Masonic Home; and
Whereas, The obligations of this fraternity should not be greater
than the obligations of a father; therefore, be it
Resolved, That Sections 163, i, j and k be repealed, and 163q be
amended by expunging all that following the words "Masonic Lodge
for assistance," and inserting in lieu thereof the following: "And the
daughter of a deceased Master Mason shall not be entitled to relief
after reaching the age of 21."

181

Whereas, These practical Lewises are many in this Grand jurisdiction, sacrificing all, arid striving to uphold the principles of Masonry
in its strength and purity; therefore,
Be It Resolved, by the Masons of California in Grand Lodge assembled, That it is the sense of this Grand Lodge that the Lewis, as an
emergency tool, be at once ins.tituted in the Grand Lodge, and the age
limit of Lewises in this Grand jurisdiction be fixed at whatever age
the United States Government fixes for enlistment into service, either
as volunteers or by selective draft system.
Resolved Further, That the privileges of the Lewis shall be granted
only to "candidates who have actually enlisted or been drafted or commissioned officers in the United States forces in the great war, and during the term of said war," and shall be extended to such candidates
regardless of whether the candidate's father be a Mason, or infirm,
and on the same terms and conditions, and with such privileges as the
Grand Lodge grants to persons of similar service in the government
who are over the age of twenty-one years.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.

Brother A. H. Alderman introduced the following resolution:
Resolved, That Section 163q of the Constitution of this Grand
Lodge be amended by adding thereto the following:
Section No. - - . That the son or daughter of a Master Mason
after having attained his or her majority as recognized by the laws of
California, and having changed his or her name in any way, is not (as
a matter. of right) entitled to relief as an orphan by the subordinate
Lodges of this jurisdiction.

of brethren assembled for the purpose of renewing their
allegiance to the government of the United States, and to
do honor to the nearly six thousand members who have
answered the call of country and taken up arms in defense
of decent democracy.

REPORTS OF BOARDS OF RELIEF
The Grand Secretary presented the reports of the
Boards of Relief, all which were referred to the Finance
Committee.
SAN FRANCISCO BOARD OF RELIEF
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

We hereby beg to present the following report for the year
beginning August 28, 1917, and ending August 26, 1918, both dates
inclusive.
Like every other social agency, our organization has been confronted,
during the year, with unusual conditions owing to the rnost trying period
in the world's history, and while the attention of the Fraternity is
focussed upon the activities incident to this unfortunate war, we are
pleased to state that our own needy ones have not been neglected. The
calling to arms of the large number of young men has made it possible
for our older men and women to get employment, some of whom
would be unable to get anything to do but for this condition, and were,
heretofore, a charge upon the Fraternity. Were it not for this elimination of cases, our expenditure for relief would have been a great
deal higher during the year on account of the increased cost of everything appertaining to food and wearing apparel, but as it was, our
disbursements were a little less.
The members of the Board at all times assisted with their hearty
co-operation, an<l to them is due the thanks of the Fraternity for their
untiring devotion to a branch of Masonic activity, whose only reward
is their own knowledge of having assisted in this noble work and to
which is attached no glory and public applause.
We were ably assisted, as heretofore, by our good Brethren of the
medical profession, and our thanks are due them for their untiring
devotion without recompense to the needy ones who called upon them.
We were ably assisted during the year by the following: Doctors H. I.
Block, J.' C. Egeberg, Aaron S. Green, Otto Freyermuth, Jacob Schwarz,
W. Wal<leyer, and A. L. W. Zillmer.
The amount shown in our report which has been expended for
relief does not, by any means, represent the whole activity of the Board.
The members of the Board at all times have been divided into
visiting committees for the sick Brother who is a stranger in our midst,
