l<J.'.l'ORT OF THE MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU OF
SAN FRANCISCO.
We hereby beg to submit our report for the year ending August
.II. 1918.
Notwithstanding the abnormal demand for labor during the past
.1·mr, our Bureau has been most active in helping the employer to adjust
his husiness in accordance with the demands of the times. The large
1111mber of young men who have been called to serve their country have
l1·ft a vacancy which employers have found hard to fill.
A great many women have been able to secure positions which
paid them sufficiently to live comfortably without assistance, who have,
la·rctofore, been aided by the Board of Relief.
A great many of our older men who were hard to place before,
arc now doing their share. It is heartily gratifying to note that men
of seventy or thereabouts are doing their bit to help win this war and
have come into their own.
It was not an easy matter to convince employers at first that old
men could be of use to them, but they have taken the place of office
hoys and errand boys so successfully that we are convinced they will
he retained in such positions.
It is a novel sight to see an e.rrand boy of seventy five, or thereabouts, and brings strongly to mind the fact that we are passing through
unusual times.
The Fraternity at large deserves our thanks for the valuable aid
rcnderea by them at all times and it is a pleasure to be able to serve
where service is so much appreciated.
Fraternally submitted,
THOMAS IRWIN, Secretary.
CHARLES H. S. PRATT, President.

The Masonic Board of Relief of the City of Los Angeles, herewith presents the following report of its labors from September 1,
(1>17, to August 31, 1918.
The Masonic Board of Relief is composed of the Masters (exofficio) of the 28 Blue Lodges of this City and two members appointed by him, together with the· Past Grand Masters residing
within the City of Los Angeles, the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts of Los Angeles City, one representative from each of

CEMETERH'.S

The Masonic Fraternity of Los Angeles has had no satisfactory
place for the burial of its dead until this year, when arrangements
were made with the Forest Lawn Memorial Park, to set aside a
beautiful tract of land within its boundaries, which will receive perpetual care and be forever kept g:een. This tract of land is known
as the "Masonic Plot," and in which only Masons or members of
their families will be interred. The cost of these interments is considerably lower than can be obtained for a like situation in other
cemeteries.

INVALIDS COMING

We are proud of the fact that the steadily increasing success
11f the Bureau demonstrates that on longer acquaintance with the
11hjccts and aims of the Bureau employers and employees share
alike and better results are obtained, but space forbids showing in
dl'tail the great amount of good accomplished.

Invalids coming to California, particularly consumptives,
quote from the statement of Dr. John W. Trask, Assistant Surgeon
General, United States Public Health, who says: "No locality has
a climate that is favorable for all the year. In one's quest for
favorable climate you must not forfeit suitable food, rest and peace
of mind. The consumptive can usually obtain the most favorable
conditions for recovery, including outdoor life, suitable food, rest,
medical attention and nursing, at or near his home. Leaving home,
except to a sanitarium, is fraught with much danger, unless one is
financially able to meet all possible demands. It should be most.
carefully considered, even then." In the foregoing, I most certainly
concur.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS

Brother J. F. \Vest, Chairman of the Committee on
By-Laws, presented the following report:

Brother Frank Tade, Chairman of the Committee on
( 'harters, presented the following report:

To the J1ost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

To the Jfost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on By-Laws has received, carefully considered and found that the following applications for changes in bylaws conform to the Uniform Code of this Grand jurisdiction, and
it recommends that the same be approved as follows:

Your Committee on Charters, to whom were referred the petitions for charters of the several Lodges to whom dispensations
have been issued during the past Masonic Year, to-wit: Lincoln
Lodge, at San Francisco; Delta Lodge, at Stockton, and Yorba
Linda Lodge at Yorba Linda, now reports:

1. Twelve petitions increasing dues: 1 from $6.00 to $7.50 per
annum; 8 from $6.00 to $9.00 per annum; 1 f'rom $6.00 to $12.00 per
annum; 1 from $7.50 to $12.00 per annum; 1 from $6.00 payable
semi-annually, to $6.00, payable quarterly in advance; 1 reducing
dues from $18.00 to $12.00 per annum.
2. Four applications reducing initiation fees: 2 from $75.00
to $50.00; 2 from $100.00 to $50.00.
3. Four applications increasing initiation fees: 1 from $30.00
to $40.00; 2 from $30.00 to $50.00; 1 from $50.00 to $75.00.
4. Four affecting affiliation fees: 1 providing for an affiliation fee of $15.00; 3 abolishing affiliation fees.
5. Seventeen petitions changing date and time of stated meeting.
6. Three sets of By-Laws of Lodges under dispensation.
7. Your Committee also considered one application to reduce
dues from 75 cents per month to 50 cents per month, but as no
substantial reason was given for the change, your Committee recommends that same be denied. (This refers to Plumas No. 60,
denied approval by the Grand Master.)
8. Your Committee carefully considered standing resolutions
of four Lodges providing for an increase in fee for life membership.
All of these conform to the provisions of Section 129 of the Constitution.
Your Committee recommends that all four b~ approved.

J. F. W:i;:sT,
E.W. Fox,
CHAS. F. FURY,

H. M. WALLENSTEIN.

Adopted as presented.

Your committee followed with precision the examination of the
records of said Lodges prescribed by sections 74 and 75 of the
Constitution. We examined the records, including the reports of
said Lodges to the Grand Lodge, their dispensations and by-laws
and books ·of records of meetings; also their certificates as to proficiency of their respective Masters and Wardens.
We find first, that the said records of Lincoln Lodge and of
Delta Lodge were in proper form and kept in an orderly and commendable manner. Further, that said Lodges were clear of all
debts. We, therefore, recommend, as to Lincoln Lodge, at San
Francisco, to be numbered 470. and Delta Lodge, at Stockton, to be
numbered 471, that charters be granted.
As fj~l'Yorba Linda Lodge, at Yorha Linda, Orange County,
we found that the minutes of their meetings exhibited certain omissions of necessary actions with respect to tl\e issuance of a dispensation and the spreading thereof upon the minutes, and also the
adoption of their by-laws and the spreading of said by-laws in
full upon the minutes of the meeting after they were adopted.
Certain other rectifications of the minutes we deem desirable, in
order that the records may fully and accurately exhibit the necessary actions of the Lodge in the essential preliminary matters required by Masonic Law. \Ve, therefore, recommend in the case of
Yorba Linda Lodge that the minutes be amended in the respects
wherein they are deficient, and that upon certification by the Inspector of the 62d District, in which said Lodge is located, to the
effect that the minutes have been properly amended and the submission of said certificate to the Grand Secretary for his approval,
a charter be issued to Yorba Linda Lodge, to be numbered 469.
Your Committee further reports a recommendation to the effect
that the request of Germania Lodge No. 438 of Los Angeles, for

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRANL> LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

perm1ss10n to change its name to Acacia Lodge No. 438 a.nd to
render the ritual in the English language hereafter, be granted, and
that said Lodge be commended for its patriotic action.

Special Building Fund

Your Committee on Finance has also considered the claim of
Arroyo Lodge No. 274, of Arroyo Grande, for reimbursement for
overpaid Grand Lodge dues. It appears that in February 1917
,\rroyo Lodge received an application for affiliation, accom~anied
hy a certificate of standing from King David's Lodge No. 209 of
lhis jurisdiction, and that the affiliate was duly elected and his
11ame entered upon the books of Arroyo Lodge, but the Secretary
of Arroyo Lodge neglected to notify the Secretary of King David's
I .odge of such election, and did not procure the demit from King
David's Lodge. The error was not discovered until after King
David's Lodge had made its annual report and paid dues to the
(;rand Lodge on the brother in question. Hence it is clearly evident that dues were paid to the Grand Lodge in the amount of $2.40
for the year 1917 on the name of Brother James Eugene Wilson by
both Arroyo Lodge and King David's Lodge.

Adopted.
Your Committee has had under consideration the claim of El
Centro Lodge No. 384, of El Centro, for reimbursement for expenses
amounting to $252.20 incurred for the relief of Brother Isaac Harry
Todd, a member of Gothic Lodge Xo. 852, of East St. Louis, State
of Illinois.
It appears from the correspondence that Brother Todd was
brought to the hospital in El Centro with a serious case o.f dropsy.
that the officers of El Centro Lodge wired Gothic Lodge of the
serious condition of the Brother, and received an answer to give
Brother Todd whatever assistance they deemed necessary and
draw a draft on Gothic Lodge for the amount. El Centro Lodge
followed instructions to the letter, but when the draft was drawn
for the balance due for $252.20, payment was refused, and El Centro
Lodge has ever since been trying to secure the refund of the above
amount.
Our Grand Secretary has written the Grand Secretary of Illinois
in regard to this matter, but so far no reply has been received.
The date of the Grand Secretary's letter being September 20th,

This report contains recommendations that this Grand body reimburse its constituent Lodges and Boards of Relief in the sum of
$8,966.47, expended by them for the relief of Masons and the families
of Masons of other jurisdictions. It is not only right, but it is n
privilege to take care of these needy when within our doors. If the
Masons of this jurisdiction did less, they would not be living up to the
obligations of the fraternity. But your committee is strongly of the
opinion that some other jurisdictions are not doing their full duty when
they permit the expenditure by this jurisdiction of such sums for the
relief of their needy without reimbursement.
We are informed by the Boards of Relief that the matter of reimbursement is always taken up with the responsible Lodges and often
with the Grand bodies, and much of the money expended is returned,
but the recurring reports of this Grand Lodge show that there is a
large sum each year which is never returned.
This committee is strongly of the opinion that if the matter of
reimbursement was promptly and energetically taken up to the last
resort, it would result in the recovery of more of the sums expended.
Your committee therefore recommends that Lodges and the
Boards \if Relief be required to render quarterly, to the Grand Secretary, and before they shall be enabled to come before this committee
for reimbursement, a complete report of each case where relief has
been extended for the benefit of outside jurisdictions, and where such'
expenditure has not been repaid, together with copies of all correspondence had in connection therewith; provided, however, that each Lodge
and Board of Relief shall be required to exhaust all reasonable means
for the collection of all items before including the same in such report,
and that the Grand Secretary then take up with the Grand bodies of all
sueh jurisdictions the matter of reimbursement.

Referring to Decisions 2, 3 and 4 of the Grand Master :
As we understand Decision 2, the ruling of the Grand Master was
to the effect that it is not an appropriate function of the Grand Lodge to
conduct dedication ceremonies of a room occupied by a Lodge for its
meet~ngs, where such room is not owned or controlled by the Lodge,
~nd is not ~rimarily and principally devoted to Masonic purposes, but
is one used m common for meeting purposes by the Lodge and several
non-Masonic fraternal societies, all of whom hire the same from one
who is conducting and controlling it as a purely commercial enterprise.
We do not understand it to apply to halls owned by Masonic Hall Associations, conducted primarily for the purposes of the Craft.
\Ve think the correctness of this decision is manifest and recommend that it be approved.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

The Grand Master rendered a decision to the effect that the
<'xception in favor of persons in the army or navy of the United States
contained in section 96 of our Constitution does not apply to officers
and men of the army or navy who entered the same purely for the purposes of the present war from the National Guard, or as volunteers or
hy way of the selective draft. That section provides that the application of one "belonging to the army or navy of the United States" may
he received by a Lodge, though he has not the qualification of residence
ordinarily prescribed, by dispensation from the Grand Master.
Sub. 5 of section 43 authorizes the Grand Master to grant a dispensation in such a case, while section 107 provides that no such dispensation shall be issued in such a case unless application therefor be
made by the Lodge by unanimous vote, by ballot, and requires the
usual reference and ballot after issuance of dispensation. The language in all of these provisions is a person "belonging to the army or
navy of the United States," and, of course, is applicable to anyone who
comes within the description at the time of his application. We do not
feel authorized in reading into this plain and unambiguous provision
any limitation based on the manner in which the applicant became a
member of the army or navy of the United States, or on the term for
which he enlisted or was commissioned, whether for a term of years,
or for the duration of the war, of for an indefinite time. Nor do we
think it can be disputed that one who has entered such service of the
United States by volunteering for the period of the war, or under the
selective draft, or from. the National Guard, is a person "belonging to
the army or n,avy of the United States." In our judgment, there is no
room left for construction, in view of the language in fact used. The
exception includes all persons in fact belonging to the army or navy
of the United:iStates.
The decision of Grand Master Keesling in 1917, which was
approved by this committee and by the Grand Lodge, was with reference to a member of the National Guard who had )tot been mustered
into the service of the United States. We held that prior to being so
mustered in he did not belong to the army or navy of the United
States, but we further said that as our Constitutional provision now
reads, the exception does include all persons belonging to the army or
navy of the United States. This question therefore has already been
decided in accord with our views by this Grand Lodge.
Of course, all this means simply that the Grand Master has the
power to grant such a dispensation. Whether he shall do so in any
particular case is a matter for him to decide in the exercise of a wise
discretion in view of the circumstances of that case. Jt is to he pre-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

238

239

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

sum.ed that he will discharge that duty with a view to the proper protect10n of the Craft against the admission of unworthy candidates and
that if in any case he concludes that the applicant should be req~ired
to ap~ly to the Lodge of the locality in which he has a legal residence,
he will deny the dispensations. The members of this committee all
believe that, as a matter of policy, application for such dispensation
should be scrutinized with extreme care, and should not be granted in
any case in the absence of exceptional circumstances. Whenever reasonably practicable, the applicant should be required to apply to the
Lodge of the locality from which he has a legal residence, or obtain a
waiver of jurisdiction therefrom. If it be desired to limit the power
of the Grand Master in this regard, we deem an amendment to our
Constitution essential.
We recommend that the decision be not approved.

The Grand Master recommends that section 100 of the Constitution relative to reports of investigating committees be amended, so as
to require such reports to set forth in detail the facts respecting the
applicant, as well as the conclusion of the committee, and the reading
in the Lodge of the full report except the names of the committee. As
the law now stands, there is no requirement as to the furnishing in
the report of anything but the conclusion of the committee, and nothing is read but the conclusion. The question presented is one of policy.
We see no objection to the proposed amendment if it is desired
to adopt the method recommended, and we believe that the proposed
change is a desirable one.
We
adopted.

therefore recommend

that

the proposed amendment

be

Adopted, and section 100 amended by unanimous
vote.
The Grand Master recommends that sections 149 and 150 of the
Constitution be amended so as to require the giving of bonds by the
Treasurers and Secretaries of subordinate Lodges.
We see no objection to either proposed amendment, except that
we deem the proposed proviso in regard to the Treasurer undesirable.
Under the provisions of our Constitution, the Secretary is required to
pay over moneys col!ected to the Treasurer. We are in accord with
the views expressed by the Grand Master as to the desirability of
bonds as to these officers, and
We recommend the adoption of the proposed amendments, eliminating, however, the proposed proviso in sub. 6 of section 149.

The Grand Master has recommended that the privilege extended
by resolution at our last Communication to our brethren serving or
visiting in France, Italy and Belgium to hold fraternal intercourse with
the Masons of those countries and to visit in their Lodges, be extended
to cover the countries of Holland and Switzerland.

The Grand Master recommends an amendment of section 128 by
raising the minimum Lodge dues from $6 to $9 per annum.

If such a privilege is to be given at all, we know of no logical
rvason why it should not cover the two last-named countries.

The proposed amendment is in proper form and there is no legal
objection to the same, but as it presents purely a question of policy on
which we do not feel qualified to express an opinion, we report the
same without recommendation.

We therefore recommend that the Grand Master's recommendation be adopted.

We are in accord with the recommendation of the Grand Master
that our law be so amended as to permit an applicant elected to
receive the degrees who has entered the military or naval service of the
United States or its allies prior to or within three months after his
election, to come forward for initiation at any time within three
months after his discharge from such service. As the law now stands,
the applicant who does not come forward to he initiated within three
months after his election forfeits certain rights.
,We recommend that section 2 of Article IV of the Uniform Code
of By-Laws be amended by the addition of the following proviso, towit:
"Provided, however, that this section shall have no application in
the case of an applicant who entered the military or vaval service of
the United States or any of its allies, prior to or within three months
after his election to receive the degrees, who comes forward for
initiation within three months after his discharge from such military
or naval service."
We deem any further amendment in this regard unnecessary and
inadvisable at this time.

Adopted, and section 2 of Article IV of the Uniform
Code of By-Laws unanimously amended as recommended.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
Brother Irving J. Mitchell, Chairman of the Committee
on Masonic Education, reported as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Masonic Education report as follows:
We are confident that the hour has arrived when the craft in
this jurisdiction are willing and anxious to give a larger measure of
time, attention and effort to the understanding of the vital teachings,
purposes and needs of Freemasonry.
There permeates our Institution a longing for a fuller conception
of its duties and its possibilities along the broader lines of human
activities.
It is recognized as never before, that to achieve results which
are really worth while, we must give more freely of our time to the
understanding of the spirit of our fraternity and less time to the
letter of its work.
We recommend to your especial consideration that part of the
Most Worshipful Grand Master's Address under the caption, "Conditions of the Craft," which refers to the need for greater educational
endeavor. He has truly said, "The Lodges throughout the jurisdiction
are devoting an immense amount of time to the work of initiating,
passing and raising Masons, but find little time to instruct or help, or
minister to their members."
This very condition has proved an unsurmountable barrier to
effective work on the part of this Committee. Again and again we have
been told that as the Lodge's time was so completely absorbed by the
pressure of degree work, no time could possibly be given to addresses
which might illuminate, direct, and inspire both candidates and
members.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

245

Keen regret has been expressed by many of our Lodge officers
and members that such are the unfortunate circumstances.
Heretofore this Committee has . voiced the imperative need of
!.ringing to the c~aft a broader vision of the purposes of our fraternity.
We have emphasized the need of understanding the basic principles
for which we stand and the practical application thereof.
We have tried to impress the idea that in our Masonic work we
should depend less on formalism and more on enlightenment. If we
may correctly judge from the sentiments expressed in this Grand
Lodge; if we mistake not the spirit which broods over this Communication, it is no longer necessary to reiterate these statements. ·There
is no question but that the craft longs for the inspiration which shall
he found through the application of Masonic truths to our civic activities. There is a strong desire to drop generalities and to consider the
specific and the concrete.
Many now feel that Masonry should inspire men to render a
larger public service.
We heartily agree with the Most Worshipful Grand Master that
"Little interest is taken in the reading of lectures or themes, no
matter how excellent the subject ·matter or how attractive the method
of its presentation. To be of value there must be a personal touch
;ind many will throng to hear a speaker or teacher who is a master
of his subject and imbued with the Masonic spirit."
We are of the opinion, that, in these larger days, men are not so
much interested in the musty things of the past, as they are in the
vital issues of the present. For this reason we believe that to attract
and hold interest, Masonic addresses should measure up to the demands
of the new era we have just entered, with its complex problems of
human relationship.
The walls of every Masonic Lodgeroom should echo and rel'Cho with the great questions which deal with the welfare and progress of humanity.
If some plan can be arrived at hy this Grand Lodge whereby
there will he a reasonable opportunity for time to carry on the work
11f Masonic Education through addresses, we would suggest the following plan :
First: That Lodges throughout this jurisdiction co-operate with
the United States Government by inviting at frequent intervals, members of the fraternity who are enrolled as "Fonr Minute Men" to
;iddress them. Application can readily he macle in most practical
fashion of the duties we owe as Masons and citizens. We can thus
perform a patriotic duty and give to our gatherings an added interest.
Second: That Lodges throughout this jurisdiction organize a
corps of Masonic speakers. following the same system as that cm-

246

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ployed by the Four Minute Men's organization, but devoted to the
discussion of purely Masonic subjects.
Third: That Lodges throughout this jurisdictfon hold meetings
now and then to be known as a "Masonic Forum," where an address
will be given, followed by a general discussion.
Fourth: That joint meetings be held by several Lodges in a
community, to be addressed by some well informed Mason. \Ve
believe that the influence of such meetings will result in immeasurable
good.
Fifth : That the Committee on Masonic Education exercise a
helpful influence toward all Lodges who desire tlieir counsel and
co-operation. That this Committee shall foster and encourage throughout this jurisdiction, the study and research of Masonic history, law,
philosophy and especially the dominant fnwposes of this Institution.
Respectfully submitted,
IRVING J. MITCHELL,
JESSE \VHJTED,
HARVEY D. LOVELAND,

Committee.

The report was adopted.

Referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which
· Committee through Chairman Angellotti subsequently reported thereon as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is really a proposition to amend two decisions of this Grand
Lodge by substituting the word "shall" for "should" in two places.
Regardless of any question of the propriety of amending a decision,
we consider the proposed change entirely unnecessary. The decisions
mean exactly what the maker of the proposed amendment would have
them express in different words. When the Grand Lodge decl~res
that under our law a certain practice "should not" be followed, it
necessarily means that such practice "shall not" be followed. .
We recommend that the proposed change be not made.

The recommendation was adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was referred that portion of the
:1<ldress of Past Grand Master Keesling at the last Communication
relating to the so-called "group plan" of initiation, have considered
the same and beg leave to report as follows:
The Grand Master says:
"The fact that Lodges doing a great deal of work are compelled
particularly to initiate and pass several candidates in an evening, and
that under Constitutional requirement this must be severally done, has

251

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

no <loubt influenced attendance adversely. The required repct1t10n
consumes so much time that before conclusion many brethren depart
owing to the lateness of the hour. I am satisfied that repetition also.
influences brethren to remain away. Fully appreciating the evident
purpose of severally initiating, passing and raising of candidates, I am
of the opinion that modification permitting of exemplification of portions of the ceremonial on groups would not in the least detract from
effectiveness and, by lessening the time and avoiding repetition, conduce
to an increased attendance by reason of the fact, and, permitting of the
employment of a portion of the time for educational purposes and social
intercourse, would thereby materially increase efficiency. I therefqre
recommend that consideration of the subject matter be referred to such

for report and recommendation at the next stated communication of

lu• the product of a degree factory. Quantity and quality relatively
rii11si<lcrcd, we adhere to our preference for the result of individual
dfmt.

250

Obviously the Grand Master coul<l not state in his address what
portions of the ceremonies might be performed in groups, and for the
same reasons this Committee is unable to incorporate in this report
some of its findings, which must be left for oral presentation at its
hearing.
For precedent we have made inquiry in regard to the practice in
other jurisdictions, and learn that several have a plan similar to the
one recommended. We are not informed, however, that in their Lodges
any more time is devoted to educational purpos~s and social intercourse
than in some of the Lodges in California. On the other hand, we do
know that many Lodges in California which are enjoying a period
of prosperous popularity, have ample opportunity to indulge in. fraternal intercourse and are continually absorbing the truths of Freemasonry through intimate association with the ritual, which expounds
our lessons in terse and beautiful language, well calculated to impress
the novitiate and the adept as well.
It is admitted that there are cogent reasons why the initiate
should receive the individual instruction, and they are so apparent as
to need no exposition here.. Here follows the inquiry if the gain
in time and opportunity for other purposes is sufficient to balance the
loss to the novitiate of the impressiveness of the work caused by
divided attention. After a careful snrvey of the ceremonies of initiating, passing, and raising, we are unable to fin<! that any other
portions than those now so conferred, can be as effectively done on
groups as on indivi<luals, and the time saved in any event is negligible.
First impressions are often the most lasting, and a proper dignified initiation is more apt to produce a Mason inspired with a veneration for the Institution and its forms and ceremonies than would

W c believe that poor attendance and lack of interest are not at1rili11table in any manner to the length of time consumed in conferring

t !1t· degrees, but rather to the absence of the effort or ability to make
t !1<·111 <luly impressive. The officer with the necessary degree of dignity
:ind efficiency should find no difficulty in making the ritual attractive
111 all members who are equipped with the essential qualities of under•,t a1uling and appreciation. If the ritual properly rendered does not at1rat'l members to the Lodge, no other form of proper social intercourse
11r c<lucational facilities will draw them away from their homes or
places of amusement.
If it is deemed advisable to- shorten the ritual, it can be done by
, 1111itting certain parts which are now ~onferred on groups without harmf11l results, and these portions communicated as is now done in other
parts by reference to the Monitor. We have not undertaken this task,
:1s we consider it to be within the province of the Committee on Ritual.
We also believe that much time might be saved to the Lodges for
the purposes mentioned were it not for the apparent desire of some
of the officers to extend the princip~e of the universality of Masonry
t" the entire community in which they reside, regardless of the fitness
of the candidates to appreciate or be benefited by the lessons which we
attempt to inculcate. To obviate this, and to limit this misdirected amliition, we would recommend an amendment to the Constitution to the
<"ffect that not more than three degrees be conferred at one meeting, and
that at least one calendar month must elapse between the degrees confcrred on any candidate.

FORM FOR INSTITUTING LODGES UNDER
DISPENSATION
The Grand Lecturer presented a form for instituting
Lodges under dispensation as follows:
The dispensation for the formation of a new Lodge is issued by
order of the Grand Master, and is sent to the Inspector of the Masonic
J)istrict in which the Lodge is situated, who should acknowledge receipt
thereof to the Grand Secretary. The Inspector should arrange with
the Master regarding elate of institution, and the members named in the
Dispensation notified by the Master to assemble in their Lodge room at
the time determined upon.
If the Inspector cannot attend, he may deputize some competent
Past Master to institute the new lodge.

After the brethren are assembled, the instituting officer will assume
the East. He then causes the Dispensation to be read, after which the
names of the officers appointed by the Master of the new Lodge will be
announced, together with the names of the Treasurer and Secretary
srlectecl by the brethren. As these names arc called, the officers will
form in line west of the altar and facing the East, the Master at the
right of the line, and the instituting officer will then descend from his
station and invest each officer with his jewel. The Master named in the
Dispensation will then be seated in the East, on the right of the in·

258

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

stituting officer. The other officers will take their respective stations
and places. If convenient, music should accompany these movements.
The instituting officer will then open in the third degree.
The instituting officer tben addresses the Master (who should
rise) as follows:
CHARGE To THE MASTER. The Grand Lodge havinz committed to
your care the superintendence and government of the brethren who are
to compose this new lodge, you cannot be insensible of the obligations
which devolve on you as their head, nor of your responsibility for the
faithful discharge of the important duties pertaining to your appointment.
The honor, reputation and usefulness of this Lodge will materially
depend upon your skill and assiduity; while the happiness of the members will be generally promoted in proportion to the zeal and ability
with which you propagate the genuine principles of Freemasonry. For
a pattern, consider the great luminary of Nature, which, rising in the
east, regularly diffuses light and lustre to all within its circle. In
like manner it is your duty to spread light and instruction to the
brethren of this lodge. Forcibly impress upon them the dignity and
high importance of Masonry, and seriously admonish them never to disgrace it. Charge them to practice out of the lodge those· duties which
they have been taught in it, and, by amiable, discreet, and virtuous conduct, to convince mankind of the goodness of the institution, so that,
when a person is said to be a member of it, the world may know that. he
is one to whom the burdened heart may pour out its sorrow; to whom
distress may prefer its suit; whose hand is guided by justice, and whose
heart is expanded by benevolence. In short, by a diligent observance
of the laws of our Grand Lodge, ancient landmarks, and regulations of
Masonry, and above all, the Holy Scriptures, which are given as a
rule and a guide to your faith, you will be ,enabled to merit the contidence reposed in you.
CHARGE To THE WARDENS. Brothers Senior and Jm_1ior Wardens
(who are called up by two knocks): You should be examples of good
order and regularity, for it is only by a due regard to the laws, in your
own conduct, that you can expect obedience to them from others. You
are as~duously to as~ist the Master, in diffusing light and imparting
know'.edge to all whom he shall place under your care. In the absence
of the Master you will succeed to higher· duties; your acquirements
must therefore be such that the Cr:::ft may never suffer for want of
proper instruction. From the spirit which you have hitherto evinced, I
entertain no doubt that your future conduct will be such· as to merit
the approval of your brethren and the testimony of a good conscience.

Resolved, That there be levied upon the subordinate Lodges of the
State of California for the current fiscal year, in addition to the clues
prescribed by the Constitution, the sum of 15 cents for each member
borne upon the respective rolls at the date of the annual reports. Said
levy shall be for the payment of Representatives, Grand Officers, Past
Grand Masters, and Inspectors, and shall be paid at the same time and
in the manner prescribed for th~ payment of the annual dues.

JEWELS AND FLORAL PIECES
Past Grand Master Murphey, from the Committee on
Jurisprudence, reported concerning the proposed amendment
to section 88 as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

This proposed amendment to the Constitution will, if adopted,
abrogate the expressed will of the Grand Lodge on the matters
embraced therein. The Grand Lodge has expressly inhibited the
purchase. with Lodge funds, of either floral pieces for deceased
brothers or jewels or other mementoes to be presented to distinguished brethren. The subject matter of the amendment is purely
one of policy, and your Committee is disposed to submit it to the
consideration of the Grand Lodge without recommendation. Should
the Grand Lodge favor this legislation your Committee would suggest the following as a substitute for the amendment proposed by
Past Master Smith:

The. R.". W.". Charles Albert Adams, of Excelsior

REPORT

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
OCTOBER, 1918

BY JOHN DOUGLASS MURPHY, P. G. M.
Introduction
The matter contained in this report is in the nature of an innovation from the beaten path of the "Correspondence Round Table."
lt is very much an assemblage of matters relating to the war and
war activities; and I do this without apology, as at this critical time
in the world's history there is nothing really worth thinking about,
talking about, living for or dying for, except such matters as in some
way are in$~rumental in helping directly or indirectly to win this
war.

'

In my judgment the report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence is matter for home consumption. Nearly 95 per cent
of those who read the report of this Committee on Correspondence
are members pf California lodges, and it is needless to say they are
not vitally interested in the small details that go to make up a very
large prop,o;tion of the reports of the several States.
What do Californians care that in Illinois the Grand Lodge
opened in ample form; that practically all the Lodges were represented; that forty of the representatives of other jurisdictions were
present; that a cordial welcome was extended to a distinguished
brethren; that certain distinguished members were present that
were introduced, and appreciated responses were made; that the
printed proceeding is a volume of excellent taste; that the Grand
Master, judging from his picture, is a fine-looking fellow, etc.?
These matters constitute a third of the space of the report of each
of the Grand Jurisdictions.

\,

2

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

In this report I have endeavored to assemble information that
will int~est and inform such brethren as feel disposed to read it,
and I trust that my efforts in this respect may not be wholly in vain.
In 1914, at my suggestion, this Grand Lodge adopted legislation
liberalizing the physical qualification requirements. Since that time
many jurisdictions, as will be observed from this report, have broken
away from the cast-iron rule of "literal conformity." Some, however, fearing an encroachment on ancient landmarks, still adhere to
the old rule. My own judgment is that this liberal legislation is in
strict conformity with ·the best and oldest admonitions we have
received as Masons. It will immediately recur to any brother that
very early in his progress in Masonic work, he was informed that it
is the internal and not the external qualifications that recommend a
man to be made a Mason.
This question is of vital import at this time. Are we who stay
at home and enjoy the fruition of the loyalty and heroism and sacrifices of our sons at the front, to deny to them the benefits and
privileges of our order when they return to us full of mental vigor
and industrial usefulness, but unfortunately suffering from some
physical defect as a consequence of valorous conduct? Let the
Masons of the world answer this question.
I have given in these pages sufficient data on the question of
recognition and fraternal intercourse with the brethren of our allies
to present the question in all its aspects. I feel that the least that
should be done is to permit full fraternal intercourse with the
Masons of our allies during the period of the war, and trust to a
satisfactory adjustment of any differences when 11111tters of less
vital import are demanding our attention.

RELATIONS WITH FOREIGN JURISDICTIONS
ALLIED WITH THE UNITED STATES
IN THIS GREAT WAR.

Following the lead of the Grand Lodge of California in the year

1917, there is a strong and growing disposition on the part of

Masonic Grand Jurisdictions on this continent, as well as the Austndian Grand ] urisdictions, to clear the way, as far as possible, for
f'n·t• Masonic intercourse among Masons who are fighting shoulder
lo shoulder in this terrific world contest.
the following pages I give all the information on the subject
that I have been able to assemble. To procure which, communica1ions have been sent to all of the Grand ] urisdictions on this conti111•nt. Many of these communications have not as yet elicited a
reply, occasioned, no doubt, by the fact that no action has been
taken in the respective Grand Lodges.
I may add that most of the Lodges in the United States working in the German language have displayed a commendable and
1•atriotic spirit, becoming to all Masons in this country, by renouncing the German language and conducting their ritualistic work in
English.

A haze of conflicting records, discrepancies in dates and disagreements between historians and writers cloud authentic details
in regard to the establishment of French Masonry and much of its
subse9uent develol-!me_nts. So~e writers hold t.hat a Lodge was
orgamz;d a! Dunkirk m the ear!1est part of the eighteenth century.
Most historians agree that the first authentically known Lodge was

founded in Paris in 1732 by Lord Derwentwater.
Organized
Masonry in France apparently dates from 1735, when Lodges at
Paris petitioned the Grand Lodge of England for a Provincial Grand
Lodge, which had been refused on account of political reasons. In·
1743 authorization was granted to the petitioning Lodges by the
Grand Lodge of England for the organization of a Provincial Grand
Lodge under the name of the Grand Loge Anglaise de France. Its.
constitution is said to have been a model of that of Anderson which·
was framed in 1723.
EARLY FACTIONALISM R(SillT(D.-Almost co-incidental witli. the 1.•
granting of the warrant and the constitution of the French Grand'•\
Lodge, factionalism sprang up between the Parisian and Provincial,,
Lodges and anarchy resulted. The Provincial Grand Lodge declared ,
its independence of the Grand Lodge of England in 1755 and assumed
the name of the Grande Loge de France. It is said to have recog- ··.
nized only the first three degrees and was composed of Grand ·Officers
to be elected out of the body of the Fraternity and of the Masteraf
for life of the Parisian Lodges. It formally excluded provincial Lodges
from participation. Such a period of dissensions followed that meetings
for a time were forbidden by the civil authorities.
In 1771 the factions were united. In the meantime, hodies conferring higher degrees had been organized. Recognition was der
mantled and finally granted by the Grand Lodge of France.
Shortly afterward apparent peace was broken by members of 'the.,.
provincial faction, who had been expelled but afterward reinstated."
This faction succeeded in having a new constitution adopted and
December 24, 1771, the Grand Lodge of France was declared extinct
and another substituted with the new name of the Grand Orient. The
Grand Lodge of France, however, continued its existence and the
conflict was waged until the French Revolution terminated the struggle. With the restoration of civil order, both bodies resumed their
contentions until June 28, 1779, when the Grand Lodge of France
was united with the Grand Orient under the name of the latter organization. The Grande Loge Generae Ecossais de France was organized
in 1804, but union was shortly afterward effected by treaty.
THI( GRAND ORJl(NT OJI FRANC(.-From the time that the Grand Orient
became the ruling organization its history was ma~ked by what appears
to have been continued conflicts and violation of landmarks and constitution, which finally resulted in recognition being withdrawn by practically all English-speaking Grand Lodges. The Grand Orient was first
engaged in dissension over the control of the degrees higher than the
first three. The organization afterward abolished the office of Grand
Master in 1871. Recognition was granted to a spurious Louisiana
Scottish Rite Body which invaded the jurisdiction of the regular Louisiana Grand Lodge. The name of Diety was expunged from the Constitution and the ritual and it was stated that the Holy Bible was
removed from the Altars. it was also the contention of a prominent American Masonic writ< r that the Grand Orient extended recognition to bodies admitting r. ~groes.

THE GRAND LODGE OF FRANCE.-The Grand Lodge of France claim.s
to have been organized in 1804, and cons~ituted by t~e. Supreme Council

The Grand Body claims 136 Lodges under its jurisdiction, among

almost exclusively British and American. Its membership m its
Grand Jurisdiction is estimated at 8,000.
The Grand Lodge of France requires its subordinate Lodges to
open and close with an appeal to the Grand Architect of the 1:.Jniversc ..
Candidates are obligated with the same appeal. It has ilpon its altar:;

THE NEW GRAND LODGE.-The Independent and Regular National
Grand Lodge of France and the French colonies was .founded ~n
December 1913. It claims ·to be the only regular Masomc power 111
France ac'cording to Anglo-Saxon Masonic principles. It is said that
its constitution was favorably influenced by the Grand Lodge of England which has extended recognition and exchanged representatives.
It i~ also recognized by the Grand Lodges of Scotland and Missouri.
It consists of three, probably four, Symbolic Lodges with an estimated
membership of 150.
The Lodges constituting the Grand Body withdrew from the Grarid
Orient and its Grand Master is a Prof. E. de Ribacourt, who was formerly a member of the Grand ·Orient of France.
The new Grand Lodge has practically the same constitutional requirements as the Grand · Lodge of France, viz. : The appeal to the
Grand Architect of the Universe, "the sacred writings on the Master's
desk," the ban on political and religious discussion and jurisdiction
over only the first three degrees.
Discussing the recognition of this Grand Body by the Grand Lodge

Lodge, but rather as a sort of colonization on French soil of some
new Lodges under English patronage or autonomy with French sovereignty, agreeing to comply with English regulations, but with no
inspector or censor on the spot to •ee that they do as they agree.

THE GRAND ORJl1NT 01' Bl1LGJUM.-The first Lodge said to have
existed in Belgium was established in 1770 at Mons, under the name
of "Perfect Union." lt is said to have held a warrant from the Grand
Lodge of England. Sixteen Lodges were reported in 1785, but the
Order was interdicted during the French Revolution. Under the protection of the Grand Orient of France. labor was resumed. When the
French dominion was terminated in 18i4, independence was declared by
the Belgian Lodges. The Grand Lodge of Belginm and the X ether lands
was organized in 1817, but dissolved by mutual consent in 1830.
In 18J2 the Grand Orient of Belgium was formed. Excommm1ication of the members was declared in an edict of the Bishop of Luxemburg in 1845. The matter was carried into politics and the Grand
Orient of Belgium attempted to justify their unmasonic position upon
the grounds of self-defense. A protest was made against such a sti!nd
by practically all the Grand Bodies of Europe and the Grand Or~nt
ceased to be recognized as a legitimate Masonic body.
It is stated that conditious improved some time afterward. The
Grand Orient of Belgium is the snpreme body in Belgium for· the
three degrees of Symbolic· Masonry. It controls 25 Lodges, two in rlie
Belgian Congo, and four Circles.
·~
The Grand Orient of Belgium is recognized by fifteen Englishspeaking Grand Bodies, including the Grand Lodges of Utah, New
Brunswick and New South Wales.
Upon the requirements of the Grand Orient of Bclgimn your
chairman has no positive first-hand information. It is stated hy a
number of Masonic writers that the Grand Orient of Belgium adopted
the same platform in regard to the absence of a Bible upon the altar
as that of the Grand Orient of France and the Grand Lodge of Franc~:
At the same time we are in fraternal relationship with the Grand
Lodges of Utah, New Brunswick and New South Wales (which are.
also in fraternal relationship with the Grand Lodge of England) by
which the Grand Orient of Belgium is recognized.

MANITOBA.
The chairman of the Foreign Correspondence Committee of
the Grand Lodge of Manitoba submitted the following very just
solution of this problem. The Grand Lodge continued the matter
by further investigation.
Since that report was presented the subject has been before many
of the Grand Lodges of the United States of America, ancl several
American Grand Lodges have authorized their members to visit lodges
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of France. The enlistment
of thousands of A111erican Masons now fighting on French soil in defence of France, civilization and Christianity has brought home to the
people of this continent ·and of Great Britain the realization of the
weakness of a divided craft and the advantage to our co111111011 interests
and the welfare of the western democratic nations of a re-union of
those who ought never to·have been separated. As has hcen well saicl
by those who have commented on this situation-what was impossible
industrially, linancial!y and politically in 1914 has been found easy of
accomplishment under the stress of war, and Masonry should he ready
am! willing to drop dogma for the great cause of universal Masonry.
Your Ctnnmittee lwlieves that the events of the past year have only
strengthened the reasons for such a reunion of Masonry and intensifiecl
the desire of all the craft for the breaking clown of the Masonic harriers now existing between those who arc allies in arms in dcfem·e of
humanity and freedom.

MASSACHUSETTS.

In December, 1912, the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts passed
on the recognition of French Masons as follows:
At the June Quarterly Communication, M.'. \V:. Brother Gallagher presented a Memorial relative to the possible recognition of the
Grand Lodge of France by this Grand Lodge.
It will be remembered that there are three several bodies claiming
authority over Symbolic Masonry in Fnmce; the National Independent
and Regular Grand Lodge for France and the French Colonies, the
(~rand Orient of France, and the Grand Lodge of France.
The Xational Independent and Regular Grand Lodge for France
and the French Colonies asked for recognition in 1914, and, on report
of a Committee, recognition was refused in 1915. (See 1914 Mass.,
page 233 ffg., and 1915 Mass., page 168 ffg.)
Thus while the flags of our two Nations float side by side with
that of England in the common cause of civilization, let us extend to
the Brethren of the Grand Lodge of France our expressions of good
will and, by sending a copy of this memorial say to them that when•·ver they can adopt in their Grand Lodge the spirit herein expressed
as a part of their Masonic principles, and embody in their Constitution
a belief in Deity or a recognition of the. Supreme Being in all their
obligations, we shall hail with delight the opportunity to be first to extend to them the right hand of fellowship, and enter into Fraternal and
official relations with them, as one of the Masouic powers of the world.
After receiving the Memorial the Grand Lodge passed the following vote:
"That the Grand Secretary. be directed to send a copy of the
Memorial, as presented, to the Grand Lodge of 1:ra11ce, with a request
that an answer he returned stating the action taken hy them, and also
the form in which such action will appear in their Constitution."
Before this Memorial and vote were transmitted a communication
was received from the Grand Lodge of France soliciting the opening of
fraternal relations.
The Memorial and vote were then transmitted to the Grand Lodge
of France, with an expression of satisfaction that their desire to open
fraternal relations had been anticipated by the action of this Grand
Lodge.
No answer has yet hecn received from the Grand Lodge of France.
Fearing that our communication, or reply thereto, may not have been
delivered because of the uncertainties of ocean transit during the last
year, I have directed the Grand Secretary to send a duplicate commtmication and thus reopen the subject.

ALABAMA,

The Grand Lodge of Alabama adopted the following recommendations of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence:
Your Committee on Foreign Correspondence has had referred to it
a communication from the Grand Lodge of France, extending an invita·
tion to the Grand Lodge of Alabama to enter into fraternal reliitions
with it, and to ~rr'.lnge for an exchange of represeqtatives. It is !?roper
to state that this 1s not the recently formed so-called "National Independent and Regular Grand Lodge for France and the French. Colonies,"
to which we refused recognition one year ago, but a Grand Body organized in 1879 under the auspices of the Supreme Council 33° Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite. In 1904, it, however, became entirely independent of the Supreme Council and now controls the three symbolic degrees.
The claims of this Grand Body to recognition have never been fully con- '
sidered by the Grand Lodge of Alabama. The nearest approach to such
consideration was in 1912 when the Grand Master answered an inquiry
from New Mexico 'that we did not recognize the Grand Lodge of France
because it did not require the Bible to be displayed in its Lodges. This
action of the Grand Master was approved by the Grand Lodge.
Your committee has also received a communication from the Grand
Orient of France, a separate and distinct body from either of those
already mentioned, which controls many degrees including the first
three. In 1878, this body was carefully considered by the Grand Lodge
of Alabama and fraternal relations with it were severed, because it had
in 1877 eliminated all reference to Deity from its constitution and· ritual
and no longer required of its initiates a declaration of belief in Deity.·
During the recent months, circumstances have given renewed importance to the subject of the relations between the Masonic bodies of
France and those of the United States. Thousands of American Masons, including many from Alabama, find themselves in France an·d
companions in arms with French Masons. It is not at all certain that
there ~ill be among them Lodges chartered by their own Grand Lodges
wherem they may enjoy the pleasures of Masonic intercourse and labor.
But whether there are or not, it is highly desirable that there should be
during the war, the fullest possible measure of social and fraternai
intercours.e between ;'\mericai;i Masons and those of France, not only
that nothmg may arise to disturb the harmony already existing, but
that the people of these two great republics and traditional friends may
be knit together even more closely than ever.
At the same time, your Committee is not possessed of sufficient data
and has been unable to give sufficient consideration to make a recommendation at this time as to what shotild be the permanent attitude of
the Grand Lodge of Alabama towards these two Grand Bodies. With-

1111t deciding this question the Grand Lodges of California, Kentucky
1111<1 New York have recently taken action authorizing Masons of ~heir
11ht'<liences to visit Lodges of the Grand Lodge and Grand Orient of
France and to hold Masonic intercourse with their members, pending
lnrther consideration as to what shall be their final action. This app1·ars to us as a cautious and at the same time fraternal course, and
w1· have decided to recommend that this Grand Lodge take similar
11rt ion. It can certainly do no harm and will afford an opportunity for
11' to learn more of French Masonry than we have heretofore known.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the following:
1. Resolved, by the Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted
Masons of Alabama, That Masons holding membership in its Lodges
111'1', until otherwise ordered, privileged to visit Lodges of the Grand
l.11dge and of the Grand Orient of France and to hold Masonic interr1111rse with their members, and that Lodges holding under this Grand
I ,odge are authorized to admit as visitors Masons holding under said
t :rand Bodies of France.
2. Resolved, That the Committee on Foreign Correspondence
11ather all obtainable information and report to the next Annual Com1111111ication of this Grand Lodge its recommendation as to what should
lo1· the attitude of this Grand Lodge towards those Grand Bodies.

FOREIGN RELATJONS.-In these days of world turmoil I find it rather
difficult to speak of our foreign relations. An almost universal war
dividing into conflicting elements all governments, aligning the forces
11f Democracy against the evil influences of Autocracy, rending political
1111d econG1mic relations seemingly beyond the possibility of reorganization, has unquestionably worked incalculable injury to the best interest
of an institution whose Master roots are planted in the doctrines of
1.iberty, Equality and Fraternity. We, of America, at least, are
,1/,asonically at peace with all the nations engaged in this superhuman
l'1111f!ict. No inhibitory measures against free, liberal and unequivocal

fraternization have been adopted by the Grand Lodges of America. We
still respect the Masonic rights and privileges of our enemy brethren,
and true to our principles, not unmindful of the experiences of our own
Civil \Var, we can still recognize the Masonic worth of those brethren ·
who by force of circumstances, environment, or other influence, may be
sincerely opposed to us. I admit it requires a supreme confidence in the
purposes. aims and aspirations of Masonry to view with equanimity
and confidence of result the raging conflict of the present day and its
possibilities. In these times of trial, however, let us not despair; let us
strain our vision through the darkness which surrounds us and ·seek the
ray of light which will lead us to the practical philosophy of Peace and
good will to all men.
.
·
True to its ideals, American Masonry is. today paving the way·
to Universal Brotherhood, and he is blind to the signs of the time who
does not see its realization in the very near future. What a formidable
front would be present as a world force for honorable and enduring
peace based upon the eternal principles of Justice and Right, if as an
institution we had been mindful of our teachings ! •
'
It is not my purpose, my brethren, to keep you in longer suspense.
Briefly and as clearly as I can, I desire to call your especial attention..
to a matter which has been a subject of considerable thought. There
is hardly a Grand Lodge in these United States which, during the past
few months, has not given thought and consideration to the matter
which I desire to bring before you, viz.: our relations to our French
Brethren. Most of our Grand Bodies partially have solved the problem. It is fortunate that we have a record which enables us tci solve' '
it completely.
"The history of the Fraternity in France, as we all know, is cone
fused and difficult to follow, but as France in its every political change
has not lost sight of the principles of the Revolution, reaching over to a
higher and broader conception of liberty, so has French ·Masonry,
through its struggles and in spite of many mistakes, worked consistently and determinedly to a more complete realization of the humanitarianism that is the foundation and raison-d'etre of our Institution."
Our French Brethren have always felt that in its pragmatic philosophy
lies the logic of .'.\fasonry's lieing and t.hat the conclusions of that philosophy cannot be avoided. It is in that spirit that they are still holding
to the Con.stitutions of 1723 which have proclaimed that all men, regardless ot race or religion, can freely and fraternally meet on the
Level.
As a matter of history, let me recall that it was only in 1849 that
the Grand Oric11t of France declared "that the basis of Freemasonry
is a belief in God and the Immortality of the Soul." Prior to that time,
it held to the spirit of the Ancient Constitutions as evinced in the
wording of the first article of the original draft of the said constitu·
tion. Let us not forget also that prior to 1849 and for twenty years
thereafter, the Grand Orient of France was in frakrnal relation with ·
the entire Masonic world.
In 1869 the invasion of the territorial jurisdiction of this State
through the chartering and recognition of clandestine lodges. both of
white and of colored membership, caused the Grand Lodge of Louisiana
to adopt a resolution recommending the severance of fraternal relations
with the Grand Orient of France. Ostensibly we have no other griev-

ance with this Grand Body; that is, no other grievai1~e of recor4. This
resolution remains the only obstacle to the resumption of cordial and
' fraternal intercourse between the two Grand Bodies, and it would seem
to be logic as well as good law that where conditions producing certain effects have ceased to exist, the effects themselves should no longer
prevail.
While all of the above is absolutely true, the current of opposition
to the recognition of the Grand Orient does not flow from its attitude
in regard to the Grand Lodge Sovereignty hut :ath~r from t.he. conception unfounded and _unp:oven that the Gram! 0;1~1~t ts an athe1sttca\ bo~y
for the reason that 1t fails to demand from its 1111tiates the profession 111
the belief in a Supreme Architect. I am again compelled to repeat that
prior to 1849, the Grand 9ricnt of France held strictl.y tp the first arti~le
of the Ancient Constitut10ns of 1723. In the later s1xt1es or the earher
seventies, realizing that its platform of princi1>les was not sufficiently
broad and liberal, the Grand Orient, through a resolution proposed by
Hrother Desmons, a Protestant Divine, whose belief in the Supreme
Architect of the Universe cannot he questioned. reverted to its original
plan and in accord with the true spirit of Toleration, declared that
Fre~masonry being an "institution essentially philanthropical, philosophical, and progressive, has for its object the seeking after Trnth, 1he
study of Morality, and the practice of Human Soli.darity; that its obj~et
is the material and moral improvenu•nt, and the 111tellcct11al an? soctal
perfection of Humanity ; that it is based upon m~1tual tolcrattoi:, the
respect of others and for one's self, and ahsol11te liberty of consctencc,
and that it considers metaphysical conceptions as belonging to the exclusive domain of the individual appreciation of its mcmhers, and that
it refuses to interfere in dogmatic qm·stions." The Masonic world went
wild. Not a single English-speaking Grand Lodge looked upon this
declaration in the true light of Masonic Philosophy, and the Grand
Orient of France hecamc an 011tcast in the Ma sonic World,

16

I submit, my brethren, that in the misconception of the position of
our French hrcthren regarding their inkrpretation of Masonic Philosophy English-speaking Masonry is clearly in the wrong, and we as
:.\fa~ons should he ready to admit it. While French Masonry is religiously tolerant, it is not in itself a religion in the restrictive :;cnse of the
word. l t proclaims no dogma ; it demands no profession ; it respects all
opinions, and in that tolerance is an exemplar of that tru~ relig~on
which is the basis of Freemasonry-the Brotherhood of Mankmd which
leads 11s through the love of our fellow men, a spark of his Own Divinity-to the Love, Honor, and Glory of the Great Architect of the Universe.
As a great many of the Grand Lodges of America have submitted
through resolutions a modus vivendi between Amttrkan and French
Masons permitting unrestricted fraternization with the members of the
several Grand Bodies of ,France, let us go a set further, heing true to
ourselves and to the Institution of which we arc memhl·rs and resume
once and for all, free and fraternal intercourse with the Grand Orient
and the Grand Lodge of France, leaving time and results to prove the
rectitude of our line of action.

So much of a general statement concerning the Grand Orient, and
French Masons, appeared to be necessary in order that we might have
something of a background upon which to project other details which
may seem to have a closer connectio!1 with the matter in hand.
It must be obvious, too, that in dealing in this general way with
the Grand Orient, we have at the same time indicated, in faint outline
at least, certain facts essential to an understanding of the Grand Lodge
of France. The different threads of their history were so closely interwoven through so many years that they seem to form one, rather than
two strands, and after their separation, and independence of organization came, there would still be, in things fundamental, such a community of interests and similarity of ideals, as to make the annals of the
one, bear many of the marks of the history of the other. And in the
great ends sought, they are one. For the practical mission of Masonry
in France, as was recently pointed out by a member of the Grand Lodge
of France, is "* * * to promote and sustain liberty, to further equal
conditions and opportunities for all men, to urge a true fraternity among
the people."
The Grand Lodge of France had its birth in 1804-1821, say$ another French writer, and became an independent, sovereign Body in
1895, as already indicated. It has 150 Lodges under its. jurisdiction
with a membership of 8,000, according to recent reports.·
In the matters upon which the Grand Orient and English-speaking
Lodges differ, the Grand Lodge of France appears to be more tolerant,
in that it permits its Lodges to exercise their own judgment. At least
one Lodge under its jurisdiction is composed for the most part of
English-speaking members, and follows the Grand Lodge of England
in its religious requirements.
The Grand Lodge of France, like the Grand Orient, stands squarely
on the Constitutions of 1723, and these, as already intimated, seem not
to justify any such insistence upon the three points in dispute, as characterizes the attitude of Grand Lodges in this country. It may not be
amiss to note in this connection, just what is demanded by that Article
"Concerning Goel and Religion".
It declares that "A Mason is obliged by his Tenure, to obey the
moral law." It further declares, that, "if he rightly understands the
Art, he will never be found a stupid Atheist, nor an irreligious Libertine." Without pausing to consider the possible or probable meaning
of the words "Atheist," and "Libertine," as used in the year 1723 you
notice that the condition is found in the words: "if he rightly u;1derstands the Art". It does not say that he may not be both an Atheist
and Libertine, as well as a Mason; nor does it say that an Atheist or a
Libertine may not be a Mason. It does say that "if he rightly understands the Art" (but this he may not do}, he will be neither the one
nor the other. Then follows a statement of what formerly was requi;ecl of the Brethren, vi~.,_ t~. be of the religion .of the country in
which they lived,. b?t n?w 1t _is thought more expe?1ent m~ly to oblige
them to that Religion m whtch all men agree, leavmg thetr particular
opinions to thernselves; that is, to be good Men and true, or Men of
Honour and Honesty, by whatever Denominations or persuasions they

may be distinguished." In this, then, we have the religious platform
ttpnn which the Grand Lodge of France takes its stand. In explanation

11itiate the proper conception of the G. A. 0. T. U., believing that with
111tr aid they will rightly understand our art and not be 'stupid atheists

The question of Military Lodges is of great interest at this time
and I include in this report the action of several Grand Lodges on

In connection with this subject I may say that the question nf
eonferring degrees by courtesy has assumed tremendous magnitude

responsibility cordially and willingly.

This move frequently and generally involves the conferring of
degrees nearly every night in the we~k and not infrequent afternoon sessions.

The attitude of Oregon may be had from the following:
Petitions were signed asking for Special Dispensations to form
Military Lodges in the different organizations forming the Oregon Contingent of the U. S. Forces at Camp Mills to be sent ahroad; but these

of the rights of other Jurisdiction;;. However, if these petitions could
have been presented while the applicants were still within our State,
the Dispensations could have been consistently issued. I believe that

those of our boys who have enlisted in the cmrnc of Democracy, but we
should even remember that conferring degrees is only a mca.ns of

"I desire also to call your attention to the Grand Lodge of California, on this subject. It says :
"'An army lodge is an anomaly in Masonry. Its meetings are held
at any place where the exigencies of the military service may cause a
temporary encampment. If held in our own country, such meetings are
necessarily an invasion of the jurisdiction of other regularly constitute(!
lodges. During the clash of battle in our late Civil War, it sometimes
happened that army lodges, with their charters ·and records, were swept
from existence, and the unfortunate members of such lodges were thus
deprived of mcmhenhip, without dimits or other records to show that
they had received the degrees of Masonry in a regularly chartered
Masonic Lodge.'
"There are many other authorities holding to the same effect, but
it woul.d seem unnecessary to quote them further. For the good of the
fratermty generally, throughout not only the Grand Jurisdiction of
Kansas, but throughout the world, 1 am constrained to deny your petition for letters of dis1iensation for such military lodge."
on JO,
The Grand Master of Ohio has this to say of Military Lodges,
which m~t with the approval of the Grand Lodge:
I have received some informal requests for the establishment in the
state of Ohio of military lodges, sometimes called traveling or army
lodges. I have answered these requests by stating that it would not be
conducive to the best interests of Freemasonry, in my opinion to authorize such lodges. I have explained that the Grand Master ha~ no power
in the premises, but that the initiative would have to be taken by the
Grand Lodge, I am opposed to this idea. With fifty Grand Jurisdictions in the United States of America and no General Grand Body over
all, each Grand Jurisdiction is a law unto itself. 1f each Grand Lodge
of the fifty should unckrtakc to establish military lodges, the result
would he untold confusion, and, in my humble opinion, disastrous to the
cause of Freemasonry. All honor to the man who has gone forth to
battle for this glorious country of ours and who is offering his life as a
sacriticc to the cause of Lilwrty and Humanity; hut what real benefit
can he derive from hecoming a member of one of these military lodges?
All of the benefits of Freemasonry will accrue to him from association
with his companions in arms who are members of the Order. and by
being permittcd to visit regularly established Lodges near the camp or

cantonment where he may be located. No proper place can be h.ad .for

this country, and it is not practicable elsewhere, I trust the Grand Lodge

MASONRY AND THE WAR-UNANIMOUSLY PATRIO.TIC.
From the moment when this Great Republic bowed to the will
of the inevitable and cast its lot with the nations that were struggling to death with the unspeakable barbarism of the central powers,
Sovereign Masonic Bodies of this country immediately allied themselves with unbroken unanimity back of the Government. This
unanimous sentiment of the grand jurisdictions of the United States.'
pervades all the Masonic jurisdictions of the colonies and countries
arrayed against Prussian barbarism. The Masonic grand bodies' of
Australia and Canada have evidenced their devoted loyalty by taking an unalterable and unyielding stand to support the Mother
Country and her Allies until such time as further fear of the Uomination of Prussianism shall have been beyond the pale of possible
resurrection.
The spirit that pervades the Masonic world is exemplified in
the splendid patriotism which runs through the acts of every Grand.
Lodge that has convened since April, 1917. It would be impossible
and unpracticable to atte~npt, within the limit of tpis review, to give
each Grand Jurisdiction a representation; but it may be said to the·
credit of all that what follows is not an exaggerated exemplification
of the judgment of Masonry.

vVhen a storm gathers in the heavens black clouds shut out
from sight the face of the sun. But when the rage and madness of

Every school boy is taught and we all remember various dates
which mark great steps in the progress from a worid of autocracies
lo that goal of every liberty-loving people-a world oi democracies.
There is the year of 1215, marking the grant of the Magna
Charta.
There is the date of the Declaration of the Independence of our
own beloved country. July 4th, 1776.
There is the date of that proclamation by which our great
!'resident Lincoln gave freedom to the slaves, the Emancipation

There is the date of the birth of the present French Republic,
1870.
There is the year 1913. when China took its place among the
republics of the world.
The year 1917 we all hope may go down in history as the year
of the end of autocratic rule in Russia.
'
The dates, marking steps in the triumphant onward march of
democracy, as distinguished from autocracy, are familiar to everyone.
But there is one period which, unfortunately. cannot be distinuuished by a definite or positive date, marking the greatest single
;tep toward democracy which the world has ever known. of which
the general public knows and hears but little. Could the step be
attached to a definite date, the world might know more of it. But
we Masons, who should and do know the most of it. have positive
information as to no definite date and know but the period of the
great step.
I refer to the birth of Speculative Masonry.•
In ancient times we Masons existed as lodges of actual workmen-operative masons, practicing the principles and following to
some extent, as is shown by the old charges, the doctrines we now
teach, though probably only in an incidental way, for we were primarily concerned in the proper application of the useful rules of
architecture. But at some time prior to 1717. our ancient operative
brethren admitted to their ranks, as members of their order. individuals who were not operative or actual builders.
Our history previous to the year 1717 is cloudy; dates cannot be
definitely fixed; records were either not kept or were destroyed.
Just how long before 1717 men were admitted to lodges oi Free
Masons, who had no connection with the builder's trade or profession, we do not know. Rut we do know that in the preceding century, many, among those whose names are familiar to ns being Ashmole and Mainwaring, both scientists and philosophers. and not at
all eligible as builders, were admitted to memhership. The presence

ever, and over its shining portal we shall read in letters of living
light the words: "Liberty and union, freedom and fraternity, now
and forever, one and inseparable, world without end."
No stronger statement of the real Prussian situation as represented by the Hohenzollerns-its origin and growth-can be found
anywhere than is expressed in the following oration delivered before
the Grand l~odge of Minnesota by Worthy Brother Harry G. Gearhart, Grand Orator, and I commend it for the careful perusal and
consideration of all thoughtful Masons. It demonstrates that which
we all knew, that this most momentous struggle in history was
inevitable.
He said, in part:
These forms of government by which the world was for so long
ruled, whether we call them autocracies or monarchies, early gave
birth to the theory of the divine right of kings-the theory that the
ruler was the ruler by divine right-and to such sayings as "The
king can do no wrong", "Might is Right", and that famous truism
of that king of France, "The State; I am the State."
Plato, that old Greek philosopher, in his "The Republic," cynically yet truly for his time and for many centuries thereafter, maintained that political governments existed for the benefit of the governors and not for the benefit of the governed, and makes his char-·
acter, Thrasymachus, say "Might is right; justice is in the interest
of the stronger."
Prior to the middle of the seventeenth century, the government
of autocrats which existed throughout the world, had received but
one substantial check. In the year 1215 there was wrung from King
John, of England, that great document, the Magna Charta, or Great

of these non-operative Masons had an effect upon the workings of

Whether the birth of Speculative Masonry is placed in the year
1717 or at some time prior thereto, I say that its birth marks one ot

Think of the countless ages previous to the birth of Speculative
Masonry, during which time autocratic rule was universal, and the
influence against autocracy was wielded by so few people. From
the very birth of the human race up to the eighteenth century, the
world had been ruled by might, and the principles of whi~h we are
reminded by the square, the compass and our other workmg tools,

But taking the year 1717 as the earliest starting point of Speculative Masonry, and the time from which we Masons were bound

There is no question but that the Constitution of the United

France first endeavored to throw off the yoke of tyranny in

I have in mind. And that fact is this: That these numerous and tre111cndous changes and efforts toward changes in the form of govc•rnments, from autocracies to democracies, have taken place since
Speculative Masonry came into being.
At first we were naturally few in numbers. But our growth has
been most marvellous. The voices of the few who, as individuals', so

equality and liberty in past ages, have, since the birth and growth

We arc sending to the European battle front hundreds of. thousands, possibly millions of men, with the idea that, through the

possibly be produced hy a less number. So with Masonry; its principles are urged with the combined force of all its members-a force
which should he tremendous. And, therefore, considering the principles in which we Speculative Masons believe and for which we
