'Vhy. then, is Germany not only fighting this war against the
peoples having and believing in a liberal form of government, but
the instigator of and leader in the war?
Jn my judgment, the answer to the question is found, primarily,,
in the form of government which obtains in the German empire,
and secondarily, in the peculiar tastes, beliefs and mental characteristi~s of the members of the Hohenzollern family, of which Kaiser
William II is the present head.
The German empire is composed of what were once a number
of independent kingdoms, duchies and states, now generally called
states, each governed by a king or other hereditary ruler. T.he
kingdom of Prussia is one of these, and the Hohenzollern family
has for centuries been its reigning head. •
The empire, consisting of these several so-called states, has
what is called a constitutional form of government; that is, the conduct of its affairs is regulated and the powers of its ruler fixed by
a constitution adopted in 1870. which also, in theory and only in
theory, grants to the people a voice in the government.
This constitution is a very ingenious document. It was adopted
practically at the dictation of Prussia, and provides that he who is
king of Prussia shall be the ruler of the empire-the German kaiser.
It also provides for two legislative bodies corresponding in a faint,
though very faint, degree to our Congress-there called the Rundesrath and Reichstag. The members of the Bundesrath, or upper
house, are appointed by the reigning heads of the several states and
kingdoms comprising the empire. But the ingenuity of the practical working of this develops in the fact that, through the methods
by which members are appointed. and the exceptional numbers
allotted to Prussia, and the powers given the Prnssian members in
affairs concerning the army. the navy and taxation. the voice of
Prussia dictates the action of the body. Therefore, in such matters
the voice of the Bundesrath is simply the expression of the will of
the king of Prussia-the German kaiser.
The other legislative body. the Reichstag, is composed of members who are elected by the people. This sounds like democracy;
hut it is not as encouraging as it sounds. For here, again, Prussia
furnishes a great majority of the memhers (232 out of a total of
397), and, what is more important, the kaiser .can, at his will, dissolve the Reichstag and compel another election of memhers. .If
he has an unruly Reichstag, which will not yield to his dictates, he
can dissolve it and compel another election and continue so doing
until he secures a Reichstag where a majority will do his will and
indorse measures passed ,by his BundeHath. By these constitutional provisions the kaiser's autocratic power is limited, in that he
is refused the right to make laws by his word alone. as he could
were the powers of government vested in him and in no other individual or body. But by that most ingenious constitution of Prussian manufacture, the kaiser has merely to conforpl to or put up
with a little red tape, and his will is law.
At the beginning of the present war we hear much from German sources as to how Germany had been attacked by France and
Russia, and how Germany was forced into the war in self-defense.
The reason for this is found in another provision of this remarkable
constitution which gives the kaiser the right to declare a war only

in defense of the empire, and which all authorities agree impliedly
prohibits him from declaring an offensive war. Yet the constitution fails to state what shall happen if he does declare a war of
offense; and, as it is a fact that every German soldier and sailor is
bound by an oath of allegiance, not to the empire and not to the
particular state from which he comes, but to the kaiser personally,
it is not difficult to see that the kaiser, with the army and navy
under his absolute direction, can actually declare and prosecute a
war of offense and conquest, without any serious consequences by
reason of his overrnling the provisions of the constitution.
I have no doubt but that the argument that Germany was the
country attacked in the war, was made by the German people in
order to defend their constitution to themselves and to the outside
world, and to justify their kaiser's declaration of war.
From these facts, it will be seen that Germany, though assuming to he a so-called constitutional monarchy, is really an autocracy
-an autocracy which, headed by an individual of decidedly autocratic tendencies, can be as pronounced an autocracy as ever existed,
And what are the peculiar tastes and beliefs and mental characteristics of the members of the Hohenzollern family, of which the
present kaiser is the head?
In the first place, from the rulers of the original kingdom of
Prussia, which containea approximately 24,000 square miles. the)'
have extended their rule over what is now the German empire, an
area approximating 209,000 square miles; and practically every
square mile of that additional territory has been brought under the
rule of the Prussian reigning family by force of arms or coercion.
For several centuries past the heads of this house have been
believers in the doctrine of the right of might. and have had the
physical and mental attainments necessary to enforce that doctrine
upon their own and neighboring peoples.
This family also holds another belief, one of which much has
been said and written, but one which l doubt is thoroughly appreciated by anyone who is not imbued with the spirit of democracy.
That is the belief that the Hohenzollern family rules by Divine right
-that it has been especially chosen by the Almighty to rule over
the people of the German empire, and that the Almighty and the
kaiser, working together, can do no wrong. Many expressions hy
various German rulers can be found which prove such beliefs, but I
,,.ill quote but two hy the present kaiser-William 1I.

with a people believing that the brutal incidents inseparable from

\Ve can have no sympathy for people who conduct a war in
violation of all codes of civilized warfare; who wreak their vengeance upon women, children and non-combatants, generally; who
do not respect the Red Cross; who wantonly and unnecessarily
wreck and ruin those magnificent monuments erected by our operative brethren centuries ago.
These things are not in accord with our Masonic principles;
therefore we, as Masons, must oppose them.
It is a matter of personal regret to me that our Blue Lodges, as
Masonic institutions, cannot or do not take a more prominent part
in matters v.ital to our communities, or to our country. The Blue
Lodge stands, upon principle, for everything that is good and is
opposed to everything which is bad; yet my personal belief is that,
as an institution, it does all too little in a public way; that it should
not be content merely to impress its principles upon its members
and, through them, exert its influence for good, but that it should
itself take its place as a direct and open advocate of its principles,
striving to directly impress them upon all the world. However, our
conservatism is the result of centuries of conservatism, and no one
can expect any such change as I hope for to be brought about in
any manner other than the most gradual. So we cannot expect that
Masonic institutions, as such, can take any prominent part in the
conduct of the war or in the adjustment of conditions which must
obtain when the war is over. But, as individual Masons, if we are
true Masons, if we believe in the lessons which are taught us in our
Lodges, we, every man of us from the youngest Entered Apprentice
in the northeast corner of the Lodge to the Master, must do everything in our power to support our country during the war and until
it is brought to a successful conclusion.
Our obligation to do this is twofold. We are American citizens, and it is the duty of every citizen to stand solidly behind our
government at Washington. But we are also Masons, and we are
under the additional obligation of defending our principles and our
teachings. Therefore, I say to you, Brothers, that we Masons of the
United States are doubly obligated to uphold and fight for the principles urged. by our government, and t0 annihilate that German
system of government which is the primary cause of the war.
Most of us are beyond the age when we would be permitted to
actually bear arms for our country and our principles. As the
situation is at present, that must be done by younger men, But the
use of the rifle and the work in the trench is but one form of the
fighting in this war.
The man who supports the Red Cross, the ~an who furnishes
the government with his money, either through the purchase of the
government's bonds or the payment of taxes, the man who contrib·

utes to the work of the Y. M. C. A., the man who eats less meat and
less wheat and, in general, regulates his food supply according to
the requests of the authorized government official, the man who
if he be an employer or an employe, for the time being adjusts hi~
grievances arising out of labor conditions so that a strike or a cessation of work is impossible, the man who produces the food and the
materials necessary to the conduct of the war-each of these is
doing a share of the fighting just as surely as the man who is in the
first-line trenches in Belgium and in France.

There is still another and a very practical way in which we
Masons can support and be of service to our government and our
country.
There is still too much German sentiment among our people.
There are still those whose sympathies are with their fatherland
rather than with this land where they have prospered and which
they have chosen as their home in preference to the fatherland.
There are still those who, maliciously or because of selfish political
reasons, criticize our government for entering into the war. There
is still too mucla seditious talk. There are many who still spread German propaganda, the intended effect of which is to cause some
measure of weakness in the spirit of some of our people. Along
this line are the stories of the mismanagement of our soldiers'
camps, the immorality in the army, the ravages of disease, etc .. the
misappropriation of Red Cross funds and supplies. More talk of
this kind is that to the effect that we are in the war because munitions makers want to keep busy, or that this is a Wall Street war,
and that, now we are in the war, France and England are not exerting themselves to the utmost, and are shirking their part of the
burden.

If such stories are believed, they will naturally create in our
minds some measure of dissatisfaction with the government's conduct of the war. And German propaganda is calculated only to
sow seeds of dissatisfaction in the minds of her opponents.
We have, doubtless, made mistakes in grasping the new problems which we have had to confront. \Vhen one considers the vast
number of people in our country, suddenly called upon to meet in a
practical and efficient manner conditions entirely new to them, is it
any wonder that these people upon whom new duties are thrust are
not immediately JOO per cent efficient? Mistakes have been made
and will continue to be made, but I know that our government is
weeding out the incompetents, and will continue to weed them out,
and to, as rapidly as is possible, render us as nearly 100 per cent
efficient as it is humanly possible for us to be.
There are still those who, for selfish reasons or to help Germany, talk about the unfairness of the draft.

Here follows a practical common-sense talk given before the
Grand Lodge of New York by a worker with the United States
forces and the Allies. It touches the heart of every true patriot and
makes us feel proud to know that we are Americans:
Brother Charles W. Whitehair: Brothers, it is not easy to come
and speak when, within the last hour, you have told your kiddies
good-bye by long-distance telephone, and turned your face out there
for the fourth time. It is not easy. Money could not bring me here
today. This organization could not give me a check that would
tempt me to come here today. But I did come, and I have come,
because I feel that in this organization, our organization which is
close to the heart of every one of us. are possibilities and power
which will mean much to the boys out there.
And, then. when I left that Western front last year, I said, "I
am going back to America to do anything I possibly can do to back
up the boys overseas."
I don't like this talk that food will win the war. I don't like
this talk that Liberty Bonds will win the war. I don't like the talk
that the Y. M. C. A. or the Red Cross or any other organization witl
win the war. If you had gone with me last September from the
French front on down the British front to Arras. Armentieres.
Vimy, Messines. Bixshoote. Ploegsteert and Kemme! Hill, on down
through the mud plains of Flanders on that September morning,
and you had stood with me in the front-line trench, and seen them
crawl out of their trenches to go over the top and die by the thousands before your eyes, you would come back and ask God's mercy
to forgive you if you ever talked about anybody winning this war
but the boys that go over the top. (Applause.)
These are serious hours. \Ve are facing one of the crucial
periods of the war. I am going to talk on the square this morning
-there aren't any newspaper men here, I take it-we are facing a
crucial hour of the war; in fact, the most crucial nour since August,
1914; more critical than the Marne, more critical than the Somme;
more critical than Verdun, the most critical hour the war has gone
through. It is the time for the blow of the strong man who knows
that he has met his match. and that he is going down if he does not
strike and strike quick; and that is the blow of Germany today.
But, they did get through, and we have got to admit it. But they
are not going to take Calais. (Applause.) They may go further
through our lines; but if you think afteT three years and over going
and coming out there, that we are not going to win, then you don't
know anything about it. We are going to win. (Applause.) We
are going to win if it takes every drop of American blood and every
dollar of the world. (Cries of "Hear, hear," and great applause.)
It is not alone a question of making the world safe for democracy. Quite frankly, it is a question of self-preservation, and we
might as well face the truth.
\Vhen Mr. McAdoo asked me to delay my trip two months ago,
he said: "\Ve want you to go out and tell the truth to the country,
uncensored." That is what I have been trying to do; but I hope I
will speak here more frankly than I have spoken at other places,
because I can.

The last day before I left France, General Pershing stood up at
the end of our interview and said: "You have got to go back to
America, to help kill that damnable German propaganda that we
cannot break the Western line." (Cries of "Hear, hear," and applause.) We can, and eventually will break it, and, men, as God is
my witness, I believe to the very bottom of my feet that we are
going to win this war and we are going to smash that line to pieces.
(Applause.) But, it won't be tomorrow, and it won't be the next
few months, make up your mind, because the bloodiest parts of this
war are ahead.
When ex-President Taft told me last Spring, just before I
started on my third trip, that he thought it might t<;lke two million
American lives to win the war, I think he put it right. We are facing a united Germany. . . .
It is a united Germany; but, friends, why did I say that they
would not win and we would win? Because I am in the large army
where we believe in God, and ours is a righteous cause, and we are
going to win because we are on God's side. (Applause.) That is
the spirit out there.
But, quickly let me jump to the other questions. You are cone
sidering our American boys. They are a remarkable lot and you do
not need to ask me how they act under shell fire. I know. I have
been under it. I spoke one night in a tent up near the front line,
and a German aeroplane came around and began dropping bombs.
Well, I have been going to war for quite a while, and I thought, out
of courtesy to the chap up there, we would adjourn the meeting.
A tent is not shell-proof. Don't think that. It is not bomb-proof.
On either side of me was the camp-one was here and one there.
And I was talking about the one subject which I have found men ·•
will sit for hours and listen to. They will sit and listen to you talk
if you have a real message. I have talked ·to them on the far-flung
plains of the Albion Desert, on 1'he Suez Canal; and within a shorter
number of hours than I dare say, I will turn my face out there again
to go to the Turkish frontier of Transylvania. I have talked to
them all along the Western front on the one subject they want to
know: "What does God have for a man out here, who has given up
everything, home, and life?"
I was talking to our American soldiers, and I thought we would
adjourn the meeting, but one big Yankee sergeant stood up beside
me and did not say a word, but just blew out the candle, and never
left the tent; and there was nothing for me to do hnt go ahead and
talk. There wasn't a boy that left that tent-not a hoy. The shells
were bursting one after another overhead, and the German wa.s
throwing bombs around us, and I want to say to yoti there is only
one man in this war that counts. I don't count, and you don't
count. It is the boy that wears the khaki, and the blue, that is doing
his bit. (Applause.)
They are doing their bit, but will you do yours? Don't put this
off on Tom Brown or John Jones, or somebody else. I want to
know: Will you do your bit?' Do not ever be guilty of talking
about somebody being a slacker, somebody who is sorry and trying
to get .out of the fight because he has been conscripted, when you
have kept your hands down in your pocket and won't fork out your
money. You are just as much of a slacker as he is. (Applause.)

great September push was ready to begin. Up between the lines I

The shells are falling. Five-thirty. Five-forty-five. Down the ·
line co.mes the word, and there they stand. Oh, don't any man ever
dare talk of sacrifice, for there they stand! Do you think that any·
of us could ever sacrifice like that? Fifteen minutes. You bare
your chest to it. Six o'clock. Every gun speaks, and into hell they
go, with machine guns firing four hundred or six hundred shots a
minute, with high explosive shells, with the shrapnel; and they are
running over ground that has been mined, and barbed-wire fences;
and last of all, the battle. And you have never heard of one like
that. And over they ga for us. And as I stood there that morning,
I thought of back home, and I said, "With God as my witness, I
am never going to say anything on any American platform-no
man, I don't care if he is the president of the biggest corporation in
America-any man, be he the president of the great labor unions
holding up shipbuilding-be he the man grafting half of the price by
giving them inferior material that he is sending out, shoes and clothing, and endangering their lives-be he German professor or professor preaching in the university and in the German schoolroom,
German class, preaching propaganda-be he preacher preaching
pacifism-I say pacifism, that is worse-German propaganda-any
man today who wilfully hinders military preparation or hinders our
backing the boys to the limit out there, if he is the biggest man in
America, he deserves only one thing-what they get out there:
Stone wall, in front of a firing squad! (Great cheering and ap-.
plause.)
I have only a few more minutes and I want you to hear what I
have to say, and then I leave you. I must go.
?.1en, any enemy back here is worse than an enemy out there.
You cannot get a way from that. There are our boys on the French
front. I have gone over the ground. I have heard them speak when
I was in Verdun. \Veil, God forgive any of us who now pick the
Americans to settle it. I walked over the graves of the men in
1915. I was in Verdun on the last Sunday in September. Those
once beautiful hills now are hills of graves-graves of their sons.·
There are a million of her boys under the sod for us; and it does
not do well for us to talk about how we are going in to settle it..
When we have tasted of th<; true sacrifice we won't want to boast.
Now, let me lift the curtain on what I call the most horrible
act of the war, and yet the most Christ-like. I stood along that line
of the white posts. I have spared you the scene of that field there
of No Man's Land. But, I stood on the line of the white posts, and
there they come; not by the score . but by the hundreds they are
coming back. Well, I won't spare your feelings! I saw them there
with arms shot off; undressed, with twists taken around to stop the
flow of blood; I saw them coming with both arms shot off; I saw
them staggering back with an eye gone, with the nose shot off,
with the chin gone, shot through the body, the legs were shattered,
and every stitch of clothing below the waist torn off.
You say men cannot walk hack like that. No. they cannot!
They cannot walk back, shot like that; but it is walk back or die,
ai1d they walk back. The stretcher-bearers are only bringing those
who cannot move; and back they are coming.

And, men, I have seen this war, and I want to say to you that
I am an American from the bottom of my feet to the top of my
head, and I went to this war two years ago, in spite of the fact that
my little wife is a Quaker we declared war in 1914; and I went out
there, and I want you to hear what I have to say. That talk that
America will never quit is all right, as long as you don't make insinuations. But the talk that Britain and France may quit-but we will
never quit-I don't like! Wait until we have played the game!
Wait until we have paid the sacrifice! But I will say this: Nobody
can talk with me about France breaking down. I have been in the
front-line trench with the French and seen their dirty, ragged uniforms; but, thank God, I have got their spirit, and the French will
never say quit until they have won, if it means death.
But, consider, for the sake of argument, that France might be
forced out; Italy might have to quit, and America, through faint
hearts back here and through German propaganda, should lie down.
But thank God, I can say to you today, from all that I have seen
and' heard that Great Britain will never quit until the last man is
under the sod. If any man tells you that Great Britain is not in
this war, he doesn't know the truth. I have been there; I know,
and the British Tommies are going forward to die, because God is
on their front, and they believe in righteousness, and they are giving their lives not for any false ideas of the issue.
God pity the German people. I say it honestly. They are misled. But General Pershing said: "We have got to kill, kill, kill,
until we have so dissolved their man-power that they cannot ever
again put on to the world or attempt to put on the world the Prussian yoke!" And we are going to do it, if it takes all of our money
and men.
But, alongside of the sacrifice out there, may l say this in all
kindness: I cannot make a sacrifice and you cannot make a sacrifice that would be worth touching the old, muddy, bloody coat of
the boy that goes over the top to fight our battles.
I don't know what you are going to do. I don't know what the
purpose of your plans are, but I do know this, men: In spite of all
the organizations that are working, what is done is only a drop in
the bucket. It is only a drop in the bucket. One man said to me in
Seattle-I went to see him to have him interest himself in a certain

cause. They said they might get two thousand dollars. He is not a
Christian man, not interested in these things. And I said, "This is
not my war any more than it is yours." I said, "We have got to
hack the boys up out there. I thought you might like to start this
I hing with ten thousand dollars." He looked at me and said, "Every
damn thing I have got is in this war; my two boys are in"; and he
said, "I am not going to say to any organization, 'Why do you do so
much for those boys?' I am going to say, 'Why do you do so
little?'" And he said, "I will give ten thousand dollars-in fact, I
will give twenty-five thousand dollars, because they are all my
hoys."
And, men, we will win this war, and with this war goes the
heart of every man, woman and child in America, who boasts of

Men, stand back of them! Stand back of them to the limit!

Russia-we would have won before this, I firmly believe, if

The Grand Master of Kansas promises a generous response by
the Masons of his state to the call of duty:

64

"What a man does for bread and butter
Is worth its market value and no more;
But what a man does for love's sake
Is gold, indeed, and rings well upon
God's touchstone."
It is assuring to us that now linked upon one side in this great
struggle are, as we know them, all the Masonic countries of the
globe. The declaration of the greatest republic on the Western
Hemisphere to become a partner in the defeat of ruthless villainy
and revolting tyranny is a contribution to Christianity and the cause
of humanity. The United States of America, with its millions of
Freemasons, casting its stupendous weight on the side of common
justice, marks historical.Jy a Masonic event, in that it inseparably
forever links the Anglo-Saxon Masonic world. In the union of arms
between the two great English-speaking nations, we find forged
with increased strength the chain of our fraternity. Through the
agency of the combined military endeavors we can perceive tke
dawn of the day when peace, with its charitable mantle, will once
more cover the blood-stained peoples; of the work for which we are
banded together progress unhampered and. the cardinal virtues
become the dominating influences of all governing powers. It will
hasten the better, the happier day. It gives courage to the faith
that is in us-a faith such as expressed by Fay Hemstead, poet
laureate of Masonry, when he penned:
"But over the war-cloud, rolling low,
And above the tide of tears and woe;
And through· the blight of harrowing fear,
His higher purpose shineth clear.
For like the light of the opening day,
His hand shall sweep the mists away;
And over that hour supreme shall span,
Blest Peace, and the Brotherhood of Man.
"God grant it so. And grant we may
Sooner usher in that gracious day;
When men shall turn to war no more;
And peace abide from shore to shore;
When states be ruled by kindly thought,
And sword and spear be held for naught;
And evermore among us dwell,
The reign of Prince Immanuel."

We stand today amidst a world in flames fanned by a universal
whirlwind of violence and destruction for which history affords no

Never in the history of our beloved country have more important and perplexing problems puzzled the minds of the wisest and
wittiest of men than at the present hour. As we convene 'here
tonight, in every part of our land. are assembled the soldiers ready
to do and die for the cause we all hold dear. If we are to remain
true to the immortal declaration, "Millions for defense, but not ane
cent for tribute," the hour is here when we must all do our best.
It is, however, in behalf of those who are members of our own
fraternity that I plead. It is hardly possible that there is a single
subordinate Lodge in all our country that does not have at least
one Brother who sleeps this night in a soldier's tent. If there was
ever an hour when there should be an united effort to aid in all
possible ways to make camp life pleasant, pure and home-like, that
time is now. For years, to do good to others has been a theory;
today it is a practical reality. One of the District Deputy Grand
Masters of this Grand Lodge is authority for the statement that
nearly one-third of all the young men now in training at one of the
officers' training camps of our country are Masons. If this be true
of all the camps of the nation, what is the present duty of our
fraternity?
I know n.ot what is best to do in the present pressing situation.
I am confident, however, that it is an hour for action. The solution
of the problem and the plan to add to the happiness of our brethren
who are "somewhere" tonight should enlist the best of heart and
bi:ain. May I dare even to suggest for your maturer consideration
two or three ways in which we can help in some small manner to
keep in touch with our brethren, wherever they may be, and cause
them to feel and know that we shall be interested in them every
hour, and our daily prayer shall be that success may crown their
efforts, and that the hand of Him, who neither slumbers nor sleeps,
sha:tl finally return them safely to home and loved ones.
First-I recommend that this Grand Lodge remit to each subordinate Lodge the annual Grand Lodge tax chargeable to each
brother now in the service so long as he shall remain in such
service.
Second-If deemed advisable, I further recommend that an
effort be made to ascertain the number of brethren in our Grand
Jurisdiction who are already in the service, and add thereto such
others as may hereafter enlist; that a committee be appointed for
that purpose, and that this Grand Lodge, in session now convened,
consider seriously the proposition of appropriating a fund sufficient
to enable said committee to dispense such financial aid as will add
to the comfort and happiness of our brethren as are deservedly
needing the soothing balm beneficial to their immediate circumstances. That sublime precept, "Inasmuch as you have done it unto
the least of these my brethren, you have done it unto me." should
be the daily doctrine of every American citizen, and particularly of
us as Masons.

ALBJiRTA,

The Grand Lodge of Alberta approved the following liberal views
of the Grand Master:
The dispensation to act on applications of candidates with physical
defects were as follows:
Lethbridge Lodge No. 39, to initiate a returned soldier who had
lost his right arm below the shoulder. He had an artificial, mechanical
arm, and was able to fulfill the necessary requirements.
Bow River Lodge No. 1, to initiate a returned soldier who had
defective hearing and was obliged to use an ear trumpet. I was present
at this initiation and was quite satisfied that the candidate was able
to fulfil the necessary requirements.
I feel that the broadest possible view should be taken in the matter
of granding dispensations to initiate ottr returned soldiers. who have
been wounded in the service of the Empire, provided they can fulfil
the necessary reqttirements, and I therefore granted these dispensations
gladly.·
Speaking of the constantly increasing number of applications for

proclaimed and generally understood in this jurisdiction. While this

The Grand Lodge of Texas applies the rule set out in this preamble
and resolution :
\VHl\Rl\As, The perfect man is an ideal being, and absolute perfection does not exist among men, neither physically, mentally, nor
morally; therefore, be it
Resolved, (1) That it is not obnoxious to the Ancient Landmarks
and Charges of Masonry that slight maims or defects of body should
debar an applicant for initiation or advancement in Masonry; and
(2) That an applicant for initiation must be sound and hale, without maim or defect in his body that may render him ineligible to be a
Mason; that is, physical maims and defects should be considered on
the basis of his ability to receive, practice and impart freely and without
artificial or other aid all the rites and ceremonies of Ancient Craft
Masonry, including :\fasonic work in the Lodge room, and shall possess
the mental and physical ability to earn his livelihood in his chosen
occupation outside the Lodge room; and
Resolved, That when an applicant for initiation has a maim or
defect, the Lodge to which the application is made shall refer the case,
with a faithful description of such maim or defect, to the Grand Master,
who shall thereupon rule upon the eligibility of the applicant in the
light of these resolutions.
ALABAMA.

The rule in Alabama is stated by the Grand Master as follows:
At the last meeting of the Grand Lodge, an amendment to the
Constitution was adopted, placing the decision as to the physical qualification of a candidate in the hands of the Lodge, subject to the written approval of the Grand Master.
I had .been of the opinion that the intention of this amendment was
only to 111odi'fy to a limited extent the laws previously existing, and the
Grand Lodge having declined to make any interpretation of the new
law, but leaving each case to the judgment of the Grand Master I
adopted for myself a rule that where the candidate could, either
with his own person, or with the aid of artificial limbs, place
himself in the necessary positions and give the signs and grips, that I
would approve the action of a Lodge in accepting snch candidate.
I think that the language of the amendment would permit the
acceptance of one who was so maimed that he could not comply with
this rule which I outlined for my guidance, but I acted upon what I
considered the spirit of the amendment, rather than the strict letter of
the law.
The several cases acted npon by me are not here reported in detail,
but the rule which I have just given has governed my action throughout the year in all cases on this subject submitted to me for action.

CHAIN LETTERS.
As expressing the attitude of the several Grand Jurisdictions
it1 the Chain Letter humbug, I ca11 attention to the following:
The Grand Master of Rhode Island has this to say:
In spite of the fact that much has been written and said with a view
of discouraging the evil of chain letters in general and of the "Masonic
I 'rayer" chain letter in particular, many members of the craft in this
jurisdiction appear to have thoughtlessly let their superstition get the
!Jetter of their good judgment and have aided in perpetuating and in·
ercasing an altogether foolish and useless undertaking.
It may not be amiss to quote from an article by Bro. Newton appearing recently in the Builder:"Perhaps half a hundred brethren have sent us the following prayer,
saying that it had been sent to them with the request that they send it on
to nine brother Masons, forming an endless chain of prayer: 'O Lord,
I implore Thee to bless all mankind. Firing us to Thee. Keep us to
•lwell with Thee." So far, good; it is a brief, wise and universal prayer.
like a line caught from a vast litany of humanity. But the usual form
of the letter adds that this prayer was sent by all :\fasons in the olden
ti111e, and that all who wrote it would be free from calamity, and that
I hose who did not pass it on would be in danger of misfortune. What
a pity to spoil the beauty of it all, breaking the links which Tennyson
said bind us as with 'chains of gold about the feet of God.' with such a
hribe and such a threat! It becomes a matter of luck, like wearing a
rabbit foot, or some other token handed down from old-time magicwhereas, prayer, if it has any meaning, much less worth, is a wish sent
( :odward, a law of life."
I suggest that the Masters of Lodges bring this matter to the attention of their members urging them to discourage the practice and assist
in minimizing at least, the evil of an undertaking which appeals only
to superstition and not at all to intellect or reason.

The Grand Master of Massachusetts says:
Again it seems necessary to call your attention to another epidemic of chain letters that has recently broken out. I have personally
received large numbers of them. Chain prayer letters seem to be the
present most popular form and are being widely circulated in additio.11
to those seeking money for various objects. Such letters are unmasomc
and prohibited in this jurisdiction. They are calculated to appeal to the
superstitious and are a rank imposition upon those to whom they are
sent. Every loyal Masonic officer and memher should use every reasonable effort to rid the Fraternity of this pernicious practice so contrary to
Masonic ethics and authority.

MASSACHUS!lTTS.

In Massachusetts the Committee in War Relief offer the following suggestions that must appeal to one's sense of justice:
The committee have held several meetings and have sent out a
general appeal for voluntary snbscriptions to the War Relief Fund.
These subscriptions are being collected through the various constituent Lodges. It is confidently hoped and believed that a large
sum will be raised and that we shall be able to take care of our
wounded Brethren and their dependents in a way that is in keeping
with the standing and professions of our fraternity.
It is our purpose to ket•p in touch with our memhers who are serving in any branch of the military or naval service of their countrv, and
to give thetn and their dependents such assistance as may he needed.
Letters are constantly being received from men who have· enlisted and
who are now stationed in the various camps (some acros~ the water)
telling of their experiences and needs.
One case came to my attention yesterday of a member of our fraternity who was drafted and who was obliged to leave a wife and twomonths-old baby to live on an income that would not exceed fom lumdred dollars a year. It would be to the everlasting shame of our Brethren if we did not seek out just such cases and provide suitable food,
clothing and housing. We ean and should supply all of the dependents
of our Brethren who are in the service with the actual necessal'ies of life
without their being obliged to call for them.

The attitude of the Grand Lodge of Alberta is shown by this action:
At the convocation of Grand Lodge held in the city of Red Deer,
i11 May, 1915, there was established a Patriotic Fund for Masonic De1w11dents. Two thousand ($2,000) dollars was appropriated to this fund
;11 the convocations of 1915 and 1916.
Subscriptions from the various
J ,mlges within the jurisdiction have augmented these appropriations, and
at this date there is a balance of three thousand six hundred and ninctvfour ($3,694) dollars standing at the credit of the fund.
•
The objects of the fund arc as follows:
(a) To assist our .Masonic retnrned vett•rans in case of need,
diher by way of immediate grants of money, or to procure hospital and
1m·dical attention, employment, homes, etc.
(b) To aid dependents of our soldier brethren overseas needing
:i'sistance.
( c) To provide assistance in cases of need for the widows and
orphans of our soldier brethren, deceased, also to procure homes for,
and advance the education of their children.
·
( d) To assist in work of the Y. M. C. A. and other kindred insti111tions at the front.
Our obligations to our brethren at the front and their dependents
a1 home are very great, and as a fraternity, we have done little up to the
pri:sent time to discharge them. In this connection, I cannot do better
lhan quote the words of our Past Grand ::Vfaster. M. \V. Brother E. T.
Bishop, in his address to Grand Lodge a few weeks ago:
"As I went from place to place I saw in our Lodges the names of
nnr men who have gone; the records of the men who have fallen .. Very

98

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

many of our brethren arc now at the front; many of them will never
return. All this is throwing upon us a responsibility which we cannot
ignore, and which it will be our greatest honor and our highest privilege to meet. The welfare of the widows and children of our departed
brethren must be, for years to come, the principal concern of this fraternity. Our obligation in this regard will not be answered by subscriptions suitable to our convenience, or given with consideration as to what
others give. Not until the giving hurts us <lo we really begin to give.
If the money and effort that are expended in less laudable ways in the
name of Masonry were directed to the help of the relatives of our brethren who need it, then would Masonry, indeed, be a great benefit to the
community, and not merely a hope but partially realized.
"If it were a question of the price to be exacted from us that we be
aJlow<.>d to remain in our own country that we might be with and care
for our loved ones, what would we not give, what would we not do?
This, 1 take it, is the nature of our obligation. This great privilege is
being purchased for us by the sacrifices of our Brothers overseas, by
the anguish of their wives, by the sorrows of their children. To pay
this debt we may easily do too little; we cannot do too much."
My aim is to bring the present fund up to $25,(X)() before the next
convocation of Grand Lodge, in May, 1918. With even slight effort at
organization this can be clone, and if the Masters, officers and brethren
of all Lodges take this matter as a sacred Masonic <luty, even more than
this might be accomplished.

NEW MEXICO.

In New Mexico the Grand Lodge, by a unanimous rising vote, took
this stand:

The undersigned, the committee appointed to consider and report
upon the advisability of investing a part of the permanent funds of this
Grand Lodge in bonds of the Second Liberty Bond issue of the government, after due consideration, begs to submit that in this extraordinary
crisis, the Grand Lodge of Masons can consistently show its deep patriotism and attachment to the principles of our government, by subscrib··
ing for ten thousand dollars of the Liberty Bonds of our national government, such sum to be taken from the Masonic Home Fund, and we
recommend that the committee having charge of this fund immediately
causr such subscription to be made in the name of the Grand Lodge.
We also recommend that the subordinate Lodges be advised and
counseled to purchase such number of these bonds as the funds in their
treasuries will warrant.
The Committee on Grand Master's Address, having referred the
last section of the Grand Master's address to this committee, we recommend that the same he published in the press of our state for the immediate information of the brethren of the craft. together with the fact
that this Grand Lodge has subscrillf'd for $10.000 of the Liberty Bonds.
The sentiments expressed hy the Grand Master should meet with the
hearty approval of every Mason.

UTAH.

The Grand Master of Utah has this to say of Libcrt.Y Bonds:
My understanding is that every Masonic organization within the
state; including not only the Blue Lodges, but the several Chapters,
Commanderies, Council, Scottish Rite, Shrine, and also Eastern Star
bodies, both state and subordinate, holds one or more Liberty Bonds,
and that the amount subscribed by the bodies alone is more than $20.00
per capita for each of our members.
Of even greater importance, however, is the fact that the influence
of the fraternity was everywhere directed to the furtherance of this
important work. A few illustrations of the effect may not be out of
place. Canyon Lodge, one of our country Lodges, having a membership
of only about eighty Masons, found itself able to purchase only $500.00
worth of the first issue of bonds, but it is reported to me that the membership of that particular Lodge purchased, at the time of the first issue,
bonds to the value of more than $15,000.00. The Lodge also took $500.00
worth of the second issue. In another country community within the
state, the individual subscriptions aggregated more than $200,<XXl.OO worth
of the first issue (with no individual subscription exceeding $500.00), and
over $400,000.00 worth of the second issue. It is not possible to identify
absolutely the Masonic work done in that community at that time, other
than to the extent that our membership at that point not only co-operated to the utmost of their ability, but also were very largely instrumental in the promotion and sale of the bonds. .

VIRGINIA.

The Grand Master of Virginia sent out this call:
Early in the summer of this year the President of the United States
and those in authority under him, realizing the demand for financial aid
in the great struggle in which our country is engaged, appealed to the
people of our nation to purchase bonds generally designated as "Liberty
Bonds." Deeming the matter of the utmost importance to the present
and future welfare of all the people, I dared to issue a circular letter to
each of the subordinate Lodges in the Grand Jurisdiction calling attention to. the proposition and suggesting in a very general way that such·
Lodges as were in position financially so to do, could safely invest such
,;urplus money as they might have, and at the same time lend a helping
hand to one of the noblest movements that has ever demanded our attention as a fraternity. No complete report of the amount of money subscribed has heen received, but from several Lodges it has been asce1·tainc-d that bonds in various amounts were purchased, and I have the
fullest belief that the Lodges, so far as possible, have done their full
duty.
OREGON.

The Grand Lodge of Oregon adopted the following report of a
special committee :
Your special committee, to whom was referred the portion of the
Grand Master's address treating of an Emergency War Fund for the
special relief of soldiers and sailors who are Masons, recommend that
no action be taken in the matter because of the limited state of our
finances and for the reason that creation of special funds leads to duplication of effort in a field already covered more effectively by the American Red Cross and the Y otmg Men's Christian Association.
Concentration of effort, under efficient .central control, is far more
beneficial to the cause in view.

ADDRESS OF GRAND MASTER
The Grand Master th,en delivered his annual address,
as follows:
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

As we approach the conclusion of one of the most significant aml
portentous years in the history of the world, I cannot forbear to direct
attention briefly to the conditions which prevai:cd one year ago, when
I entered upon the discharge of the duties of Grand Master.
The entire civilized world was more or less actively engaged in a
death struggle, was just beginning to sec gleams of light in the darkness, was just beginning to feel that the end was dimly in sight, to feel
that the forces of Ught and Civilization were bound to triumph. But
few, if any, had any reasonable hope, much less assurance that the
victorious end was near, and that the forces of darkness, r~prcscntcd
and functioning through the mightiest military machine in the world's
history, had met their Waterloo.
It was then, with almost a fce!ing of stupefaction, that when the
armistice was signed, early in N ovcmbcr, we realized that the feared
and hated German machine had collapsed, and that the mighty menace,
\Var'. .no longer .was to be , feared, if the problems arismg rrom that
cond1t10n were rtghtly and wisely faced and handled.
But it was no light or conventional task which the leaders of civilization faced in the attempt to restore order out of chaos, and to so
handle the situation that a· just and lasting peace might ensue.
If such were the difficulties and pcrp'.cxitics attending the lcaclcrs
of forty nations, it is no tmlust thing to say that such were the difficulties of the worlcl and humanity as a whole. ] low much more significant a_nd . importa.nt . was the ;espon.sihility resting upon that great
humamtanan Institutton of which tlus gram! jurisdiction was and is
a component part. Neither to this country nor to this State had come
the most trying features of war. Our lands had not been devastated
nor invaded. But we had been callecl upon to pour out of our blood

334

PROCEEDINGS 01!' THE

and our treasure, and business, social and family tics had been rudely
broken and disorganized.
It remained, then, for us as Americans and above all as Masons,whose sole reason for existence rests fundamentally on our recognition of the essential bonds of this common humanity,-to gird up our
loins, and enter heart and soul into the weighty problems of reconstruction and rehabilitation. So that in proportion as we have realized
the problems and risen to our responsibility the history of that struggle is to some extent the history of California Masonry throughout
the past year.
With this recognition of our responsibility, I conceived it to be
the duty of California Masons to lend a hand wherever possible, to the
furtherance of the work of those great organizations which had distinguished themselves so signally in the fields of human service. I
therefore gladly circularized the Lodges of this grand jurisdiction in the
interests of the Red Cross; and believing that the objects of service to
and for our devoted heroes could best be accomplished by centralized
bodies already organized, I declined to lend the aid of this Grand
Lodge to the more or less sporadic efforts of well-intentioned and
devoted brethren to initiate new movements under exclusively Masonic
names and labels.
The fact that other organizations, such as the Knights of Columbus,
were doing good and efficient work in a limited way, and securing unlimited advertising thereby, seemed to me no good reason for spending
time, effort and money to dup'.icate the noble and efficient work already
initiated am! splendidly carried on hy the Red Cross, the Y. M. C. A.
and the Salvation Army. I therefore declined an invitation to participate
in a conference of Grand Masters held in Iowa' early in the present
year, and which. had for its object the organization of an Overseas
Mission to carry on distinctively Masonic service overseas.
I believed then, and I still believe, that the same time, energy and
expense lavished 011 this abortive attempt to do something distiHctively,
Masonic among our boys overseas, might better and more efficiently
have been employed in the service of those agencies already established,
Knowing that one of the greatest and most urgent prob'.l'.!ms of·
reconstruction was the re-employment of those who had given
up their places, in order to enter the service of their country, I .·cir-·
cularized the Lodges of this grand jurisdiction, requesting the appoint-.
ment of a committee in each Lodge, to· have for its S[)Ccial care the
taking up of that problem for the members of that Lodge, believing
that by thus segregating and placing the responsibility, each Lodge conld
take care of its own; and I have reason to believe from the reports
which have reached me, and the ahscnce of complaint, that this work
has been efficiently and faithfully carried out.

NtCROLOGY

Our dearly beloved Brother Frederick W. Clough, for many years
Inspector of the 23rd Masonie District, contracted the dread influenza
at or in1111ediately following our session of 1918, in which he participated
with his usual earnestness and enthusiasm. He was unable to overcome the attack and passed to his rest on October 24, 1'918, to the
great sorrow and distress of his devoted family and many friends ~n.d
brethren. It needed no such experience, but during a subsequent v1S1t
to Brother Clough's home and the region where he was most active,
I found his name a household word, and throughout the district it was
evident that in the passing of Brother Clough a great and irreparable
loss had been suffered, not alone by the Lodges, but hy the communities
of that district, and we know that the memory of his many virtues is
safely recorded in every Mason's heart.
On the arrival of Brother Baker and myself at Chico, January
23, 1919, we were greatly shocked and grieved by the receipt of a telegram from our Grand Secretary, announcing the sudden death of the
M:.w:.wmiam Sewall Wells, Grand Master of this jurisdiction in
1901. \Ve immediately returned, convened the Crand Lodge in special
session at Oakland, the home of Brother Wells, and at the Scottish
Rite Cathedral in that city and subsequently at the crematory, I conducted the funeral of our deceased brother in accordance with the
so?emn rites of the Order.

Brother Wells had been so long and intimately associated with
the larger activities of the Grand Lodge, and particularly with the
organization and management of our Homes, that it seemed impossible
that that important feature of our work could go on without him. His
work for the Homes was so manifestly a labor of love that he had
endeared himself to the hearts of the Trustees and residents alike, and
no words of mine can adequately portray our profound sense of ~;orrow
and bereavement in the transition of our distinguished brother to that
Supreme Lodge above where his great heart of love can find untrammelled expression and where the wicked cease from troubling and
the weary arc at rest.
Our official family suffered another severe loss in tlic sudden
passing on September 12, 1919, of Brother Frank E. l'viorrell, Inspector
of the First District. Brother Morrcll's earnest and sympathetic
handling of that sparsely settled district, extending from Ferndale to
Crescent City, a distance of 125 miles, had endeared him alike to the
Grand Lectnrer and the brethren of his district, and our deepest and
heartfelt sympathy goes out to the brethren who have lost a most
efficient Inspector, and more particularly to his hcloved family, wh~.
have sustained a deep and lasting personal loss.
This Grand Jnrisdictio11 has suffered Sl'Vt'rPly in the loss at the
front and in cantonments of those brave and va!iant ia<b of our membership, who made the great and supreme sacrifice in the cause of
Country and Liberty, and it has therefore been deemed fitting to extend
the purview of our annual memorial service to our brave soldier dead.
To that end, the program has hccn arranged for such service, so that
this grand !Jody may properly and fittingly express in that service its
:ippreciation of the noble sacrifice of those heroes.

All these functions were enjoyable, and the details were worked
out hy the committees in charge to the last degree, each guest being
attended to as though he were the only person to be looked after. The
great and crowning event of course was the Peace Jubilee meeting.
To adequately describe the meeting at Albert Hall on the afternoon
of June 27, a book would be required. The actual registered attendance
was as follows: Masters, Wardens and Past Masters, 7523; Visitors,
182; Grand Officers, including Grand Stewards, 625; total, 8330. This
in addition to many Master Masons in the galleries not in regalia.
As was stated in the London Times of the next morning, "Craftsmen
were present from all parts of the British Empire-dignity and brilliance being added to the stately ceremonial by the many gradations
of color which distinguished the clothing of the brethren of the many
jurisdictions now spread over the surface of the globe. Men came
from the .City of London and from every province in England; from
Scotland and from I relarnl. Australia, Canada, New Zcalond, South
Africa, and a dozen or more dominions and dependencies sent their
representatives. Guests were gathered from America, where Grand
Masters and Grand Secretaries arc as numerous as the stars and
stripes that embellish the hattlc-staincd folds of Old Glory. When
the battle trenches stretched from the North Sea to the Mediterranean,
the United States sent her sons lo light for the salvation of Europe.
Now specially-chosen messengers came to hear part in common thanksgiving that Peace was once more within sight. Altogether it was
an assembly worthy of a great and historic occasion. As a spectacle
alone the scene deserved record. Massed around the Grand Master
on the platform were the purple and gold of the Provincial Grand

Brother Hervey and I took with us to England, by your direction,
a trowel as the gift from the Lodges of California to the Mother Grand
Lodge. I hand you herewith a photograph of this artistic piece of
work. It was my privilege to present this trowel on Saturday evening,
June 28, at a banquet given by Jubilee Masters' Lodge, there being
present probably five hundred brethren. My. remarks on this occasion
were substantially, as follows:
"I came to your land at fhe gracious invitation of Ili~ Royal
Highness the Duke of Connaught, Grand Master of the United Gram)
Lodge of England, knowing you only by tradition and through your·
good work and good influence as Masons, for which we of Atnerica
had formed an opinion which amounted to genuine affection. I have
now for a full week tasted of your sweet hospitality, and can say with·
·truth that I have spent a week in a paradise of good fellowship, the
memory of which I will carry back with me to my distant home as a
precious souvenir like unto sweetest forgctmenots. Ilut I cannot let'
this glorious week pass into history without executing a pleasant duty
commanded of me by the Grand Master of Masons in California, six
thousand miles to the westward.
"Your Masonic brethren-not cousins-but brethren, of the jurisdiction which I have the honor to represent, are but yotiths in the
great work of the Masonic Institution, but we are inspired to effort
by the traditions of our Mother Grand Lodge of England. In our
humble but earnest way we, like you, are fighting the good fight for
civic and personal righteousness, and are keeping the faith as taught
by our forebears of old England. And as visible evidence of our esteem,
our reverence, our love for the United Grand Lodge of England, I am
commanded by my Grand Master to present to you, and through you
to the proper custodian of your Grand Lodge, this trowel, ancl with it
the greetings of your brethren of the land by the sunset sea, on the
western shores of America. If I am correctly advised, it is an instrument not known to the ritualistic work of the Lodges of England,
except possibly in the Province of Bristol. Its use in the hands of the
operative Mason is obvious, that of spreading the cement which unites
the building into one common mass; and of all operative tools it is
the most indispensable. Therefore have we sent you our most precious

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

345

working tool, which all American Masons are taught symbolically to
use for the noble and glorious purpose of spreading the cement of
brotherly love and affection; that cement which unites us and all Masons
into one sacred band or society of friends and brothers, among whom
no contention should ever exist but that noble contention, or rather
emulation, of who best can work and best agree.
"This trowel is typically and essentially Californian. Its component parts of gold quartz, of onyx, of silver and of gold, were taken
from the rugged mountains of our golden State, and fashioned by the
loving hands of Masonic artisans, true descendants of that first artificer
in metals whose name is known to all Masons. The casket in which
this trowel rests was made from the burl of the sequoia gigantea, the
largest and noblest tree in the world. This tree, which is found only
in California, can trace its genealogy in direct descent beyond history,
and is the oldest Ii ving thing on the earth. It flourished full grown Jong
before the building of King Solomon's temple at Jerusalem; it was a
giant of the forests when Moses was rocked in his cradle of rushes;
and if Jethro's flocks had wandered afar to our shores, they might
have browsed in peace aild plenty beneath the shade of these monarchs
of arboreal beauty. To my mind therefore, this casket is a fitting
resting place for this gift of my brethren to the oldest Masonic body
in the world; and I have much pleasure, sir, in placing it in your hands
as tangible and visible evidence of our loyalty and 'love to you and
your brethren, in the hope and with the prayer that the legend engraved
on the face of this trowel will stimulate you, and all who view it, to
heartily assist in the great work of spreading the cement of Brotherly
Love."
Brother Sir Alfred Robbins, President of the Board of General
Purposes, accepted the gift with every manifestation of pleasure. It
would, he said, serve to commemorate a most wonderful week. In the
history of Freemasonl'y that week would stand out as marking the first
occasion on which so many representatives of the English-speaking
world had foregathered from all parts of the globe. He said the Grand
Lodge of England would treasure the trowel as a link between them
and the Grand Lodge of California.
I devoted as much time as I could to a study of English methods
of raising revenues for their poor, and heartily commend their manner
of teaching their members the glory of giving voluntarily. A brief
sketch of their several charities is herewith submitted:
The Royal Masonic In.rtitution for Girls, located at Clapham Junction, London: Number in institution, 377; girls out-educated and
u1aintained, 328. Expenditures for year ending December 31, 1918,

$200,000. The expenses include girls' holiday traveling expenses, $3200;
for gratuities and outfits to girls leaving the school, $1700; girls educated and maintained out of the school, $50,000; office expenses, $26,000;
and pensions to former governesses, $3000. It is of interest to note that
of the office expenses, $13,000 go to salaries, and $1600 are paid for

Girls are admitted to the bene8ts of the Institution for "out-education" and maintenance on practically the same terms and conditions as
those who elect to attend the school at Clapham.

346

The fixed income of this Institution is $55,000, and the donations last
year amounted to $300,000. Unexpected balances are invested, and
go to swell the fixed income. Lodges are not taxed for the maintenance
of the Institution, it depending entirely, as above indicated, on voluntary donations from Lodges, Chapters, etc., and from individual Masons.
Some money is received yearly from legacies. The form of bequest
adopted and found to be legally sufficient is as follows:
"I give and bequeath unto the Treasurer, for the time being, of
the Royal Masonic Institution for Girls, Clapham Junction, the sum of
........................ , to be applied for the general purposes of the lnstituti~n."
Girls whose mothers desire to have tbem at home during the
holidays are permitted to leave the Institution for the purpose, their
traveling expenses being paid by the Trustees. Holidays are three
weeks at Easter, six weeks in the summer and a month at Christmas.
Other ho:idays are the last Saturday in ] une (ex-pupils' day), and
afternoons of each Wednesday and Saturday.
No girl is eligible for admission to the Institution undeF six
or over eleven years of age, and must be recommended by two subscribers and the Master and Wardens of a Lodge; nor unless her
father has been a member of a Lodge under the English Constitution
for seven years. "No girl shall remain after the age of sixteen years,
except upon the recommendation of the Head Mistress and with the
approval of the House Committee."
If it be shown that any girl in J:he Institution exhibits marked
talent for a particular branch of education, calculated to be practically
useful to her in after life, the Trustees have discretionary power to
afford such girl the means of extra instruction. Under this rule
many girls are sent to other schools.

Children under the age of six, who require Masonic aid, are looked
after by the Board of Benevolence.
Before any girl be received into the Institution, a written guarantee
must be given by two responsible "householders to remove her if required by the Trustees, to receive her upon leaving, and in case of death,
to bury her free of expense to the Institution.

Daughters of ] ewish parents may be educated Gut of the Institution,
if their guardians so desire.
All the members of the resident staff received their early education in the school. The girls receive a sound education, including hospital nursing, shorthand, typewriting, pianoforte, singing, swimming,
and calisthenics, and are employed by turns in the domestic duties of
the house. Great pains are taken to render them skilful in needlework,
dressmaking, and practical cookery. Dinners served to the Trustees
are cooked by the girls, and the prii1cipal dishes bear the names of the
girl cooks. The Trustees always call in the girls after dinner, and
praise-or censure-each dish and girl.
The Royal Masonic Institution for Boys, at Bushey, Hertfordshire:
The Institution for Boys is supported largely in the same way as the
Institution for Girls-by voluntary contribution from Masonic bodies
and from Masons. Nearly eight hundred boys receive the benefits of
the Institution, of which four hundred are at Bushey, the others-being
between the ages of six and ten-are receiving "out-education" socalled, many of them being with their mothers. The conditions of
admission are much the same as at the Institution for Girls; Sixtyodd boys beyond fifteen years of age are being retained this year for
higher education. The fixed income of this Institution is about $50,000
a year; the ordinary annual expenditure is $210,000 and not less than
$160,000 is required to be raised each year by voluntary contributions.
At the annual festival in May, 1919, the donations to the Boys' Institution aggregated $435,000. The boys are well cared for, ancl sent out
from the Institution well equipped to battle with "life ancl be self-supporting members of society. Through Scholarship Funds a consiclcrablc
number of boys are sent to the best universities and technical schools.
The Masonic Bene11olent Institution at Croydon provides for and
pays annuities to aged Masons and the widows of Masons. No Mason is
eligible under the age of sixty years, ilor unless a member of his Lodge
for at least fifteen years, and whose income is in excess of $150.00 a
year. And no widow is eligible under the age of sixty years whose
income is more than $150 a year, nor unless her last husband had been
a member of a Lodge for ten years. This Institution costs about $150,000 a year, and all the funds are raised by yearly donations.
In aclclition to the three charities above mentioned, there is the
Board of Benevo!ence, associated directly with Grand Lodge, intrusted
with a special fund raised annually, devoted solely to relief. Brother
John White, Deputy Past Grand Master for Kent, is Chairman of the

Committee charged with raising funds for this benevolence for the

To summarize the voluntary yearly donations of English Masons, as
shown by last year's receipts:

The membership of the jurisdiction is about 200,000.
These donations do not come alone from wealthy members . . On
the contrary, they come from the great body of "average" Masons,
who are taught from the day they apply for the privileges of Freemasonry that it is the glory of our Institution that its ritual and
practice arc to regard the human species as one family, and that to
relieve the distressed is a duty incumbent on all Masons; that Masonry
gives a foremost place to the privileges and obligations of practical
benevolence; and that actual giving of something for the distressed
brother, his widow and orphan, is an indispensable quality in all
members of our ancient and honorab!e, craft. The novitiate and members arc enjoined that while benevolence is not the only good quality
of Masonry, yet they arc urged to remember that it is the outward
and visible sign of the inward and spiritual grace which exists in
our Institution, and which ought to be the ideal of its members.
The ritualistic work in English Lodges is much the same, in aJJ.
essentials, as in American jurisdictions. The lectures and opening
ceremonies arc shorter, and more time is given to the social side of
:Y:Iasonry than to ritualism. Lodges with large memberships are not
known, it being the rule that members must know one another and
be personally "grata." The usual meeting hour is six o'clock, and
Lodge work or business is finished by seven o'clock, when the members and visitors repair to dinner. By ten o'clock, or a little later, •
the brethren go to their homes.

349

I have no recommendations to make, but call your serious atten·
tion to the good points of Masonic practice as established by our
brethren of the Grand Lodge of England, particularly with relation
to the social side of Masonry, which they deem of more importance
than the ritualistic side. They teach, enough of ritual to inculcate in
the minds of their novitiates that Masonry stands first and foremost
for the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man; for personal
righteousness; for law and order; for good and orderly government by
orderly men; and that man is his brother's keeper. At their social
gatherings they aim to, and do, bring to the surface the good qualities
of their members-and never lose sight of their obligations to the
poor and distressed in their midst. The matter of relief is not referred
to the Lodge treasury, but to the individual member, who, as I stated
above, is early taught that his obligations as a Mason extend to his
personal purse, with the result that nearly every Mason of an English
Lodge yearly contributes not only to his Lodge treasury sufficient to
pay the ordinary running expenses of the Lodge, but to the several
charities maintained by Committees of Grand Lodge, as well to Scholarships to aid poor boys and girls to extend their education even to the
larger universities and schools of technology.
The visit across seas was expensive in time and energy and money,
but I believe it was well worth it all. And if any of the suggestions
noted appeal to you or to Grand Lodge as being worthy of even further
investigation, I shall be amply repaid, and content.

JOUN WITTCHER,

I referred previously to the zealous cooperation and inestimable
assistance of our V.'.\V.'. Grand Lecturer, and I want to repeat again,
and as a basis for the recommendation which follows, that travels with
him have brought home to me with great force that Brother Baker has
111 ade of the office of Grand Lecturer a vital and valuable force in the
Ma sonic life of this State.
At no time has he spared himself or limited his efforts to the
activities which might naturally be supposed to belong to the sphere of
his duties. On the other hand, there has been no s.lightest suggestion
n f officiousness or interference with the prerogative of any other office.
Nothi.ng but the most zealous cooperation and kindly and disinterested
~ympathy has marked his intercourse with the brethren of the State.
It is difficult to define in words what I mean when I say that Brother
Baker has made of the office of Grand Lecturer a monumental factor
i 11 Masonic life. It needs to be seen and lived with day after day and
month after month, as I have been privileged to do while traveling with
Brother Baker. The physical and nervous strain of the office is
st upcndous, and I know from personal observation that an average of
sixteen hours a day is devoted by Brother Baker gladly and sympa1hctieally to the duties of his office. In view of the marked increase
in his labors, due in great part to the phenomenal growth of the Instil nlion and the vastly increased expense of all the means and incidents
of cxi stence, and, above all, the unique place which Brother Baker has
made for himself and his office in the State, I strongly recommend a
snhstantial increase in his salary.

By the presentation of a petition and resolution from San Fernando
Lodge No. 343, seconded by the action of Elysian Lodge of Los Angeles, the Grand Master and Grand Lodge have been requested to grant
San Fernando Lodge concurrent jurisdiction with the Lodges of Los
i\ngeles-thus bringing to the front the troublesome question of j urisdiction.
It is evident that a very manifest hardship is worked upon San
Fernando Lodge by the curtailing of its territory, dne to annexation
of surrounding territory by Los Angeles, and the operation of our
present rigid law governing these situations. San Fernando Lodge is
entirely surrounded by the city of Los Angeles, and necessarily is conlined to its own city limits in its territorial jurisdiction, so that while it
originally had 700 square miles of territory to draw from, it now has
but one.
Under our present law, the Grand Master has no power to remedy
this situation, as Sections 82 and 92A apply only to defining limits of
exclusive jurisdiction, and not to concurrent. It seems to me, however,
that this and many similar situations throughout the State deserve a
remedy, and I would strongly recommend that our law be so amended,
or added to, that concurrent jurisdiction could be granted Lodges in
similar situations, where it would be manifestly just to do so.
As an alternative, it has hcen suggested that our entire policy with
reference to jurisdiction be changed, and that we adopt the same rule
therein which now prevails on application for affiliation. In other words,
that we permit a petitioner for the degrees to apply to any Lodge in
the State, upon notifying the Lodge nearest his place of residence, of
his intention so to do.
I firmly believe some definite action should he taken in one or the
other direction at this communication, for the present law bears particularly hard upon many Lo(Jges and <listr:cts.
I approved the consolidation of TuG!umnc Lml"c No. 8 and Cconyc
Washington Lodge No. 62, although constitutional requirements could
not be complied with strictly hy Cconi;c Wa~hin'.'J<m, owing to its inability to hold meetings or reach all its members.
Since 1913, when a similar situation arose, in that it was impossible for one of the Lodges desiring to consolidate to ho~d the meeting
required by the constitution, it has been prrmittcd to take the written
ballots for or against the proposed consolidation, and when the assent
of three-fourths of the members of said Lodge was so ohtain,~d, the
consolidation has been permitted and such action hy P.'.G.".:\1.'.Angellotti and the Committee on Jurisprudence has been repeatedly approved by the Grand Lodge. No change in our organic law has been
made, however, definitely permitting such procedure.

In the case of George Washington Lodge now before us, we were
confronted with an additional obstacle. It was impossible to locate
and obtain answer of any sort from nine of the members of George
Washington Lodge, and there were but twenty-eight members on the
rolls. The nineteen members located, unanimously voted for the
proposed consolidation. Confronted then with this impasse, it was
either necessary to let the proposed consolidation go by the board and
permit George Washington Lodge to languish still further, and ultimately
forfeit its charter, or I must go one step further along the road'tnarked
out by my illustrious predecessors, and approve the consolidation upon
the unanimous written consent of all the members of George Washington Lodge who could be located, after diligent search, certified to by
the Secretary, even though such number of consents fell short by two
of the constitutional three-fourths required. Believing it to be in the
interest of justice and sound common sense, and the other party to
the proposed consolidation, Tuolumne Lodge, having performed in
strict accord with the Constitution, I accepted the action of (;corge
Washington Lodge as a substantial and sufficient compliance with
the requirements, and approved the consolidation. That it may not he
necessary in the future to so strain the legal requirements, I would
recommend that our constitution be so amended that si111ilar situations
be taken care of within the strict letter of the constitution.

Throughout the year I have hem 1·cpcatcdly asked to decide the
eligibility for admission to our Order of candidates who have suffered
the loss of one or both hands or feet, and in every case I have decided
that it was the intent of 'the amemlm('nt of 1913 to Section 94 of the Con'.·,
stitution, substituting therein the word "substantially" for "literally,"
to relax the rigidity of our former rule, and vest the Master and the
subordinate Lodge with discretion to determine in each individual case
whether or not the applicant could conform su/Jsta11ti111ly to the require- ,
ments of the different degrees; and with such preamble, have held
that an applicant who had lost his left hand or arm or either foot or
leg below the knee, especially where the loss had been supplied by an .
artificial limb, was not by reason of sueh loss ineligi!Jlc.
Our sister jurisdiction of Iowa bas p;one a skp fortlwr, rmd
definitely provided that where the loss has been replaced hy an artificial·
member, permitting a substantial compliance with the requirements of
the degrees, he was not ineligible, the Grand Master of Iowa stating
in his reeornmendation for such amendment, that we had better accept
members with wooden legs than with wooden heads.
