GROWTH OF THI\ ORD!lR.

At tlic conclusion of the last Grand Lodge year, it was seen that
the net gain in membership for the year l9l'l had Ileen phc110111cn;;l and
unprecedented, and it was undoubtedly felt by many that this phenomenal growth was due in large measure to war conditions. Today, however, upon a survey of the year just past, most of which has "been
without the period of war, we find that the phenomenal growth has
still continued, and that the net gain of last year, 3591, has been surpassed in this, and that the membership in this State has been increased
to the extent of 3887 members. This in itself, and so far as numbers·
go to indicate strength and interest, is an encouraging indication of tiie
general . con~ition, not alone of our Order, but of thinking men, .in
that tlit:tr 111mds and attention are being turned to an Institution based
upon principles such as ours, and which promises something in the
way of self-development and self-expression. Sufficient has been said
by earlier and abler kaders and writers in Masonry to prevent anv
undue elation over large accessions in numbers. We are constantly;
ringing the changes on the doctrine that it is quality and not quantity
that we seek and that we are not at all interested in acquiring members,
unless they also shall be, or appear likely to become, Ma sons, in fact
as well as in name. I do not desire to trespass on tlic attention of the·
Grand Lodge in reiterating at tiresome length the very evident truth
of these propositions, and that our attitude should continue the same
upon this all vital point. I have the courage to believe from my observation throughout the State, and my correspondence with other
jurisdictions, that a greater and more vital interest is being taken
in what Masonry stands for than ever before, but whether or not•
that awakening of interest in vital topics is a by-product or in any
sense clue to war conditions, is really not important. The sa 'icnt thinq is
.that there is this awakening of interest, and it is most decidedly a
feature which must be taken into account in our calculations, and
as we recognize the fact, we realize that more and more it is true that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

359

the eyes of the world are upon us, and that our responsibility is correspondingly enhanced.

In the light of this view, I watched with intense interest the responses of the Masters of this grand jurisdiction to my request for suggestions for the Good of the Order. Many of them have been both
illuminating and instructive. To draw a composite conclusion from the
great mass of suggestions I have received, I should say that I find a
pronounced undercurrent of dissatisfaction at undue emphasis placed
upon ritualistic activities. In other words, the remedy, if such there
be for these conditions, seems clearly indicated to confer fewer degrees,
take less time of the Lodges in so doing, and emphasize the social
features by the maintenance of club rooms, by holding frequent social
and educational meetings, which shall be devoted to these purposes
alon~, without the addition of any ritualistic work; and to the encl of the
promotion of the social feature, I find considerable sentiment in favor
of more frequent banquets as a means of furthering social interest
and feeling. I realize that it is hardly possible for a large Lodge,
especially if it lets its intention be known, to banquet its own members and receive hospitably the visitors who would naturally come to
such occasions. So that we are confronted with a practical difficulty,
even though this feature be, and I believe is, most desirable.
In conclusion, then, it seems that so far as we can make a
general recommendation, it should be along the line of emphasizing
the social and fraternal features of our Order. If we can once get
the great mass of the brotherhood to realize that there is nothing
more important than the recognition of the common bonds of humanity, that the doctrine of brotherhood means in very fact just
what it says, that we are all descendants of one Almighty Father, that
we arc linked together, in fact as well as in name, by an indissolub!e tie of sincere affection, I venture the prediction that we will
see the Masonic Order take its rightful 11lace as a dynamic force
in the Na ti on, and in the life of the people, and that it will command
recognition not alone for its professions, not alone for the beauty
of its doctrines, but des<;rvcdly for its solid, practical accomplishment
in all constructive po!icies and endeavors for the uplift and unity of
Humanity.
BRADFORD WEBSTER,

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
I have the honor to report herewith the transactions of the
Grand Secretary's office for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1919,
together with a detailed account of all moneys received within the
year, and a detailed and itemized statement of the dis bur semen ts of
the Grand Lodge. In addition thereto, I have appended an account o'f receipts since the close of business July 31 to and including October 2, 1919, and all uniinished business of Grand Lodge.

For the first time in many years the report is not complete
as to all the Lodges on our registery. Mokelumne Hill No. 298
and Loyalton No. 359 have not reported; Los Banos Lodge No,
312 has sent its annual report, but has not paid Grand Lodge du~s.
In my tabulation of membership I have included Los Banos Lodge
and estimated the two other delinquent Lodges.
Because of the scourge of influenza the Craft in California
suffered many losses, the toll of death being 50 per cent more
than last year. llut notwithstanding the fact that for many
months our Lodges were not permitted to meet, the great numbei;
0£ 17,233 degrees were conferred, being 3114 degrees more than
last yt·ar, ancl the net increase of membership for this year is 3904.
The net membership now is 67,890.
At the close of the last annual communication there were 382
Lodges on our regis_try, with a membership 'Of 63,986, a net gain
for that year of 3593. Charters were ordered issued at that cornmunication to Yorha Linda Lodge No. 469, located at Yorba
Linda, Orange County, constituted November 23, 1918, by Samuel
E. liurkc, Junior Grand Warden; Lincoln Lodge No. 470, located
at San Francisco, constituted October 11, 1918, by Bradford Webster, Grand Master; Delta Lodge No. 471, located at Stockton,
constituted December 12, 1918, by Bradford vVehster, Grand Master. And by resolution of Grand Lodge, after due petition, Lodge
Maui No. 472, located at Kahalui, Territory of Hawaii, was
granted a charter and was duly constituted December 14, 1918, by
James F. Fenwick, Inspector of the Sixty-sixth Masonic District.
Lodge Maui has been working for a long period of years under
obedience to the Grand Lodge of Scotland, which body generously
relinquished all claim to the Lodge and its property.

Unfinished Business.
At the last annual communication the following resolution was
adopted:
"Resolved, that it is the intention of this Grand Lodge, acting
on behalf of the whole craft of Masonry in the grand jurisdiction of
California, to erect, in this our Temple, as soon as may be after the
close of the war in which our nation is now engaged, a tablet in
hronze as a lasting testimonial of love and memory to those Masons
who have gone forth from the Lodges of this jurisdiction to fight
for justice among men and nations and to exalt the sacred cause of
democracy." (Proceedings 1918, page 95.)

Constitution and Ceremonies.
Immediately after the close of Grand Lodge in 1918, I caused to
be printed six thousand copies of the Constitution and Ccrcm'onies,
at a cost of 39.6 cents each. The postage on a single book is S cents.
It was sold to Lodges and Brethren for SO cents a copy, postage
prepaid. In July of this year the entire edition was sold, and an
edition of fifteen hundred copies was printed, at a cost of S2 cents
each-being the actual cost to the printer. This lot has now been
sold, at the old price of SO cents a copy. I find that because of the
increase of wages, paper and cloth it will he impossible to secure
another edition of the book for less than SS cents a copy, ancl if
many changes arc made in the Constitution, that price may be increased slightly. I therefore ask that Grand Lodge intimate the
price to be charged for the hook to be printed this fall, and recommend that it be fixed at SO cents, Grand Lodge absorbing the loss.

Suspensions for Non-Payment of Dues.
Every year the suspensions for non-payment of dues indicate
that we arc probably unnecessarily losing members. It will not he
seriously disputed that one who has been suspended will feel hurt
and refuse or neglect to take further active interest in Masonry.
Some of our best Lodges-Lodges whose members maintain the
keenest pride in keeping their fellows enthused with the notion that
theirs is just a little the best Lodge in the jurisdiction-have small
losses for non-payment of dues. This spirit should pertain in all
onr Lodges. And I therefore again urge upon Masters to provide
committees whose particular duties will he to personally interview
det!nc1uent members and ascertain in a friendly way the cause of
the delinquency. If the committee reports that the delinquent member has met with misfortune which his pride will not permit him to
report to his Lodge, that fact should he reported and the Brother's
ciaes remitted and a receipt for dues sent to him without the asking.

37S

If the committee finds that a member is spending too much money
for non-essentials, the Brother should be kindly admonished-and
experience has proved that this sort of endeavor ~ill result in fewer
suspensions and a better spirit of Lodge fellowsh1p.

MEMORIAL SERVICES
A_ very ~olernn service in memory of our dead-Inspectors Frederick Warren Clough (died October 24, 1918),
Frank Edward Morrell (died September 12, 1919), Past
Grand Master William Sewall Wells (died January 23,
1919), and those of our members who lost their lives in the
service of their country, was held.

Most Worshipful Gmnd Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

The greatest tragedy of life is death. And just as we are aho11t
to realize the hopes of our ambition in our travels thro11gh this
transitory world, often the cold finger of death touches us and we
are called to our eternal home. It was the privilege and pleasure of
the Grand Master at the last Convocation to :mnl'!unce to the brethren that the linger of death had not touched any member of the official family of the Grand Lodge during that year, and we had sincerely hoped and trusted that the past year would also giv~ to \lS

388

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

such a record; but hardly had the goodbyes been said and the exchange of departing messages given by our brethren, before one of
our worthy and honored Inspectors, Brother Frederick W. Clough,
was called to his eternal rest. Brother Clough was one of those
!"fasons who endeared himself to the members of his constituency
m the Lodges which he served so faithfully and so well for a num?er o~ years, .and his loss is deeply felt not alone in the community .
m which he hved, but amongst his brother Inspectors and members
of the Grand Lodge. It was his privilege and his pleasure to be
~resent ~t ~he last session of the Grand Lodge, and he took a deep
mtere.st m its proceedings, I can picture him now, in my mind's eye,
standing upon this floor and claiming that the Inspectors had at last
been recognized in a ruling in which he was deeply interested. It
was a pleasure in his heart, and a pleasure for us to know that he
was taking such deep interest in Masonic affairs. In his home life he
was kindly and generous. The members of his neighborhood respected him as a citizen and friend, as we respected him as a true
and upright Mason. He labored in that portion of our jurisdiction
known as ."the ~outher~ ~ines," in Angels Camp, where the people
are open m. their hospttahty, true in their friendships, and firm in
acknowledgmg what is right and for the benefit of manki.nd.
Brother Clough grew up in that sturdy atmosphere and became one
of the leaders in its affairs, as well as a leader in Masonic principles.
We exten~ today our heartfelt sympathy to his survivfog relatives.
We feel his loss deeply and keenly, and we trust that his life has
set us an example to follow, and we· will long revere his memory.
Another memher of the Inspectors, one in the far North came
to his death during the latter part of this Masonic year, Fr~nk E.
Morrell, of the First District. He, too, was deeply imbued with
Masonic principles, and also undertook the work of spreading the
~o~pel of ~asonry and endeavored to hring out its purest teachings.
m its true light, and for the benefit of his brethren of the First Disirict; Raised in the mountains of the grand redwoods, where God's
sentmels have kept vigil over mankind, Brother Morrell was honored
and .r~spected by his fellow men. He was esteemed for his manly
qualities, as well as for his superior knowledge of the Masonic law.
The Inspectors and Grand Lodge, I feel certain, recognize that
in the demise of these two worthy brethren, our Grand Lodge has
suffered a loss which it will be hard to fill. Now, brethren let us
follow in the footsteps of these two Masons, whose lives' left a
lasting impress upon the communities in which they lived. Time
alone will replace their us.efulness with other good men and true.
We say to them, farewell, and sincerely trust that in the future we
shall meet' again in a higher plane.

Eulogy-William Sewall Wells-Frank M. Angellotti:
On the 23rd day of January of this year, William Sewall Wells,
l'ast Grand Master of this jurisdiction, in the prime of life and apparcnt'.y with many years of useful service before him, quietly passed from
us. For almost thirty years he had faithfully attended the annual communications of this body, giving to its work all of the splendid ability
of which he was possessed. By reason of his natural talents, his pleasing personality, his devotion to Masonry and his active interest in all
matters pertaining to the Craft, his had become a most familiar figure
to all those who have been attending the communications of the Grand
Lodge, and his absence from our midst today brings home with fu:I
force the realization that he is gone from us forever. Justly had he
rnme to he considered one of the pillars of Freemasonry in California.
Universally respected as he was by all of the Craft and beloved by all
those who cainc into intimate association with him, it is hard for us to
reconcile ourselves to his loss. The tribute that we offer to his memory
today is no merely formal thing, accorded so'.cly bt:causc of the high
official positions attained by him in Masonry, but something that truly
comes from the heart of each and every one of us who knew him well.
In preparing my few words of eulogy of Brother vVells, I have been
somewhat burdened by the feeling that what in simple justice I must
say concerning him, would be distasteful to him, could he hear, as
seeming llattcry. vVhile always desirous, of course, of the respect and
conliclcncc of his fol!ow men, which he with full right uniformly enjoyed
from the heg-inning to the eml of his line career, nothing could he more
repugnant to him than even the appearance of adulation. Indeed, he
cared little for words of commernlation at any time. vVhatever he did
was done simply because he felt that in vh:w of all the circmnstarn:es it
was the right aml proper thing to do, and he had no thought that he
was entitled to special praise for being faithful to the ohligations resting
upon him as a man and a Mason. That, with him, was a mere matter
of course-the essential thing for any honest man. Certainly he never
did anything for the mere purpose of ohtaining the praise of others. 111
all my long and intimate acquaintance with him extending over a
period of thirty years or more, I never knew him either here or elsewhere to say a word or do a thing designed to ohtain the applause of
the moment. To the contrary, always brave and fcnrless, he was ever
ready and willing to strike a blow for what he conceived to he the
right, regardless of any possible loss of immediate favor. All of you·
who knew him long and well will bear witness with me to this attribute
of Brother vV ells. It was as though there were engraven upon his
heart, as the rnlc am! guide of his life, the immortal words put by
Shakespeare into the mouth of Polonius:

390

l'HOCEEDlNUS 01•' '.l'H.El

"This above all-To thine own self be true;
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man."
Always conscious of his own honesty of purpose, he was content to
await such vindication as the sober thought and judgment of his contemporaries might bring, and he scorned, as involving an e'.ement of
dishonesty, the idea of resorting for his own glory and gain, to the
wiles and arts of the shrewd and cakulating seeker for popular favor.
\Vould that in this period of stress all over the world, when at times it
seems that the fate of civilized government is almost trembling in the
balance, we all lived more nearly up to the standard of our departed
brother in this respect, for never before were simple honesty and 'unselfishness of purpose more essential to a settlement of the difficulties
besetting mankind.
Brother \Veils was a faithful and devoted Mason. As a lover of
humanity, the principles and teachings of our fraternity appealed to him
with special force, and having become a Mason he henceforth to the
end of his life gave to Masonry the best that was in him. The bare
records demonstrate his devotion to duty and the confidence reposed in
him by his brethren. Made February 25, 1889, passed March 2, 1889,
and raised March 9, 1889, in Martinez Lodge No. 41, he continued .an
honored member of that Lodge to the time of his death. Within nine
months from the time he acquired membership iu the Lodge he was
e'.eeted from the floor to be \Vorshipful Master, and having been first
installed as Master on January 4, 1890, he was re-elected and re-elected·
until he had served in that exalted office for eight successive years.
What more convincing evidence of duty well performed and unfaltering
confidence on the part of his brethren could be given? During all thi>
period he was also the incumbent of the responsible office of Inspector
of his Masonic district, being first appointed to that office in April, 1890.
In Octohcr, 1890, he attended his first communication of this body, and
from the very outset took an active part in its work. He served on
various committees at the Communications of 1890, 1891, 1892 and 1893,
and in 1893 was appointed to the Committee on Grievances. On this
important commitee he served until and through the Communication of
1898, being from 1895 its chairman. At the Communication of 1898 he
was elected R.'.W.'.Junior Grand \Varden of the Grand Lodge. In 1899
he was elected R.'.W.'.Senior Grand Warden, and in 1900 he was
unanimously elected R.'.W.'.Deputy Grand Master. At the Communication of 1901 he was unanimously elected M.' ·\V: .Gram! Master of
Masons of California, thus being selected in a little over twelve years
from the time he was made a }.Jason to occupy the most exalted position
in Masonry in this jurisdiction. Of his administration, the committee
appointed to review his official acts, expressing their "great appreciation

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

391

of the zeal, the fidelity and the ability displayed by him in the discharge
of the trust committed to his charge," succinctly, and truly said: "We
honored him; he has faithfully served and honored us." He retired
from his high office but to continue in the service that he loved. Immediately appointed to the Committee on Jurisprudence, he continued to
he an active and faithful member of that committee, except for one
year, until in 1917, by reason of the responsibilities and labor imposed
on him as President of the Board of Trustees of our Masonic H.ome, he
felt constrai~ed to give up all other official positions in the Grand
Lodge. To the latter office he had been appointed in 1908, and he held
it by appointment each year, until his death. W c all know how unreservedly he gave himself to the work of this great practical charity of
our Fraternity, and how near and dear it was to his heart.
It was my privilege to be intimately associated with Brother \Velis
in much of his work in this Grand Lodge. \Ve were together prefcnt
at twenty-seven annual communications. For two years we were fellow
members of the Committee on Grievances. During my term of office
as Grand Master, he was Junior Grand \Vatden. For fourteen years
we were together members of the Committee on Jurisprudence. I feel
that I know of what I speak when I say that he was ever faithful
to duty, efficient in performance, wise in counsel and a loyal friend.
Surely we will sorely miss his kindly and helpful presence in this
Grand Lodge. His death means a loss to Freemasonry in this jurisdiction as to which we may well use the words of lamentation of an
o'.d Moorish ballad: "A tower is fallen, a star is set! Alas! Alas!
for Celin."
The career of Brother Wells in Masonry is but typical of his
career in every other walk of life. In selecting his life work he followed in the footsteps of his distinguished father, William S. Wells,
one of our pioneers, and was admitted to the bar in the year 1884.
After having practic<>d law in Contra Costa county for fifteen years
he was appointed judge of the superior court of that county, and was
subsequently twice elected to that office. Jn April, 1909, he was appointed judge of the superior court of Alameda county, and occupied
that important position to the time of his death, having been twice
elected to succeed himself. As a judge he stood unexcellcd among
the j udgcs of this commonwealth. His conscientious devotion to the
duties of his important and responsible office, his knowledge of legal
principles, his inherent love of justice, his sound common sense, his
fearlessness and freedom from demagogism, and his sympathy with the
unfortunate and oppressed, all combined to make him an ideal officer,
possessing at all times the respect and confidence and affection of both
the bar and the people. He was equally efficient in all the varied
duties that devolve upon a judge of the superior court, but it was

392

perhaps in the discharge of his duties while presiding over the juvenil~·
court work that he showed most clearly some of the traits that endeared him to the people of his county. The welfare of the unfortunate or wayward child who came before him, and whose future was
thus to some extent committed to his determination, was to him a!ways
a matter of supreme importance, worthy of his best consideration. and
utmost effort. One of the memories of Brother Wells that will ever
remain with me is of a call that he made one afternoon at mv cha~­
bcrs in this city, having come from his own chambers across .the bay
solely for the purpose of discussing wjth me how best he could dis- '
pose of the case of one of these little unfortunates. For over an hour
he talked with me about the case from every possible angle, his sole
desire being to adopt the course that would be for the child's best
interests. His abso'.utc devotion to the matter of this little child made
a lasting impression on my mind. I remember that a friend who was
with me that afternoon, meeting Brother Wells for the first tim·e. and
hearing the conversation, said, after he had gone: "That is a good
man." And so truly, he was. Many there doubtless arc who in the
years to come will realize that it is due to his kindly words, fri~ndly
council, patient consideration, and wise determination they were started
upon the way that has made of them worthy and self-respecting. men
and women and good and useful citizens.
Brother Wells was born in Fairfield, Solano County, California,
on Jtme 24, 1861. All his life was lived in this, his native State, indeed, within a range of a hundred miles from the place of his birth.
lfr was cllucatcd in the schools of this State. He was twice married,
first to Ella O'Neal on November 4, 1885, who died July 3, 1913, and
second to Frances Bancroft Lemon on September 9, 1915, who survives him. He also leaves surviving him two chi:drcn, i!'.suc of his
first marriage, a son, William S. Wells, and a daughter, Ella Mildred
B:trhour. Our heartfelt sympathy goes out to those who were nearest.
and dearest to him and who have been deprived of an affectionate ·and
devoted husband and father.
To his fricn1ls he was ever loyal and devoted, as those who ·hat!
the priceless treasure of his fricncbbip will ever remember. Truly,
he grappled them to his soul "with hoops of steel."
As a citizen he was right in the head and right in the heart.. He
loved his country and firmly believed in its institutions, and never
failed to give of his hest in its service.
In every relation of his life Brother Wells hn.s left a stainless
page. \Ve who loved him, in thinking hack over his record, can think
of nothing that we would have preferred otherwise. He was true and
faithful to every obligation. More can not be said of any man.

At the time of his death Brother Wells ha<! not yet attained his
fifty-eighth birthday. vVe had every reason to believe that he would
he spared to us for many years to come, and in our grief we may at
first have questioned in our minds the wisdom of the Divine decree
that took him from us while still in the full strength of his glorious
manhood. But we know that his going was in accord with the Divine
plan, and that he has simply preceded us a little on the road along
which we all must journey. His life was such that there can be no
sorrow on our part for him. The time of his departure was at hall(!
and we can not- doubt that it found him ready. In the words of the
apostle he truly could have said: "I have fought a good fight, I have
tinishcd my course, I have kept the faith." His death was hut his
passing to that place not made with hands, eternal in the heavens,
where the Supreme Grand Master of the 'Universe forever presides,
there to enjoy the reward .that we hclievc awaits all who have hccn
faithful.here. \Ve who arc for a brief season left hhind will mourn
his absence and long for the sight of his familiar figure, the sonnd of
his kindly voice, the touch of his friendly hand. nut in truth he is
not wholly lost to us, for he will always live in our memory as one
who was ever our loyal friend and faithful brother. Jn conclmling,
we may truly say of him in his own simple words spoken in eulogy
of another distinguished rnemher of our Fraternity: "An honrst,
upright man and Mason, truthful and jnst, loyal to his frirnds ancl
to his Fraternity-may he reap the reward of a wcll-sprnt life; and
to the will of our Heavenly Father we, in sorrow, rrvrrcntly bow."

Address-California's Departed Heroes-William D. Stephens.
It was on the 19th clay of November, 1863-almost fifty-six years
ago-that Abraham Lincoln dedarccl at Gettysburg that the living owe
it to the heroic dead to dcclicate themselves to the completion of the
task begun in blood and sacrifice. He saicl that from the honored
cleacl the living should take increased clevotion to the cause for which
the dead had given the last full measure of devotion.
So today, we may best honor our heroic dead by dedicating ourselves anew to the ideals they defended and for which they laid down
their lives that not alone this Republic they loved hut the entire civilized world might have a new birth of freedom.
The war from which we so recently have emerged has taught us'
the real meaning of mobilization. We have learned that the mobilization of a nation is vastly more than the marshalling of its armies,
the gathering of its material resources anti the transportation of men
and munitions to the scene of conflict. Men who had all their lives
abhorred war as an instrument for imposing on the weak and rlcfcnsclcss the will of the strong, hafl to learn that there is a justified
war of defense which is the very highest possih!c expression of loyalty
to principJc and devotion to justice. One of the hran~st deeds of the
whole war, let it not be forgotten, was registered on the battlefields
of France in the valor and heroism of an ohscnre, poorly-edncatcd
son of the Tennessee mountains who not only knew nothing of war,
hut as a "conscientious objector" had to he convinced of the moral
justification of even a war of national defense.
.
The mohilization of America was more than the httilding of
ships, the rnantt factnrc of equipment and the arming, drilling and
transportation of trorips. Dack of all that was the fine universal spirit'
of service, the sp\•ndid grasping of an ideal that was to Cl'ntt•r the
hearts ancl nerve the purpose of millions of men in a high common
intent. This intelligent understanding of the fundamental issue of
the war and of the part we were to play in it, was the hasis of the
wonderful nmrnle that chara<'terized our troops on the lmttlcficlds of
Europe. Tt was this that gave them their dash and high courage and
made them in effectiveness the superiors of professional foreign
soldiers.
There is little indeed of real service that we now can render our
heroic dead. We may and we wi!l care for the survivors who have
returned to tts maimed am! crippled for life, hut there is no service
we may now render those who in the language of Lincoln pair! the
"foll measure of their devotion," except as we St'rve the country

they loved with a devotion equal to that which they gave. To do

As our heroes so bravely died that their country might live, shall
we not as unselfishly live that our country shall never die? Shall
we not devote our purpose and our strength toward making America
wholly American? Must we not make sure that American citizenship
shall mean a larger freedom, under the law-a due regard for the
rights and comforts of others and a loyalty to home and country that
shall be unquestioned?
You and I, if we would measure up to our departed sons, must
so conduct our business affairs as to give no reason for or encouragement to the spread of anarchy in America. Neither ana1-chism, nor
I. W. W.ism, nor Bolshevism, nor any other traitorous ism should
be tolerated in this free and God-favored land of ours. Ii1decd in

must sec to it that if a citizen assail our flag he shall be promptly
arrested and promptly punished, and if an alien speak or act ;:igainst
America, he shall promptly be put out of America.

in history and treasured in the soul of humanity. They fought for

human, they were oblivious to danger and fearless of death. It was
as though heaven opened to them and the greatest glory enwrapped
their souls. Their translation was ecstatic and their end, peace.
They are with God. But the living arc still with us. They, who
went down into the jaws of death, into that hell on earth created
by the Huns,-they, who went through those nameless horrors, are in
our midst, 'impressing upon us, if we arc heedful, the great lesson
America taught the world; that glorious faith in God and justice, the
United States and her sons have exemplified. Let us turn for a
moment, my good brethren, to the description of the horrifying experiences our boys had to endure.
Down in the trenches, in mud and slime, strnggling agaimt vermin
and cold, with shot and shell in continuous vo'.ley, hovering over and
around them, fighting all day, nmrching' all ni)!ht with rr feverishness
and excitement that numhcd their senses, cheering and singing in the
face of death. Rumble and explrn;ion, and rumble and swish of shots
as they flew and the earth trembling beneath their feet, while the
deafening tumult continued throughout the night, hrot1ght no rest or
relaxation. All through the night, the sky am! the field, made to resemb!e a hell, that outrivalled in hellishness any description of hell
thus far known. And then, in the miclst of the din and the roar,
while cannon atlfl airship vomited forth certain derrth, over the top
sprang these intrepid hrothcrs of ours to defeat injustice and crime.
Nor was this the only terrifying experience. J\11 along the ocean
path, as the transports plm1ghcd on to land !111111rrnity'~ champions on
the field of hattle, stealthily plied the suhmarinc, the terror of the

Some of them have hecn wound('d, ancl so carry the marks and

But they have had time to find themselves. In the long hours of

Many of you brethren still remember our awful experience of
1906, when the earthquake shook us into a condition bordering on
insanity. You may recall numerous instances of people affrighted
by the terror, nuining aimlessly about, uttering meaningless jumbles
of incoherences. Then, too, were seen trifles and empty bird ·cages
in the hands of those who had left valuables behind to be devoured
by the fire. It was a case of shattered nerves all around. And this
was the result of but a few moments' dreadful menace of destruction
and death. \Vhat, then, do you suppose, is the condition of those
stalwarts who, unwounded, are returned to us? Theirs was not the
abject terror of <l moment's awfulness, but the continuous nerve strain,
a century of fears extended over months. How, then, will you descrihe their condition, brethren? Strong men, apparently hale and
hearty, have almost wept as they dec!ared to me that, in spite of. the
pl1ysician's declaration that there was nothing the matter with them,
that there was and that something was holding them back. There was
-sha ttcrcd nerves. And no time to rediscover themselves.
From the earliest times, men have always cried out against injustice, and no period of history has yet been chronicled but that that
cry has been recorded. Not that men are designedly unjust, but that
our own growth enlarges our comprehension of justice and shows
the insufficiency of our present mode of satisfying justice. Still, we
strive to do our best. And it is true hcyond all contradiction, that in
the matter of recompense, we can never do exact justice to our nervestricken boys. It is yet manifestly our duty to do all we can, especially
we of the· fraternity who speak and teach justice. Getting these men
jobs immediately placing them in positions as soon as they return (I
mean those who went across to France) is almost futile. None of
them is sufficiently recovered to stay. steadily at anything. They
should be given time to recover, and the six months' pay idea shoulcl
have been so strongly backer! and fostered hy all of us that they
would have been able to enjoy the required respite.
Still, we can persevere to render them that mead of respect and
affection that may solace them for our neglect and in this manner
endeavor to give them some justice. Let us encourage them to get
together and to keep together, that their getting together may stimulate
us to conserve and to conform to those great ideals, now the admiration of the entire world. Let it not be said that we, who went forth
to obtain justice for the world, fail to uphold justice in our own midst.
Let not all the admiration and praise showered upon them before
they left, ooze out of us now that peace is here and they are back.

behalf of the whole c'raft of Masonry in the Grand Jurisdiction of

The Grand Master, however, concurred in the op1111011 of the Coi11111ittee that if a memorial was to be erected it should be fully worthy

Resolved, That Grand Lodge hereby requests its Finance Committee to consider and report for action by Grand Lodge the appropriation of a sum which in its judgment will be a proper compensation to Mr. Daryl B. Miller for his services in connection with the

404

In view of the circumstances above related your Committee did
not feel authorized to direct Mr. Miller to proceed. The situation
was explained to him, however, and he consented to proceed with his
work up to and including the delivery of a perspective drawing of
the design upon which he and the Committee had agreed. This perspective drawing has been completed, and is at the present time displayed in the main vestibule of the Temple.
The Commiftee believes that the design is, indeed, "worthy of
the Order and of the Temple," and would rejoice to see Grand Lodge
make the necessary appropriation for the casting in bronze of this
artistic monument. Under the circumstances, however, the Committee
desires only to submit the matter to the judgment of the Grand Lodge,
If erected, this memorial would cost between $5,000 and $6,000 completed and erected.
As will be noted from a study of the memorial the feeling e~­
pressed is appropriate, both with respect to Masonry and with respect
to those of our Brethren who participated in the service of the Gov-•
ernment during the war.
The base of the monument, which would be situated in tlic center
of the main vestibule, is approximately three feet square ,;nd three
feet high. It is designed to represent the altar of Masonry as ab
altar of service. Upon the altar rests an ornamented drum: encircling
which in bas-relief, appear representations of men in all the various:
branches of war activities. Above this drum rests a circular fluted
column with a handsome capital in classic design, whic11 capital is
surmounted by a ground glass globe representing the world. This
globe is to be lighted in token of our recognition that the service of
our brethren, based upon the foundation of Yiasonry and patriotism.
has helped to diffuse light throughout the world. The monument is·
approximately eleven feet in height.
Your Committee believes that Grand Lodge, in view of the sacrifices made by our brethren, and in testimony of its appreciation of
such sacrifices, could well afford the expenditure involved in the erec-.
tion of this memorial.
In conclusion, you'r Committee feels that in any event, Grand
Lodge should, as. a matter of fairness, offer compensation to Mr.
Daryl B. Miller, the designer of the memorial. He has expended a
large amount of time in this work, and in fact devoted his summer
vacation very largely to the development of this monument. Y01.1r

Committee therefore offers. the following:

condition of the Lodges. It can safely he said al the outset, that a
very large majority of the Lodges have never before heen called upon
to confer so many degrees, and there seems to he no end to the
petitions. Many of our hoys who were overseas have since their return sought admission to our Lodges, on arriving nt their respective
homes. It is apparent that the cau;;e for this great increase must he
the general prosperity of the country, and a favorable opinion con·
ccivcd of the fraternity, as well as a sincere desire to he S('rviccahlc
to their fellowmen. I smcly 1H'lieve that most of the boys who wl're
on the other side have returned with a far diffcn•11t viewpoint, and
look at life a bit more seriously.
Shortly after the c'.osc of the last session of the Cram! Lmlge
many localities an<I Lodges were sadly <lisorganizcd on nccount of the
epidemic that prevailed at that time. No meetings hcing permitted,
many of the Lodges were not able to hold their clection.s on time.
Many of mtr hrcthren were victims of this tcrrihlc scourge. Brother
Frederick Warren Clough, Inspector of the 24th District at J\nc;ds
Camp, contractc~l the disease while in attendance at the Crand Lod:,c,
and after returning to his home died on the 24th of Octoher. Brother
Clough was Inspector for many years, and always was ready and

be said of Brother Clough, "Well done, good and faithful servant,

presence in the Grand Lodge.
Brother Frank Edward Morrell, Inspector of the First Masonic
District at Arcata, died on the 12th of September. Brother Morrell
had been Inspector of that District for several years and had given
good service to the Lodges. He will be greatly missed by the brethren
of Humbo!dt and Del Norte counties. We regret his untimely taking
off, for he had many years of usefulness.
I desire to express my sincere appreciation to the Inspectors of
the jurisdiction for their untiring efforts and assistance in the work
of the year, and to congratulate them on the condition of the Lodges
in their respective Districts.

I have received reports from almost all the Inspectors aml they
report the Lodges, at least most of them, to he in prosperous condition and all gaining in membership. Brother Reese, Inspector of the
Fifty-third District, conceived the idea of forming an Officers' Assa~
ciation. Meetings are held monthly, alternating in the respective
cities. A dinner is served and a business meeting held, then the.
officers repair to the Lodge room, where either a degree is conferred,
a Lodge of instruction held, some Masonic topic considered, or to
hear a Masonic lecture. These meetings seem to have produced th~
purpose for which they are held, namely the get-together spirit, and
to perfect themselves in the ritual and Masonry in general. It was
my pleasure to attend one of these meetings while holding schools
of instruction in the District, and I was impressed with the splendid
spirit of good fellowship that prevailed, as well as furnishing an •
opportunity for the officers to get better acquainted, and it appeared
that the desired results had been accomplished.

THE AMERICAN'S CREED
Brother Eugene S. Elkus presented the following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, There appears to be a world-wide and organized movement fostered by enemies of law and order to subvert and destroy
government, which movement is very manifest in our own free Amer~
ira; and
Whereas, Masonry recognizes that all nature is and must be subservient and obedient to law _and order, and
Whereas, Masonry believes in and inculcates obedience to human
laws and enjoins loyalty to established government; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California in annual co1111111111ication assembled does
renew its pledge of absolute fca'.ty to our Government, and further
pledges the entire membership to use all lawful means to check the
growth of the destructive and treasonable doctrines that now threaten
our free institutions;
Resolved further, That the American's creed as accepted by the
National Publicity Committee on behalf of the United States give.s
expression to the loyalty of every true lover of country, and as
Masons we and each of us affirm our belief therein as fol'.ows:
"I believe in the United States of America as a government of
the people, by the people, for the people, whose just powers arc derived from the consent of the governed; a democracy in a republic;
a sovereign nation of many sovereign States; a perfect Union one
and inseparable, established. upon those principles of frecclom, equality,
j usticc and humanity for which. American patriots sacrilicecl their
lives and fortunes. I therefore believe it is my duty to my country
to love it; to support its Constitution; to obey its laws; to respect
its flag; and to defend it against all enemies."
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary cause these Resolutions to
be printed in sufficient number to supply every Mason in California
with one copy, that he send them in suitable quantities to the Secretaries of our Lodges with instrnctions to mail or otherwise clclivcr
to each member a copy thereof.
Resolved, That the Master of each Lodge at the next annual
meeting, cause the same to be read, and to direct his brethren in
):..odge assembled to repeat with him the American's Creed.
Respectfully submitted,
EuGENE

S. ELKUS.

The resolutions were adopted as read, except the paragraph which provides for printing and circulating the same,
which matter was referred to the Committee on Finance.
That committee subsequently reported, recommending "that
in view of the fact that this Grand Lodge now has an Educational Committee, that this matter be referred to said
committee for disposition." Later, the Finance Committee
recommended that the resolutions be printed and distributed under the auspices of the Committee on Education, and
it was so ordered.

REPORTS OF BOARDS OF RELIEF
The reports of the several Boards of Relief were presented and referred to the Committee on Finance:
RE'.PORT OF TH}t MASONIC IlOARD OF RltLlEF OF SAN }'RANCJSCO

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California, and the Lod1;es constituting the Board:
We herehy beg to present the following report for the year beginning
August 27, 1918, and ending August 25; 1919, both d:ites inclusive.
A year of great activities has just closed, and this Board has justified its existence by extending its labors beyond those heretofore under~
taken.
The relief work done is fully shown in our report annexed, and we
have nothing to add thereto, except to praise those jurisdictions which
show a true Masonic spirit by responding readily and liberally to the
calls of their distressed brethren. Some of the j urisdietions are models
which we wish others would imitate.
The Masons of San Francisco fully realize their responsibility in
caring ,for those in their midst, and do not try to shirk, and it is a matter
of congratulation that letters from which the following paragraph is
taken arc not numerous. (This letter is in answer to one requesting
relief for a brother aged eighty years.)
"It seems to me that if we should assume the burden of seeing him
through, together with our other demands, thM our members would
soon. feel that being a Mason r.,qas not worth while, and wou·ld all desert
us. If he has been in the Poor House four years, we should thinli
he would as soon die there as any where else."
We wish to add that this brother is being taken care of by this
Board, notwithstanding the fact thnt the Lodge to which he has belonged for a great many years, refuses to do its duty.
The thanks of the Fraternity arc due to our brethren of the Medical Profession, who have given so unstintingly of their time and ability
for the unfortunate ones in need of their services. Without them we

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

419

should fall far short of doing our duty to the sick, and we hereby thank
Doctors ]. C. Egeberg, Aaron S. Green, Otto Freyermuth, William P.
Read, Jacob Schwarz, Wilhelm Waldeyer and A. L. W. Zillmer.
The epidemic of Spanish Influenza tested the ability for our relief
work more than anything has done for years, and we are glad to report
that we were able to attend to all cases coming to our notice, being ably
assisted by a great many volunteers.
During the month of April a Children's Health Center was conducted by us in our rooms, in the Masonic Temple, where 211 children
of Masons, up to the age of six years, were examined, and the following
table shows the results:

}'RAUDS

While the fraud and the impostor are always abroad in the land
and their cunning will at times deceive the most watchful, I believe
they were fewer this year than usual. On the other hand, there is
undouhteclly an increase in the number of wives seeking to locate
runaway husbands, and Brothers are trying to locate runaway wives.
This latter is to he deplored.
INVALIDS COMING

Let me again call attention to the wrong that is done to your
invalid Brother. and to the Masons of California hy sending your sick
out here, unless they have money sufficient to proviclc for thcmsclvc5.
Tt is just as expensive to live here as anywhere, and costs more for
burial expenses. Just look at the burial record in this report.
Rcmcmhcr a sick man. CAN'T get hy the examining physicians
for the larger corporations, and it is of no use to try.
The officers upon. v. hose shuulclcrs falls the work of this office
do it cheerfully and elevate their entire time thereto. I hcrcwitT1
present a compact statement of its magnitude, viz., since September

I, 1918.
More than 5000 letters sent.
More than 300 telegrams sent.
More than 400 investigations.
And arranged for the disposition of 136 deaths, besides other
miscellaneous matters attcnclccl to on the spot in the office.

The Manager reports as follows:
Just a few years ago, the Masonic Em1)loymcnt Bureau was struggling through disconragcmcnt and adversity to maintain its place, and
fn~fill the God-given duty of helping others to help themselves, for which
purpose it wns organized. The Bureau was considered the last hope of
the applicant for employment, and the employer for help.
Today, the Bureau is building a structure of service to humanity
which will stand as an enduring monument to the beneficence of
::\lasonry; for instead of the last hope, it is as the brightness of the
Eastern horizon at break of day to him who is seeking maintenance of
self respect, honor and manhood, by honest toil, the Mecca for the
employer an<l the employee.

Your Committee desires to congratulate our worthy Brother, the

account of the official visit of hitnself and Past Grand :.\faster Hervey
to the Especial Peace Jubilee session of the Gra11d Lodge of England in

gratulated upon the great opportunity of hearing such a vivid and intensely interesting personal report from Brother Whicher, forming a
most life-like picture of the details of the great celebration. This jurisdiction is most fortunate in having been represented by such ahle and
distinguished members of the era ft on that important occasion.
The Grand Master's references to the Masonic Homes are instructive
and illuminating, hut as we confidently assume that his address will be
widely read by the brethren, we do not conceive that extended reference
thereto is necessary at this time, further than to express our approval of
the Grand Master's recommendation that he he given authority to appoint
a special committee to thoroughly investigate various plans for the hcttcr
support of the Masonic Homes, and report thereon with recommendations.
W c heartily concur in what the Grand Master has said of the loyal
and faithful service of our Grand Lecturer, Brother Thomas ]. Baker.
His recommendation as to appreciating the salary of Brother Baker is
something which your Committee believes shoulcl he acted upon by the
Grand Lodge itself.
A clifficult situation is presented to this Grand Lodge by the report
of _the Grand Master upon the circumstances conccrning Acacia Lodge
and Herman Lodge. Your Committee believes the recommendation of
the Grand Master to he in the interests of justice and equity and sug·
gests that this he referred to the Committee on J urisprndcnce.
The Committee is in accord with the Grand Master's interpretation of what should be the physical requirements for membership in our
order, and hopes the Grand Lodge, through the Committee on Jurisprudence, will concur.
Your Committee is also in hearty accord with his recommendation
with reference to the matter of permitting the subordinate Lodges to

JNCORPORATJON

For some years past there has periodically arisen the question
of the advisability of conducting the affairs of the Homes as a
corporation. We have always realized that we were proccerling in
a somewhat loose manner in carrying the legal title to our properties
in the name of an individual; and that it would be better to have
the title stand of record in the name of the real owner. On the
other band there was a somewhat pronounced feeling that in carrying
on the business of the Homes as a separate legal entity there might

449

6

We therefore "muddled along," recognizing the fact that embarrassments might ensue upon the death of the individual in whom
the record title to our properties was vested; but trusting that if
the necessity therefor should ever arise, some way would he found
to me~ the situation. That necessity confronted us when Past Grand
Master Wells clied with the title to our properties standing in his
name.
After consulting .with Past Grand Masters Angellotti, Weller,
Keesling and other memhers of the Jurisprudence Committee, and having
considered the matter at length with the Grand Master, it appeared
in the jndgment of the Board that it would be advisable to create
a Benevolent Corporation to he known as the Masonic Homes of
California, in which should be vested the title to all property acquired
for the purposes and benefit of the Ho111cs; and the Grand Master
having authorized and directed the incorporation, if in the judgment
of the Board it was deemed advisable, it was dccicled to immediately
incorporate. It was, however, specifically understood that the Trustees
who are to manage and direct the affairs of the corporation should
he selected and appointee! as provided '>y the Constitution of the
Grand Lodge; that no power was to be given the Trustees under
the corporation not now vested in or exercised hy them; and that
the rights, powers and privileges of the Grand Lodge and Grand
Master to control and direct the affairs of the Homes were to he
in no way altered, limited or abridged; the sole intention of the
Trustees in incorporating heing to devise a cldinite legal entity
authoriz('cl aml empowered to take, receive, hold and transf~r in the
name of the Masonic Homes of California title to real and personal
property howsoever acquirC:d; and that the relation of the Trnstees
to the Grand Lodge and to the Grand Master should be in no
wise changed or altered by the incorporation.
We have therefore provided in our Articles of Incorporation
that everything is to he done "in accordance with the rules, regulations and discipline of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of California, which said mies and regulations and discipline
as now existing and as hereafter amended shall always be a part of
these 1\ rticlcs of Incorporation and this corporation shall always be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

subject thereto"; and that the "Trustees shall be elected and appointed as provided by the rules and regulations of the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of California."
In the by-laws of the corporation it is provided that "In accordance with, and subject to, the rules, regulations and discipline of
the Grand Lodge of .Free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California, the corporate powers of this corporation shall be vested
in a Board of seven Trustees who shall be elected, designated or
chosen in such manner and for such term as the said Grand Lodge
shall from time to time determine or by its Constitution prescribe;
and the persons who shall act as Trustees of this corporation shall
be those selected, appointed, designated and elected in accordance
with the provisions of Section 33 of the Constitution of the said
Grand Lodge as adopted on the 11th day of October, 1917, which
said provision is as follows, to wit:
"Sec. 33. The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California shall
be seven in number, four of whom shall be appointed by the Grand
Master, and the three others to consist of the Deputy Grand Master,
the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens, who shall be ex-officio Trustees. The term of office of the four appointed shall be respectively
one, two, three and four years, to he designated and determined by
the Grand Master appointing. Two of the Trustees shall be from
Lodges in the vicinity of Covina.· Succeeding Grand Masters shall appoint successors who shall hold office for four years. They shall he
the successors of the present Trustees and of the Trustees of the Masonic Widows and Orphans' Home hereinbefore appointed under the
resolution of the Grand Lodge adopted in 1892 and subsequently
thereto, and shall be vested with all the powers given such Trustees
and with all the rights by them or any of them acquired."
There is also a provision that "vacancies in the Board of Trustees
shall be filled by appointment by the Grand Master and the term
of office of the person so appointed shall he the unexpired portion of .
the term of the Trustee whose office bcean1e vacant. At any time
upon re{Jttest of two-thirds of the members of the Board the Grand
Master may remove a Trustee and appoint another in the place of
the person so removed.''
The officers of the corporation are a President, Vice President,
Secretary and Treasurer. The Preshlent and Vice President arc
under the corporation selected by the Board from their own number,
just as was the procedure prior to incorporation, and in accordance
with the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, the Secretary shall be
the person holding office as the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge
and the Treasurer shall be the person holding the office of Grand
Treasurer.
The question of whether or not there should he a provision for
mcmhership in the corporation of those who were at the time

members of Grand Lodge or of a certain number to be selected
by Grand Lodge was considered at some length. It was finally
determined, however, that that plan would he best which entailed
no change i_n the Constitution of the Grand Lodge and which could
in no wise be construed as changing the relation between the
Trustees and the Grand Master and Grand Lodge. In other words,
under the present plan the Trustees to all intents and purposes
act exactly in the same manner they have always done, reporting
directly to Grand Lodge and being at all times under the control and
direction of the Grand Master; the only material difference being
that the title to properties is in the name of the Masonic Homes of
California instead of an individual; and that in dealing with those
properties the Trustees act as an incorporated body. It will of
course he understood that in referring to the properties belonging
to the Homes we have in mind particularly not the Homes themselves, hut the detached individual pieces of real estate which under
Rule 16 arc conveyed to the Homes by those who are admitted, and
which arc not required or necessary for the purposes of the charity.

Rl!SIDEN'l'S

At Decoto our aged brethren are well cared for and comfortable.
There naturally is a great contrast between this Home and that
at Covina. Here our plan is to make the last days of our brethren
comfortable and to furnish them with those things that will make
life happier, while at Covina we are developing the bodies and minds
of those who are to take our place. The Superintendent and his
assistants are to be congratulated upon the condition of the Home.
It should be mentioned here that during the influenza epidemic . of
last winter, no cases developed in either institution.
The Covina Home is running smoothly and beautifully in well
organized, steady, and dependable progress with the children. The
health record has been almost perfect. The children have been
unusually attentive to school work and home duties. The merit
system practiced the past year has given an incentive to applied
effort and created an interest in effective results in all their
work. Their discipline is quite satisfactory and their interest in
athletics, sports and diversions displays a desire to excel in competitive recreation as well as in their school and home activities.
The children have made a remarkable improvement due to
splendid work in physical and mental corrections which can be made
with growing children. It is desired that all Lodges make themselves
familiar with this work through the report of· the Medical Department
of Stanford University made to the Grand Master, showing results
of their survey of the children.
PHYSlCAL CONTHTJON OF PROPERTY

As the years pass by, the buildings at Decato become more and
more in need of repairs. This is particularly true at this time, as
the Trustees felt that they could not increase the deficit by the
expenditure of money on the lmi:dings. We have now reached a
point when it would be to the detriment of the best interests of
the Homes to longer delay certain needed repairs, and it will he
a real economy to spend money at this time, to do that which is
necessary to preserve the buildings and properties. we, therefore,
purpose during the year to do all the painting that the conditions of
the buildings indicate to be necessary, and to repair and replace
such woodwork as ti111e and decay have rendered unsafe, and to
rebuild the fences around the property. These things can be delayed
no longer.
At Covina the property is in good condition. The wagon-sheds
and barns completed this year from salvage of the old temporary
buildings meet all present needs. The fence around the lower
garden should be rabbit-proofed and an area of about two acres

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

453

added to our deciduous orchard. The citrus orchard is doing well
and the lemon trees doubled their production this year. A new
cottage was built for the men, replacing the one destroyed by fire.
Xo repairs have been needed except some interior painting during
the vacation season.
FARM

It has been found ih1possible to economically take care of the
entire farm at Decato. The original intention in purchasing the
tract occupied by the Home, was to cultivate the ground with the
aid of the residents. This did not work out, as the majority of our
fap1ily are too far advanced in years to be of real value. Only
enough land has been worked under the Home management to keep
the table supplied with vegetables. The remainder of the land, with
the exception of the orchard, is leased on shares. The in<;ome from
farm rentals and sale of fruits is to be found in the financial
statement in this report.
The farm at Covina is too new in general improvement to show
much resu!ts. The garden docs well, but the trees, while showing
exceptional growth, arc not old enough to bear fruit, except about
three acres of five-year- old lemons. Table grapes and berries are
now being set out and ground is prepared to seed alfalfa in the
spring.
I'INANCES

Owing to the conditions arising from the war and the constantly
increasing high cost of living, the expense of maintaining the
l lomcs has been, as it was· last year, greater than our income.
Such economy as we believed justifiable has been practiced both
at Covina and Dccoto; and it is pleasing to know that the percentage
of increase in the cost of living at our Homes has been iess than
the average as ascertained from C6vt~rnment reports. The daily per
capita cost at Decoto was $1.01 and at Covina 87 cents; the difference
in cost b<otwcen the ·two Homes being accounted for by the fact
that included in the cost at Decoto is the expense of maintaining
the hospital and farm. To meet the deficit we were compelled to
borrow the sum of $11,755.44.
There arc only two ways to prevent a deficit in the conduct of
any business. One is to reduce the expenses ; the other is to
increase the income.
The Trustees are of the opinion that it is practically impossible
to further reduce the expenses of maintaining the Homes. The
alternative is to increase the income. The Trustees realize that
even the present per capita tax has proved 'a burden upon certain

454

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodges; and they arc therefore unwilling to recommend an increase.
They are unanimously of the opinion that any change in the per
capita tax for maintenance should be toward a reduction rather
than an increase. It is, however, obtrusively apparent that if the
per capita tax is to be reduced, or even if it is to be maintained
at the present rate, some plan must be devised whereby additional
income can be derived from other sources. To this matter they
have given their best thought and have had under consideration
several suggested plans. In the consideration of the problem they
have not only conferred with brethren of the craft in California, ·but
have sought information from other jurisdictions.
After mature consideration they are inclined to believe that
the best method is that generally known as the "Pennsylvania Plan,"
but modified to meet conditions peculiar to our Lodges.
In Pennsylvania every applicant for admission to the fraternity
pays, in addition to the initiation fee required by the Lodge, the sum
of $20.00 for the support and maintenance of the Masonic Home.
Had this plan been in operation in California during the two
years last past, which of course were abnormal ones, the income
derived from this source alone would have amounted to the sum
of $224,0JO.OO, a sum far in excess of the entire cost of maintenance;
and it would have rendered unnecessary the levy o'f any per capita
tax on the Lodges. Of course, as we have said, the two years last ·
past were abnormal ones; but we may rcasonahly expect that the
annual increase in our membership will be not less than 4000. With
the payment by each new member of the sum of $20.00, if any per
capita tax at all would be required, it would be an extremely low
one; in no event probably more than 10 cents instead of $1.00 as
at present.
This computation, you will however note, is based on a uniform
fee of $20.00 to be paid by each new member
Therein lies the objection to the plan, because it may militate
against the smaller and less prosperous Lodges. An additional
charge of $20.00 to an applicant for membership in a Lodge where
the initiation fee is $100.00 would not be a serious objection. In
other words, whether the total fees would be $100 or $120, would not ·
in all likelihood affect the increase in membership.
Where, however, the initiation fee is $30.00 or even $50.00, an
additional charge of $20.00 might materially reduce the number of
applications made to those Lodges.
A provision for a uniform charge of $20.00 might therefore
perhaps prove to be a detriment to the less prosperous Lodges. This
of course must be avoided; and that objection to the plan suggested

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

455

will be obviated by a modification we have discussed, which is as
follows:
Instead of making the additional charge on all applications
for membership uniform, the amount to be paid for the support
and maintenance of the Homes might be made proportionate to
the initiation fee charged by the Lodge. If instead of making a
fixed charge ?f $20.00 there was a provision for the payment of
a sum equal to 20 per cent of the initiation fee, a member admitted
to a Lodge in which the initiation f~c was $100 would pay $20,
while a member admitted to a Lodge in which the initiation fee
was $30 would pay only $6.00. There. could therefore be no suggestion of any discrimination in favor of or against any particular
class of Lodges.
It is hardly conceivable that an additional charge of $6.00 would
prove an obstacle to an applicant who is able and willing to pay
$30.00 for membership in the fraternity.
In order merely that the members of the Grand Lodge may
know that the Trustees have not failed to consider the matter
from every point of view, and not because we believe it a valid
one, we may say that another objection made to the so-called
Pennsylvania Plan was that it "might produce an unfavorable
impression upon the minds of those aspiring to obtain Masonic
light, inasmuch as they may well assume it to be strange that the
great Imtitution of Masonry should require an applicant at its
doors to contribute directly to a fund for maintaining the Homes".
It seems to us that the exact converse· would be true. At the
very threshold of our door he who knocks would have impressed
upon his mind the fact that the care of the widow nnd the orphan
is an obligation every Mason take.s upon himself; and he could
not but be favorably impressed with the fact that of the amount
paid by him for the privilege of becoming a member of the fratcrnitv
one-fifth was devoted to the maintcna11ce of an institution whi~I~
should be the pride of every Masonic heart.
If the Pennsylvania Plan, as modified in accordance with our
suggestion, had been in operation this year, we would have obtained
for the Homes from that source the sum of $68,930.00. This would
have warranted even at this time, a recommendation for a decrease
in the per capita tax. With the increase in membership which we
can reasonably expect, the amount derived in this way, together
with the income from the continually increasing Endowment Fund,
would warrant the expectation that in a few years the per capita
tax might be not only materially reduced, but dispensed with
entirely.

456

PlWCEEDINGS OF '£HE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This much at least is certain: If that plan were adopted it
would not in any event increase the burden the Lodges are now
bearing; but on the contrary would offer the hope that it might
be diminished.
\Ve can not therefore escape the conviction that · it should at
least be given a trial. None of the other plans which have been
suggested appeals so strongly to us as does this. N evcrtheless, in
view of the fact that there arc those who prefer some other
method of providing for the revenue required for the maintenance
of the Home·s, and because other plans may be submitted, instead
of making a recommendation for the adoption of the plan we favor,
we have asked the Grand Master to appoint a committee to which
the entire question may be submitted, with instructions to report
thereon at this communication with such rccommcndntion as may
seem to its members meet and proper.

The situation with reference to children is even more embarrassing. In the event of the death of the father, if the mother is
compelled to seek employment and therefore unable to care for the
child, it is adrriitted to the Home at Covina. In the event of the
death of the mother, however, the child is not admitted if the
earnings of the father are sufficient to provide for the support of
the child.
Under the discretion vested in the Trustees, if the earning~ of
the father are not sufficient to pay for some one in whose care
the child may he placed while the father is absent from home, the
child is admitted. If, however, the earnings of the father are
sufficient to maintain a home and hire a housekeeper, or if he is
only able to pay for some one in whose care the child may be
placed, the child is not eligible for admission to the Horne. We
are compelled to disregard entirely the question of whether or not
the best interests of the child will be subservcd hy p'.acing it unde;
the care of such a person as the father is ahlc to find.

whom the care of his child may be safely entrusted. Under those

THE DECOTO HOME

of not only their own rooms but also the halls, stairways, wash
rooms, reading, linen and reception rooms, also the Assembly Ha!l
in the bui:dings occupied by them.

During the past year the affairs of the Decoto Home have been
very satisfactory.
The permanent improvements and repairs made for several
years past ha vc enabled the management to render a higher standard
of service in meeting the physical, mental and spiritual needs of
the family.
1'hcrc has been a greater individual effort to interest themselves
in the general routine. work and to contribute according to their
strength to the general welfare of the H omc, with the result that a
splc11did spirit has been created which exerts a harmonious influence
in the daily life of the Home.
The social side of our Home life has been carried out by means
of diversions of various kinds. Suitable entertainments, out-of-doors
recreations, picnic parties, excursions to nearby places of interest,
etc., have enriched the social and farni'.y life of the Home.
There arc now at the Home 85 men and 46 women. During the
past fiscal year there bave been 21 admissions, 14 men and 7 women.
Twenty-seven have passed away.
The licalth of the Home has been good. Those now being
cared for at the Coleman hospital are hy reason of the inlirmities
of advancing years. There arc now 16 members of the family being
cared for at the hospital.
The operation of the heating, laundry, pumping and cold storage
plants and the blacksmith shop has been satisfactory.
The water supply has hccn plentiful for household, garden and
irrigating purposes. The reservoirs have at all times 700,000 ga!lon5
of water in storage.
The greater part of the hill ranch has been leased either on
shares or cash rental. 1'bc orchards, hay fields, the chicken and
hog rancb, vegetable and berry gardens bavc given good returns
the surplus being sold in the San Francisco markets. A larg~
quantity of fruit has been dried and 13,000 eggs have been put up
for future use.
A number of the brethren have contributed to the welfare of
the Home by their labor i11 the carpenter, tailor, shoe and barber
shops, picking fruit, watering lawns, garage, library, kitchen and
pa11try and dining room work and light chores, also work in the
drug, dental and optical departments.

markmg of tbe household linen, and have taken charge of the care

COVINA HO.ME
The ·children of the Covina Home furnish a living example of
a due appreciation of Masonic practice. There they demonstrate the
happiness that can be provided to disp:ace the sorrows that brnught
them there. There, as one family, they try to prove to Masonry
as an adopted parent, that they can make themselves worthy of the
favors the fraternity extends to them. As they reach an age that
gives them a producing value, they are ambitious to succeed and
to do honor to the fraternity by making a creditable record. In
the daily care of the Home, the children do all that their time
and ability will permit to assist in reducing our maintenance cost,
and offset the severe influences of the H. C. L.
A splendid example of the voluntary desire to employ their time
usefully, is the ready and willing spirit manifested in wanting a
part in the general improvement of the place. The walks, trees,
lawn and grounds have the appearance of being cared for by
experienced gardeners. \Vhen the farmers' cottage burned down
one Sunday morning, the boys changed clothing at once, and worked
with both judgment and daring. They refused the wild and conflicting advice from the bystanders, and observed only the directions
of those in authority at the Home. Their loyalty in this regard
with their brave and well organized worked saved the barns, wagonsheds, and implements, and without accident to any of them.
Our remarkable standard of health, while due in a general
sense to a carefully selected diet and a watchfulness for all irregular-

482

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ities, is much influenced by the out of door diversions of the
children. Their interest in athletics will be intensified and more
systematized with the installation of a play ground equipment now
being provided. The frequent hikes in which many of the smaller
ones. participate, the regular Easter trip to the mountains, and their
summer camp at the beach give them unusual physical endurance.
For example, twenty-six children climbed a trail seven miles on
o'.d Baldy with a raise of 4300 feet one afternoon. Next day they
went to an elevation of 6600 feet on a sever~ trail to the heavy
snow, and returned to camp for six o'clock dinner, then went down
the seven miles grade the following day, and reached home at
Covina for six o'clock dinner. At the beach fifty-seven of the sixtysix children were swimming, and thirty-nine of them swam the bay,
which was more than a quarter of a mile across, through a strorig
tide current. The boys won the valley pennant for their school in
the baseball contest, and brought home a majority of the ribbons
in the field and track· meets this season.

The question is frequently asked about indoor diversions. While
the climatic conditions invite and favor outdoor diversions, the
indoor features are not neglected except for the gymnasium work.
This is because our gymnasium is not yet furnished. The boys
have a good library, a game room, a work shop and play room for
small boys. The girls have their music room, sewing room, library
room and reception rooms of the main building for mixed games,
music and dancing. Both have pianos, victrolas and other music.
Both have access to the plunge and gymnasium room for dances and
drills. Amateur shows, contests and other competitive features are
arranged between the boys and girls. The Sunday school is so
conducted as to make it very entertaining and instructive, without
the tiresome features too prevalent in religious work. The Grand
Chapter of Royal Arch Masons has set aside $5()()() for a :vocational
building for boys, and the Grand. Council of Royal and Select
Masters has appropriated $2500 for a Domestic Science bungalow.
When these buildings are constructed, a delightful, useful and most
instructive diversion will be provided for the older boys and girls.

The usual health survey was made at the c'.ose of school, and
all operations for tonsils, adenoids, circumcisions, etc., were performed
by the most skilled physicians of Los An_gelcs, who are members
of the eraft and who accepted no compensation for their services.
Our dental work has been employed, but our brethren of the pro-·
fession are now organizing to take care of this work for us. The
psychological and physical survey made annually by the Medical
Department of Stanford University was conducted this year by
Dr. Arthur J. Ritter and Dr. Herbert I. Bloch. Their report to
the Grand Lodge will probably accompany this report of the
Trustees. The Trustees desire to acknowledge the greatest improvement and advancement in the mental and corrective work with the
children through the recommendation of Dr. Ritter and his able
assistants. The children are appreciative of this work, and their
co-operation in our efforts to obtain results is admirable.
A health feature worthy of mention was the epidemic of influenza. The Trustees, knowing the fraternity desired every safeguard against this dangerous disease, closed the Home to all visitors.
At first some objection was made by relatives, but later when
fatalities were being recorded and we were free from the malady,
our action was highly commended. The local school Trustees
governed their quarantine by ours, and we lost little in the progress
of the school work. Much credit must be given to our loyal
employes who stayed at home, denying themselves all diversions
for the safety of these children. The children were patient and
checrfnl and provided their own entertainment during this period.

483

The visitations this year were greater in number than any
previous year. The increasing interest in our big family shown
by local Masonic bodies and members is pleasing. Never before
have the good ladies of the Eastern Star contributed so much to
the happiness and comfort of our big family. We may attribute
some of it to the fact that two· of our Trustees are Patrons of
Chapters this year. The greatest asset the children have is their
acquaintance in the fraternity, and they can best meet their friend>1
through these visitations to the Home.
\Vhile we cannot of
course name all visits of individuals, we must call attention to the
visits of the Lodges and Chapters which the children so much ap·
predate:
Sept. 8th, 1918--Garvanza Chapter No. 266 0. E. S. visited the
Home with a good attendance of members, including their Sunshine
Club. A program of entertainment was arranged for the visitors,
and they left a contribution of jams and jells for the children.
Sept. 27, 1918--Buena Park Lodge No. 357 and many , ladies
visited the Home. Children were well remembered with treats
and program. They responded with a good program.
Sept. 27, 1918--Grand Matron Order of the Eastern Star, Mrs.
Ivy Crane Shelhamer, with several grand officers, visited the Home.
Sept. 29, 1918--A committee called from Arab Patrol, Al
Malaikah Shrine, and gave each child a War Savings stamp. Grand
Master Wm. Rhodes Hervey accompanied the patrol and stayed for
supper with the children.

April 18, 1919-Twenty-six children took their annual hike
above the snowline on San Antonio inountain, known as Old Baldy,
to spend their Easter in the snow. Three days were spent on the
trails with no illness or aeddents, taking with them their own
foQd supplies and most of their equipment.
April 27th-Hollenbeck Lodge and Chapter have so well
