·
certainly was a day, long to be remembered.
May 4th-The Masonic Board of Relief met in the Library of
the Boys' building. After their regular business, the members and
their ladies went through the buildings and were entertained by the
children.
May 4th-"University Day," marking ·the annual visit of the
families of University Lodge No. 394, is one always looked forward
to by the children. This Lodge is most generous in their methods
.of ·entertaining as well as judicious in their selections of favors.
They have many members who arc all the year round visitors and
contributors.
May 11th-Glendale Commandery No. 53 chose to celebrate
"Mother's Day" with our children, and they so enj8yed themselves
they determined to make their visit an annual affair. Each mother
present adopted a chi~d for the day and a real family gathering
was enjoyed.
May 17th-Boys' cadet team was guests of Jinnistan Grotto and
gave an exhibition drill at Shrine Auditorium. The Grotto is a new

live and very active organization.

June 28th-The Southern California Past Masters' Association,

the Past Masters. There was more fun than business accomplished,
but the day will long be remembered.
June 30th-Pasadena Chapter No. 100 0. E. S. visited the

rooms and mended for the children all day. Thank you, Pasadena.

The sanitary conditions were found to be good. Toilets have
sewer connections. The problem of the proper disposal of garhage
is the same as exists in all camps.
The daily routine of the camp was followed during our four
days' visit with much interest. What particularly impressed us was
the careful attention given by every child, from the youngest to the
oldest, to their teeth and personal hygiene.
The daily responsibilities were carried out the same as they
are at the Covina Home. Their pleasures included rowing, swimming,
fishing and hiking. All the children, excepting those helow the age
of six years, swim. The day was concluded with a bonfire about
which the children gathered, singing an.d telling stories.
While at Camp Tucker, mental and physical examinations were
made of those children who had entered the Home subsequent to the

Camp Tucker has been made possible through the $2000 donation
to the Horne by the late Brother John Tucker, of California Lodge
No. 1. This donation enabled the Board of Trustees to purchase
the camp site at Balboa island, Orange county.
The camp is arranged in the form of a quadrangle; the front is
made up of five tents, one occupied by the Matron, another for the
Trustees, and the remaining for the use of guests. To the right
a large dormitory tent for the boys; to the left a similar one for
the girls. These tents are divided into subdivisions. Behind each
of these tents occupied by the children is a permanent building
containing shower baths and latrines. Another permanent building
is that used as a storeroom, kitchen, and mess hall; the latter
completes the quadrangle.

survey made m 1918. The other children were re-examined after
their return to the Covina Home. These examinations were conducted along the same lines as in the two preceding years. All
recommendations made m 1918 for tonsillectomies and circumcisions
were carried out, and a number of those for dlintal work and
orthodontic corrections. During the current year the teeth of every
child will be examined, and receive the necessary attention. The
recommendation made in 1918 regarding the examination of the eyes
of the children should be carried out. While some improvement has
been noticed in posture, there is still much to be desired in this
direction. It is recommended that the gymnasium be equipped, and
that an instructor in physical culture be placed m charge. Without
such a person to direct the work the results will not be all that
might be desired.
Comment was made in last year's report upon the excellent
sanitary conditions of the kitchen, refrigeration, and stores. The
food supply is abundant, and the meals well prepared. During the
past year there has been an increase m the amount of butter fats
and fresh vegetables consumed. Each child receives a dai'y allowance
of one and one-half pints of fresh milk.

One child, Case No. 84, who had recently been admitted to the
Home, was found to be considerably below normal inteJlect, and
showed physical deformities.
In the interest of the remaining
children, it was necessary to advise the removal of this boy.

Recommended removal

With the exception of Case No. 84 and one Dull Normal child,
the remaining 63 children vary from normal to normal superior
intelligence. There is no doubt that this showing is due to the
personal interest of the management, the excellent environment and
the educational opportunities offered.
The physical and mental
standard is higher than expected. It must be admitted that some
of these youngsters come from more or less shipwrecked families;
the results are therefore so much more gratifying.
Feeling the importance of an investigation as to the conduct
and behavior of our children when away from the protecting inflnC'nce
and supervision at the Home, we interviewed the Principal of the
Covina Public School, and she expressed her opinion in a letter as
follow&·

l'UOCEEDINGS OF THE

OFFICE OF PRINCIPAL
CHARTER OAK SCHOOL,
Cov1NA, CALH'., Sept. 8, 1919.
Dr. Arthur J. Ritte•r,
Care of Stanford lJniversity Medical School,
San Francisco, California.
Dear Sir:
Referring to our today's conversation in regard to the conduct
and behavior of the children of the Masonic Home at Covina, I
wish to state that the children are above the average in mental
ability, refinement and athletics.
I should be very glad to co-operate with you in every way possible·
in the interest of the cause.
Very truly yours,
.
CLARA THOMPSON,
Prin. Charter Oak School.
It is strongly advised that children who are about to enter
nigh school be placed in the homes of Masonic families.- We believe
they would have more opportunities for exchanging ideas in larger
educational centers. At Covina there are limited opportunities for
girls and boys during their high school careers to enjoy the social
privileges which children of that age crave. In addition, we feel
that it would contribute vastly to their education and the development
of their characters, if they could receive the individual attention that
is obtained only in a private home circle. Until the high school age
we feel there are no better environment or educational opportunities
to be had than at the Covina Home, but during that period they
require the broadening influence which i;an only be obtained from
association with children of the same age and those more advanced
than. themselves. The plan that has been suggested to the Board
of Trustees is that during the time children are attending high
school they be placed with families, and that the Board of Trustees
continue their supervision, receiving, at stated periods, reports of
their progress and conduct, until they 'ilrc no longer subject to the
authority of the Home.

The report was adopted as presented, except as to the
request for an appropriation for $11,755.44, which was referred to the Committee on Finance.

AN>IUAL ORATION
Brother Charles H. Victor, Grand Orator, then delivered his annual oration, as follmys:
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
'.fhe duty of your orator at this time is both a pleasant and a
serious one; a pleasant one because we have so many reasons for
congratulation, and serious in that we are confronted by conditions
that are at once fraught with menace and danger not alone to our
fraternity but to the land we love.
One year ago when we met together in annual communication
we were engaged in a war, the equal of which has never been
known in the annals of history. It seemed at that time, and we
felt, that the whole structure of civilization was threatened; we
were hopeful that it might be ended soon, but even the most optimistic of us had no idea the end was so near or that complete
victory could so soon be achieved.
The clouds of war passed, and today the banners of our gallant
allies float beside our own starry emblem, bathed in the sunlight of
a glorious victory. We cannot at this time refrain from congratulating ourselves, because now that the record has been made up,
we find that the destroying Death Angel passed lightly through
the ranks of our fighting men and our losses, severe though they
have been, were light when compared to the tremendous sacrifice
made not alo.ne by our allies, but inflicted upon our adversary.
Before the great Architect of the Universe we humbly bow in
thanksgiving for His goodness and mercy vouchsafed to us. Brethren, we would be untrue to our calling if at this time we did not
likewise refer to our 11llies who, through the many weary months
preceding the time when the strong urge and ca11 came upon us
as a nation to enter the conflict, stood in the breach and fought to
maintain the civilization in which we rejoice today.
We are prone to forget; we are prone to look to the future
always, rather than to the past, so let us remember our gallant
allies, and let us remember that they are allies still, and that in the
great fight that must be waged in the coming mq,nth and in the
coming year, and in the years that are ahead of us, the great fight
of reconstruction that must be made for the fulfillment of the
dream we had when we entered the c'anflict, that our allies must

PROCEEDINGS OF 'rHE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

stand with us and that they must fight with us and that the burden
cannot be borne by them or us alone. We must still be allies.

Oh, let us today not alone congratulate but likewise pay our
respect, our feeling of intense thankfulness to our sister across
the water for the fight that she waged, and let us stand unflinchingly forever against any propaganda that may be spread abroad
to separate these two nations whose lives and whose futures have
been brought together in bonds of blood!

506

What a wonderful record it is that they present to us. We
can spend a moment profitably in reviewing it. We all know how
~ur hearts were burdened when the first news· came that war had
been declared away back in 1914. It seems so long ago, it appears
to be a relic of almost a past age, and yet we were burdened
with an oppressive thought that things were not altogether right
in the world, and then those who afterwards became our allies in
the conflict stepped into the breach. France had her part. France
.vas true to the promise that she had made prior to this conflict.
When the hour came that she must fight-fight she did. There
.v:::s no sacrifice too great for her to make, and she poured out not
alone her manhood but likewise her womanhood upon the altar
of her patriotism. She fought and fought against odds that seemed
almost too 'great for human strength, on and on, willing if necessary to be annihilated rather than submit to a conquest she
knew would be worse than destruction to her national life.
And Belgium-glorious Belgium-who, rather than 1acrifice
her honor for temporary safety and peace, threw her puny strength
into the breach and fought back the invader who would at once
have raped and then destroyed her. Her puny strength was sufficient for the moment, and although she lay des6lated and almost
destroyed in the path of the conqueror, still that strength was sufficient to allow others to rush into the conflict and hold until the
hour when the death knell of autocracy could be sounded.
And then Britain-oh! we hear much of Britain in these days.
I want to say to you, l:l'rethren of the Grand Lodge, that we of
Anglo-Saxon origin can never cease paying our debt of gratitude to
that great Anglo-Saxon people, that great Anglo-Saxon nation
who had been so misjudged, who had been so misunderstood by
our adversary, that they were counted upon to violate the pledge
that they had made and leave their small neighbor in her hour of
trial. But Britain stood as Britain has always stood, ready to fight
for the right.
As we look over the record, England and Scotland and India
and Australia and New Zealand and our near friends on the north,
Canada, we find their blood and treasure poured out without stint,
poured out in a sacrifice unparalleled in the history of mankind,
and they stood and they fought and they waited until their AngloSaxon brethren on this side of the water came into the conflict
and finally assisted in the settlement of the difficulty.

507

And so the record runs on: Italy made a gallant and great
fight, at some times fighting up in the snow-covered Alps and at
others down on the plains-betrayed but never willing to give in;
yes, Italy was a gallant part of the host of righteousness that
fought in the conflict. And so with the others-Serbia, Roumania,
the blacks from Morocco, Japan and China and Russia.
And friends, let us not forget the part that Russia played in
this. struggle. For many weary months she fought; she fought
~t times almost with bare hands, attacked from behind by traitors
m her own camps, but ever fighting until resources were gone. But
credit must be given for one thing: It was due to Russia that
the horde of Huns was held back until their possible hour of
triumph had passed and their fate had been written in lurid letters
of fire on the sign-board of destiny. Russia played a splendid
part until she was practically destroyed.
So we can congratulate our allies for their part in the conflict
and it is only fit and right that we should remember. Yea, breth~
ren, let us never forget the part they played! Shame on him and
shame on those who in this hour of triumph, in this period of reconstruct.ion, would try to spread dissension in our ranks by
ende.avormg to allot to any one particular nation the supreme palm
of victory. All are conquerors, all have their part all have made
their sacrifice; so let us today congratulate and' commend our
allies and seek in no way whatever to take unto ourselves greater ,
credit than is our due nor to take from any full credit for service
rendered.
We are likewise to be congratulated as a fraternity. The
reports that come from all jurisdictions show that many have
been prompted to solicit the privileges of our fraternity. Our
growth has been unparalleled in the history of Masonry. We
cannot help but feel that these initiates of ours have come prompted by a desire to be of service to their fellow men. And Brethren
if that is true, and we cannot doubt it, then we have great caus~
for congratulations and great hope for the future, for it demonstrates that at heart the great mass of our people are sound. It
demonstrates that the desire to serve has not left us ;ivith the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

war; it demonstrates that the principles that we have enunciated
for these many years are finding a responsive echo in the h1iarts
of more and more as the days go by. These numbers have augmented our material prosperity, so we can congratulate ourselves
and our sister jurisdictions today upon the great increase in numbers and material prosperity. This 1::1 the bright side of the picture,
and I would that I could spend the time allotted me in contemplation of a theme so pleasant and so delightful.

Oh, yes! We had a big ideal and we felt that we could sacrifice for that ideal. Then the war ended. Immediately there was a
relaxation-immediately a letting down of the tense feeling we had
had before. Some felt that duty was done; others that they had
really played their part, and then the element came that desired
to place a fallacious and absolutely wrong construction upon the
reason for the sacrifice and is endeavoring to break up all or.ganized society.

But there is another side to the picture and a side perhaps not
quite as inviting.

Now, that is what has led up to our present condition. We
must face that condition and I know of no institution, I know
of no organization that is better fitted to meet it than our great
fraternity.

508

The war is over and the days of relaxation have come, and
In the hearts of
many the blood-lust still remains and we find dissension-we find
indifference-we find active and open propaganda to destroy organized society-we find effort being made to spread confusion
among the ranks of those who labor-we find an effort being made
to destroy the. pleasant alliance that has been formed between
ourselves and other great nations who fought for liberty and for
freedom, and with that problem, we as Masons and we as citizens
are largely concerned, and we can readily afford to spend a few
minutes of our time in this session of Grand Lodge in trying to
find a soluti.on to the difficulties that confront us.

no~ the period of reconstruction is upon us.

To understand something of the problem we will have to revert
again for a moment to the reasons why we entered the conflict
that has just closed. Regardless of acts that may have been committed, there is no question in the minds of those who have studied
the matter and who have been close observers, that our participa- ·
tion in the conflict was due to our following a great ideal. We
fought the war for no mercenary motives-no thought of indemnity
-no thought of political aggrandizement-no thought of material
gain in any way whatever.
We felt that human rights and human freedom and liberty
of all peoples were at stake, and with that splendid idealism before
our minds we went into battle. No sacrifice was too great for us
to make. Our blood and treasure were poured out; our young
manhood was enlisted; conscription was accepted without a murmur; the onerous rulings of the Food Administration were taken
as a matter of course. Economy was practiced that the Nation
might have the funds wherewith to prosecute the war, and when
the call was made by those organizations that were ministering
to the comfort and to the welfare of the boys in camp and at the
front, our purses as well as our hearts were opened to them.

509

Why? Because from the very beginning of our government
the principles of Freemasonry have been inculcated in the minds
of our people. We hear statements made from time to time that
we have no real political influence, and far be it from me, Brethren, standing before you this morning to advocate that a Masonic
Lodge or the Masonic Grand Lodge or that any or all of our jurisdictions should in any time seek political preference. I rejoice
this morning that we have no machinery, no organization, that
can go into the political arena and demand things to which we
are not entitled by our rights as American citizens. And I hope
the day will never come when we will seek for the Masonic fraternity anything that she is not legitimately entitled to have.
E'ut let us look, Brethren, to see whether the statement is altogether true that we have no influence. Let us go back to the
very foundation of our government. We find that many of the
men who organized this government were Masons. Our leading
Colonial fathers were inspired by the lessons that have inspired us,
and in the foundation of our government they endeavored to inculcate in the minds of our people those lessons of Freemasonry,
and down through the years they have passed Masonry and Liberty, not with the many but rather with the few, and through those
few have reached the many, until the idea of liberty and the idea
of freedom and the \dea of the rights of men have been planted
in the hearts of our citizenship. And I say to you this morning,
and I do not believe that any will refute the statement as I make
it, that the idealism of the United States of America, that carried
it through this great war for civilization, was the idealism that was
planted through no other agency than the teachings of Freemasonry
through the years that preceded it. And I want to ask you a question, that if that is a fact and if it be true and if you do not dispute

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOHNIA.

:t-is it not better that we have the substance rather than the
shadow? Is it not better that our teachings through these years
have built up in the hearts of the people a desire for that which is
right, a desire for that which is true, a desire for that which
is good, and has led them forth to lay their lives upon the altar
as a sacrifice for those principles, rather than to gain some temporary advantage by political machinations? Brethren, we have
the substance; let those who desire the shadow play the game as
they will.

to be a Mason. He must be a man whose record as far as we can
ascertain it, at least, is clean. We are not a reform institution, but
religion has for one of its prime duties the building up of men
who have fallen and reclaiming the lost and instructing the young
and providing inspiration and meeting places for the sex that we
do not admit to our membership.

510

This opposition, this unrest, this indifference is the enemy we
have to fight. Now there is no new-there is no startling remedy
for this condition. I cannot stand here this morning and instruct
you in the ways of life that will lead to the solution of this problem,
but I can remind you, Brethren-I can only remind you-of the
lessons which you have learned and to attract to your thought the
fact that the promulgation of those lessons in your community
through the medium of your daily life and your activities will
bring about a solution to the problem.
Freemasonry stands today, as it has ever stood, for certain
well·defined principles. Freemasonry stands first for a belief in
God. It is primary and it is fundamental, and I want to say to
you this morning, Brethren, that without a belief in God you can
have no faith in your fellow man. Faith in fellow man is absolutely founded upon a faith in a higher or Supreme Being, so we can
profitably think for a moment upon the principle that we enunciate
-our belief in God.
Every Mason as he enters the Lodge is required to declare
that belief. He is not required to accept a creed. He is not
required to express an allegiance to any particular type of religious
denomination. Freemasonry does not stand as a religion. We are
not a religious organization, and yet there is another fact in the
same connection, Brethren, that we want to remember and never
lose sight of-Masonry is not a substitute for religion. Masonry
never can be a substitute for religion. I for my part would. not
want a religion that would be as narrow a religion as Freemasonry,
if Freemasonry were a religion. Freemasonry bars so many people.
I cannot take my children to the religion of Freemasonry. My
wife cannot go with me when I attend the inspiring ceremonies of
Freemasonry. My friend who has perhaps fallen, who has wandered
from the paths of rectitude, cannot come back and be reformed by
Freemasonry, because Freellllasonry is not a reform institution.
The man who comes to solicit our privileges must be a good man
and true. He must be a man who in his heart has been prepared

511

And so, when I think of my religion, I want a religion that is
broad enough and inclusive enough to include my family and my
friends along with me. Therefore, I do not this morning advocate
the thought that Masonry is a religion, but I do say this and I
believe that you can find an echoing response in your heart, that
each and every one of you will be a far better Mason if you will
ally yourselves with and support some type of organized religion.
The Church has its place in society. The Church has been
teaching for many years, and Masonry can support the Church
in so far as the Church does not attempt to impose upon it an
authoritative religion. Religion by authority, by direction, that
does not allow for the free use of the conscience and the develop·
ment of the int~llect that God has given to man in the working out of his relation between the Diety and himself has no part
in the support of Freemasonry.
So, let us, Brethren, endeavor as a means of meeting the
spirit of unrest-let us endeavor as a means of meeting the
anarchistic teachings that are.. being spread abroad today, support
the churches that are building up true piety and righteousness in
our several communities, so that their hands will be strengthened
in the fight that they are making along with us.
Masonry likewise teaches certain very pronounced doctrines
in regard to duty as citizens. Americanism is becoming a subject
that is on all tongues. And some say "Well, your doctrine of
Americanism-your doctrine of Nationalism does not confonn to
the universality of Masonry."
Brethren, let us get that idea or notion out of their minds!
The universality of Masonry teaches us that at heart men are alike,
and so they are. At heart we are inspired with the same feelings.
We love, we hate, we work, we play, and regardless of the modes
and the methods that we use, the feeling that prompts our motives
is largely the same, whether it is in the heart of the white in San
Francisco or the black in North Africa, so that universality is the
feeling that we can account for when we talk of the universality
of Masonry.

512

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Masonry does teach this: that we should render a proper· due
to all mankind. We are as much obligated to be just and to be
fair to our brethren who have the black skin or the yellow skin
or red skin as we are to our brethren of the white skin. That is one
of the phases of the universality of Masonry, but Brethren, never
think for one minute that the universality of Masonry denies the
doctrine.of a splendid nationalism or a splendid Americanism.
A man can be a true Frenchman and a good Mason:
A man can be a true Scotchman and a good Mason:
A man can be a true Irishman and a good Mason: ·
A man can be a true Canadian and a good Mason:
But I assert to you this morning, Brethren, that no man can
be a French-American; no man can be a Scotch-American; no
man can be an Irish-American or Canadian-American and owe
allegiance to those people and be a good American Mason.
Our safety as a people depends upon our loyalty to our own
country. If we find those in our midst who are Americans; if we
find those ·in our midst who have been born here and who have
been trained here and are yet concerned in plots to destroy the
liberty that has been built up through these many generations of
toil and bloodshed, then let us deal with them as traitors should be
dealt with. If we find in our midst those who have come from
other shores and are accepting our hospitality, our benefits and our
privileges, and yet are working as thieves in the night, ready to
stab us in the back and destroy the institutions that have made our
land what it is, then let us send them back to the p!ac·e whence
they came and rid our country of an undesirable element.
So Masonry teaches good citizenship; Masonry teaches good
Americanism. And Americanism today in its best sense can be
exemplified by the spirit that is willing to work in ·these problems
of reconstruction as men inspired by that spirit that is willing to
make the same sacrifice, who are willing to pay the same price that
our country may be perpetuated and may go on in peace as it did
in war, and if we can get that spirit in the hearts of our people then ·
our American Nation is safe.
·
As a citizen there is .one very important duty and that is the
duty as a voter. Our registration shows some remarkable things,
and one of the sad as well as remarkable things is that we are not
as a people as careful and as zealous and as jealous of the privilege of the ballot as we should be. Many are indifferent even to
registration, and of those who do register, large numbers of them

Gl<AND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

513

do not vote. Brethren, in every Masonic Lodge at the time when
an election is on, mention should be made that the prime duty of a
voter is to express his opinion-not the opinion of the Lodge, not
the opinion of Masonry, but his opinion as a voter.
Let us, Brethren, lay just a little bit more stress on the observance of this privilege and this duty and a little less stress on
who and what we are voting for. Oh, it is so easy to get up excitement over an individual; it is so easy to get up a temporary
excitement over an issue, but it is hard to get up enthusiasm and
excitement over just ordinary duty. But voting is not an ordinary
duty. It is the greatest duty that we as citizens have to perform.
Masonry should likewise enter into the everyday life of t~e
individual if these problems are going to be solved. Masonry ts
not a thing for the Lodge-room alone; it is not a thing. for our
festive occasions alone, but it is a practical everyday philosophy
of life. A man to be a good Mason should be a good business
man should be a good lawyer; should be a good bricklayer or a
good mechanic. Into his everyday work should go the. principlt;s
that have been inculcated in his life through the medmm of his
Lodge. He should feel that he is endeavoring to dignify his craft
or his profession,. he should endeavor at all times to show tha~ the
word of a Mason in business or as a laborer or as a professional
man is absolutely inviolable. The fact that he is a Mason should
be sufficient recommendation of his character. And in our Lodges
we should lay emphasis upon that fact. We should teach the
fact not alone in the beautiful phraseology of our ritual, but in the
common ordinary language that every man can understand, and
if we find in our community Masons who are not living up to
the teaching of Masonry in their everyday business life and affair~,
then so.!11e means should be found to show them the .error of their
ways.
Brethren, the teaching of Masonry is nothing more or less
than old fashioned, common honesty and common sense. T~o~e
are the things that are particularly needed in this hour of crisis.
There is no new panacea for the ills of the world. Work honestly
performed, duty faithfully done, will bring peace and happiness
and contentment to our land. Let us in our Lodges as we go back
from this communication of the Grand Lodge give consideration
to the old fashioned virtues; let us bring them before our membership as we have never brought them before. Let us put greater
stress upon the social side of our Institution, so that ;ve can come
to understand and know our Brethren better; let us give them the
inspiration of our companionship; let us give them the helpful and

514

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

strengthening influence of a closer acquaintanceship; let us have .
them feel that as they go out in their several walks of life that
they have the interest and support of the brethren of their Lodges.
Let us endeavor by this close, active connection and acquaintanceship and frequent meetings together to weld ourselves into one
solid mass that will stand for righteousness and for honesty· and
for uprightness in our civic as well as our private dealings; let us
be bound together into one great mass that will move forward as
a solid unit for righteousness.
Just a little while ago I heard a soldier telling of his experience with the army of occupation. He was sent to the Rhine after
the armistice was signed and reached the border or edge of the
river at night. In the morning, when he went out from his tet'\t
and went to the river to look across at Coblenz, he saw over the
great fortress of Ehrenbreitstein the American flag flying. It
made a wonderful impression on his mind. He said he had never
been thrilled before as he was thrilled by the sight of the American flag over Ehrenbreitstein, and he turned to his comrades and
found that they were feeling just as he felt; and so morning after
morning, during the time they spent with the army of occupation
they went out and saw Old Glory floating over Ehrenbreitstein
and as they returned to their native land he said the thought came
home with them. His whole company seemed to be inspired with
the thought that as they returned to their land they would endeavor
to so live and act that they might keep that American flag flying
over Ehrenbreitstein-Ehrenbreitstein, not in its physical character
but Ehrenbreitstein as it typified the ascension of righteousness
and of truth and of freedom over autocracy and sin and error.
And so, Brethren, in these, my closing words to you, I would
urge that' as we go forth from this communication of the Grand
Lodge, we go with the feeling and inspiration that we are going
to keep Old Glory flying over Ehrenbreitstein and that error and
unrighteousness and ignorance and lack of patriotic fervor shall be
forever cast forth from among us and that the principles that we
are so pleased to enunciate as the principles of our grand order
may animate and inspire mankind, to the end that we may have a
better, brighter and more glorious land in the future than even our
glorious record of the past.

Were it not for the modesty of the Orator, the transcript above would show the applause which frequently
greeted the speaker. On motion of the Junior Grand Warden a rising vote of thanks was extended to Brother Victor.

PETITION OF ACACIA LODGE TO WORK IN GERMAN
Los Angeles, Calif., October 11, 1919.
Most Worshipful Bradford Webster, Grand Master of Masons, State of
California, and Brethren of the Grand Lodge.
Most Worshipful Sir an.d Bri;thren:

As the representative of Acacia Lodge No. 438, F. & A M., I have
to report, tlrnt at the stated meeting of the month of September, and
after all members were duly notified, it was unanimously decided to petition t1ie Grand Lodge to allow us to confer the work in the German
language.

516

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Just a year ago one of our Past Masters read a telegram before
your honorable body, expressing the desire of the Lodge to voluntarily
desist from using that language, because our country was at that time
at war with the German Government, people and tongue.
This war having now been won by America and to a great extent by
the loyal, actual, financial and economical support of the millions of
citizens of German descent, the members of our Lodge deem it proper
at this time to petition you, Sir and the Brethren, to allow them again
the use of the German language.
As the Lodge was founded to spread the cement of friendship and
brotherly love among those foreigners of German tongue who come to
our free country in search. of freedom in speech as well as development,
the members are sure that by joining our body of men they will not only
become better men but a!so more loyal citizens.
They have asked me to convey this sentiment and desire to your
most careful and kindest consideration.
Yours fraternally and obediently,
H. M. WF,GF,Nl\R,
Master.

REPORT OF WAR FUND COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

The undersigned, Masonic War Fund Committee, appointed by the
Grand Master, beg leave to report as follows:
That during the year your Committee has administered the said
War Fund in strict accordance with the rules and regulations governing
its administration as set forth on page 30 of the Proceedings of this
Grand Lodge for 1918, and as authorized by a resolution of this Gtand
Lodge set forth on page 238 of said Proceedings.
At the time of the appointment of this Committee the balance of
the War Fund in the hands of the Grand Treasurer amounted to
$60,188.29. During the past year contributions have been received and
paid over to the Grand Treasurer amounting to $4,077.25, making a
total of $64,265.54. Disbursements have been made from this fund
amounting to $5,160.16, and there is now in the hands of the Grand
Treasurer belonging to the Masonic War Fund the sum of $59,105.38.
To this balance must be added sundry items. of interest on bonds and
bank deposits, which will be shown by the report of the Grand Treasurer. (The net amount of the fund as of October 1, 1919, is $60,893.54.)
Annexed hereto is a detailed report of all receipts and disbursements
during the past year. An examination of the detailed report will show
that 104 Lodges have made contributions to the War Fund since October
4, 1918, and that the money disbursed has been almost entirely for assistance in the support and maintenance of social rooms and other instrumentalities of Masonic hospitality and brotherly attention to members of
the craft in the Army and Navy of the United States and its Allies.
Very little relief has been given to or required by California Masons

519

The Grand Master in his letter announcing. the establishment of a
Masonic War Fund, and asking for contributions thereto by the brethren
of California, stated that "in the event of the termination of war leaving
an unexpended balance in said fund, the same shall be donated pro rata
to the Lodges collecting the same, or shall be paid into the Masonic
Home Fund, in the discretion of the Grand Master." It seems to your
Committee that not only the best interests of the craft, but also the
desire of the subscribers to this fund will be served by turning the
largier part thereof over to the Masonic Homes of California. Expressions have been had from many Masons on this subject, among whom are
more than fifty Masters of Lodges that were large contributors to this
fund, and without exception it is their opinion that the Masonic War
Fund should be given to the Masonic Homes and that the same should
not be given back to the Lodges that acted as instruments for the collection of the same. Moreover, during the year of the collection of this
fund no general effort was made to increase the Endowment Fund of
the Masonic Homes.
Your Committee, therefore, recommends that the Grand Secretary
and Grand Treasurer be authorized and directed to transfer from the
Masonic War Fund to the Masonic Homes of California the sum of
$55,000, and that the balance remaining in the Masonic War Fund continue to be administered according to the rules and regulations relative
thereto adopted in 1918.

REPORT OF ENDOWMENT COMMITTEE,
MASONIC HOMES
Los Angeles, California, October 1, 1919.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

We, the members of your Endowment Committee of the Masonic Homes of California, appointed by the Grand Master at the
close of the last Grand Lodge, beg to report that our activities
during the past year have resulted in a very material increase in
our Endowment Fund.
Early in January of this year, the entire Committee was c.alled
together for consultation at the Grand Secretary's office; the general plan of campaign outlined and unanimously approved. It also

523

It is needless to recapitulate the plans adopted for the Victory
Drive held from April 21st to May 10th, of which the members of
the Grand Lodge are undoubtedly familiar. The State was divided
into regional districts-the members of the Endowment Committee
taking charge of the districts in which they resided.
There have been some criticisms, and, in some cases, lack of
enthusiasm. In most instances we have had the most whole-hearted
cooperation and wonderful organization. Generally speaking, however, it is a source of great pleasure for us to extend our deep and
heartfelt appreciation for the cooperation received from the officers
and brethren of subordinate lodges in this Grand Jurisdiction.
In the last report of the Endowment Committee, the status or
the Endowment Fund was given as follows:
August 1, 1918Cash on hand ....................................................$ 2,468.54
Securities, etc ................................................... 145,912.50
Total ..........................................................$148,381.05
Our Grand Treasurer, E'rother .Filmer, under date of September 20, 1919, advised that the status of the Endowment Fund on
that date was as follows:
Cash in bank ....................................................$ 35,387.83
Securities .......................................................... 219,003.86
Total ................................................... :.............. $254,391.69

It will be readily noted that we have made an excellent showing as a result of the Drive, and our brethren are obtaining a more
thorough knowledge of the needs of an ample Endowment Fund
for the care of our Masonic charities. The great difficulty confronting this Committee seems to be that the brethren generally
have no intimate knowledge of the magnificent homes for the
elderly at Decato and the Orphans' Home at Covina; and it has
been suggested that a motion picture film be produced so that the
brethren in all the lodges may have an opportunity of seeing f<;>r
themselves, if unable to make a personal inspection, just exactly
what Masonry in California really is accomplishing.
It has been suggested, and the Endowment Committee earnestly recommends the approval of the recommendation, that a proper

scenario be prepared and that a moving picture film be produced1000 feet for the Decoto Home, and
1000 feet for the Covina Home,
which would tell a most interesting story on the screen, lasting for
approximately one-half hour. The Committee has an understanaing with one of the largest picture producing companies that the
work will be done at cost. The directors and camera men will be
Masons, who will naturally take a personal interest in the work.
The Committee on Investigation has ascertained that the income from the per capita tax-$1.00 per member per annum-has ·
not, during the past year, on account of the abnormal prices prevailing for every commodity entering into the conduct of the
Homes, been sufficient to provide for all of the necessary expenses
in connection with same. This clearly indicates the necessity for
active work in materially increasing the Endowment Fund so that
the income thereof can be turned over annually to Trustees of the
Masonic Homes, thereby preventing, if possible, an increase in the
per capita tax on the subordinate lodges.
It is the opinion of j:his Committee that the Endowment Fund
for the Masonic Homes of California cannot be construed as a
Grand Lodge Fund, as referred to in the Constitution of the Grand
Lodge. It is our understanding that the donors to the Endowment
Fund contribute for a specific purpose and that it is in the nature of
a trust. Hence, we recommend appropriate action on the part·
of the· Grand Lodge as to the investment of the funds of the
Endowment Fund and also the safeguarding of the securities, so
that the Constitution of the Grand Lodge shall be clearly defined in
this particular.
We beg to submit herewith in detail as near a complete report
of the result of the Drive up to September 15, 1919, as possible.
We do not in any way guarantee this report to be correct, but
the figures submitted are the latest available and have been procured either from the Master or Secretary of the lodges. In some
instances it has been necessary to write four or five letters before
replies were received, and it will be noted in some cases, that no
reports of any kind have reached the Committee, all of which is
fraternally submitted.

Brother ·wm H. Fischer, for the Committee on Grand
Lecturer's report, presented the following:
To the .41ost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your committee heretofore appointed to consider the annual report
of the Grand Lecturer desires to submit its report as follows:
The report of the Grand Lecturer makes clear the fact, \vhich was
previously reflected in the report of the Grand Secretary, that the doors
of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction are at the present time being sought
by an unusually large number of men who are attracted to our fraternity
hy reason of a favorable opinion conceived of it, and a sincere desire to
he serviceable to their fellow men. It likewise is easily to be observed,
from a study of the report, that the upright, courageous and manly conduct of our brethren who went overseas in the service of the government
during the late war has had a profound effect upon many young men;
for among those who are now seeking admission to our privileges, many
indeed come from the ranks of the gal!ant boys who fought under Old
Glory on the fields of France.
The work of the Grand Lecturer during the past year has been
rendered more than usually arduous by reason of the extended interruption of Lodge meetings on account of the influenza epidemic last fall
and winter; but as· usual, counting no inconvenience to himself, and
sparing himself naught of effort, the Grand Lecturer has fully made the
rounds of the Lodges. and has ministered to them all with the efficiency
for which he is so well known.
W c note with deep regret the passing from life of Brother Edward
Warren Clot1gh, Inspector of the 24th District, and Brother Frank
Edward Morrell, Inspector of the 1st Masonic District. Grand Lodge

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOUNIA

already has given suitable testimony of its grief and the loss it has
sustained.

vVe note with particular interest that paragraph of the Grand Lecturer's Report dealing with the formation of an Officers' Association in
the 53d Masonic District, and unite with the Grand Lecturer in extending to Brother David J. Reese our compliments upon the organization
thus alluded to. Your Committee coftlmends this plan to the consideration of the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts, doing so in the
belief that frequent meetings of the Officers of the Lodges composing ·
districts will result in much good.
In c:osing, your Committee desires to testify in the strongest manner possible to its appreciation of th~ high service constantly rendered
to Freemasonry by our Grand Lecturer, Brother Thomas J. Baker. We
feel sure that no expression of commendation which we might be able to
write would be considered extravagant by the Inspectors, Officers or
brethren of the Lodges constituting this Grand Jurisdiction. Insistent
always on efficiency, demanding ever a full respect not only for the
discipline but as well for the principles of Masonry, Brother Baker, at
the same time, is a gentle, gracious and kindly guide, philosopher and
friend of the rank and file of the Fraternity, and we rejoice in commending him once more to the most generous consideration of Grand
Lodge.

Brother \tVilliam A. Sherman, chairman of the Committee on Finance, submitted the following report:
To "the Mast Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ccdifarnia:

Your Committee on Finance begs leave to report as follows: Pursuant to annual custom, your committee, through Accountant E. S.
Valentine, ~as e;i<:amined the books and records of the Grand Secretary
and Grand Treasurer and compared the totals of the books of both
offices and are pleased to report that every item of receipt and disbursement has been properly entered and accounted for by these two efficient
Officers of Grand Lodge. Inasmuch as the Grand Treasurer was compelled to leave San Francisco to attend the Supreme Council of Scottish before the opening of this annual communication, two mem ·
hers of your committee examined the securities of the various Grand
Lodge funds, which are deposited in the vaults of the :Mercantile Trust
Company of this city, and found them to check correctly with the report
of the Grand Treasurer. All unmatured coupons are intact on the
bonds and otherwise properly segregated and in good form. It is the
intention of the Grand Treasurer to have the bonds of the various
Liberty issues registered, which will relieve him of considerable work in
the cutting of coupons. The work of the Grand Treasurer has materially increased because of the success of the Endowment Fund drives
and is entitled to the thanks of this Grand Lodge for the conscientious
and business-like manner in which he has conducted the duties of his
office.
Your Committee on Finance has received and carefully considered
the reports of the Boards of Relief of San Francisco, Los Angeles, Oakland, San Jose, Sacramento, San Diego and Honolulu. The reports
show conclusively the earnest and capable manner in which these Boards
of Relief are being conducted. Although th.e work of the Boards of
Relief is increasing very rapidly in the cities of San Francisco, Los
Angeles and San Diego, nevertheless the Boards are being operated
economically, which is due, no doubt, to the employment bureaus which
arc conducted in these three large cities with increasing efficiency. The
Board of Relief in San Diego has materially increased its work and as
it started without any capital it finds itself ha.ndicapped in its work to
such an extent that it needs a larger amount this year than it will in the
future when it will be reimbursed only for the money expended for
Lodges and J uris<lictions not now reimbursing it. In furtherance of the
work of the Board of Relief we offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
Brother Irving J. Mitchell, chairman of the Committee
on Masonic Education, reported as follows:
To the 1l1.'.

w:. Grand Lodge of California:

The Committee on Masonic Education report as follows:
It is quite apparent to all intelligent men that today humanity
stands face to face with conditions of tmparalleled difficulty. Everywhere social and economic problems baffle the sagacity of the wisest.
From the chaos of war man has entered a period of confusion and discontent. The threatening voice of force is heard in the most unexpected
quarters. Lack of respect for law, order, and the rights of others has
become all too common.
How shall Freemasonry concern itself with the storm and stress
through which suffering mankind is now groping its way? Shall it he
in deed and in fact a helpful, constructive power in the civic life of the
present, or shall it be indifferent and unconcerned?
Never before has the need for right thinking !lnd clear understanding been so manifest as today; Never in this generation has there been
greater necessity among Masons for voicing and keeping constantly in
mind the potent principles for which this institution stands four-square.
Masonry can and should be a stabilizing force in a world filled with disturbances .. If we mistake not, the thought of larger service is a matter
of profound concern to the Craft.

549

m~st not commit itself to partisanship.

The exigencies of the past year have made educational work upon
the part of our Lodges extremely difficult. Meetings have been held
necessarily in many Lodges twice or three times each week, and every
moment has hcen required for degree work. With all the gain in ·
membership, however, and the apparent prosperity, the average attendance of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction is approximately 15 per cent.
This very con(lition evidences the fact that all is not well, and we need
to do something to awaken the interest of the missing 85 per cent.
The need for a better understanding of the basic principles for
which this institution stands, and the practical application of those principles to the great prohlcms of the clay, is just as pressing as ever. This
conviction is voiced on every side. The same old question p;esents
itself, "How shall we find the time?"
Upon the direction of this committee an <'Xperimcnt has l:ccn tried in
Los Angeles. l n July the Masters and 'War deus of the Lodges of that
city were formed into an organization. It is not a social organization.
It is devoted solely to the Cause of Enlit;htenmcnt.
It has gathered together a permanent board of local speakers,
whose services arc available to all of the Lodges of that city and vicinity. They comprise some of the ahlest men of the Craft. Mass meetings of the Fraternity have hccn addressed hy Ma sons of national cminc11cc and similar meetings arc planned for the near future. Through
these addn•sscs, practical application has been made of Masonic princi~
pies to the problems of the day.
The work tints far accomplished has shown clearly that what is
particularly needed today is concert of action among the Lodges. It has
been demonstrated that by the Masters and Wardens meeting together
frequently, getting hctter acquainted, thinking together, planning together
and working together toward a common ohjcctivc, practical results in a
large measure will surely he attained. Such results can be accomplished
throughout the State by organized effort in each city or inspection district.
Quoting from the address of the M.'. \V.'. Grand Master: "A
greater and more vital interest is being taken in what Masonry stands
for than ever before, hut whether or not that awakening of interest in
vital topics is a by-product or in any sense due to war conditions, is

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

really not important. We realize that more and more it is true that
the eyes of the world are upon us, and that our responsibility is correspondingly enhanced."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE

550

We recommend the following:
First-That the Committee on Masonic Education shall consist of
three members from each of the following' districts: Northern California, Bay Counties Region, Central California and Southern California, together with a general chairman; a local chairman to be appointed from the committee in each district; this committee to be appointed by the M.'. W.'. Grand Master and to be directly responsible
to the Grand Lodge.
Second-That each District Committee organize the Masters and
Wardens of the district in such groups as may be most convenient, for
meetings at regular intervals under the direction of the committee.
Third-That the committee procure (!st) a series of subjects for
discussion, (2nd) a list of local speakers available to the Lodges, and
(3rd) addresses at Masonic mass meetings by speakers of established
reputation.
Fourth-That through the organization above outlined, the Lodges
of this jurisdiction be encouraged to participate actively in the solution
of the problems of the day.
Fifth-That the committee also promote a proper understanding of
and interest in the sublime teachings and ritual of the Craft.
Sixth-That the Committee on Masonic Education shall in every
way be helpful to all Lodges who desire its counsel and co-operation.
That this committee shall encourage the development of a broader
understanding among the Craft of the fundamental principles of this
institution, and the practical application thereof.
Respectfully submitted,
IRVING }. MITCHELL,
DENMAN

S. W AGSTAil!o',

ROBERT B. GAYLORD,

RESOLUTION-SAN JACINTO LODGE
The following was introduced:
·whereas, On April 21st, 1918, the Masonic Temple at San Jacinto,
Calif., was totally destroyed by earthquake, and as there was no available place to meet, San Jacinto Lodge No. 338 had to rebuild, and the
officers and members of said Lodge were forced to borrow the sum of
four thousand ($4000), pledging the good faith of San Jacinto Lodge
No. 338, F. & A. M., through a few of its members; and
Whereas, The efficiency and the life itself of said Lodge is endangered from the heavy debt overshadowing it, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the sum of $4000 be hereby appropriated from the
funds of this Grand Lodge to be expended through the Grand Master
and Grand Secretary to remove the burden from the shoulders of said
San Jacinto Lodge No. 338.

Referred to the Committee on Finance.

Committee.

The report was adopted, together with the recommendations. On motion the Grand Secretary was directed to
write to Brother Clarence Berry, giving expression of the
appreciation of Grand Lodge for his efforts in holding his
Lodge together, and our sympathy in his domestic afflictions.

APPROPRIATIONS

Since 1917 the Grand Lodge has appropriated for the use of this
committee the sum of five hundred ($500) dollars for the purchase of
books and she'.ving. The sum of $81.75 was expended in 1918, and your
committee has not expended any money during the past Masonic year.
There is now a balance of the appropriation not expended in the sum <;>f
four hundred e.ighteen dollars and twenty-five cents ($418.25). Your
committee might have expended this money, but it was dec;med advisable
not to make any purchases during the past year, or until our social conditions had become more settled.
Your committee is of the opinion that the balance above shown
should be left to the credit of the Committee on Library for the ensuing
year.
And your committee desires to impress upon the members of the
Grand Lodge that we still have shelving for over two thousand books,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
Brother Albert A. Rosenshine, chairman of the Committee on Charters, presented the following report:
To the Most Worshipful .Grand Lodge of California·:

Your Committee on Charters begs to report as follows:
During the past Masonic year dispensations were issued to two
Lodges, namely, Blythe Lodge, at Blythe, California, an<l Victory
Lodge, at San Francisco, California. Each of these Lodges has petitioned this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge for charters.
Your committee has made careful examination of the records of
each of said Lodges and w.e find that the same substantially conform to
all the requirements of the Constitution and that they arc kept in an
orderly and careful inanncr. In the case of Victory Lodge, the minutes
fail to set forth in full the by-laws adopted hy that Lodge, and we rec-

'

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ommend that the by-laws as .adopted by said Lodge be spread in full
upon the minutes.
The communities in which each of these Lodges have been established are sufficient both in population and resources to justify the
chartering of these Lodges. Each of the Lodges are free from debt
and have substantial cash balances on hand.
We therefore recommend that a charter be issued to Blythe Lodge
situated at Blythe, California, to be known as No. 473; and that a
charter be issued to Victory Lodge situated at San Francisco, California, to be known as No. 474.
There was also referred to your committee the request of Meridian
Lodge No. 182, situated at Arbuckle, California, asking that it be
granted permission to change its name from Meridian Lodge .No. 182 to
Arbuckle Lodge No. 182.
Your committee finds this request to be in proper form and that the
Lodge meets at Arbuckle and not at Meridian, and that the facts
brought out before your committee justify the granting of this request.
'We therefore recommend that the name of Meridian Lodge No. 182
he changed to Arbuckle Lodge No. '182 and that this Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge grant said change of name.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PLANS FOR
HOMES REVENUE
Past Grand Master Keesling, chairman of the Special
Committee appointed pursuant to the Grand Master's recommendation to survey and _report some plan for providing
revenue for the Homes, presented the following report:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your special committee appointed with the duty to thoroughly investigate the various plans and suggestions to adequately provide for
the maintenance of the Masonic Homes respectfully submits its report
as follows:
The plans considered were the one pending as unfinished business
by resolution providing for the devising of ways anti means for charging
the individual members of the Craft at the rate of one dollar ($1.00) per
year for this purpose, an endowment insurance plan, the so-called Pennsylvania plan, and the modification of the Pennsylvania plan as reported
by the Trnstecs of the Masonic Homes.
We have given these various plans careful consideration, and with
definite objects in view submit our recommendation.
We believe in a permanent endowment fund; that that fund should
be at least two and one-half million dollars; that any plan for obtaining
money must provide for an allocation of part of the money collected to
the endowment fund, thereby providing a means for lessening the burden as time goes on and the fund increases; that the problem is not so
much to provide a means whereby the present per capita charge may
be reduced, but, owing to increasing demands and responsibilities which
must he assumed by the fraternity, the Prevention of ati increase in the
per capita.

Whether or not the value of money and its decreased purchasing
power will continue is at kast a problem for present consideration and
the fact is that if the cost of maintenance continues, it will be necessary
to raise the per capita or restrict our activities and not fully perform our
duty. An increased per capita would mean an additional hardship on
those lodges which are now complaining of the burden and would cer
tainly mean in some instances a readjustment of dues with its attendant
difficulties. It is quite likely that the conditions affecting the value of
money will prevail for some time. Our responsibility grows in_ propo~­
tion to the growth of the membership. As the expenses grow, if that is
to be relieved by a permanently invested fund, it is self-evident that the

569

amount of the endowment fund must be increased. We all realize the
importance of the endowment fund. Conceding its importance from
the point of view of a possible reduction of the per capita it becomes
exceedingly more important if we consider the possibility of in.crease of
the Per capita. It may be well to note what has happened with reference
to institutions which have considered themselves sufficiently endowed
and no": find that, by reason of growing responsibility, if they are to
keep their proper p!ace and perform a sufficient duty, they must meet a
s_ituation which demands increased funds. Stanford University, at one
tune the most largely privately endowed institution in America, if not in
the wo:ld, ".'as consi<!cred to be beyond all question of necessity, and
today hnds itself laclong funds by reason of a change of circumstances
an_d_ increased rc.sponsibilitics and under the necessity of imposing a
tmt10n fee when 1t was the hope and the aspiration of the founders that
an education should be furnished free to the boys and girls of California
and elsewhere.• The exigencies have compelled that action or a restriction of activities. Harvard University and other universities largely
endowed arc making strenuous drives for money. A study of the
appropriations for the University of California would indeed prove
interesting.
Therefore, it seems that the plan for charging the individual member
One Dollar ($1.00) per annum for the benefit of the homes, even if such
IL:gislation _could he effectively enacted, would be but a temporary expedient and, m the end, mean but a compulsory addition to the <lues of the
Lodges and the transfer of the present per capita in that manner.
There was submitted a plan for endowment insurance contemplating

A financial secretary employed by reason of special ability to col!ect
funds was suggested. Believing that the voluntary activities of the
brethren under direction of a committee of this Grand Lodge will more
than equal the activities of any paid official, we believe the suggestion
should not be considered.
There remains for consideration (1) the recommendation of the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of the "Pennsylvania Plan
modified to meet conditions peculiar to our Lodges," which in a few
words is a substitution for a uniform membership charge, an amount
proportionate to the initiation fee charged by the Lodge, and (2) the
so-called Pennsylvania plan itself.
Careful consideration has been given to both plans. We believe that
the theory of the charge for the maintenance of the homes is based upon
the requirement that the individual member shall bear an equal .proportion of the burden. That is the basis of the per capit~ tax. That a
Lodge charges Nine Dollars ($9.00) or Twenty-four Dollars ($24.00)
dues or a Thirty Dollar ($30.00) or One Hundred Dollar ($100.00)
initiation fee makes no difference and that we believe to be perfectly
proper. The dues and the initiation fee of a particular Lodge are based
upon what the members conceive to be the requirements for administration and other standards established for their membership. We believe
that the proposed fee, if it may· be so defined, is in the nature of a
capital contribution and should not be entirely expended for maintenance,
but a portion thereof should be allocated for the purposes of permanent
improvement or become a part of the permanent fund. It is our opinion
that no man who is desirous of membership in the fraternity will be
balked by a Twenty Dollar additional charge; that it will be willingly
paid; that it is a most feasible plan and will have a salutary effect of
impressing upon the initiate the responsibility of a Mason toward the
less fortunate, which probably would not have been amiss hitherto. It
may be claimed that this is imposing an unfair charge upon the initiate.
It should be unnecessary to comment upon the fact that the present
members of the Fraternity have been bearing the present burden continuously since the establishment of our homes, and, if they have not,
they should have contributed at least the amount expected of the initiate
and that, under the plan, a portion thereof being used for permanent
improvement and a permanent fund will result in reducing responsibility
in the future. It can just as well be claimed why should any initiate be
permitted to enter now and avail himself of the privileges without bearing a portion of the burden thereof which those in the fraternity have
borne. It is a well recognized system in some institutions to add to
initiation fees any amount which has been paid by members by way of
assessment.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

571

payment by each m1tiate m addition to the initiation fee for the purposes
of the homes: one-half thereof to be allocated for maintenance, one-half

a.llocatto~ of the surplus in either fund to the endowment fund from

To the Jfost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

With regard to the application of San Fernando Lodge No.
343, either that it be granted .concurrent jurisdiction with the
Lodges of the City of Los Angeles, or that its exclusive jurisdiction be defined to be the same as it was previous to the annexation of the San Fernando Valley by the City 6f Los Angeles, we
beg to report:
It is manifest that the situation is such as to make it proper
for this Grand Lodge to grant relief. By reason of the annexation
by the City of Los Angeles of all of the territory surrounding the
. little city of San Fernando, wherein is located San Fernando
Lodge No. 343, the jurisdiction of this Lodge is now confined to
the territory within the town limits, about one mile square, while
prior to such annexation its jurisdiction extended over some 700
square miles of territory. The Grand Master correctly concluded
that under our existing law the Lodge could not be given concurrent jurisdiction with the Lodges of the City of Los Angeles
over territory within the legal bounds of the City of Los Angeles. But we see no reason why it cannot be given, under the
provision of Section 92A, exclusive jurisdiction over the City of
San Fernando, and over all the territory outside of said city over
which it had jurisdiction prior to the annexation by the latter city
of. the San Fernando Valley. This is exactly the character of ·
case contemplated by Section 92A. The procedure had is in
substantial accord with the requirements of Section 92A. The
notice required by such section has 'been given to every Lodge
where jurisdiction will be affected by the proposed change, and
no opposition has been recorded on the part of any such Lodge.
Th~ section requires as a prerequisite to action by the Grand
Lodge, the recommendation of the Grand Master. That recommendation has now been made. \Ve believe the Grand Lodge
should in this way grant the relief sought by San Fernando Lodge
No. 343. If this be done, there will be no necessity for any
amendment of Section 92A in so far as the needs of this Lodge
are concerned, and we are not at the moment sufficiently advised
::s to the necessity of any amendment or as to what should be
the provisions thereof. We doubt very much whether it would
be expedient to amend our law in such a way as to permit a
petition·er for. the degrees to apply to any Lodge in the State

WORK IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE
Past Grand Master Angellotti presented the following
report:
To the i"tfost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Certain recommendations of the Grand Master, arising from
difficulties in Acacia (formerly Germania) Lodge No. 438 of Los
Angeles, have been referred to your Committee for consideration.
At the last communication, upon a request based on the unanimous
action of that Lodge, held at a stated meeting, to the effect that the
name of the Lodge be changed from "Germania" to "Acacia," and
that its work thenceforth be given in the English language instead
of German, it was in effect resolved that the name be so changed
and the ritual thereafter rendered in the English language.
In view of internaltdiscord in the Lodge resultant of this change,
the Grand Master recommended either that the privilege of using

576

PROCEEDINGS .OF THE

the German language be restored to the Lodge, or that all Lodges
working in foreign languages be required t() adopt the English language in their work. In this connection it should further be stated
that the Grand Master is of the opiniori that "in the interest and
furtherance of that thoroughgoing Americanization which is the
dominant hope of the nation today, we should require all the Lodges
holding allegiance to this Grand Lodge to uniformly adopt and ~se
the English language in their work." At the very outset we desire
to state that your Committee unanimously concur in this last expressed view of the Grand M<1ister as to any Lodge that may .hereafter be instituted.
With relation to the matter of allowing Acacia Lodge to resume the rendition of the ritual in the German language, we are satisfied that no action should be had at this time. This conclusion
is based on the information given us by the Inspector of the Masonic District including that Lodge, and the Master of the Lodge.
There is no difference between these two brethren as to the cause
of the trouble that now exists in the Lodge. The great majority
of the members of the Lodge, including the present Master, who
opposed the making of such request, have loyally conformed to the
new policy inaugurated therein at the request of the Lodge, and
have faithfully endeavored to carry on the affairs of the Lodge
thereunder. The only difficulty now existing is due to the action
of a very small minority, the members of which substantially declared that they would not conform, and that for so long as the
Lodge failed to go back to the use of the German language there
would be no degrees conferred in the Lodge. A$ a result, such
applications for degrees as have been made ha_v: been :ejected. In
view of our decisions, the members who participated in such conduct have been guilty of a serious Mas.onic offense. In any event,
neither this Grand Lodge nor Acacia Lodge can allow itself to be
thus dragooned by such conduct on the part of these few recalcitrant members into taking the action they thus desire to accomplish.
We, therefore, recommend that no action be taken at this co~1munication looking to the restoration of the German language m
the ritualistic work of Acacia. Lodge.
With regard to the recommendation that all Lodges working
in foreign languages be required to adopt the English lapguage in
their work: As already stated, we heartily concur in the view of
the Grand Master, if the same be limited to Lodges to be hereafter
instituted. Rut we see no such exigency as now requires us to
take action which would have the immediate effect of depriving
several of our oldest and best Lodges, among others our Lodges

working in the French and Italian languages, a privilege given
them by our predecessars many years ago. We have only recently
registered in express provision of law our approval of these Lodges.
(S<'e sec. 121, Constitution.) If any necessity therefor hereafter
arises, we can easily take such action as may be desirable.
\Ve, therefore, recommend that no action be now had on this
recommendation of the Grand Master.

LIFE MEMBERSHIP
Past Grand Master \:Veller, for the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following report:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration
the approval of the Grand Master of standing resolutions adopted
by Lodges creating life memberships, and finds as follows:
That Southern California Lodge No. 278, West Gate Lodge No.
335, and Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469, have each complied with the
requirements of our Constitution in all respects, and we therefore
recommend that the action of the Grand Master in approving the
resolutions of said Lodges be approved.
The record submitted in connection with the action of Hawaiian
Lodge No. 21 and Argonaut Lodge No. 461 shows that neither of
said Lodges followed the procedure prescribed by our law.
Section 129 of our Constitution provides for a system of life
membership by the adoption of a standing resolution wherein shall
be provided the sum to be paid for the life memberships, the securities in which the funds may be invested, and also the duty of the
Secretary. to report to the Grand Lodge annually the number of
life members, the amount of the fund thus created, and the manner
in which it is invested.

579

Hawaiian Lodge No. 21 merely adopted the recommendation of
a Committee that life members be created upon the payment of
$150, and no provision was made for the investment of the funds
or report of the Secretary.
Argonaut Lodge No. 461 adopted a resolution as follows:
"Resolved, That this Lodge does hereby establish the fee for a
Life. Membership at the sum of $200, subject to the provisions of
Section 129 of the Constitution."
·
It does not in terms provide for the creation of life membersh.ip, but purp?~ts only to fix the fee therefor; nor does it comply
vv 1th the prov1S1ons of Section 129 that the resolution itself shall
specify the securities in which the fund may be invested, nor for
the Secretary's report.
The method prescribed by Section 129 is simple, and there
should be no difficulty experienced in following the plan outlined
the;ein. This statement is fortified by the fact that all Lodges
:Vh1ch have heretofore adopted the system, have complied with
its requirements before approval by Grand Lodge, and we can see
no reason for countenancing any deviation therefrom.
We, therefore, recommend that the action of the Grand Master
. in ·approving the resolution of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21 and Argonaut Lodge No. 461 creating life memberships, he not approved and
that the Lodges affected be permitted, if so advised, to take the
necessary action to adopt a valid resolution creating life membership.

CHAS. L. PATTON,
DANA R. WF.!.LF.R,
AI.ll>'.RT G. BURNF.TT,
F. V. Kr.;:sr.rnc,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
Hrother Bernhard, chairman of the Committee on
Grievances, presented reports as follows:
To the l.!ost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee to whom was referred Trial Record No. 251,
Crescent Lodge No. 45, respectfully report as follows:
The accused was found guilty on three specifications; first, that
of having disobeyed a summons sent from within the Lodge.
Second, that of having made disrespectful remarks relative to
said summons; and
Third, that the accused had failed to assist a needy sister of
his and thereby made her a charge on the fraternity, he having
the ability to aid her and also that he wrongfully wi.thheld certain
personal property from her.
On the first and second specifications there is absolutely no
evidence in the record on the subject; the record disclosing ouly
the accusation and the answer denying the same on the part of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

582

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

accused. The record does not even show that the summons which
the ~ccused is charged with having disobeyed was ever issued or
served on the accused.
, In support of the third specification the only evidence offered
is a letter from the sister of the accused to a third person with
reference to making certain collections from the accused and recovering certain personal p~operty claimed by her from him.
This letter is not under oath nor does it appear from the eviderice that any deposition of said sister or any one, was ever taken
in said matter.
While no appeal was taken by the accused, your Committee
nevertheless feels constrained to reverse the findings of the trial
commissioners on all three specifications, for the reason that the
same are absolutely unsupported by the record.
Your Committee begs to call attention to the fact that trial
commissioners frequently accept the unverified statements filed
with them as evidence; these do not rise to the dignity of proof,
and are only to be taken if at all as admissions, where they constitute admissions of the person making them, and not for any other
purpose. This practice is not to be commended and often results
in grave injustice~
Your Committee therefore offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
Resolved, That the verdict of the Commissioners in Trial
Record No. 251 be and the same is hereby reversed.
Respectfully submitted,
WALTER F. HAAS,

J. P. BERNHARD,
LEO YouNGWORTH,

GEo. L. JONES,
E. B. POWER,
Committee.

The report was adopted, and the accused was restored
to membership.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances to whom was referred Trial
Record No. 259, Crockett Lodge No. 139, begs leave to report as
·follows:
The accused was found guilty on three specificationsFirst, that of using violence on the person of a brother Master
Mason.
Second, that of using vile and threatening language toward
said brother.
Third, that the accused testified falsely in a Police Court with
reference to state~nts alleged to have been made by the Master of
said Lodge.
The Commissioners found the accused guilty on all three
charges and sentenced him to be reprimanded.
Your Committee, after a careful review of the evidence. believes
the sentence to be inadequate to the offense proven. The record
shows that the accused, to use his own language, "heat up" a
brother Master Mason, knowing him to he such, two days after the
accused received his third degree, for the reasons as claimed by
the' accused, that the brother had opposed his advancement in
the Lodge and had spoken ill of him. It also appears from the
reeord that the accused intended to beat .the brother as soon as
he learned of the statements, but was advised by a subordinate
officer of the Lodge to wait until the accused received his thirtl
degree and then to heat up the brother who was claimed to have
made the statements about the accused and opposed his advancement. This conduct on the part of the subordinate officer n[
said Lodge was in our opinion most reprehensible, partic11larly
as such officer knew that he was giving the advice to a brother
not versed in Masonic law or practices. We feel that this circumstance must be taken into consideration in the fixing of the
penalty and that under all the circumstances the ends of justice
and the best interests of Masonry will he best suhscrvcd by suspending the accused, rather than expelling him.
Your Committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and
moves its adoption:
Resolved, That the findings of the Commissioners in trial
record No. 259 as to the guilt of the accnsed be and the same

f'HOCEEDINGS OF ·.rn rn

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

are hereby sustained, but that the penalty to be imposed upon the
accused be and the same is hereby fixed at suspension ..

Resolved, That the decision in ~ach of the cases herein above
mentioned, and t~ action of the Lodge thereon be, and the same
are hereby approved.
