To the },fost Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred Trial
Record No. 260, from Reading Lodge No. 254, reports as follows:
The accused was found guilty upon the following charges:
1. Battery upon the accuser, a brother Mason; 2. Personal violence upon a brother; 3. Striking a brother; 4. \Vounding a
brother; 5. Adultery; 6. Divulging contents of a trial record.
Charges one to four embrace the same offense. All of the acts
charged were done at the same time and against the same
brother, and are sustained by the evidence.
The divulging of the contents of a trial record was the act of
the accused in allowing one of his witnesses to read the charges.
·While this act might be considered a technical violation of Masonic law, yet, under the peculiar circumstances of the case it
was a natural thing to do, and is not such a Masonic offense as
to warrant expulsion.
The transcript in this case contains 779 typewritten pages.
The entire evidence directed to the charge of adultery is hearsay.
The chief evidence relied upon by the accuser is a letter said to
have been written by the woman at the home of the accuser.
The woman denies having written this letter. This witness is
impeached by the accuser, and claimed by the accuser as unworthy
of belief.
T.his charge, under the rules as laid down in Section 202 of
our Constitution, that hearsay evidence is not admissible, is not
sustained by any competent and credible evidence.
We are of the opinion that the circumstances under which
the contents of the Trial Record were divulged, and under which
the battery was committed,-the accused acting under· great provocation and excitement and at the time when he had just been

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

586

accused of rape-are mitigating circumstances, and we think th~t
the penalty of expulsion as fixed by the Commissioners is too
severe and that the penalty of reprimand is a sufficient punishment. ' \Ve therefore offer the following resolution and move its
adoption:
Resolved, That the action of the Commissioners in Trial
Record No. 260, in finding the accused guilty of adultery and
divulging the contents of a trial record, be reversed; and
The action of said Commission in finding the accused guilty
of battery be sustained, but that the punishment be fixed at
reprimand.
Resj;lectfully submitted,
J. P. BllRNHARD,
Gm. L. JoNlls,
Lto YouNGWOR'fH,
E. B. PowllR,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred certain petitions for restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry, report as
follows:
,.
Case No. 84-A. ]. F., expelled March 4, 1910: It appears that
notice of the intention to petition for restoration in this case was not
given to the Lodge which expelled him until September 8, 1919, whereas
the Constitution provides that such notice shall be given at least sixty
<lays before the annual communication. This necessary provision not
having been complied with, the application should not be further considered at this communication. We, therefore, recommend that the
application be denied without prejudice to a renewal thereof by the
applicant.

The recommendation was adopted.
Case No. 144-William S. R., expelled October 16, 1913: Petitioner
was found guilty of defrauding his emp'.oyers out of large sums of
money and was expelled. His application for restoration is supported
by a letter of his father, but no other affirmative showing is made that
•the petitioner has so conducted himself since his expulsion as to compel
the conclusion that he has made amends for his offenses 'and is now
worthy of being restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the petition of Willi;un S. R. for restoration he
denied.

Adopted.
Case No. 148-]. P. R., expelled December 5, 1913: The pet1t10n
in this case has been indorse<l by the Lodge which expelled the petitioner, and there have been presented several affidavits and letters in
which the petitioner is favorably recommen<lc<l. Your Committee, however, feel that in view of the character of the offense for the commission
of which the petitioner was expelled, the time has not yet come for his
restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry, for we arc not fully
satisfied that the petitioner has under control the morbid temperament
which it ·is averred was the cause of his trouble.
Your Committee therefore offer the following resolution and rccom-·
mend its adoption:
Resolved, That the petition of]. P. R. for restoration he denied.

Grand Lodge refused to concur in the recommenclation,
and on motion the petition was granted and T. P; R. was
restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Past Grand Master Henderson offered th.e following:
Whereas, The work in Lodges, in the desire to clear their calendars,
has become a burclcn; and
Whereas, Such rapidity betokens no great good to the brotherhood.
Whereas, A Committee on matters of policy has been orclcrcd to be
appointed; therefore be it
Resolved, That the incoming Committee on General Policy report at
next annual communication whether it woulcl not be best for this juriscliction to return to the practice of conducting all business in Lodges
while open on the first degree, ancl thereby pursue a more leisurely
course in conferring the other clegrccs, when full worth of association,
fraternal and otherwise, determines that the honor thus conferred is
placccl upon those who can worthily wear said honors. For Masonry
shoulcl honor no man that docs not fully honor it, and one that has fully
proven himself entitled thereto.

Past Grand Master :Murphey, for the Committee on
Jurisprudence, reported as follows:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which was referred that portion of the Grand Master's Address with reference to physical qualifications of candidates, beg leave to report:
That in view of the language of Section 94 of the Constitution, we
are not prepared to go to the extent reached by the Grand Master in
holding that an "applicant who has lost his left hand or arm, or either
foot or leg below the knee, especially where the loss has been supplied
by an artificial limb, was not by reason of such loss ineligible."
When Section 94 was liberalized in 1914 the then Grand Master
said: "I feel that this great Fraternity would be taking a long step in
the right direction if the requirements as to physical qualifications were
eliminated from our laws, or the law amended so as to require only substantial physiqil conformity' leaving a very large discretion in the subordinate Lodge to determine what shall constitute substantial conformity. Jn other words, where the local Lodge shall favorably pass
upon the physical sufficiency of a candidate, that finding shall he practica:Jy the final determination of the issue."
In response to the Grand Master's recommendation, the Committee
on J urisprudencc reported: "Your Committee concurs with the Grand
Master in this recommendation and therefore submits the following
amendmcn t to the Constitution and recommends its adoption :

"Resolv~d, That Section 94 of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge
of California be ame11dcd by striking therefrom after the words 'able to
,-onform' the word 'literally' and by inserting in lieu thereof the word
'substantially'.
"If this amendment to the Constitution is adopted it will render
inapplicable in the futu.re Sections 94j and 94k and will accomplish the
object of leaving the matter practically in the hands of the local Lodges."

Under this law and the interpretation of. it hy the Cram! Lodge, the
Master of a subordinate Lodge should, in the exercise of a wise discretion, determine the question of fact for himself. It was the hope of
the Gr;ind Master and the Committee on Jurisprudence that succeeding
Crand Masters would not be further burdened with the determination

616

PROCEEDINGS OF THI!.

of this question in individual cases. Each case should be determined on
its merits without fixing and promulgating any hard and fast rules.

METHOD OF REIN STATEMENT
Brother Patton also presented the following:
A question as to. the proper method of reinstating a brother
sentenced to reprimand in his own Lodge and. after an appeal suspended by the action of this Grand Lodge itself, has been submitted.
The Grand Lodge unquestionably exercises this power to originally suspend a Mason after trial in the Lodge and appeal as an
original power inherited by the Grand Lodges from the General

618

PROCEEDINGS OF 'l'IIE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Assemblies of Masons and not parted with by this Grand Lodge in
its Constitution.
In this view of the matter it is clear that the Lodge has no
jurisdiction to restore such a Mason, for under Section 210 the
Lodge may only annul a sentence of suspension pronounced by
itself.
By the provisions of Section 211 the Grand Lodge may reswre
to the rights and privileges of Masonry any Mason who has been
suspended or expelled within its jurisdiction.
Your Committee is therefore of the opinion that when it is
desired to restore a brother so suspended by this Grand Lodge the
procedure prescribed in Sections 211 and 212 of the Constitution
must be followed.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK M. ANGl\LLOT1'T,
CHAS. L. PATTON,
DANA R. Wl\LLl\R,
ALnl\RT G. BuRNl\TT,

F. v. Kl\l\SLING,

J. D. MuRPHl\Y,
Committee.

Adopted.

If we read Sections 159, 161 and 248 and 247 of the Constitution together, we find that it would be possible for a brother desiring to affiliate by the use of his Certificate of Standing instead of· a

MASONIC SERVICE ASSOCIATION
Past C rand Master M urphcy, for the Committee on
J urisprndcnce, presented the following:
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Jurisprudence has been referred the
following resolution, introduced by Past Grand Master 1l ervey:
"Whereas, The organization of a Masonic Service Association of
the United States has been effected, and more than forty American
Grand Lodges have joined the Association and ratilied its constitution; and
"Whereas, The formation of this Association represents a significant advance movement of the craft and inay become an instrnment of noteworthy service to our country and to Freemasonry; and
"Whereas, This Grand Lodge has been invited to join the Association and to send accredited representatives to the meeting to he
held on November 11, 1919, at Cedar Rapids, Iowa; now, therefore,
be it

620

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of California approves the
constitution of the Masonic Service Association of the United States
and accepts membership therein; and be it further
"Resolved, That the Grand Master be and he is requested to
attend the meeting of Kovember 11, 1919, in person or by representative, and that the Grand Secretary also be and is requested to
attend said meeting."
The prospect to which said resolutions relate seems alluring and
to constitute a scheme of co-operative effort through which the purposes of our Institution may be promoted; but the proposition
comes to us late in our deliberations and we have not been able. to
devote to it that careful and mature consideration to which it is
entitled, and we are not prepared now to recommend its adoption
by the Grand Lodge. Moreover, the adoption of the resolution
would necessarily impose a financial burden of uncertain extent
upon this Grand Lodge, and therefore, if the members of this grand
body deem it advisable to take definite action in the premises, the
Finance Committee should first have an opportunity to consider it
in the light of the condition of our treasury. However, we believe
the matter should be deferred to some more convenient season, and
we recommend that no action be taken at this time on the resolutions.

The. report was adopted as presented and subsequently
Past Grand :i'v1aster Burnett moved that the matter he referred' to the Committee on General Policy and Purposes,
and it was so ordered.

626

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

PUBLIC EDUCATION
Drother Charles Albert Adams offered the following:
Whereas, It is our belief that there is no higher duty devolving
upon us as Masons than the duty we owe the State as citizens; and
Whereas, we believe that the hope of a free and untramrpelled
democracy depends upon the enlightenment 'and education oi the
citizens of this Republic, the Americanjzation of its alien population, and the instruction of its illiterates; and
Whereas, We believe certain measures now pending in the
Congress of the United States give promise of the fruition of that
hope by the passage of an act introduced as House Bill No. 7 by
Representative Towner of Iowa and as Senate Bill No. 1017 by
Senator Smith of Georgia; and
Whereas, Those measures provide for the creation of a Department of Education and for an annual appropriation of one hundred
million dollars to encourage the States in the promotion and support
of education and the strengthening of the public school system; and
Whereas, The traditional policy of the craft, which precludes
the consideration of political question~ by the ftaternity, finds its
origin in its desire to preserve harmony in the Lodge and to avoid
the discord which might possibly arise from the expression of differences of opinion existing among the brethren; and
Whereas, There are certain fundamental principles concerning
which there can be no difference of opinion among Masons, and one
of those principles finds its expression in the support of the public
school system; now, therefore, be it
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California, while not feeling justified in formally indorsing any specific measure, indorses the spirit and purpose of the
measures referred to, and its members express the hope that they
will receive careful consideration.

Adopted by unanimous vote.
It being intimated to Grand Lodge that the mqther of
Past Grand Master Bledsoe had this clay passed to the Great
Beyond, on motion the Grand Master appointed a committee
to convey to our distinguished brother the sympathy of his
brethren in Grand Lodge; and this Committee sent the following telegram :

ORA::-JD LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

627

"Hon. Benjamin F. Bledsoe,
Federal Building,
Los Angeles:
Your brethren assembled in Grand Lodge learned today of the
passing of your mother 'to the realm where the rainbow never
fades,' and we are directed to express to you the profound sympathy
of Grand Lodge.

FRANc1s V. Kn:sLING,
JOHN WHICHER,
EDGAR F. GEE."

REPORT
OF THE

Committee on Correspondence
OCTOBER, 1919

By JESSE M. WHITED
To the Most Worshipful Grand Masters, Officers and Members of
the Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
I submit my first report on Foreign Correspondence.
A retiring member of a Supreme Court gave to his successor this
injunction : "Give your decision, but if possible, never the reasons for
the same. Men will agree with your rnling, !mt very seldom with your
arguments." Having this in mind, I am making no apologies for the
scope of this Report, or giving my reasons for presenting it to you in
the form that I have.
That great Mason and scholar, Albert Pike, after drawing 011 various
sources for his work, "Morals and Dogma," prefaced it with the statement that he could, on that account, claim little of the merit of
authorship, and did not care to distinguish his own from that which he
had taken from other sources, but was quite willing that every portion
of the book, in turn, should be regarded as borrowed from some old and
better writer.
As that method was followed by me, I era ve the same indulgence.
Thanks are due to the Secretaries of the several General, Grand
Bodies of the United States, practically all the Grand Secretaries of the
various Grand Lodges, the. National Masonic Research Society of /\namo~a, Iowa, and the Editors of a numher of Masonic periodicals, for
statistics and other valuable :ind interesting data, which make up this
Report.
Jf the information in some cases, as to certain Jurisdictions is missing,
or not up to date, it is due to the failnre of partit's to answer comnnmications.
A rural newspaper once made the statement that the only imlividuals
privileged to use the pronoun, "we," were editors and men with a tapeworm. To this classification should also be added the Chairman of a
Correspondence Committee. It is of course understood that the view• or
opinions expressed in this Report arc those only of myself,

AMERICAN HISTORY
There is a tendency among Masonic writers to make American
Masonry responsible for the American Revolution and everything '
connected with it, arid subsequent thereto down to the present
time. As a matter of fact, Masonry, as an organization, so far as
we have been able to find out, has never done anything that has
become historic, unless it was to furnish the ground for the AntiMasonic Movement. Even in that time, the majority of the Brethren "took to the tall timbers," by surrendering their charters, and
disbanding their Lodges.
When American Masonry, as a body, does something, or suffer because of their activities and belief like our French, Spanish,
Italian or South American Brothers have done, it will then be time
enough for us to talk along this extravagant line,
District of Columbia:

The orator said that all the officers of the Revolution were Masons
except Benedict Arnold. Arnold was expelled for his treason. But
the exception was Charles Lee-no relation to the Virginia Lees.
The records of the Lodhe in Poughkeepsie, N, Y., extant today,

BALLOT
We believe if a stricter investigation was made of applicants,
and the black ball used a little more freely, perhaps Masonry would
not have some of the "black sheep" that it undoubtedly has today,
particularly in large cities. This is so because of the "Degree
Mill" tendency.
When a man makes an applicatlon for a Life Insurance policy,
a Surety bond, or asks a financial favor in every-day life, he is
usually required to give some history of his family, himself, and
his financial condition. If this procedure was followed with applicants for preferment in our Order, and a close investigation made
into their answers, it would ultimately work to the advantage of
the Craft. Doubtless a large number of applications would never
get to the ballot box.
Illinois:
It is not supposah'c, among Maste1· J\:fosons, that there arc any
who would reject a candidate through malice, envy, ill will, anger,
jealousy, or spleen; if any lod!!L' bas admittPd to its fold any one who
can be guilty of such base conduct, it is her misfortune-perhaps
her fault-and for which there is no Masonic remedy. The right to
reject a candidate is a clear sequence of the right to vote, and it is
as clear and sacred as the right to elect. The ballot is not spread
to elect a candidate alone, but to determine whether tl1e candidate
shall be rejected, and for the further protection of the weak, of
the timid, or the poor, the secret ballot is spread. The duty to reject
is also as clear as the duty to vote; and that duty is to he the result
of conscientious convictions in each hrothcr's hrenst, and he votes upon
those convictions in the presence of Diety alone.

REPORT ON CORRESPONimXCE

REPORT ON CORHESPONDENCE

The rejection of a candidate, when declared, is to be shared in
silence by every brother, no matter how unpleasant; for if any one
states how he voted, he violates the secrecy of the ballot, and thereby
violates his obligation. The more shields there are thrown around
the ballot, which is the great safety-valve of Masonry, the better.

Pennsylvania:
The Masonic ballot is sacred. HP who knowin"lv misuses it
should be promptly expelled from the Fraternity; and it is a clear
misuse of it when objections are raised to a petitioner for any other
than Masonic reasons. Private pique, business transactions and personal differences which do not relate to the character of tbe petitioner,
have no place in Freemasonry, and the Lodge whose members continue to abuse the ballot by such practices deserves to lose its warrant. "While the blackball has its place in Freemasonry, it should be
used only in the true Masonic spirit. Its abuse cannot be tolerated,
and they who abuse it should be promptly a11d speedily dealt with.

Virginia:
We are all making Masons too fast, and it is desirable that every
member of every lodge should know who is to be subject to a ballot.
Men are constantly l1eing black-hcil.ed, to the surprise of. perhaps, all
but one member, and frequently it later develops that tbis one memher knew what none of the others <lid, and which, if known. would
have resulted in unan"imous rejection. Still, it is not kind, or even
Masonic, to let the profane world knows who is to be subjected to a
ballot, and printing names on notices, even those sent in sealed

BIRTHDAYS
The date of the establishment of the first Masonic Lodge in
America continues to interest the Brethren of certain Jurisdictions.
Pennsylvania's' claim that in 1731 four Lodges of that Colony
formed a Grand Lodge seems to be clearly established. Under the
procedure the:i in vogue, it would seem that these Brethren• had
as much right to do this as the Brethren of the four London Lodges
did when they established the first Grand Lodge of England.
The question for us has as much real importance as the ancient
wheeze, "How old is Anne." The claim of one of the Deputy District Grand Masters of South Carolina is more interesting and entertaining.
As California can usually produce anything, perhaps when explorations are completed in the asphalt beds of Southern California, we may uncover a prehistoric Lodge.
Canada:
After all, these arc questions of little real importance. Masons
outside of Massachusetts and Pennsylvania care very little which
of the Grand Lodges had priority of existellce. The great fact
that interests Masons is that both are in the very front rank of
the world's greatest lodges, and both are doing Masonic work
worthy of the position they hold .
Massachusetts:
The first known warrant, deputation, commission. or other authority. issuing from the Grand Lodge of England or its Grand Master
(or from any other Masonic org;111ization or officer, for that matter)
to he exercised in America was that (April 13, 1733) by virtue of
which Henry Price founclccl a Provincial Grand Lodge in Boston,
July 30, 1733.
The first particular lodge in America to he duly constituted was
the first lodge in Boston, July 30, 1733.
The first lodge in America to he registered hy the Grand Lodge
of England in the official list of lodges was the Jirst lodge in
Boston.
Missouri:
Because a Freemason has a thigh hone docs not prove that an
Egyptian mummy was a Freemason, because a thigh hone was discovered in him. It is related that a Freemason, with a Moslem pin
on the lapel of his coat and a combination watch charm of the
double eagle, cross and crown dangling from his vest, accidentally happened on some Egyptologists as they uncovered the grave of a man of
the late stone age; in the grave were the remains of the man, food ancl
other things usually found in such tombs, also a stone hammer with a
wooden handle attached hy withes. When the Freemason saw the hammer he exclaimed: "Eureka, this man was a Freemason and the master
of his lodge, because here is his gavel." This incident may not he true,
hut it is in keeping with some of the eloquence dispensed from Masonic
platforms and Masonic papers about "the great antiquity of our great
and magnificent order."

BUTTONS
Some enterprising Brother in Salt Lake City, the home of the
"American Masonic Federation," conceived the idea of having a
copyrighted universal emblem to be worn by members of regular
Lodges. This found favor only in Wyoming. The fraternity in
California have a remedy in Section 538-B of the Penal Code.
The best solution of the problem might be to follow the custom
of our English brothers and wear no emblem at all.

CANDIDATES
The Questionnaire adopted by Mexico and sent to all Candidates
could be followed undoubtedly with good results in any Jurisdiction.
The average man is prompted to make an application to become
a Mason, we think, either by curiosity, a desire for "worldly wealth
or honors" acquired by reason of his membership, or an admiration
for what he has heard or read regarding the Lodge. Too often,
the motive is one of the first two. If there is any method that
could be used to impress upon a petitioner that these should not
have a place in his thoughts it should be adopted.

CATHOLICISM
We have known some, and there are still some good men in
the Fraternity who were Catholics and Masons at the time the
ban was placed upon the organization by the Church. We have
known, and do know, good Masons who were born and raised
Catholics, but afterwards became members of the Order, very properly renouncing their Church connection. It is truly said a man·
cannot serve two masters, and by reason of the natural conflict
between the two ideals represented by each, a person cannot we
believe, be both a Catholic and a Mason.
·
'
The part that the Knights of Columbus played in war work
with their continuing efforts, and the criticism which has been lev:
eled against the Y. M. C. A., has naturally tended to make the
difference more marked. If the War Department had 'kept all
organizations based on sectarianism of every kind out of the army
we believe it would have been better for all concerned. All did
good work, but "the leopard cannot change his spots, or the
Ethiopian his skin." Hindsight is better than foresight, however.

There is one thing that we must acknowledge. The Catholic
Church has an organization and uses it. Masonry has one, but
does not. The Jesuits say that if given a child for the first seven
years, he belongs to them forever.
What has Masonry done, or what is it doing to train and guide
the sons of its members? What has it done as a body to remove
illiteracy from our midst? Echo answers, "nothing," not only to
these two, but various other living questions of the day.
Stop, we forget the good brothers who believe and practice
that Masonry works through the individual only and accomplishes
its greatest good that way.
In business life, we have a sincere admiration for organization,
service, and the following individual:
"The man who has a thing to sell,
And goes and hollers down a well,
Is not as likely to collar the dollars,
As he who climbs a tree and hollers."

He (Grand Master of Mississippi) reports that on July 6th he refused to lay the cornerstone of the Government building at McComb

Wisconsin:
Persistent attC'mpts on the part of certain persons to draw Masons
and Masonry into religious controversies require active vigilance by
those in authonty to prevent such a violation of the principles on
which this institution is founded. No discussion so quickly tends to destroy harmony of thought and unity of purpose as does that which pertains to religious creeds, and it is very properly prohibited in the Lodge
room. Yet it sometimes creeps in that sacred precinct to the detriment of Masonry, and into the writings and speech of Masons as such.
This is contrary to the dignity and high character of our profession,
and in direct antagonism to the declared attitude as set forth in the
First Degree in Freemasonry. This attitude has been shown to be
correct by years of experience, and was assnmed for the very purpose
of avoiding contentions which would arouse the passions and appeal
to the prejudices of the individual member. It therefore rests with us
to counteract by every force which lies within us those influences which
would make the institution of Masonry an ally of any movement directed against any creed or which assumes it to be the supporter of any
doctrine contrary to a broad tolerance based on the underlying principle of the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man.

Rhode Island:
The occasion which brings us together this evening is both unusual
and appropriate-unusual in that it is seldom in this jurisdiction, composed as it is of so many old lodges, that the Grand Master is called
on to consecrate an altar of Freemasonry-and appropriate because it
brings prominently to our attention the most important feature in the
furnishings of the lodge. Tt is not without reason that the Mason
holds in highest veneration the altar of our order. Here the novitiate
first proclaims to his future brethren his belief in the Great Architect of
the Universe. Herc, on bended knee, he. is made a Mason in due and
ancient form, and here also he finds spread before him the Holy Bible.
which he later learns is the Great Light not only of the spiritual, but of
the Masonic world.
CHAIN LETTERS
The McKinley chain letter having petered out, some genius(?)
prepared a Masonic prayer, which was brought to the attention of
the world by a system of chain letters. Various Grand Lodges
and Grand Masters took notice of it, judicially and otherwise, but
it remained for the United States Government to give it its death
blow through a Post Office ruling.

Arkansas:
It is a deplorable fact that some of the lodges of this jurisdiction have allowed sister jurisdictions to care for their sick and
bury their dead, and then repudiated the debt, on account of being

utter contempt for a lodge that refuses to pay for the care of a sick
brother or the burial of a dead one. If it is wrong to defraud a
Lodge of Master Masons, under ordinary circumstances, it is doubly
so to refuse to pay the expenses incurred hy a sister lodge in caring
for our sick and afflicted, and a lodge that will not do that, should
have their charter arrested and have their organization wiped off
the map, for of all the contemptible, mean things it is oossihlc for a
lodge to do, I think that is the worst, and I would feel more kindly
to a lodge that would wilfully violate every edict of the Grand
Lodge than the one who obeys every edict implicitly and then refused
to pay the funeral expenses of a deceased brother, when such expense was incurred by a sister lodge.

CLANDESTINE MASONRY
The main agency for the operating of spurious Masonry is the
"American Masonic Federation," with headquarters in Salt Lake
City, Utah, and the Cerneau Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite,,
in New York. The first was incorporated in 1917 under the laws
of the State of Idaho. Its leader is one M. McBeth Thompson.
The moving spirit in the Cerneau was one Captain W. Bayliss,
who died in Washington, D. C., on March 16th, 1919.
This Jurisdiction has not been invaded by the Cerneau clan,
but it is to be regretted that the "American Masonic Federation" is
active. Through the efforts of Past Grand Master William P.
Filmer, Grand Secretary Whicher and Brother Henry M. Owens,
these peddlers of fake degrees are slowly but surely being exposed
and receiving attention at the hands of the law.
There is an old saying that "There's a sucker born every
minute, and two persons waiting to catch him." Such being the
case, we suppose these fakes will always flourish.

CLUBS
"A man cannot live by bread alone." The average attendance
at Masonic meetings is evidence enough that there is something
lacking. The success of the clubs established in this Jurisdiction
shows that they are filling a long-felt want, and so far as we can
learn are vital factors in practical Masonry.

The ~uestion of the benefits, and the advisability of forming these
clubs, is still in its infancy. The idea of the club and club life is growing
all over. In fact there seems to be little of social life outside of
c'.ubs of one kind and another. I don't know of any reason why a
Lodge might not maintain a club room wherein they may hold their
social events, if they see fit to, so long as it does not materially and
seriously interfere with the good of Masonry and its proper administration.

District of Columbia:

\Ve have no disposition to emasculate from l\fasonry the fellowship which is horn of club intercourse in that portion of a Masonic
temple which is occupied as a cluli house, hut we do not feel that the
profane world should be brought to believe that Masonry is a social
organization, and that it occupies no unique position among the various
social and benefit orders of which we have so many.

* * * * * *

. The Masonic Clubs and the Masonic Bowling League continue to he
important and commendable features of our social activities. The clnhs,
in addition to other important work, to which reference will shortly
be ry:iade, hold monthly 1'.1eetings for which interesting programs of
music, addresses and special features are prepared, while the Bowling
League offers to Master Masons clean sport with desirable surroundings.

now thirteen of the clubs, with an aggregate memhership
of almost
thousand. The first one was organized in 1908 in the

g-ot together informally for the purpose of rendering him assistance.
Out of this volunteer organization there came the Trowel Club, which
now covers the whole of the Interior Department, and which was
followed in due time by the Ashier Club, composed of Masons in the
\Var. St~te and Navy Departments. the White House and the Civil
Service Commission; the Compass Cl uh, composed of Masons in the

CONFERENCES
There has been and is a growing tendency in all Jurisdictions
to "get together." The Bogie of a National Grand Lodge of
course will always haunt some, and selfishness and petty jealousy
will continue to have their place in any movements looking towards the uniting of the Craft into a National organization. We do
not believe, on this account that there will ever be a General
Grand Lodge.
As the American Colonies surrendered part of their rights, without any harm, to make a great Nation, we believe that Grand
Lodges could well follow the example. Might we inquire if the
Supreme Councils of the Scottish Rite, the General Grand Chapters,
and the Grand Encampment have worked any great hardship in
their respective organizations?

The kind, size, value or qlfantity of the Report of the Reviewer, the Chairman of a Correspondence Committee, or a Committee itself, is guided by no fixed rule- Some Jurisdictions believe them a waste of printers' ink and paper, others that they
should be merely a recital of events without comment or criticism,
and the remainder allow an open field.
In most cases, it is a labor of love, and as such, its greatest
benefit is to the person compiling it. In its practical application
it reverses the proverb that "It is more blessed to give than to
receive," for undoubtedly the time and labor given is not appreciated by the readers, or ever given a thought, except by a few_

CRIMES
From time immemorial, a Mason has been obliged to be a lawabiding citizen, not only in his Civil relations, but in his moral
ones. The charge to the youngest entered apprentice Mason is
specific enough along this line.
We believe that .when a man has been finally convicted by a
Court of last resort of a felony, or an act involving moral turpitude
that should, ipso faci:to, sever his relations with Masonry. However, as in every-day life, we have our "sob sisters." There have
been cases, and undoubtedly now are, where men have been finally
convicted of felonious acts, and who are in durance vile without
hope of release, but are in good standing because the formality of
a Masonic trial has not been gone thru with, or some technicality
has not been observed, and the case is on appeal. Too often sentiment imposes an inadequate punishment.
Connecticut:
On the ground that a man is presumed to be innocent, until proven
guilty, he (Grand Master of Oklahoma) ruled that a complaint in
court against a Mason does not of itself act as an objection to his
advancement. We dissent. On the principle that the Lodge, not the
can.didate, should have the benefit of every .doubt, an objection should
be promptly filed, staying advancement at least temporarily.

DISPENSATIONS
If there is a law, enforce it. If it is a bad law, the enforcement of it will cause its repeal. This applies to Masonry as in
every-day life. The growing disrespect for law or authority is
shaking the foundation of our country. The persons who have
been or are in power are responsible for this. The easiest way
to stop it is to have less law, and allow no one to set it aside by
dispensations or otherwise.
British Columbia:
The fact that no dispensations were granted to shorten the time
between degrees seemed so surprising that the reviewer went back and
read the list again, thinking that he had overlooked one or two. There
was, even before the war, as Brother Williams (Ohio) says, a tendency
among Grand Masters to allow the interval between degrees to be
shortened upon the flimsiest excuse or none at all, and as one reason for
these dispensations the war has been worked to the limit. In view of
the fact that Canada is in the war "good and strong," as Brother
Williams says, he had expected to find the Canadian Grand Masters
inclined to ignore precedent and to allow candidates to hurry through
the degrees simply because they were called to military service. Fortunately, so far as British Columbia, at least, is concerned, our Grand
Masters have not caught the disease.
Illinois:
One thing which has impressed the writer more than any other in
the review of various proceedings, is the utter senselessness of the dispensation habit, which seems to have fastened itself on all grand lodges.
A dispensation is merely the means whereby a grand master permits
himself to violate the law and to escape without censure. What is the
sense of having constitutions and by-laws if their provisions are to be
made subject to the will and caprice of one man.
If laws are good why not live up to them? If they are bad, then
repeal them and get them off the statute book. Where is the consistency in enacting a law forbidding a lodge to do a certain thing and
then investing a grand master with the power to set aside that law and
permit the lodge to do the prohibited thing? If the clispensatic ..1 ha hit
continues to grow in proportion to its present clay development. Free·masonry will wake up some morning and find itself in a ridiculous
predicament. It is most refreshing to note that in two or three grand
jurisdictions, grand masters refused to take advantage of the dispensation privilege, giving as a reason that they believed the laws as
enacted to be good and cou~d sec no reason for thC'ir llC'in~ set aside
to the detri111C'11t of the hest interests of the fraternity.
Kentucky:
Is there ever a necessity for such relaxation of the laws? Aside
from the fact that every suspension of the operation of a law tends to
l('ssen respect for all law, we can hardly imagine the existence of conditions that would make necessary the initiation and advancement of a
candidate in any wav. manner, or time different from the initiation and
advancC'ment of all Masons.

New Mexico:
All decisions of the Grand Master were approved. One that looks
wrong to an outsider is in effect that a boy can petition and be balloted upon before he reached manhood (21 years of age) and then
can be initiated on the evening of his twenty-first birthday. If in
such a hurry why not have an early morning session? We believe
that we should wait until our applicants are men before we have anything to do with the petition.
Ohio:
I have been compelled to refuse more requests for Dispensations
than I have granted. In each instances, however, the granting of these
requests would have been in direct conflict with the Code and well established decisions of the Grand Lodge of Ohio. Requests for Dispensations to confer degrees out of time became so numerous on account
of men being called from ho11Je for military service in other states before
they could receive the degrees in regular order, that I was compelled to
issue a cautionary letter on July 19, 1917.
I do not deem it wise to confer degrees out of time. I am of
the opinion that much harm will be done to Freemasonry and little good
to the petitioner by this method. It were better to return to the old
law requiring a man to remain an Entered Apprentice for one year
before becoming a Fellow Craft, and to remain a Fe'.low Craft one
year before becoming a Master Mason, than to resort to this unseemly
hysterical method of conferring degrees wholesale, thereby destroying
the Constitution, Landmarks, and Code of the Masonic Institution.
The following, taken from his address (Pennsylvania), will cause
a howl on the part of the writers of the Correspondence Reports:
"Permission was granted .to Washington Lodge, No. 59, to receive
and act upon a petition for initiation and membership of a youth under
age, and by virtue of my presence I caused the petitioner to be made a
Mason upon the approval of his petition."
We do not helieve that there can he any excuse on earth for either
receiving the petition of a man who is under age, or of making him a
Mason, and we very much douht the wisdom of creating Masons at
sight, although we are bound to admit that Qhio ·has been guilty of
this very thing.
Utah:
Among dispensations granted we note three which permitted the conferring of two Degrees upon candidates at one and the same meeting.
We assume, of course, that there were imperative reasons for such action, but that does not change the fact that Masonry can mean but little
to such machine-made products. We would suggest-with a good deal
of diffidence- that Connecticut Lodges be equipped with a preparationroom in which such candidates may be trephined, and have the ritnal,
lectures, and charges of the Degrees laid away in the brain cavity, without the usual and unnecessary trouble of conferring them. To he sure,
this would necessitate the presentation of a lapel button npon the conclusion of the operation, so that the candidates, the Craft, and the public, might know that they were members of Masonic Lodges. There are
no restrictions upon this suggested course of action, and we would
modestly recommend it for adoption, by those Jurisdictions which permit
their Grand Masters to grant dispensations for the initiation, passing,
or raising, "of more than five, and not over thirty, at one and the same
meeting."

EDUCATIONAL FUNDS
Practically every Jurisdiction in the United States should take
off its hat to the "Sage Brush" State. The Grand Lodge of Nevada provides an educational fund to assist children of deserving
Brethren, whether alive or dead, to secure an education. The
money is loaned to be used for the purpose of attending higher
institutions of learning. It is supposed to be repaid when possible.
The Grand Lodge of West Virginia has also swung into line.
This is practical Masonry.
The San Francisco Bodies, A. & A. S. R., and San Francisco
Pyramid No. 1 of the Sciots have each made an annual appropriation to be used in this way for some of the wards of the fraternity
at Covina.
Let the Knights Templar, Eastern Stars, Amaranth and
Shrine follow suit.

FLAGS
It is only a small bit of bunting,
It is only an old colored rag;
Yet thousands have died for its honor
And shed their best blood for the flag.
An elaborate flag ceremony has been adopted by certain

Jurisdictions, and the use of it made compulsory at all times.
This, we believe, is a mistake. The simple tribute paid to the
American flag and what it represents, as outlined in Army Regulations, is .ample.
The flag should have a permanent place in the Lodge room
and Masonry. The average ceremony, however, tends to become
either a mere routine, or an excuse for fiddle-faddles.

6. The Grand Lodge of Arizona "recognized" the "Masonic Bureau
for the Allied Armies," which is only a committee, composed of members of the Grand Orient of France, and appointed by that Grand Body.
We are somewhat at a loss to understand just how much our Arizona
Brethren meant by this action. It would seem to be a tacit recognition
of the Grand Orient of France, but perhaps our Brothers did not mran
it to be such.
The Grand Lodge of Michigan appropriated $200.00 to he used by the
same Bureau in its fine work for the soldiers. This, of course, does not
commit the Grand Lodge of Michigan, or show a leaning toward the
Grand Orient, any more than a similar contribution to the general fund
that is being gathered, a part of which is to be administered by the
K. C., would indicate Roman Catho:ic predilections.
To summarize: The , foregoing list shows that of the 50 Grand
Lodges named, 21 gave some measure of recognition to French Masonry.
Of the remaining 29, four were avowedly opposed to any form of
recognition; 11 considered the subject, but postponed action; in 12, the
matter was not mentioned, and 2 expressed themselves only so far as
concerns the "Masonic Bureau for the Allied Armies."

THE FUTURE
Masonic principles and their practical application triumphed
after an eight-year struggle with England, though, with privations
and ordeals that at that time appeared to be unsurmountable. It
took the Morgan episode, and the Masonic persecutions to solidify
the Craft. From present indications it would appear that there
will have to be something as radical and drastic in the Masonic
situation as these two movements to impress upon us the duty that
lies before us. This applies not only to the individual, but to the
fraternity.

GENERAL GRAND LODGE
As stated in another portion of this Report, the possibility of
a General Grand Lodge is too remote to ever be considered
seriously. There is no doubt but what there should be a common
meeting ground whereby certain standards and regulations would
be fixed that would remove friction between the various Jurisdictions and work for the ultimate good of all concerned.
District of Columbia:
He seems to believe 'the General Grand Lodge question is
slowly moving into the zone of controversy.' We pray not. Our
fear our belief is that should a General Grand Lodge ever succeed that unclean' hands will be put on it and it will merge into a
polit'ical cauldron. The one good reason against it is that existing
Grand Lodges lose their sovereignty the moment. t~ey acknowle_dg_e
a superior or controlling body. That we are dnftmg towards 1t 1s

45

Georgia:
The world of thought and action has changed and many problems of weight will arise in the future, and the time has come when
the voice of individual Grand Lodges can and will have but a minimum of weight, but as a body, concentrated into one great organization with one purpose in view much can be accomplished. Jealousy .and sectional feeling is of the past, the wars of the world
have made manifest the needs of consolidation to enable us to meet
in harmony and effectiveness the future.
Our Government is formed by a union of States, States by a
union of counties and counties are divided into districts. National
laws are applicable to the whole, without interference with or infringement upon the individual State rights. The States govern the
counties and the counties the districts, yet each has local laws that
in no wise affect the others. And so it should be with us for the
perfect accomplishment of the great and magnanimous principles
which we represent.
Idaho:
The trouble is that the above points in the direction of a Supreme Grand Lodge and such a proposition could not be entertained for a moment. lt might make Masonry a living force in the
world. It might be the means of turning Masonry toward the
future and make it too great a power in the affairs of men. No, no,
such a proposition is rank heresy.
Iowa:
We cannot agree with him (New Hampshire) .when he intimates
that precious little attention is paid by the Grand Chapters and the
Grand Commanderies to the national organizations which exercise
an advisory care over them. On the contrary, our experience has
been that these Grand E'odies do listen, heed, and profit by the
advice and suggestions of the national advisory body. At any rate,
this national body has served to furnish them a powerful means
for working together in harmony, for in the story of the work of
these Grand Bodies we have been able to find none of the petty
gri~vances, matters of contention and dissension which have prevented the Grand Bodies of Blue Lodge Masonry from united and
co-operative effort along lines of true progress in the great civic
life of America.
Everyone who is familiar with the facts knows what a wonderful
lack of unity and co-operation the Grand Lodges have presented in
the present crisis of the great world war. It has been in many
cases a most humiliating spectacle-one which has excited the derision and contempt of other fraternal organizations who have
worked together most beautifully by means of a national organization which furnished them with a means of national unity and cooperation.

\Ve are convinced that the time is at hand when some way, some
means will be found to unite and solidify Masonry in the United
States. \Ve simply must work together. \Ve cannot work separate
and apart any longer, for the situation has become simply intolerable. There is no use denying it; no use blinking at it; the problem
has become a burning one, and presses for an immediate solution.
The Grand Officer or Past Grand Officer who is not willing to
sacrifice something of his power, pomp, and prestige for the sake of
making Masonry really worth that much more all over the land,
should go and take a look at himself.
Brother Cheney cannot deny that we are working under a total
lack of unity between sister Grand Jurisdictions; that under ,our
present system we are as powerless to supply that want as were the
divided American colonies to throw off the voke of George III. If

they did, how will we then get the peace, the unity, the harmony,

Minnesota:
Because, in this country, Masonry is divided into forty-nine separate jurisdictions with forty-nine diverse policies, we have lost one
of the greatest opportunities that ever has knocked at our door.
Let us not mourn over the fact, but profit by our mistake. Let us
not be caught napping again.
Pennsylvania:
The General Grand Lodge question is slowly moving into the
zone of controversy. The cloud, no larger than a man's land, to
which reference was made in the conclusion to our report last year,
is assuming a more portentous aspect, and electrical discharges,
faint yet, may occasionally be seen playing about its periphery. A
meteorological chart is not yet possible. The idea is obnoxious to
us. We may discuss it at a later date.
We do not reproduce the above as a 'sign of the times' or as a
warning to Pennsylvania's pride in her sovereign power, but merely
as a subject which some day may furnish the correspondents pleasant discussion-if, indeed, it has not already begun.
Vermont:
The great activity of Masonry is upon the individual. Its object
and purpose is to give strength and character to the individual.
The scene of its greatest activity is in the local community. Its
work as an organization is little seen. No Grand Lodge was
thought of until after the institution became speculative. For generations it existed as a practical helpful organizaion without
thought or need of any Grand Lodge whatever.

GERMAN EXCLUSION
The Grand Lodge of England, her colonies, and Scotland,
during the war, excluded from their Lodges all Masons of alien
enemy birth. Ireland did not go so far, but let each case rest on
its own merits.
As an abstract proposition, we believe they were wrong, but
it was undoubtedly a case of safety first. We now know what
war is first hand. Sherman was right.

He quotes the remarks of one Brother who spoke against the proposed regulation, and follows with the statement of another Brother,

g-ation of peoples of one nationality under the guise of Freemasonry.
The fathers in Freemasonry who formu'ated the principles under which
the fraternity is today working never contemplated the organization of
class lodges wherein men of different nations, creeds, and professions
might segregate and use the lodge as a means of propagating their own
peculiar ideas and practices. The purpose of Freemasonry as originally
conceived was that of a fraternal democracy, wherein men of every
country, sect, and opinion, religious belief and political party, might
come tog-ether around a common altar, upon a common equality and meet
their fellows as children of one father. A lodge made up exc'.usively
of Germans, Frenchmen. Italians, Swedes, and using the particular
language of the constituents is not a Masonic lodge; hut a loclp-c composed of men representing these different nationalities and using the
language of the country wherein the lodge is located is Masonic. If the
war has done nothing else it has awakened us to the clanger of
class lodges and has served to bring to us a better understanding of the
object and purposes of genuine Freemasonry.

Connecticut:
A Masonic periodical states that some Arkansas Masons, who
had signed a petition to repeal the state-wide prohibition law,
afterwards tried in vain to have their names removed, on the
ground that they find their act in so signing to be 'in violation of
the edicts of Grand Lodge.' This is another 'straw' which shows
up the utter idiocy of this anti-liquor legislation by Grand Lodges,
even though their intentions are good. Further, if the majority
of individual Masons be so utterly irresponsible that they must
rely on their Grand Lodges for paternal guidance in every little
particular, the leading strings should be extended so as to cover
regulations on diet, hours of sleep, restrictions as to recreation, etc.,
even though Masonic teachings are aimed to embrace all of these in
general. \Ve thank heaven that our Masonic lines are not cast in
jurisdictions where such lunacy prevails. We hope that at some
future time these jurisdictions will awake to the foolishness and at
least partial inefficacy of such petty restrictions upon the individual. As an average proposition, the latter can better be trusted to
properly settle questions of conscience than can the holier-thanthou megalomaniacs who assume that they alone are competent to
play the paternal.
To make a logically complete job, Grand Lodges should regulate every moral question, leaving no initiative to the individual,
for of course all Grand Lodges have a few wise- men who know (at
least in their own estimation) that the average man has not sufficient brains to govern himself morally. 0 tempora, 0 mores!

GRAND LODGES
The suggestion was once made that the greatest good for the
United States and the various States would be done if Congress and
the State Legislatures would meet and then adjourn for ten years.
While t~is suggestion will never be followed, it is worth while
speculating what would occur if it .was put into effect so far as
Grand Lodges are concerned. Perhaps, if more detail was left to
the subordinate Lodges, there would lie less necessity for annual
communications. Of course, this would not be with pleasure to
the members of the Grand Lodge, but certainly it might profit the
Fraternity at large.

Illinois:
The Grand Lodge (Iowa) stopped long enough in its proceeding
to officially receive the Grand High Priest of the Grand Chapter,
the Grand Master of the Grand Council, the Grand Commander of
Knights Templar of the State. \Vhere was the Sovereign Grand
Inspector of the Scottish Rite, as well as the Grand Patron of the
Eastern Star? Can it be that the Grand Lodge of Iowa is discriminating in favor of York Rite Masonry? It may be that when these
officials find out that they were not given the same recognition as
their competitors, their noses may be out of joint.
Concerning Brother Martin's criticism of the tendency of Grand
Lodges to limit the activities of local Lodges and interfere in their
private concerns, Brother McAllister (Washington) says:
"He may as well give that up. The tendency of the times is to
usurp authority in favor of the Grand Lodge, and neither he nor the
writer can stop it."
The writer, however, is disposed to agree with Brother Martin
because there is a feeling of unrest among the fraternity and a
growing conviction that there is entirely too much legislation for
the best interests of the society. It is possible to carry this to such
an extreme that lodges will rise in their might and absolutely clean
out of their Grand Lodges those meddlesome, office-holding,
authority-seeking Brethren who imagine that the future success of
the fraternity lies wholly and solely in the enactment of petty legislation which in many cases is without Masonic precedent and becomes highly burdensome to the present overworked and much annoyed Masonic Lodge.

. More than forty years have passed since we first attended Grand

remain. No man has yet, so far as we have seen in Masonic literature, been able to account for the deep feeling aroused by these
reunions, though many have tried. The older among us realize
that ties thus formed grow stronger with the years. Possibly the
truth contained in his next words in part explains it.

Alabama:
\Ve thought views like these belonged to a past age when it was
generally taught and believed that there were Grand Masters before
there were Grand Lodges. But now that we know that there never
was a Grand Master who was not chosen by a Grand Lodge, that

Illinois:
For a long time the idea has obtained in many quarters that the
Grand Master of a Grand Lodge was a law unto himself. Jn other
words, that he could do pretty much as he pleased without getting
into trouble for his acts. Again. it has been assumed that a Grand
Master possessed certain autocratic powers, that he might create
Masons at sight and by an instanter process deprive members of
their existing rig1its. Just when this assumption of unwarranted
powers fastened itself upon the fraternity is unknown. It must
have grown out of the self-importance of individuals, for there is
nothing in the traditions or history of Freemasonry to warrant the
so-called "autocracy" of Grand Masters.
There has been in the past a practice prevalent in' some of the
larger bodies, particularly in the city of Chicago, of calling upon the
candidates raised during the year to contribute a certain amount
of money to a fund to be used in purchasing a gift for the Master.
Knowing this to be the practice, I issued an order to the Worshipful Masters of the Lodges in Cook Cotrnty, to the effect that they
were not to permit any money to be collected in their Lodges for
any purpose whatever, and particularly for the purpose of buying
a gift for the Master. I further ordered that Masters were not to
accept any gift purchased in this manner.

Kentucky:
What prerogatives has the Grand Master that the Grand Lodge
has not? If its constitution forbids initiation of a candidate yet a
minor, can the Grand Master violate it under an assumed prerogative? Whence these so-called extra-constitutional prerogatives,
anyway? Where did they originate? And when? Had any past
Grand Lodge, even the Grand Lodge of England at its first Communication, the power to endow future Grand Masters of other
Jurisdictions, themselves the creatures of Grand Lodges, with powers above the constitutions of the Grand Lodges that elect them?
And what about the obligation of installation, wherein each Grand
Master solemnly agrees and undertakes to maintain and support
the constitution? Categorical answers, please, from those good
Brethren who believe in mythical prerogatives of Grand Masters.
Louisiana:
It might be well for all of us to come to some conclusion as to
the character of the Masonic government. Is it autocratic or democratic? Our own impression is that it is a constitutional democracy.
We take it that while during recess of the Grand Lodge the power
to override the law is "almost unlimited," yet it has a limit. When

THE GROTTO
An organization with a high sounding title, "The Mystic
Order of the Veiled Prophets of the Enchanted Realm," endeavored to gain a foothold in several jurisdictions. The only relation
that the organization bears to the fraternity is that membership in
the Masonic Order is a prerequisite to admission.
The Grand Master of Indiana refused to allow them to meet
in a Masonic Lodge room. . The Grand Master of Louisiana ruled
that they were in the same category as the Odd Fellows, Druids,
Knights of Columbus and other fraternal organizations. The
Grand Lodge of North Dakota made it an offense for a Master
Mason to join. To our mind, the action of North Dakota is on
all fours with other Grand Lodge legislation where they concern
themselves with affairs that are not properly within their province, or Masonic only remotely. There is altogether too much
regulation in every walk of life, including Masonry. Why not
give the individual credit for some common sense?
·
GROUP INITIATION
If Masonry continues to increase in popular favor as it has,

California will sooner or later have to give the matter of group
initiation serious consideration, or find some means of handling
the increase. Of course, this condition naturally applies only to
large cities. A good solution of the matter without violating any
of the "ancient landmarks," and the feelings of some Past Masters-Grand, and otherwise-would be to make the use of printed
monitorial work .optional. Personally, we can see no advantage in
having a Master commit to memory the printed section of the
Monitors, which in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred the candidate has read before he receives his first degree or will after he
has been initiated. This method of instruction, as compared with
the manner in which the average Master "poll parrots" the word to
empty seats, is preferable.
Illinois:
For a long time, Freemasonry in many quarters of the world has
established the rigid rule that each candidate for Masonic honors must
receive his degrees singly and alone. This rule, unclouhtc<lly, became
the practice in the early <lays of the fraternity, when lodges were small
and candidates few. Twenty-five or thirty years ago it was an unusual
thing for any lodge to raise more than ten or twelve candidates in the
course of a year. It was with difficulty that sufficient candidates were
found to keep alive the working interest of the lodge. But conditions
have changed. Population has rapidly increased, lodges have rnu'.tipliecl
and petitions are so numerous, that it is not unusual for the average
lodge to raise fifty or sixty candidates in the course of a year. All of
this contributes to haste and carelessness in the conferring of degrees,

District of Columbia:
I am a strong believer in the thought that there should be, as far
as it is at all possible, at all times a close cooperation between Blue
Lodge Masonry and all other orders or institutions in any way related
to it or composed of Master Masons, including the Order of the Eastern
Star, in furtherance of any attempt to make the activities or principles
of Masonry a potent force for good. I have, therefore, gone as far as
seemed possible to go in the accomplishment of that end-perhaps to
an unusual length. * * * There has been no time when I thought
the promotion of any commendab!e project could be helped by a concerted action that I did not freely ask the executive heads of all the
branches of Masonry and allied orders in this jurisdiction to meet in
general conference with me and lend their aid and council; and I am
glad to report that no call I have made has failed to meet with the
most ready, earnest, enthusiastic and helpful response from all of
them.

Louisiana:
There was ·a time when the deep significance of its ceremonies,
coming. down, as they have, from the dim past, were wonderfully attractive, because they taught us not alone tlie customs of man when he
was struggling out of animalism, but they showed us how these customs
and ceremonies had been preserved through the ages. But it has begun
to appear that the show of tinsel and brass, and the blare of trumpet
and newspaper notoriety, public parades, garbed in fantastic and gaudy
costumes, have become the center of attraction, and the Sublime Degree
of a Master Mason is about to become, in the minds of the thoughtless
and the profane, nothing more nor less than a 'door mat' spread before
the portals of appendant degrees and organizations.
And the question is asked, not how useful may I become to humanity when I become a Master Mason, but how long will it take me to
hecome a 'Shriner'?
In these later days we hear much of the 'playground of freemasonry'
and the 'flower garden of freemasonry', catch-phrases invented and
put forth, often by well-meaning Masons and friends of the organization,
but Masonry has no playground nor flower garden; it is a progressive,
moral science; it respects the Ancient Landmarks; it works silently,

Vermont:
That such organizations are increasing there can be no doubt. But
the various degrees based upon symbolic Masonry exemplify some further legend. Even those orders that are not recognized as a part of
strict Masonry, are founded in furtherance of some purpose. Very
likely some of these have no other object than to afford entertainment
and pleasure to its members, but even this is not without its value.
So far as we know all these that are based upon symbolic Masonry
make membership in the Blue Lodge a prerequisite either to admission
or retention of membership in such organizations. And so long as this
continues and is insisted on and the organization maintains proper
standards, even though its purpose is nothing other than entertainment, membership in the Blue Lodge is fairly well protected; for we,
at last, have the right to say who shall be members of any of the
Masonic orders.

For a long time many thoughtful Masons have realized that there

troubles look like child's play. Ohio got into trouble by taking sides

fact that she took the right side did not save her years of discord
and contention with dandestinism. Virginia was asked to take sides,
and this writer, who was present, well remembers that our Grand
Lodge wisely said, 'we know nothing whatever officially of any organization but our own, whether or not it calls itself Masonic'. The result
was peace till this day.

Utah:
The report of the Grand Secretary (Minnesota) is exceptionally full
and valuable. His observations under the head of "Research aml
History", and "Masonic Grand Lodge Building", lay emphasis upon th.::
importance of preserving everything that pertains to the history of the
Grand Lodge and of the Constituent Lodges. He remarks that the
Grand Lodge of Kansas has been fortunate in that none of its archives
have ever been destroyed, and he describes the provisions made in the
new building for taking care of all such material. We feel that too
much attention cannot be given to this subject, and we know that lodges
are often careless or, indifferent as to the fate of documents that are
priceless. Kansas is to be commended for its work a!ong this line.
\Ve shall do well if we allow its suggestion to fructify in action in
our own jurisdictions. It is this: "Programmes, newspaper comments
and correspondence relative to official visits are deposited in the Grand
Secretary's office for historical reference". Ko one who has not had
occasion to lament the absence of such flotsam of other years, when
trying to vizualize the life and activities of other days. can fully appreciate what such a course, persisted in, would mean to those who one day
will seek to revivify our age for the benefit of generations not yet born.
Such records are the tracks we leave on the sands of our Jurassic
pedod, as it were, and will be invaluable in the restoration of forms
of life and thought of our day. There should be under the care and
direction of every Grand Lodge, a place of safe-keeping for all available
contemporaneous records.

HOMES AND ORPHANAGES
As usual, the opinions regarding the desirability of Masom.:
Homes, or the manner in which this form of relief should be
handled, is one that must be determined by the various jurisdictions according to circumstances. The idea of running these
Homes on the community or cottage plan, as a substitute for the
institutional one, is receiving favorable attention. This method
has much to commend it. It gives an opportunity for the development of the individual and removes the evils attendant to collecting adults ·and minors under one roof and attempting to handle
them under. set rules.
There are two things in this connection that this Jurisdiction
lacks. One is a place under Masonic management or influen.ces
where children may be placed, but cannot under the present rules
be admitted to the Home. Often a mother or father dies, leaving
the surviving parent with children. There is no financial aid necessary, but the circumstances are such that the minors must have
a home. About the only place of refuge in this case is an institution under sectarian control. · If our Masonic Homes could accommodate paid boarders in this class, it might solve the problem.
The other condition is the care of the physically helpless, who
are charges upon the Fraternity. It is hardly right or proper· that
they should be placed in the Homes. In sc:ime Jurisdictions the
Fraternity have been allowed the privilege of maintaining at state
institutions a separate building for the care of their own and paying for its upkeep. This might solve the problem.
In the statistical part of the report will be found data relative
to existing Masonic Homes. It is to be regretted that in a few
instances the information is missing, or not up to date, but this is
.due to the "Mafiana" habit on the part of the parties to whom
communications have been addressed.
HOSPITALS
A survey of the various States develops the fact that Blue
Lodge Masonry is doing nothing along this line.. The only work
that has been done has been thrQugh the Scottish Rit.e. . This
branch of our Fraternity also went to the relief of the State Board
of Health in Alabama, when it lacked funds to carry on a health
campaign.
The report of the special committee from the Oklahoma
Grand Lodge is reproduced in full, as it· outlines a movement that
·could be followed up profitably to all concerned if Masonry
chooses to interest itself f9r the ttood of. humanitr.

LECTURES
Uusually the average Masonic lecturer is a bore. When he
does tell something that is true, but disagreeable, his ideas get
little support unless he is in a position to continue the crusade.
You can reach a person in three ways: through the stomach, the
eye, or the ear. The first is usually the most effective, with the
eye next.
Illinois:
The system of imparting Masonic instruction through lectures is
all right provided the lecturer is sufficiently well versed in the history, traditions, philosophy and ethics of the fraternity to be able to
give to the Brethren information which they should have. The
trouble is that the suggestion of Masonic education is construed by
a lot of Jack-in-the-Box lecturers as an invitation to them to immediately get into the field and bestow upon the craft the great
wealth of Masonic information which they imagine themselves to be
possessed of, much of which is the result of their own overwrought
imaginations. In these cases it is not so much the idea of service
which actuates them as it is the financial return to themselves. A
friend of the writer listened not long ago to an illustrated Masonic
lecture on Jerusalem wherein the speaker exhibited on the screen
a picture of some rocks with the statement, "These are undoubtedly
the identical rocks behind which the three principal characters of
the third degree secreted themselves." Such assertions can only
serve to disgust intelligent Masons and have no place in any system
of Masonic education.
Nevada:
Under 'Recommendations,' the Grand Master (Utah) took a fall
out of a 'lecturer of note,' who had recently given a series of lectures in Masonic subjects in Nevada. He seemed to feel that subjects which touch the core of community life and interests should
be taboo. He appealed .to Grand Lodge to put its 'stamp of disapproval upon this twentieth century heresy.' The Committee on
Address held with the lecturer and against the Grand Master-and
Grand Lodge supported the committee. The committee expressed
the opinion that 'This matter can safely be left to the good judgment of the different Masters.' A wise committee, we think. For the
love of our brother man, give us more heretics, and more power to
their utterances, if through this channel there may come to Masons
a vivifying interest in, and an irresistible and deepening consciousness of responsibility for conditions in the midst of which they live,
New Mexico:
Personally, I am not convinced that the method we agreed
upon for this year's work has been productive of the desired results.
One lecture given in May last, by a well known Mason from - - - .
was of a character to which we cannot give the endorsement of the
Grand Lodge. Another lecture given in Salt Lake in August was
higl;ily entertaining and pleasing in character, but in my judgment.
scarcely met the requirements of our jurisdiction.

Wisconsin:
Closely akin to the above" (printed lists of members) "is the
Masonic Lecturer who seeks to obtain permission to give his lecture
before the subordinate Lodges for monetary consideration. There
may be, and doubtless are,· Masons capable of giving interesting
and valuable information to the craft by this means, and deservfog'
of compensation therefor if a subordinate Lodge wishes to so expend its funds. But I have insisted that no one be permitted to
circularize the subordinate Lodges, nor seek a hearing therein for
pay, without first proving his qualification, obtaining unquestioned
Masonic testimonials of an official character as to the nature and
value of his efforts, and having the permission of the Grand Lodge
after a full presentation of his cause to that body. What shall be
presented to the subordinate Lodges as instruction in Masonic history, philosophy and ethics is too important to permit a discussion
thereof by persons not vouched for as to ability and purpose, and
especially is this true where pay is demanded.
LIBRARY
Too often a Masonic library is nothing but a collection of
books which the average brother desires to get rid of, because
they have served his purpose and are in the way. The publjc
libraries supply the demands for current fiction, and a Masonic
library for reference use is a necessity to a small portion of the
Craft only.
The main function of a Grand Lodge library should be to
furnish traveling libraries for the use of Lodges located away from
populous towns, and where such a service will be appreciated and
used.

be in more capable and intelligent keeping.

MASONIC PHRASEOLOGY

.It is to be regretted that some of the phrases peculiar to
~asonry only have become so common as to have lost their significance. For example, "A man is on the square," is heard so
often the average person using it does not associate it with the
Masonic Fraternity. Likewise there are others too numerous to
mention.
Alabama:
I:i a very mild manner, he finds fault with the name of our fratc;rn.Ity !n .so,~th ~arolina-"Ancient Free Masons." In his Jurisdiction 1t 1s Ancient Free and Accepted Masons." He thinks "it
would appear more logical, if one must be dropped to drop 'Free'
rather than 'Accepted.' " We must explain.
'
In 1777 the Provincial Grand Lodge of South Carolina, holding
under ,~he Grand Lodge of England, assumed independence, and became The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of South
Carolina." In 1783, the illegitimate, schematic Athol or Ancient
Masons invaded the Jurisdiction of South Ca;olina and on 24th
March, 1787, organized "The Grand Lodge of Ancient York Masons." In 1808, a union of these two Grand Lodges took place
which, however, was disrupted the year following. In 1817 the tw~
Grand Lodges were merged into one under the name it still bears
"The Grand Lodge of Ancient Free Masons of South Carolina." '
As between "Free" and "Accepted" we are inclined to believe
that "Free" is the correct term, at le~st, if only one is to be used
we lean. towards "Free." Dr. Anderson first used the word "Ac~
cepted" m the second edition of his "Constitutions."
.
In Masonry, the word "Free" originally signified that the persons so called were "free" of the guild, that is, were members, and

74

~EPORT

ON CORRESPONDENCE

had all the privileges of the guild, and those who were not thus
"free" were not allowed to work with those who were. In our system of Freemasonry, "Free" means not bound, not in captivity: In
1782, the Master of Royal Military Lodge at Woolwich, England,
being in the King's Bench Prison, held a meeting in said prison,
and made several Masons. The Grand Lodge of England held this
meeting of Masons illegal, and adopted a resolution affirming that
''it is inconsistent with the principles of Freemasonry for any Free
Masonic Lodge to be held, for the purpose of making, passing or
raising Masons, in any prison or place of confinement." Note the
word "confinement," it shows the meaning attached to the word
"Free" by our Old Mother.
Manitoba:
Phrases endeared by long association, terms which have a flavor
of antiquity, habits which indicate that Masonry has a historythese give character to our proceedings and differentiate Masonry
from ephemeral associations of m'ln.
South Dakota:
In my correspondence with the various Lodges in our J urisdiction I have observed that Communications are almost invariably
spoken of as "meetings." In my conversations with many old and
otherwise well informed members of the fraternity, I have lear.ned
that they have always been accustomed to use the terms regular
and special meeting, and many of them have come to believe that
the word Communication is 9nly used to designate the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge.
The same careless and incorrect use of the terms regular and
special meeting prevails very largely throughout many jurisdictions
other than our own, showing that Masons generally have become
very lax in this regard. If this unfortunate condition is suffered to
continue, the use of the good old Masonic word "Communication,"
with the proper prefix, Stated, Special, and Festival, will ultimately
become obsolete; and the fraternity as a whole will lose terins that
have a peculiar Masonic meaning.
MASONIC PRESS
The Masonic press is in a position to render as much service
to the Craft as the daily newspaper is to its readers. There are
some of the publications that are of great value. They are interesting, readable and reliable. Others too often contain only discussions of abstract theories and chronological tables, or ride the
editor's personal hobby until it is tiresome.
Canada:
Let our excellent Masonic press, to which every brother should
subscribe, open their columns to the earnest discussion of all permissible craft questions. Masonic papers help to mould Masonic
opinion, and their unifying influence and educative power should be
practically recognized by all earnest Masons.

If lodges wi!l keep in close touch with the official circulars issued
