The several Masonic Jurisdictions were invited to attend a
conference of Grand Masters at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, the 26th .of .
November, 1918, for the purpose of taking some acthm with respect
to the then existing war emergency and the opportunity fdr Ma"
sonic service therein. Twenty-two Jurisdictions responded to the
call, and fourteen expressed their approval in general terrris. The.
meeting was held and the following plan then evolved, which has
been submitted to all of the Grand Lodges:
That there be organized the MASONIC SERVICE ASSOCIA·
TION of the United States, a voluntary association of Masonic
Grand Jurisdictions of the United States of America, for service to
mankin.d.
All Masonic jurisdictions of the United States of America shall be
entitled to membership therein on equal footing on expressing their
approval of this Constitution and acceptance of the responsibility and
privileges out.ined therein. Any member shall be entitled to withdraw
at any time on ninety clays' notice provided it shall have complied with
all of its assumed obligations. Such notice shall be delivered by registered mail to the Secretary at his postoffice address.

ambitions, cast aside petty jealousies, and act on the principle of
the greatest good for the greatest number, the situation can be
remedied; but if not, there seems to be hope for nothing but a
continuation of the existing conditions.
On December 13th, 1917, the representatives of all the fraternal
organizations in the United States met in Washington, D. C.
Little was done other than to urge the wli.ole gathering to a more
enthusiastic participation in the war. On the same evening,
twenty-five Grand Masters of Masonic Grand Lodges met in the
Masonic Temple to discuss plans for united efforts on the part
of the various Grand Lodges for welfare work for our boys at
home and abroad. Nothing definite was accomplished, for reasons
which are too numerous to mention here. The meet;ng did give
birth to a resolution commissioning a Past Grand Master who
was then in France to do missionary work in France, with an idea
of gettin~ THEM to change their constitution, by-laws, regulations
and beliefs to conform to the various ideas of the American Masonic Grand Lodge, so that fraternal intercourse could once more
be had without violating ancient landmarks, etc. Up to the present, the appointed missionary does not seem to have accomplished
anything along this line.
On May 10th, 1918, a conference of Grand Masters and representatives of several Grand Jurisdictions held a meeting in New
York. Nothing practical was accomplished, but a printed report
of 208 pages contains the proceedings of the conference.

Object
The object of the Association shall be the service of mankind through
education, enlightenment, financial relief and Masonic visitation, particularly in times of disaster and distress, whether caused by war, pestilence, famine, fire, flood, earthquake or other calamity; and presently and
immediately ministering to, cherishing, comforting and relieving the
members of the fraternity, their dependents and others engaged in the
United States forces, in the present great war, wherever they may be
stationed and upon whate~er duties engaged in the service.
Administration
For the purpose of administration the United States 1s divided into
departments as follows:
The New England Division.
The Central Division.
The North Atlantic Division.
The Corn Belt Division.
The South Atlantic Division.
The North Pacific Division.
The Gulf Division.
The South Pacific Division.
The Great Lakes Division.
The Southwestern Division.
Upon the occurrence of a disaster of greater magnitude than a local
calamity, the Grand Masters of the several Grand Jurisdictions within
the department, in which the said disaster sha11 occur, shall appoint a
committee to survey the need, appraise it and report forthwith its findings
to the department. The department shall thereupon take action on the
report of the committee to the end that the fund necessary shall be
provided and properly disbursed.
The Association may enter into correspondence and. affiliation with
similar agencies in other lands or under other governments, the better
to teach the Fatherhood of Goel, and to promote the Brotherhood of Man.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

The powers and duties of the Association may be enlarged or cur~
tailed from time to time, but no member jurisdiction shall be bound
thereby without its express assent.
Each department shall meet annually on a date and at a place to be
fixed by it, or oftener if it shall so determine. A meeting may be
called at any time on the request of three Grand Jurisdictions. A
general meeting of all departments shall be held triennially on the
eleventh day of November, or oftener on the call of ten Grand Juris-·
dictions. Notices of the time, place and object of the meetings shall.
be issued by the Secretaries.
At each meeting, departmental or general, a presiding officer shall
be elected by ballot, for the purposes of the meeting. Each department
shall select a Secretary, whose duties it shall be to keep the records and
attend to the correspondence of the department.
The sole officer of the Association shall be the Secretary, who shall
be selected at the general meeting, and shall hold office until the next
general meeting, .or during the pleasure of the Association, and his
functions shall be purely clerical.

*At a quarterly Communication of the Grand Lodge, held recently,
the matter was referred to the Grand Master, who has written Bro.
Schoonover to the effect that he will recommend that his Grand Lodge
join the Association at the coming Annual Communication.

The question is now, shall Indiana approve this constitution and

"The object of the Association shall be the Service of Mankind
through education, enlightenment, financial relief and Masonic visitation, particularly in times of disaster and distress, whether caused by
war, pestilence, famine, fire, flood, earthquake or other calamity; and
presently and immediately ministering to, cherishing, comforting and

engaged in the United States forces, in the present great war, wherever
they may be stationed and upon whatever ditties engaged in the service."
A little consideration will quickly develop the fact that under these
ohjects thus stated. an almost unlimited field of activities is opened up.

would be practically no limit to the activities in which the or:;anization may engage.
We have very great respect for the opinions of the Brethren who
formulated the plan or have since approved it. Nevertheless, it is the

have justified the call for such an organization has passed.
With the passing- of the emerrrencv there has n;issed a, so whatever
need for such organization may have arisen from the emergency.

the individual Grand Lodges have ever been ready and willing to respond liberally and generously, and more oromptly in our opinion than
could be done under the machinery proposed by this organization.
Therefore, for these purposes there is no real need for this new
machinery.
So far as the general education, enlightenment and uplift of the

There is no doubt but what the plan of the Association has
some defects. That there must be a great deal of good in it is
evidenced by the action of the Grand Lodges above mentioned. It
is a matter for careful consideration and we believe that California should swing into line with the others.

Now, what sort of equipment do Masons need to fit them for the
highest usefulness? If operative, I see some reason; if speculative, I
see a wonderful inspiration from such schools as the Iowa system provides, with its grand library and its wonderful equipment for study;
but a university involves several schools with specific courses and
teachers and esoteric work as well would involve difficulties innumerable. It shows a growing need, however, for the fellowship of kindred
spirits, who grow indifferent to the ritual, which lacks inspiration and
longs for a higher or deeper insight into the spirit of Masonry, with its
history and its influence. We are proud of the great names of good men
who figure so gloriously in our country's history. Can we trace the
connection, for instance, between patriottism and Freemasonry? Why
was the Father of His Country a Freemason? Why was a Freemason
the Father of His Country? Do we need a great school with is kaleidoscopic faculty to fit us for patriotic functions? It may be. At first
blush and with profound respect to its promoters, the scheme is too
ambitious. Is it a quartuor corona ti scheme? If so, let us have it.

NATIONAL UNIVERSITIES
This, being something practical, should appeal to the Craft in
general. Perhaps, in time, the seed planted may bear fruit. One
of the aims of George Washington was the establishment of a
national university. One was started, but never prospered. The
Catholic College at Georgetown (near Washington, D. C.), is
flourishing, but Congress has never seen fit to carry out the idea
of the Father of His Country.
Thomas Jefferson wished that he be mainly remembered as one
of the founders of the University of Virginia. Perhaps these ideas
were peculiar to our forefathers, and are now out of date.

Steps were taken, which were favorably received, looking toward

undertaking. The report does not say the university shall be located
at the Na ti on al Capital, or in one of the states. If at the capital, the
answer will be, there are already in that city several half endowed,
ha1f supported similar institutions, which could be developed into great
seats of learning, if they were properly supported. And there are but
few of the states that do not have well endowed and prosperous universities for the higher education of their young men and women;
furtherm·ore, there are scattered all over the country sectarian c.olleges
and universities of the highest order, also a large number of nondenominational, non-sectarian universities, which impart the highest
courses of study, where Masons can attend a!)d not be hampered by
sectarian dogmas or isms of any sort. Really, I can see no earthly
reason for loading on the Craft the responsibility of creating and supporting a distinctive Masonic university.

Canada:
As in other jurisdictions, there are ~wo troubles or dangers which
beset us at times. Whenever a lodge needs petitions for the degrees to
refill its treasury or meet its expenses, the door is open for the reception
of unfit material. And there is the other peril-numerical ambitionthe appetite for dimensions. It has been well said that "we need
quick recovery from the insanity of numbers". Are we not paying too
much attention to the wholesale birth of Masons and too little attention
to their care and nourishment after thev are born? Masters seem to be
possessed with an imaginary rivalry with competitors who do not exist.
The character of its people is the measure of a nation's greatness and
so with the craft. The calibre, the quality of membership, is all in all.
Quantitative totals are merely nominal rolls-Masons on paper-unless
good citizenship is added to the distinguished honor and dignity that
we have the power to bestow or withhold.

"Have committees forgotten to report whether these have 'sufficient
education and intelligence to understand and value the doctrines ancl

unworthy foot allowed to cross the threshold'?

Minnesota:

This fact must give us concern, mixed with our satisfaction, for
many of these have received the degrees without any prepai"ation, and
in many cases· I fear without much investigation. To the experienced
Freemason grave dangers to the Craft will arise from this rapid
Masonic advancement. True it is that in modern times we have lost
much of our early conservativeness, but still we have insisted that a
certain degree of restraint on newly made Masons is necessary, because
that which is quickly and easily attained is correspondingly deprived
of its due value and importance. The Fraternity must make endeavor''
to digest and assimilate this mass of raw material, some of which I
icar will cause serious internal disturbances.

We often congratulate ourselves with the remark that Masonry i:;
making such rapid progress and such large gains. Never before has
there been such an increase of membership as during the year 1916.
There seems to be a passion for members in these days. There is danger
in the popularity of Masonry. There is such a thing as the enthusiasm
of numbers working more for woe than for weal. Better material
and less of it would not be a policy wanting in both sense and judgment. It is not desirable that all men should be Masons. I am afraid
there are times when we are too anxious and too ready to take men in
for the sake of their numbers, their fees, or the making of a good
record of activity. Are we simply becoming a factory for turning out
Master Masons? There is danger that we are. What makes me a
Mason? My obligation. The best Mason is he to whom the obligation
is most intelligently and instructively given. Many of the jurisdictions
around us, and some of the largest, allow only one candidate to be
obligated at one time. The Ancient Landmarks had only one in mind.
So, too, our own Minnesota work. Moreover, every candidate is entitled
to have the whole work exemplified upon himself alone. It has been
said that lodges paying high rents must have many candidates in order
to meet their expenses. Is not tHis to commercialize the Craft and
cheapen it in the eyes of the world? Those lodges are wise who have
learned that the dues should be sufficient to care for the ordinary
expenses without the necessity of receiving candidates to benefit from
the fees. To insure independence, a sure and sufficient income is as
necessary for the lodge as for the individual. Raise your dues, Brethren,
but don't cheapen the Craft.

Louisiana:
The deficiencies caused by the rapidity of growth and the desire
for large membership, rather than care in selecting new material, are
becoming· more and more apparent. The organization in general, and
in this Grand Jurisdiction in particular, lacks that solidarity and
cohesiveness which gave us strength in by-gone days. * * * It
has begun to appear that the show of tinsel and brass, and the blare
of trumpet, a.nd newspaper notoriety, public· parades garbed in fantastic
and gaudy costumes, have become the center of attraction, and the
Sublime Degree of a Master Mason is about to become, in the minds of
the thoughtless and the profane, nothing more than a 'door mat' spread
before the portals of appendant degrees and organizations.

Massachusetts:
I have long been of the op1111on that many of our lodges are
altogether too large, and that better Masonic and equally good
financial results .would be obtained if there were more lodges, with
smaller membership.
Tt is hard to say that there is any fixed number of members which
should not be exceeded. Conditions vary in different places. It is
however, always true that where the membership is so large that each
member present cannot know all the others, and where only a very
small percentage of the members can ever have the opportunity of
serving the lodge in official capacities, the interest of the members
lessens and each individual member feels less responsibility for the
welfare of the lodge and for the exercise of the duties and responsibilities of Masonry as well. It is a practically universal rule that the
smaller the membership the larger percentage of members attend the
meetings. Elephantiasis is a disease equally injurious to an animal,
a human, or a lodge. Many lodges, however, are afflicted with it.
What is even much more necessary is the creation of a sentiment
in favor of more and smaller lodges where the Brethren may be more
united, may be thrown into closer fraternal intercourse, may have
more opportunity to serve, and where the tenets of our institution
can better be in cu lea ted.
The tendency of great lodges is to lessen rather than to enhance
the Masonic development of each individual member. The accomplishments of Masonry have never been engaged by fo1ancial considerations. When these become the criteria, then it is time to halt and
to recast our activities, for then the grand aims and purposes of our
fraternity are sure to be obscured".

in popularity and one Grand Master emphasizes the thought by the

black", as an injury to our Order. And the opinion is growing among

and go to work and improve those we have made.

Nevada:
The large lodge has its advantages when it comes to doing things
in a large way, but the real service of Masonry ·comes from doing
things in the small, quiet way. When it comes to real usefulness,
personality and close contact are essentials. In the large lodge personal acquaintance and close fellowship are unknown. Time doe~
not al'.ow for the contact of the closer brotherhood. Too much energy
is expended in hustle and too little on friendship and getting in touch
with one another. while in tl1e small lodge there is no trouble in getting
nearer to the personal needs of the individual member, and this contact and fellowship arc what count in the real usefulness of Masonry.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS.
There are three well defined rules along this subject: First a
candidate must literally comply with the Ancient Landmarks
being physically perfect, without maim or defect in body or limb'.
Second, that a candidate is eligible if he is physically able to
conform substantially with all the requirements of the Ritual and
Modes of Recognition, without the aid of artificial substitutes.
Third, a candidate is eligible, even with the substitution of artificial parts or limbs for portions of his natural person, provided
such are under his practical control.

89

We believe that the last regulation is entirely too liberal for
the good of the Craft. It is a product of the "sob-sister" sentiment or philanthropy occasioned by the war, when a soldier's uniform was a passport to everything, regardless of the mental or
moral qualifications of the man himself. It was not thought wise
after the Givil war or the Spanish-American war to go to such
lengths, and we do not know that the Craft suffered very much
thereby. It should be remembered that in lifting the ban you do
so not only for men who have served their country, BUT EVERY
OTHER CRIPPLED PERSON THAT IS OTHERWISE ELIGIBLE. There are undoubtedly individual cases of persons who
would be a credit to the Fraternity, but are now barred. Might
we inquire why they did not have sufficient interest in the Craft
to make their application before the injury? Is it not about
time we commence to THINK LESS OF THE INDIVIDUAL
AND MORE OF THE FRATERNITY, and would it not be
better to tighten the· rules a little rather than relax them? While
the exceptional case might argue for a change, still remember
that in legislation of this kind we are not dealing with the exceptions, but everyone and part1cularly some who would abuse the
privilege. There is of course a stock argument that it is better
to have a man with a wooden leg than one with a wooden head.
While one prejudice makes more votes than one hundred reasons,
still is there any necessity for Masonry having EITHER the
wooden-legged or the wooden-headed man, or BOTH of them?

The general demand is for such bodily endowment as will
enable• the candidate to comply literally and fully with all the conditions of the ceremonies. We cannot help thinking that the constitution of 1723, when dealing with this subject, has been generally misunderstood. That law declar~c! that "no Master sho;ild
take an apprentice unless he has sufficient employment for him,
and unless he be a perfect youth, having no maim or defect ,fo his
body that may render him incapable of learning the art of serving
his Master's lord. ·The intent and meaning of this appears to be
that no apprentice might be taken who suffered from any defect
which would disqualify him to serve his employer. A trifling
defect would not disqualify him for cutting stone or laying it in
the wall, and a trifling defect oug~t not to disqualify a man for
Masonry in the modern and Masomc sense of the word:

in libraries (particularly the Congressional Library) where the public
can get them to read. A few years ago a renegade (Jesuit) :Mason in
Baltimore issued a volume, using Grand Lodge records for his authority
on these "horrible examples."

reading of the bill, as the case may be, and the bill is then supposed to
have been read.
PUBLICITY
As long as there are newspapers there is going to be publicity,
more or less, as to our activities. It is to be regretted that in
some instances it has been carried to such an extent as it has; because familiarity often breeds contempt.
Connecticut:
Your committee, to whom was referred so much of the Grand
Master's address as relates to publicity, made to the Grand Ledge at its
annual communication, February 3, 1916, beg leave to report:
"They ha'fe had the subject under consideration and are of the
opinion that, within proper bounds, ·Masons may and should welcome
publicity. A secret society is one which seeks to conceal its existence
and its objects. Freemasonry is not such a society and is secret only
as to the obligations, means of recognition, ballots upon candidates
and forms and ceremonies observed in conferring the degrees. With
the exception of those particulars, Masonry has no reservations from
the public. As to everything else-its designs, its moral and religious
tenets and the doctrines taught by it, the time and place of its meetings,

the names of the officers of a lodge and those belonging to it-are
all in no way secret, and may be known by any one. The fact that
a man has been made a Mason is not a secret to be concealed from
the public, nor is it anything of which he need be ashamed. The
public notices of the time and plaJ:e of holding Masonic lodges, the
name of the degree to be worked, as seen in many of the papers published in the larger towns and cities under the heading 'Fraternal News',
is useful to members of the craft, and particularly those temporarily
stopping in that locality, in affording them information as to the opening of the lodge and the nature of the work to be performed. The names
of officers elected, their installation and social occasions following lodge
meetings, which are usually joint affairs gotten up by the lodge and local
chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star·, are all matters in no way
secret, and public knowledge regarding them can do no harm. All
unnecessary secrecy tends to narrow rather than to broaden. There can
be no reason why we should undertake to keep secret and cast a veil of
mystery around that which is not secret and which the public is at liberty to know.
· "In connection with the general subject of this report, it may be appropriate to draw attention to the growing tendency to the indiscriminate
use of the word 'Masonic'. A Masonic club is a proper, useful, and
valuable association. It emphasizes the social side of fraternal life and
fills a real need. But in its conduct and in its activities good judgment
is necessary. A million men in this country have a vital interest in the
word 'Masonic'. Any man or body of men, who make use of it in connection with private or quasi public activity, owe it to their brethren to
see that it is put to a proper and dignified use. Cheap dances and boxing
bouts advertised publicly as Masonic and under the auspices of Masonic
clubs wound the sensibilities of most Masons. To some, the advertise·
ment of a Masonic baseball league, pool match, or bowling contest. is
objectionable. Your committee does not find such advertisement within
the purview of the Grand Lodge prohibition, but is of the opinion that,
in the use of the word 'Masonic' consideration is dtte to the dignity
associated with this word for centuries."

Florida:
"It is gross unmasonic conduct for a Mason to distribute business
cards having on the back thereof a parody on a subject of Masonry, or a
piece of doggerel tending to make light of any of the Masonic lectures
or ceremonies. The Masonic ceremonies are too sacred and beautiful
to be lightly treated and ridiculed."

Of course the grand master of North Carolina was correct. A good
many Masons have a mistaken idea concerning patriotism. To be patriotic it is not necessary to be flying flags, marching in street' parades
and hallooing on the slightest provocation. The world is full of people
who fight with their mouths and lay down their lives in their minds, but
the real patriot is the man who goes quietly about his business, putting
service to his country above all else, doing everything which his government asks of him to the best of his ability, and when the time comes,
should it be necessary, shoulders his rifle and goes over the top. \Vhen
the present war is over there is going to be a new standard of patriotism
established, and like charity it will not be of the tinkling cymbal and
the sounding brass variety.

REGULARITY
The action of the various Grand Lodges in recognizing French
Masonry brought this question actively to the front. As in a large
number of other questions before us, conditions and not theories
should govern. Being in favor of patronizing home industry, we
believe that the rule laid down (under the subdivision "Argument") in the Report of the Special Committee on Foreign
Masonry, of the Grand Lodge, October, 1918, gives a reasonable
solution of the question.
Kentucky:
Upon the question of visitation and intercourse there are two distinct theories held by two distinct groups of Masonic jurists, and practiced by two groups of Grand Lodges:
First-A Mason may lawfully visit a lodge of a jurisdiction other
than his own, provided the grand lodge to which the lodge of his membership owes obedience has Masonically recognized the grand lodge to
which the lodge he proposes to visit owes obedience; and
Conversely-A Mason hailing from another jurisdiction may lawfully attend a lodge within the jurisdiction visited, provided the grand
lodge of that jurisdiction has Masonically recognized the grand lodge
to which the lodge of his membership owes obedience.
Second-A Mason, made in a just and lawfully constituted lodge,
may visit lodges of a jurisdiction other than his own, provided the grand
lodge having jurisdiction over the lodge he proposes to visit has issued
no edict of non-intercourse against the grand lodge to which the lodge
of his membership owes obedience ; and
Conversely-A Mason, made in a lodge duly constituted by a grand
lodge, may visit lodges of another jurisdiction, provided the grand lodge
to which the lodge of his membership O't'es obedience has issued no edict
of non-intercourse against the grand lodge to which the lodge he proposes to visit owes intercourse.
The first theory defines a policy which, in my opinion, is wholly indefensible, Masonically and logically. It assumes that each of the sixtyodd grand lodges of the world is the judge of, and must first fix, the
Masonic status of every other grand lodge; hence is a fruitful source of
Masonic antagonism and of hopeless confusion. It is an assumption that
rests on no basis of reason. Carried out, it results in the membership
of one jurisdiction being clandestine, at least irregular, in some jurisdictions and regular in others.
The second theory meets every Masonic requirement, is consonant
with Masonic history, is consistent with the doctrine of grand lodge
sovereignty, and does violence to no principle of grand lodge integrity
and autonomy, nor does it conflict with any rule of sound reasoning. Its
rationale is clear, distinct, definite, meets every difficulty, and answers
every objection. This Grand Lodge should go upon record and define
its attitude on this important question.

Vermont:
Eleven days from this date will mark the two-hundredth anniversary of the organization of the first Grand Lodge of Masons. On June
24, 1717, at the Goose and Gridiron Tavern in London, the representatives of four old Lodges met and organized a Grand Lodge, Anthony
Sayre being elected Grand Master. You will note that this was not the
beginning of Freemasonry. These four Lodges and others besides had
long been in existence and it was to give more definite form and add
efficiency to the institution that the bond of union was formed. Historians and scholars may search and seek to determine the exact .beginning of Masonry, but it is shrouded in the darkness of antiquity. Sufficient for us today that from this Grand Lodge thus established has descended all that we now recognize as legitimate Masonry.

The church has just as often hurt the cause of true religion as it

SOJOURNERS
We think that the Nevada rule is a good one. These sojourn·
ers undoubtedly have a place in our Masonic system because they
furnish a field from which members can be drawn, to establish a
new Lodge when such becomes a necessity or some Brothers need
office.
Idaho:
sojou:rning Mason we mean one whose home is in one
place and the lodge to which he belongs is in another. In I~aho
this condition of things is far too prevalent. The excuses given
are quite various. One man retains his membership in some
eastern state because the annual dues are lower; another because
his lodge needs his dues; anotqer becau.se he was made .a ~ason
in the lodge to which he still holds allegiance, and so ad mfimtum.
The whole matter seems to rest either on expediency or mere
sentiment. A man that is not worth more to his lodge than the
amount of his annual dues is a Masonic 'slacker.' The lodge whose
existence depends on the dues of a brother residing _in a foreig;n
jurisdiction should surrender its charter. Masonry 1s not sentimental. It is a brotherhood where united effort counts, where
duty is incumbent on each member, where his personal influence
stands for more than the mere pittance of his annual dues. One
good brother Mason has been punctual in attendance ·at every
meeting of the Boise lodges when refreshments were served for
the past 28 years, and yet prides himself in having his membership elsewhere. Comment in such case is superfluous.
A Sojourning Mason becomes ill or meets with some reverses
-in short is 'down and out.' The local lodge cares for him and
then applies to his lodge for reimbursement. Most lodges refuse,
as they ought to do. The down-and-outer should have affiliated
in his place of residence.
Nevada:
The Grand Lodge (Philippine Islands) passed an amendment
doing away with dues during suspension, claiming that it is an
unjust act to require such payment. The injustice is on the other
side. We have no use for slackers in any part of life's service.
Masonry is action. Its one great law is work and it has no use
for a shirker. A shirker is about as despicable a bit of humanity
as one can find. It is the duty of every Mason to belong to some
lodge and to contribute his proportion towards its support. At
its portal he promises conformity to its rules and regulations and
dues are an essential part of Masonry and its equality these days.
Does he work? is an important question in Masonry. Without
work, leaving the burdens to others, !nakes h_im a ~hirker, and
without work in Masonry, where labor 1s worship, he 1s of no use.

study these questions for twelve months, and you will then be in a
condition to receive and appreciate the light the unwritten book is
designed to impart."

TOLERATION
Albert Pike stated that "A man should judge others as he
judges himself; believe others honest and sincere as he believes
himself; find for their actions the excuses that he finds for his,
and look always for a good rather than a bad motive." Add this
as a supplement to the Gold,eri Rule, and we have, perhaps, an
ideal .condition.
Illinois:
When the Jewish rabbi held the crucifix to the lips of the
dying soldier in Flanders, there gleamed through ·the smoke of
battle, the roar of guns, the screech of shells, the prophecy of
a new religion, based upon that long recognized Masonic
foundation stone, the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of
Man. Anyone who follows the trend of modern thought with
an unprejudiced mind must become convinced that we are fast
approaching a new era of religious thought and action.
The
barriers of prejudice are being broken down. The jealousies and
selfishness of sects are being dissipated, and mankind is gravitating surely and slowly, toward a Universal Religion wherein
many of the old ideals will be forgotten and a better conception
of life and action adopted so far as man relates to the God of
all and his neighbor on earth. Those of us who are enthusiastically Masonic have a belief that the new religion which the
world is bound to recognize will be somewhat along the ideas
for which Freemasonry has been contending for two hundred
years. Of course no one is expecting that anything in Freemasonry will be at all accepted nor recognized in the new
religion nor will the fraternity in any way be given credit for
the new reformation, but there is a lingering suspicion that those
old fathers in Freemasonry who, two hundred years ago, conceived the society and laid down its fundamental principles were
prophets for they seem to have perceived a future understanding
to which all the world 111ust eventually come.
Louisiana:
Some day liberty will be established everywhere in this world.
The Teutonic claim to be the only people will cease. Then it
will be timely to again consider those matters. For that hour
we wait. May the bells SOOl1 ring out declaring liberty throughout not this land alone, but every land. Then Illinois will
recognize· the liberty for others she claims for herself. Then
she will recognize that our Brethren of the Scottish, living in
countries where it is . the only rite, or dominant rite, have the
liberty in working in Symbolic Masonry.

The Brethren of our fraternity have been in the forefront on

to the most humble. I do not boast that we did more than
others. I glory in the statement that every true blue, loyal
American did his full dutv. ·when the roll of honor is called,
the soldiers of the republic. will be only known as Americans; not

as Jew nor as Gentile; not as Protestant nor as Catholic; not as

VOUCHING
If there is ever a General Grand Body to consider uniform

regulations, "vouching" and "visiting" are two matters that should
receive careful consideration. If such a thing were possible, it
would be interesting to know what proportion of suspended, irregular or clandestine Masons visit the "higher" Masonic Bodies
where admission is governed by a system other than examination
by committee, or vouching.
Colorado:
Question: Will s1ttmg in a chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star constitute sufficient evidence to vouch for a man as
being a Master Mason?
Answer: Sections 217, 218, and 219 of the Book of Constitutions clearly state the "lawful information" whereby one Mason
may vouch for another.
The Order of the Eastern Star is not a Masonic institution,
and although membership in a Blue Lodge is requisite for membership in the Star, for a brother, the knowledge of this fact
is only incidental to the membership of the Lodge, and can not
be used as evidence, or as a basis of vouching for another.
Illinois:
The grand master (Florida) reported a matter of great Masonic
import. It appears that a petitioner in the Order of the Ea~tern Star
must be a Master Mason in good standing and when suspended by
his lodge he is automatically suspended in the Eastern Star. In order to carry out these provisions of the law .the Eastern Star must
have some authentic way of knowing who are in good standing in the
lodges and likewise who have been excused from the fraternity for
failure to pay dues. Hence the grand master presented this momentous question with the request that something be done to meet this
vital issue for the reason that the support of the Eastern Star
was seriously needed in the plans now going forward for the
construction of a Masonic home in the state. Suppose the Order
of Red Men or the Daughters of Isabella .should have made a

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

like request from the grand master stating that they did not
want any suspended Masons joining their organization and would
like to be kept advised on these matters that they might protect
themselves. The Order of the Eastern Star has absolutely no
connection whatsoever with the institution of Freemasonry. Just
the moment that our ·fraternity commences to recognize and
accord privileges to those organizations making affiliation in the
Masonic Fraternity a basis for membership, just that moment
it invites serious trouble.

The report of the committee was approved. Nevertheless,

Ohio:
Every Mason who has intelligence enough to be a Mason
knows that the Scottish Rite is builded upon the foundation of
the three Symbolic Degrees, and that there cannot be such a
thing as a Scottish Rite Mason who is not a Master Mason, and
if a Brother has sat in a Consistory of Scottish Rite Masons with
another Brother, he certainly has the lawful information to enable
him to vouch for him in a Lodge of Master Masons.
Virginia:

and should be known only to a Scottish Rite member, and the
G;rand Lodge which is composed of many Brethren not members
of the Scottish Rite or conversant with its requirements should
be based only on Blue Lodge requirements and practice. The
writer is opposed to any other body assuming to decide Blue
Lodge matters. Blue Lodge matters discussed in any other body
are necessarily viewed from the angle of that body and its
interests, and that is no place to settle Blue Lodge problems.
We have known personally a man s. n. p. d. for year~ in

WAR
Happily, the war, with all of its horrors, is behind us, and we
are more concerned with the immediate present and the future
than that which has gone before. Masons, as individuals, did their
duty, but that our Organization as a body did not, or was prevented as such, from taking an active part, and one that would
naturally rebound to its credit, is a question open to argument.
Whether things all turned out for the best or not is also a matter of
opinion.
The Proceedings reviewed are largely devoted to this subject,
but it is unnecessary in this Report to go into the matter in detail,
other than to spread a few facts "on the record."
Military Lodges were established by the following Grand
Lodges:
Kentucky:
W. A. Colson Lodge, U. D., July 29, 1917.
J. N. Saunders, Army Lodge, September 25, 1917.
Montana:
Montana Army Lodge No. 1, U. D., September 8, 1917,
New York:
Sea and Field Lodges at:
New York;
Paris,
Bonne,
Marseilles,
Coblentz.
North Dakota:
North Dakota Military Lodge No. 2.
South Carolina:
Army Lodge A, with 113th Field Artillery, U. S. A.
That not all of these were a source of satisfaction to their
Fathers, is indicated by the remark of one of the Grand Secretaries, who stated that he had heard nothing from them since the
charters were issued. In another case, we are informed that when
the roll was being called to ascertain if the number of Candidates·
were present, when the surname A--, was called, the answer
came, "General A-- is here." We also know of instances where
men about to be mustered out of the service spent a month's pay
to join, and are now charges upon the Fraternity. These examples would lead one to believe that we were wise in not following
some of our sister States.

113

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

On July 26th, 1917, Major-General Liggitt presented the colors
to the Masonic Ambulance Corps of this city, an organization of
124 Master Masons, all of them within the draft, but volunteered
for this particular organization, and recruited before the draft law
became effective. On May 13, 1919, these colors were returned to
Major-General John Morrison, by the same organization, standing
before him as the 364th Ambulance Company of the United States
Army.
The company was maintained intact, saw service
throughout the war and participated in all of the battles of the
91st Division. One of the many striking instances was when a
member of the Ambulance Corps picked up on the battlefield a
Captain who was the Senior Warden of his own Lodge, serving in
another regiment, and not known to be in that area.
In San Francisco the women with Masonic affiliations
formed an auxiliary to 'the Red Cross, and under Government
supervision, devoted their energies to the reclamation of army
uniforms. From August 5, 1918, to February 5, 1919, they
reclaimed 31,205 garments. Their maximum attendance for one
month was 5493. Minimum attendance for one day 440, and the
maximum attendance for one day 507. The organization has
changed its name, and with a membership of 1200 is now known
as the Women's Masonic Association, and will continue its activities for the benefit of Masonry and humanity.
In the statistical column will be found the amount collected
from the individual members of the Jurisdiction, which is being
used as the occasion requires. In addition to the collection of this
fund by the Grand Lodge, they maintained clubs at the various
mobilization camps for the benefit of the men in the service.

esteen1 for the American soldier as any person on earth, and recognize and appreciate the patriotism exhibited by him when he
casts his life and fortune upon his country's altar and goes forth
to battle in her behalf. But we do not believe that a soldier's

WAR CHARITY
The Grand Lodge of Maryland appropriated $1500 to the Baltimore fund to. be used for the relief of the dependents of soldiers
and sailors. This was perhaps a little more practical than the
action of Missouri and Wisconsin. The "Show Me" State adopted
fifty fatherless children of France for a period of one year, appropriating the sum of $1825 for the purpose, while Wisconsin appropriated $365 for the purpose of caring for ten French children
for one year.
If the foster parents continue the appropriation until their
wards attain their majority, their action might appear to be of
some lasting use, but otherwise it would look to be only a drop in
the bucket.
GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL ASSOCIATION
The last report of the Treasurer showed about $95,000 on
hand. Since then, additional subscriptions amounting to $11,450
have been made. If the original idea of this Association is carried
out, it will accomplish one thing, if nothing more, and that is
locating a half million dollar Temple in a town of approximately
16,000 inhabitants, and undoubtedly free from debt, if the entire
amount is collected before operations are commenced. This is
certainly good for the inhabitants of Alexandria and an exception
in Masonic building. We yield to no one in our respect for
George Washington, but we do believe that if these relics are so
valuable, they could doubtless be located in a place where they
would be more accessible to the world in general, and, furthermore, that the money could be better employed for the ultimate
·good of Washington's memory and the Craft in general.
Our opinion is best expressed in the words of Brother Joseph
Greenfield of Georgia, who said:
"But I would rather stand before the final judgment bar, and
proffer as my passport for admission into the Celestial Lodge, a
crippled child made whole, or a maimed soldier made self-sustaining, than all the offerings of 'frozen-music' that can be erected from
now until the end of time. * * * There is a building in India
called the Taj Mahal. It is said to be the most beautiful structure
in the world, but it is the tomb of a woman. The Pyramids are the
most stupendous example of the builder's art ever erected, but they
are the tomb of a vanished civilization. St. Peter's at Rome is
the grandest religious temple now in existence, but it is the tomb of
a dying hierarchy. Westminster Abbey is the pride of the AngloSaxon race, but its glory is in its memorials of the dead."

Pennsylvania:
Another subject prominently and frequently presented is the
George \Vashington Masonic Memorial Association, the object
of which is to erect at Alexandria, Virginia, a memorial temple
to \Vashington, the Mason. The American Grand Lodges have
very generally endorsed the project, a large majority have become charter members of the Association, and a number of them

movement is now beyond the experimental state and its ultimate
success appears to be assured. The Fraternity in the United
States will do itself honor, and at the same time accomplish a
stroke of good policy, by consummating this challenge-in
tangible, concrete form-that the Greatest American was not only
a patron of the Masonic Institution and endorsed its principles,
aims and purposes, but was also an active worker in it.
South Carolina:

APPENDIX
AMERICAN FREEMASONRY
The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States
are generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite.
Properly speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and
the Scottish Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in
its organized proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.
The Symbolic degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason.
They are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instructioi;i is by symbols.
The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Royal Arch Chapter
and are the Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent
Master and the Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests
upon those who have been regularly elected to preside over a
Chapte.r of Royal Arch Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a Chapter, the work "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called Cryptic because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight
Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take
the temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them, are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to
14°, inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh,
19° to 30°; Consistory, 31 ° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes a:ll States north
of the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees
conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4° to 14°, inclusive; Council
Princes of Jerusalem, 15 ° and 16°; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and
18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft Masons commence their era with the creation
of the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Royal Arch Masons date from the year the Second Temple
was commenced by Zerubabel, Anno Inventionis (A. Inv.), "in the
year of Discovery."
Order of High Priesthood date from the year of the Blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benefacio
(A. n'.), "in the year of the Blessing."
Royal and Select Masters date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.),
"in the year of Deposit."
Knights Templar commence their era with the organization of
their order, Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
Scottish Rite, same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used, Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
RULES FOR MASONIC DATES
Ancient CraftAdd 4000 years to the common time. Thus, 1918 ancl 40005918.
Royal ArchAdd 530 years to the common era. Thus, 1918 ancl 530-2448.
. Order of High PriesthoodTo the Christian era add 1913, the year of the Blessing (B.
C.). Thus, 1918 and 1913-3831.
Royal and Select MasonsAdd 1000 to the common era. Thus, 1918 and 1000-2918.
Knights TemplarFrom the Christian era take 1118. Thus, 1118 from 1918800.
Scottish RiteAdd 3760 to the common era. Thus, 1918 and 3760-5678.
